Russia ramps up rhetoric but wants to avoid war with Nato, Western officials say

BBC News Fri, 28 Aug 2026 19:05:23 GMT

Russian President Vladimir Putin wants to avoid a direct military confrontation with Nato, despite increasingly hostile rhetoric aimed at the UK and other allies over their support for Ukraine, Western officials believe.

Some reports have suggested the visit by CIA chief John Radcliffe to Moscow this week was, in part, to warn Russia against a possible attack on a member of the Euro-Atlantic military alliance.

But the Western officials, who asked not to be named, said recent warnings from Moscow, including that UK forces could be targeted in future or that its weapons factories could be hit, were "nothing new".

They were, they suggested, consistent with Russia's military doctrine to apply pressure on the West.

The officials suggested that the hostile rhetoric was also a reflection of the growing pressure Putin is facing at home, with slow and costly gains in Ukraine along with the impact of Ukrainian long-range strikes deep inside Russia.

Putin and his officials have repeatedly dismissed warnings of Russian plans to attack Nato countries as hysteria. And US President Donald Trump appears to believe the Russian leader – saying this week that "he's not going to attack a Nato territory".

Not long before launching his full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Putin had given public assurances that he had no intention of attacking Russia's neighbour - despite overwhelming US intelligence that such preparations were in full swing.

However, the senior Western officials said on Friday that Russia would likely continue its "hybrid activity", short of direct military action, using methods such as cyber-attacks, sabotage and even assassination attempts.

They said that was aimed at breaking Western resolve and support for Ukraine. One official highlighted the risks of that Russian strategy leading to a miscalculation -which could spark a military confrontation.

Russia is suspected of being behind a string of recent drone incidents in several Nato countries.

Earlier this month, a drone loaded with explosives reached a runway in Germany's Leipzig airport - a key logistics hub for transferring military equipment to Ukraine. There is no proof to link the incident directly to Russia, which has denied any role.

It came amid a string of drone sightings over European airports and military bases that began last year and which are also suspected of being the work of Russia, though it again denies this.

Following the Leipzig incident, the head of France's security services warned that "we must consider the possibility of direct, more violent hostile actions on our national soil".

Still, one Western official said Nato allies should remain calm but not complacent. The UK government has already made clear that recent Russian threats will not deter its support for Ukraine.

The Western officials said the Ukraine war had "escalated" this year, with both Moscow and Kyiv stepping up their own long-range strike campaigns.

Putin, they said, had not changed his maximalist objectives, despite some signs of increasing frustrations back home.

They said petrol shortages in Russia were having an impact on support for the war. They believed there was increasing political pressure on the Russian leader, but that this did not pose a critical challenge to his power.

Russia is still making slow gains in the eastern Donbas region. But it's also facing heavy casualties.

The officials said Russia was losing 6,000 more soldiers a month - either killed or wounded - than it can recruit.

That said, there is no indication yet that the Kremlin leader will resort to mass mobilisation.

Four plead guilty to arson attack on Jewish community ambulances

BBC News Fri, 28 Aug 2026 18:41:35 GMT

Four men have pleaded guilty to destroying four Jewish community ambulances in an arson attack causing £1m of damage in north-west London.

Hamza Iqbal, 20, Rehan Khan, 19, Judex Atshatshi, and Saif Ali, both aged 18, pleaded guilty at the Old Bailey to a charge of destroying or damaging property being reckless whether life would be endangered.

The attack, which took place in the early hours of 23 March, saw four vehicles operated by the charity Hatzola set alight in Golders Green.

Prosecutors had said they believed the incident was a targeted attack against the Jewish community.

The court heard three of the men set fire to the fully stocked ambulances, while a fourth had waited in a nearby car.

After the ambulances were set alight, gas canisters exploded inside the vehicles.

As well as destroying each of the £250,000 vehicles, the fire damaged four electrical charging stations and cables costing approximately £5,000 each.

Leo Seelig, prosecuting, told the court that the Crown Prosecution Service would be arguing that the four men should be sentenced on the basis that the arson attack was related to terrorism.

Mrs Justice Cheema Grubb said she would not rule on the question of terrorism at this stage - with defence counsel arguing that there was no evidence for such a connection.

The judge said that the four would be sentenced following the outcome a trial of a fifth man, Subhan Ahmed, who has denied assisting an offender.

Iqbal and Khan, of Leyton, Atshatshi, of Dagenham, and Ali, of Walthamstow, were remanded into custody.

Run by volunteers, Hatzola has served the north London community of Golders Green, which has a large Jewish population, since 1979.

Hatzola, the Hebrew word for save or rescue, is a large non-profit, Jewish-led organisation that provides a free emergency medical response and transportation to hospitals regardless of faith by volunteer medics.

Community Security Trust, a charity working to protect British Jews from terrorism and antisemitism, welcomed the pleas and said the four's actions "caused immense shock and distress across the Jewish community".

"This was an appalling antisemitic act against a volunteer ambulance service providing emergency medical assistance to people of all backgrounds across north London, simply because those ambulances belonged to a Jewish charity," a spokesperson added.

When the group are sentenced - which is expected to be in spring next year - prosecutors will allege that the incident was connected to terrorism. Lawyers for the men have told the court today that none of them are involved in terrorism.

The BBC understands that British intelligence chiefs were initially keeping an open mind as to whether the Iranian state or organisations working for it had a role in the Hatzola ambulance attack and other attacks against Jewish communities during 2026.

They later concluded that secret intelligence pointed to Iran or its proxies being involved in the attack.

That position has been further confirmed in their minds by the FBI's investigation of and allegations against an Iranian-Iraqi man facing trial in Manhattan for orchestrating a series of attacks against Jewish communities across Europe

US court papers allege that Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a commander of an Iraqi militia, was linked to attacks in London, including the destruction of Jewish charity ambulances.

In May al-Saadi was arrested in Turkey and extradited to the US, with the US Department of Justice alleging he had a role in planning more than a dozen terrorist attacks in North America and Europe.

Publicly available court papers list a series of incidents across Europe that the FBI says he is linked to. In many cases the attacks on Jewish community interests were claimed online by a shadowy group, Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya, or the The Islamic Movement of the People of the Right Hand.

The US court papers say that the social media account for the group posted claims saying it was behind the ambulance attacks - and that al-Saadi had himself posted social media propaganda videos of the attack.

"On or about March 23, 2026, at approximately 1:45 a. m., three masked individuals carried out an arson attack on four Hatzalah Ambulances in London, United Kingdom," reads the indictment before the US court.

"That same day, Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya posted on Telegram a propaganda video in which it claimed responsibility for the attack. On or about March 25, 2026, AL-SAADI posted on social media propaganda videos of the attack."

The Department of Justice also alleges that Al-Saadi posted another propaganda video relating to an attempted arson attack on a synagogue in north London in April.

US lawyers for Al-Saadi have said previously that he is a political prisoner.

More British athletes convicted in connection with Baptiste case

BBC News Fri, 28 Aug 2026 17:54:59 GMT

Leon Baptiste (left) is currently in prison in Marrakech, while Will Sharman (centre) and Lamin Deen (right) were given suspended sentences

Three British former athletes were convicted in Morocco as part of an investigation into the sexual assault of a minor by a sprinting coach, BBC Sport can reveal.

The prosecutions led to the imprisonment of Leon Baptiste, a UK Athletics coach and 2010 Commonwealth Games gold medallist for England in the 200m.

Baptiste was originally reported as missing in Morocco in some media articles published on 14 August, before a BBC Sport investigation revealed his conviction and jailing.

Now, court rulings seen by BBC Sport shed more light on other convictions relating to the same case.

Two-time Commonwealth silver medallist hurdler Will Sharman, his brother and ex-bobsleigh athlete Richard Sharman, and fellow former bobsleigh competitor Lamin Deen, who were all on holiday with Baptiste, were convicted of participating in the enticement of a minor.

Also convicted of the same offence were acquaintances Ashley O'Leary Jones and David Tuck.

The group said via their lawyers that they were never arrested and were unaware of their convictions until informed of them by BBC Sport.

A spokesperson for all five men told BBC Sport: "William, Richard, Lamin, David and Ashley are shocked and distressed by the circumstances in which they have unexpectedly found themselves.

"They reject any suggestion that they knowingly engaged in unlawful or improper conduct. They left Morocco believing they had complied with all requirements placed upon them.

"At the time, they understood that they had paid an administrative fine equivalent to approximately £40 and that the matter had concluded."

BBC Sport understands that police raided a villa in Tamensourt on the outskirts of Marrakech after a girl contacted them claiming she had been brought to the property, had not been paid money she was promised in exchange for sex with Baptiste, and that she had been assaulted by a housekeeper after she was accused of stealing a watch.

Baptiste, 41, was subsequently convicted of sexual assault of a minor and given a 10-month prison sentence, which was subsequently reduced to eight months on appeal.

Court documents refer to the girl as being 16 years old and say she suffered "psychological trauma, sexual exploitation, physical assault and injury, and the violation of her human dignity".

Court records show that in June the five men were given suspended sentences of four months and fines of 500 dirhams (£40) each after being convicted of participating in the enticement of a minor.

All five men were acquitted of a separate charge of inciting a minor to engage in prostitution.

The Morocco presidency of the public ministry, which oversees prosecutions in the country, provided BBC Sport with the court judgement regarding the group, which reads: "The defendants were in the company of [Leon Baptiste] and were seated at the same table as the minor, alongside her.

"They thereby assisted him in deceiving the minor and persuading her to engage in sexual relations [with Baptiste]. This constitutes participation in the enticement of a minor.

"The court found them guilty on this count and decided to convict them for these acts."

The group had already left Morocco by the time the decision was handed down. Their convictions and sentences were upheld after an appeal hearing in July.

In a response provided by their lawyers to BBC Sport, the Sharman brothers, Deen, O’Leary Jones and Tuck say they visited the Montecristo nightclub based on a recommendation provided by their driver, and had no reason to believe it was anything other than a respectable establishment.

They say they were unaware of the girl's age and that some members of the group do not even recall seeing her in the nightclub. The villa they were staying in was vast and the interaction between the men and Mr Baptiste while inside the villa was limited.

They also say that they were not present in court on any occasion, that the court process was not in English and that it was not explained to them.

The spokesperson continued: "What has unfolded over recent months has been a distressing and incoherent saga.

"They did not properly understand the proceedings and were completely shocked on being told that they were the subject of a criminal conviction, when that is not how they understood it."

Companies House records and a biography on one of O'Leary Jones' social media profiles show he is a director of a company operating five children's care homes in Greater Manchester.

Tuck's social media biography indicates he is a military veteran, while a CV posted online lists experience coaching women's and children's football clubs including at Stoke City, Apollon Limassol in Cyprus, and Orlando Pride in the USA.

When asked by BBC Sport to comment on the convictions and the potential safeguarding issues raised, the UK Foreign Office, Home Office, and Department for Culture, Media, and Sport declined to provide a response.

Records also show that other people were convicted in relation to the case.

They include the housekeeper of the villa and two of its security guards, who were each given a two-month suspended prison sentence and a fine of 5,000 dirhams (£396).

The manager of the Montecristo nightclub where the group met the girl was sentenced to two months in jail.

A waiter at the Montecristo was also prosecuted, as was the owner of the agency which rents out the villa.

The girl - a Moroccan national - was awarded civil compensation of 60,000 dirhams (£4,784), to be paid jointly by all of those convicted, plus court costs.

Baptiste is currently serving his sentence in Al-Oudaya prison, and resigned from his position as a consultant coach via a message sent on his behalf to UK Athletics on 18 August citing unspecified ill-health.

Baptiste will be deported from Morocco once he is released from prison.

His case was able to move through the system quickly, with only weeks between his initial arrest and sentencing, because Morocco operates a system in which Baptiste swiftly appeared before a judge and not a jury.

At an appeal hearing in July, two months were taken off his sentence.

The sprinters coached by Baptiste were unaware of the reason for his abrupt lack of contact since telling them he would be absent from training "for a while" in May.

Will Sharman won silver medals in the 110m hurdles at the Commonwealth Games in 2010 and 2014, as well as at the 2014 European Championships, and has worked on the BBC gameshow Gladiators.

The 41-year-old was also featured on BBC Radio 4 as an accomplished pianist in 2015, and appeared as a panel guest on an episode of A Question of Sport in 2014.

His brother Richard, 44, formerly competed in elite-level bobsleigh competitions for Great Britain. On social media he describes himself as an industrial engineer running his own company, as well as a pilot and investor.

Richard Sharman competed for Great Britain at the 2010 Bobsleigh World Cup

Lamin Deen, 45, is a former lance sergeant who served in the grenadier guards during conflicts in Northern Ireland, Bosnia and Kosovo, and competed in bobsleigh at the 2014 Winter Olympics in Sochi and the 2018 edition in Pyeongchang.

He worked as a pundit for TNT Sports during the 2026 Games in Milan-Cortina.

On its website, Montecristo bills itself as a "temple dedicated to partying in Marrakech [which] is undeniably the favourite place for hedonists in the city"

In some online reviews and social media posts, the Montecristo is referred to as a known meeting place for sex workers and potential clients.

The venue was closed by Moroccan authorities during the investigation and has not reopened since.

A statement referring to the case was posted on its social media channels on 15 May, saying: "Montecristo would like to provide clarification and reaffirm its commitment to the values that have always defined us.

"We are treating this matter with the utmost seriousness and are fully co-operating with the relevant authorities in a spirit of transparency and responsibility."

BBC Sport has contacted Montecristo for comment but received no reply.

On Saturday the Moroccan charity Touche Pas À Mon Enfant (Don't Touch My Child) released a statement criticising the sentence Baptiste was given.

"While fully respecting judicial independence and the decisions handed down by competent courts, we cannot hide our astonishment and deep concern regarding a sentence of such duration in a case involving the sexual assault of a minor - particularly given that the sentence was reduced on appeal," the statement reads.

"Sexual assaults committed against children are not ordinary offences - they can leave victims with profound and lasting physical and psychological trauma.

"In this context, we question the precise legal classification of the acts and the circumstances that led to the imposition of this sentence and its subsequent reduction on appeal."

In 2016 UNAIDS estimated that around 75,000 sex workers were operating in Morocco.

The children's rights organisation Humanium has called sex tourism "a thriving industry" in Morocco.

More British athletes convicted in connection with Baptiste case

BBC News Fri, 28 Aug 2026 17:54:59 GMT

Leon Baptiste (left) is currently in prison in Marrakech, while Will Sharman (centre) and Lamin Deen (right) were given suspended sentences

Three British former athletes were convicted in Morocco as part of an investigation into the sexual assault of a minor by a sprinting coach, BBC Sport can reveal.

The prosecutions led to the imprisonment of Leon Baptiste, a UK Athletics coach and 2010 Commonwealth Games gold medallist for England in the 200m.

Baptiste was originally reported as missing in Morocco in some media articles published on 14 August, before a BBC Sport investigation revealed his conviction and jailing.

Now, court rulings seen by BBC Sport shed more light on other convictions relating to the same case.

Two-time Commonwealth silver medallist hurdler Will Sharman, his brother and ex-bobsleigh athlete Richard Sharman, and fellow former bobsleigh competitor Lamin Deen, who were all on holiday with Baptiste, were convicted of participating in the enticement of a minor.

Also convicted of the same offence were acquaintances Ashley O'Leary Jones and David Tuck.

The group said via their lawyers that they were never arrested and were unaware of their convictions until informed of them by BBC Sport.

A spokesperson for all five men told BBC Sport: "William, Richard, Lamin, David and Ashley are shocked and distressed by the circumstances in which they have unexpectedly found themselves.

"They reject any suggestion that they knowingly engaged in unlawful or improper conduct. They left Morocco believing they had complied with all requirements placed upon them.

"At the time, they understood that they had paid an administrative fine equivalent to approximately £40 and that the matter had concluded."

BBC Sport understands that police raided a villa in Tamensourt on the outskirts of Marrakech after a girl contacted them claiming she had been brought to the property, had not been paid money she was promised in exchange for sex with Baptiste, and that she had been assaulted by a housekeeper after she was accused of stealing a watch.

Baptiste, 41, was subsequently convicted of sexual assault of a minor and given a 10-month prison sentence, which was subsequently reduced to eight months on appeal.

Court documents refer to the girl as being 16 years old and say she suffered "psychological trauma, sexual exploitation, physical assault and injury, and the violation of her human dignity".

Court records show that in June the five men were given suspended sentences of four months and fines of 500 dirhams (£40) each after being convicted of participating in the enticement of a minor.

All five men were acquitted of a separate charge of inciting a minor to engage in prostitution.

The Morocco presidency of the public ministry, which oversees prosecutions in the country, provided BBC Sport with the court judgement regarding the group, which reads: "The defendants were in the company of [Leon Baptiste] and were seated at the same table as the minor, alongside her.

"They thereby assisted him in deceiving the minor and persuading her to engage in sexual relations [with Baptiste]. This constitutes participation in the enticement of a minor.

"The court found them guilty on this count and decided to convict them for these acts."

The group had already left Morocco by the time the decision was handed down. Their convictions and sentences were upheld after an appeal hearing in July.

In a response provided by their lawyers to BBC Sport, the Sharman brothers, Deen, O’Leary Jones and Tuck say they visited the Montecristo nightclub based on a recommendation provided by their driver, and had no reason to believe it was anything other than a respectable establishment.

They say they were unaware of the girl's age and that some members of the group do not even recall seeing her in the nightclub. The villa they were staying in was vast and the interaction between the men and Mr Baptiste while inside the villa was limited.

They also say that they were not present in court on any occasion, that the court process was not in English and that it was not explained to them.

The spokesperson continued: "What has unfolded over recent months has been a distressing and incoherent saga.

"They did not properly understand the proceedings and were completely shocked on being told that they were the subject of a criminal conviction, when that is not how they understood it."

Companies House records and a biography on one of O'Leary Jones' social media profiles show he is a director of a company operating five children's care homes in Greater Manchester.

Tuck's social media biography indicates he is a military veteran, while a CV posted online lists experience coaching women's and children's football clubs including at Stoke City, Apollon Limassol in Cyprus, and Orlando Pride in the USA.

When asked by BBC Sport to comment on the convictions and the potential safeguarding issues raised, the UK Foreign Office, Home Office, and Department for Culture, Media, and Sport declined to provide a response.

Records also show that other people were convicted in relation to the case.

They include the housekeeper of the villa and two of its security guards, who were each given a two-month suspended prison sentence and a fine of 5,000 dirhams (£396).

The manager of the Montecristo nightclub where the group met the girl was sentenced to two months in jail.

A waiter at the Montecristo was also prosecuted, as was the owner of the agency which rents out the villa.

The girl - a Moroccan national - was awarded civil compensation of 60,000 dirhams (£4,784), to be paid jointly by all of those convicted, plus court costs.

Baptiste is currently serving his sentence in Al-Oudaya prison, and resigned from his position as a consultant coach via a message sent on his behalf to UK Athletics on 18 August citing unspecified ill-health.

Baptiste will be deported from Morocco once he is released from prison.

His case was able to move through the system quickly, with only weeks between his initial arrest and sentencing, because Morocco operates a system in which Baptiste swiftly appeared before a judge and not a jury.

At an appeal hearing in July, two months were taken off his sentence.

The sprinters coached by Baptiste were unaware of the reason for his abrupt lack of contact since telling them he would be absent from training "for a while" in May.

Will Sharman won silver medals in the 110m hurdles at the Commonwealth Games in 2010 and 2014, as well as at the 2014 European Championships, and has worked on the BBC gameshow Gladiators.

The 41-year-old was also featured on BBC Radio 4 as an accomplished pianist in 2015, and appeared as a panel guest on an episode of A Question of Sport in 2014.

His brother Richard, 44, formerly competed in elite-level bobsleigh competitions for Great Britain. On social media he describes himself as an industrial engineer running his own company, as well as a pilot and investor.

Richard Sharman competed for Great Britain at the 2010 Bobsleigh World Cup

Lamin Deen, 45, is a former lance sergeant who served in the grenadier guards during conflicts in Northern Ireland, Bosnia and Kosovo, and competed in bobsleigh at the 2014 Winter Olympics in Sochi and the 2018 edition in Pyeongchang.

He worked as a pundit for TNT Sports during the 2026 Games in Milan-Cortina.

On its website, Montecristo bills itself as a "temple dedicated to partying in Marrakech [which] is undeniably the favourite place for hedonists in the city"

In some online reviews and social media posts, the Montecristo is referred to as a known meeting place for sex workers and potential clients.

The venue was closed by Moroccan authorities during the investigation and has not reopened since.

A statement referring to the case was posted on its social media channels on 15 May, saying: "Montecristo would like to provide clarification and reaffirm its commitment to the values that have always defined us.

"We are treating this matter with the utmost seriousness and are fully co-operating with the relevant authorities in a spirit of transparency and responsibility."

BBC Sport has contacted Montecristo for comment but received no reply.

On Saturday the Moroccan charity Touche Pas À Mon Enfant (Don't Touch My Child) released a statement criticising the sentence Baptiste was given.

"While fully respecting judicial independence and the decisions handed down by competent courts, we cannot hide our astonishment and deep concern regarding a sentence of such duration in a case involving the sexual assault of a minor - particularly given that the sentence was reduced on appeal," the statement reads.

"Sexual assaults committed against children are not ordinary offences - they can leave victims with profound and lasting physical and psychological trauma.

"In this context, we question the precise legal classification of the acts and the circumstances that led to the imposition of this sentence and its subsequent reduction on appeal."

Wife of man who died after turbulence sues airline

BBC News Fri, 28 Aug 2026 17:47:00 GMT

A widow whose husband died after "severe turbulence" on a flight has begun legal action against the airline.

Lawyers for Linda Kitchen, 74, from Thornbury near Bristol, who broke her back during the incident, said her husband, Geoff, 73, was "fatally injured" when the Singapore Airlines flight from London Heathrow suddenly dropped around 6,000 ft (1,828 metres).

She has now begun proceedings at the High Court seeking damages from the airline to help her access specialist support for her back. The BBC has contacted the airline for comment.

"When I got separated from Geoff, I knew he was in a bad way, but nothing prepared me for hearing he had died. It was absolutely devastating," she said.

Kitchen and her husband, described as her "soul mate", were starting a six-week holiday to Singapore, Indonesia and Australia when the incident happened in May 2024.

The turbulence hit over Myanmar, with the flight then diverted to Bangkok, in Thailand, for an emergency landing.

"There had been some turbulence over Europe, and it had been shaky over the water, but it was around 10 hours into the flight when we encountered the main turbulence," Kitchen said.

"It was so severe; it felt like the aircraft was dropping. I noticed my Kindle and Geoff's phone had fallen to the floor, and I thought the plane was going down."

As the aircraft plummeted, Kitchen said her husband fell on top of her, squashing her into the armrest. Eventually, others helped to move him and a doctor on board began CPR.

Kitchen was taken to hospital while her husband was still on the plane. It was two days before she was told he had died.

It is understood that Geoff suffered a heart attack after the plane suddenly dropped at high altitude.

"I spent 10 days in hospital before I was airlifted back to Bristol. I was in so much pain that the journey was a blur. Once back in the UK, I remained in hospital for around a week and, following my discharge, required significant assistance at home," Kitchen said.

Anthe Korelidou, a specialist aviation lawyer who is representing Kitchen, said: "That Geoff was fatally injured and Linda suffered severe injuries vividly highlights the severity of what happened.

"While it's more than two years since Geoff's death, Linda and the rest of her family continue to have a number of questions and concerns about what happened and if more could have been done to prevent their injuries.

"All Linda wants is for the most thorough investigations to be conducted. The issuing of High Court proceedings is a major milestone in being able to provide Geoff's loved ones with the answers they deserve."

Satellite images reveal scale of flood devastation in Nepal villages

BBC News Fri, 28 Aug 2026 17:36:54 GMT

New satellite imagery has revealed the scale of the devastation along Nepal's Trishuli River caused by Wednesday's deadly flash flood, triggered by a glacier collapse.

Before-and-after images show how sections of the valley, where a torrent of floodwater and debris surged through, destroyed villages, bridges and hydroelectric power stations.

More than 550 people have been killed, Nepalese officials say, with hundreds more missing.

Among the worst-hit locations reviewed by BBC Verify was a key Nepal-Tibet border crossing, which was engulfed by a rush of floodwater and captured on camera.

The satellite imagery from US-based intelligence firm Vantor, shows the site has been almost entirely washed away. Shocking CCTV footage showed the moment as the deluge of water swept over buildings as people tried to escape.

Damage and mud can be seen more than 2.5km (1.5 miles) upstream, reaching 100m (330 ft) above the area it first hit.

A few miles further south is the village of Timure, which has now largely disappeared.

The walls of the valley at this point are steep, reaching up to 50m above the water line. The image shows most of the houses perched on this slope are now gone or covered in mud.

A further 10km (eight miles) downstream, where the Trishuli River winds through Syapru Besi, satellite imagery now shows the village covered by mud, rock and other debris. Houses and other structures have disappeared, including bridges and a hydroelectric power station.

One of the larger villages to be struck by the full force of the flood was Trishuli, where some of the earliest verified footage of the disaster emerged from.

A satellite image of the town and surrounding agricultural land, which is about 45km (28 miles) downstream from the border, show an entire neighbourhood has been essentially washed away.

Verified videos of the town show a bridge collapsing as the river surges forward. At the very same moment from ground level, footage filmed from inside a bus shows people crying out in distress and trying to flee as they see the water rushing down the river.

Other dramatic videos show people sheltering inside a house, peering over the edge of a balcony as they watch a torrent of floodwater wash away almost everything around them, knocking large metal debris and a vehicle toward the building.

Somehow the house remains intact and survivors can be seen in a second verified video standing surrounded by mud once the floodwater had receded.

Imagery from satellite provider Planet Labs released today has also provided a clearer view of the disaster's origins at the collapsed glacier, the moment of which has been captured on a verified drone video.

The satellite image shows an enormous chunk of the glacier has fallen away, carving an enormous path of rock and debris where water rushed through the valley.

At the base of the landslide, trees and other vegetation have been stripped at a height of more than 300m above the riverbed.

This destructive path continues westwards along with the swelled river, before heading southwards.

Satellite images also show the formation of a barrier lake at the base of the landslide's path, which Chinese authorities have warned poses a major risk of further flooding and has hampered rescue efforts.

Dr Argha Banerjee, a glaciologist at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, told BBC Verify that it was not possible determine from the images how stable the barrier was or how likely the lake was to drain suddenly.

But he said there was no significant increase in its surface area between Wednesday and Thursday, despite water continuing to flow into the lake.

Dr Banerjee said there was a visible drainage channel, which suggests some water was already escaping downstream, adding that the its volume was "not alarmingly large" and appeared to have stabilised.

The extent of the damage on the Tibetan side of the border remains unclear. It is a strictly controlled region which China annexed in the 1950s, where foreign media access is heavily restricted. BBC Verify has so far been unable find verifiable footage from the area.

The satellite imagery - which only provides an initial glimpse into the damage of the flood - has been published by Vantor as part of its Open Data Program to help aid authorities establish where best to focus their efforts to locate the missing, rescue survivors and recover the dead.

Additional reporting Shruti Menon, Merlyn Thomas and Alex Murray. Graphics by Mesut Ersoz and Mike Hill.

Burnham says he will not vote on assisted dying unlike Starmer

BBC News Fri, 28 Aug 2026 17:04:28 GMT

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has revealed he will not vote on the assisted dying bill for England and Wales unlike his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

MPs are likely to get the chance to debate and vote on the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill in two weeks' time.

The bill is identical to the one put to Parliament last year, where it passed in the House of Commons but stalled in the Lords after an unprecedented number of amendments meant it ran out of time.

Burnham said he has his "own personal views on the issue" but it was "a matter for Parliament to decide". Starmer voted in favour of the previous bill when he was PM but did not campaign in favour of it, remaining officially neutral.

Writing to Labour MPs on Friday, Burnham said: "My role, as the prime minister, will be to lead a government that implements the will of Parliament in this area – whether that is to change the law or not.

"I also do not want to unduly influence the debate as prime minister and for every colleague to know it is a genuinely free vote.

"For these reasons, I have taken the decision that it is most appropriate for me not to vote at Second Reading."

He added that "there is no single right position" and it was an "incredibly important and personal debate".

"It is vital that those different views are treated with dignity and respect," he wrote.

While his abstension is a departure from Starmer's support, Burnham stressed that the government as an entity would officially remain neutral on the bill.

When he was Greater Manchester mayor, Burnham indicated he was in favour of assisted dying in principle.

But in June he suggested it would be challenging to implement before social and palliative care were improved.

The assisted dying law would allow adults over the age of 18 who are expected to die within six months to be given help to end their own life, subject to certain safeguards.

Burnham has also told ministers they can vote as they wish but, in a separate letter on Friday, he told them they "should avoid being part of the public debate and should not express views about the implications of the bill for their department's responsibilities".

Health Secretary Yvette Cooper previously voted in favour of assisted dying, but her predecessor Wes Streeting had openly voiced concerns about the implications for the NHS.

Supporters of the assisted dying bill - brought by Labour MP Lauren Edwards - are hoping it will pass the Commons unamended.

This is because an amended bill in the Commons would remove powers under the Parliament Acts to override the Lords and make it law if they refuse to back it.

MPs in favour of the bill hope Lords would vote in favour, if presented the choice of some sceptical amendments versus an entirely unamended bill becoming law.

It comes after the Lords tabled more than 1,200 amendments, mainly from opponents, during the previous bill earlier this year.

That prompted assisted dying campaigner Dame Esther Rantzen, who has terminal cancer, to accuse opponents of trying to sabotage rather than scrutinise it.

Opponents of assisted dying have vowed to continue scrutinising the bill.

A separate bill that would have legalised assisted dying in Scotland was rejected by the Scottish Parliament in March 2026.

Paul Heaton scores first number one album as Dolly Parton's 9 to 5 finally reaches top 40

BBC News Fri, 28 Aug 2026 16:48:36 GMT

English singer-songwriter Paul Heaton has scored his first solo UK number one album, his sixth overall.

Heaton's latest chart-topping LP - titled Jenius - follows his three with the Beautiful South and two more alongside former bandmate Jacqui Abbott.

The former Housemartins musician reached the top on Friday, in part, by shifting more vinyl copies than any other album over the past seven days.

Dolly Parton, who died earlier this week, aged 80, has three singles in the top 40, including 9 to 5, which landed at number 12 in this week's UK chart, having previously peaked at 47 in 1981.

Elsewhere on Friday, Sam Fender and Olivia Dean's Rein Me In extended its record as the longest-running number one single in UK chart history.

In a four-star review, the Times noted how Heaton's "casually funny" and "deceptively piercing" latest album "again confirms his gift for dissecting human weakness with an unsentimental but humane eye".

Victoria Segal wrote that the Ian Broudie-produced record was full of "stylistically playful songs" - like One Eye Open and Favourite Kind of Idiot - which "weave through the personal and political".

Heaton, who rose to fame as part of Hull band The Housemartins in the 1980s - alongside pre-Fatboy Slim Norman Cook - this week told the BBC he was planning on putting money behind the bar at dozens of pubs to celebrate his 65th birthday next year.

The singer made a similar gesture in 2022 when he opened £1,000 tabs at 60 pubs.

Fellow singer Brandon Flowers' pivot from the glamorous indie rock 'n' roll of The Killers to Parton's own brand of country music saw him land behind Heaton at number three, with his new album Thrasher.

Waves of tributes poured in this week to Tennessee star Parton, whose best-loved tunes were also played across the nation, evidently.

Her biggest streaming country-pop classic 9 to 5 was written for the 1980 film of the same name, and earned her an Oscar nomination as well as topping the US charts.

Another of her tunes, Jolene - which finds her pleading with a stunning rival not to steal her man - re-entered the chart at number nine on Friday.

The country anthem originally peaked at number seven in 1976 - her joint-highest UK chart placing.

Her duet with Kenny Rogers, Islands in the Stream, also reached number seven in 1983, and it has flowed back into this week's chart at number 13.

Finally, Diamonds & Rhinestones, Parton's 2022 greatest hits collection, reached the top 10 of the albums chart - topped by Heaton - for the first time too.

"Dolly Parton's extraordinary legacy continues to shine through the official charts," noted Becca Monahan and Chris Austin, co-managing directors of the official charts company, in a joint statement.

They called it a "powerful reflection of the UK's enduring love for her music".

"A true icon whose songs have crossed generations, these chart returns are a fitting celebration of Dolly's incredible life, career and lasting impact," they added.

Violence breaks out in Ceuta as migrant crisis continues

BBC News Fri, 28 Aug 2026 16:30:59 GMT

A month after tens of thousands of migrants entered the city of Ceuta, a Spanish exclave in North Africa, there have been outbreaks of violence as tensions mount between locals and foreign arrivals.

The Spanish government has been accused by opposition parties of struggling to manage the crisis effectively.

Ceuta's residents have complained of feeling unsafe on the streets, as well as expressing concerns about the burden being placed on public services.

At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July. Most swam around a border fence and at least 100 people died during the mass crossing, according to figures from Ceuta's mayor.

The vast majority of the migrants returned to Morocco within hours of their arrival, but several thousand remain in Ceuta, many of them children, and most are sleeping rough on beaches or streets.

Anti-migrant demonstrations earlier this month were largely peaceful, but in recent days they have become increasingly violent.

On Thursday, several dozen locals prevented Red Cross personnel from distributing food and water to the migrants. Afterwards, some set fire to migrant camps on Trampolín beach, the main site where they have been sleeping, and there were also clashes with the police.

Those incidents came hours after the arrest of 12 migrants who were accused of throwing stones at a military vehicle, breaking its windows and injuring the four men inside. That same morning there were reports of vigilante groups pursuing migrants through the streets.

Journalists and film crews have also reported being threatened.

"This is a city which has been under pressure, […] which has the right to normality," the mayor of the exclave, the conservative Juan Jesús Vivas, told Antena 3 television.

"The dignity of Spain is a stake right now in Ceuta," he said.

The socialist-led government of Pedro Sánchez has appealed for calm and accused Vivas's People's Party (PP) and the far-right Vox of stoking the tensions.

José María Figaredo, a member of Congress for Vox, is being investigated for a possible hate crime after saying, soon after the migrants' arrival, that they should be "hunted down, one by one".

Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska told a congressional committee: "We have heard during these weeks rhetoric and comments that contribute to the stigmatisation of immigrants and which feed social division at a moment when what we need is responsibility and statesmanship."

Javier Celaya, who represents Ceuta in Congress for the PP, accused the government of treating "the invaders as victims when the real victims are us, the people of Ceuta".

On Friday, all the parties in the Ceuta local assembly signed a declaration condemning violence.

Earlier this week, the government centralised management of the situation, overriding the local authority, after criticism that it had been slow to respond.

Defence Minister Margarita Robles also apologised to those in Ceuta who "may have felt, or who even still feel, abandoned or not sufficiently cared", as the government unveiled plans to overhaul the country's immigration laws.

Much of the recent ill-feeling in the city appears to be driven by government plans to move migrants into existing public buildings, such as sports centres, in order to be able to process their legal status in an orderly way and return those not eligible for asylum to Morocco.

Many local people, and Vivas, oppose this initiative, due to concerns that it will move the migrants closer to residential areas.

The government is also facing questions about who was behind the mass migrant crossing.

Politicians on the right and the far left have accused Morocco of involvement, pointing to its alleged use of the border with Spain in the past to exert political pressure.

Sánchez and his Socialist Party instead blame people traffickers, insisting that Rabat is a reliable partner which facilitated the immediate return of most of the arrivals.

Nonetheless, the crisis has placed the sovereignty of Ceuta, and its fellow autonomous city Melilla, under the spotlight.

Morocco has maintained a longstanding claim to the territories, which it has reiterated in recent weeks.

Spain's Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares said he "roundly rejected" such comments by Morocco.

"I don't speak about, nor have I spoken about, nor are we going to speak about Spain's territorial integrity with Morocco or with anyone else," he told the congressional committee.

'Terrorist connection' over Trump Turnberry vandalism charges

BBC News Fri, 28 Aug 2026 16:04:25 GMT

Seven people accused of vandalism at Donald Trump's Turnberry golf resort have been charged with an offence alleged to have a "terrorist connection".

The allegation is contained in an indictment lodged with the High Court of Justiciary in Glasgow over the incident that happened at the Ayrshire resort during a protest on 8 March 2025.

It states that the offence was aggravated under Section 31 of the Counter-Terrorism Act 2008, as amended by the Counter-Terrorism and Sentencing Act 2021, because it had a "terrorist connection".

The Defend Our Juries group has criticised the move, claiming the accused could face "far longer prison sentences" despite not being charged with terrorism offences.

Kieran Robson, 35, Uzma Bashir, 56, Ricky Southall, 34, Autumn Taylor Ward, 22, Rebecca Sian Davies, 29, John Moxley, 58, and Dylan Chiaramello, 24, were all charged with criminal damage following the protest.

It is alleged the group dug up turf and sprayed weedkiller on the course, caused flooding by damaging a sprinkler system, and damaged a light.

Prosecutors also allege that slogans including "Free Gaza", "Free Palestine" and "Gaza is not for sale" were daubed on the course and buildings, along with offensive messages directed at Trump.

The seven were due to appear at the High Court in Glasgow next Monday, but the Scottish Courts and Tribunals Service said on Friday that the hearing had been adjourned, with the next hearing due to take place in October.

Robson also faces an allegation that he committed the offence while on bail. The indictment states that he had been granted bail at Edinburgh Sheriff Court on 9 January 2025.

The allegation comes after four members of Palestine Action received longer prison sentences in June after being convicted over a raid on a factory operated by Israeli defence company Elbit Systems.

More than £1m of damage was caused during that incident and the judge concluded there was a terrorist connection.

Human rights groups and supporters of those convicted criticised the sentences as disproportionate.

Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in the UK in July 2025.

The Court of Appeal later upheld the government's decision, saying the group had "overtly promoted unlawful violence amounting to terrorism".

The group's co-founder Huda Ammori is seeking permission to challenge the implementation of the ban at the UK Supreme Court.

The US government designated Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation on Wednesday.

The Trump administration said the move was part of action against what it described as "far-left extremists".

Division, drama and power - what next for Infantino and Uefa?

BBC News Fri, 28 Aug 2026 15:00:20 GMT

Fifa's investment plan has intensified tensions between Fifa president Gianni Infantino and Uefa

"On information and belief, Infantino's actions described herein rise to the level of criminal mismanagement."

"A stunning dereliction of duty."

"A fraudulently off-market price promoted by Infantino for his own benefit."

Just some of the blistering language used by Uefa's lawyers in legal papers lodged in the United States over Fifa president Gianni Infantino's now-shelved plan to sell off stakes in competitions to private investors.

A scheme, Uefa claims, that awarded the World Cup an "absurdly low enterprise value... that was neither the product of an open, competitive auction, nor tested by any independent valuer". All part of "a transaction that inflicted direct and concrete injury... to the detriment of Fifa as well as its 211 members", and was conducted under "a veil of secrecy".

The court documents, which reference Infantino's "cronies" and "co-conspirators", and include a chapter on "the enduring history of corruption among Fifa officials", request access to evidence and documents in the US for use in potential litigation in Switzerland against Infantino.

More than a month since the Fifa Forward Enterprise plan (FFE) was revealed, before collapsing days later, this increasingly acrimonious civil war shows little sign of ending.

Since then, we have seen the strongest public pressure from those opposed to Infantino with a series of cutting statements, including from former players, politicians, and fan groups.

And there was even the leaking of claims - labelled "categorically untrue" by Infantino - that his alleged lover was given a severance payment over the affair while he was at Uefa.

Now we have the threat of legal proceedings.

It is ironic that Infantino has enjoyed arguably his best week since this saga began.

On Thursday, he received the qualified backing of the powerful Saudi Arabian Football Federation, which said that "at this time [it] supports the continued efforts of Gianni Infantino to restore unity".

Despite defying calls from three confederations and various other stakeholders to stand down, Uefa's decision to drop its threat of boycotting Fifa competitions after receiving assurances there would be no repeat of the FFE scheme was seen as another victory for him.

But Uefa then raised the stakes. News that it was preparing criminal legal proceedings was viewed as a dramatic escalation, and evidence that it was not backing down in its determination to oust Infantino.

Although Infantino defended FFE as a means of unlocking the commercial potential of Fifa, before later apologising for "errors", neither he nor Fifa have responded to this latest twist, with officials insisting they are focused on delivering the U20 Women's World Cup, starting next week in Poland.

Infantino, meanwhile, fresh from trips to the Dominican Republic and Paris last weekend, posted video of a "wonderful" visit to Vietnam, the latest stop on what is increasingly resembling a world tour aimed at shoring up support.

Given that Uefa first warned of potential legal action almost a month ago, when it instructed Fifa to retain any "relevant materials" related to the plan, Infantino may well have anticipated Uefa's move, so how might he feel now?

Josh Kushner (right) is the founder of venture capital firm Thrive Capital, earmarked as the lead investor in FFE

Much may depend on whether US courts side with Uefa over its requests for disclosure of evidence related to the FFE plan. In documents seen by BBC Sport, it is seeking information from three parties; Fifa, Thrive Capital - the venture capital firm earmarked as the lead investor in FFE along with its founder Josh Kushner, and former Formula 1 chief Greg Maffei, who is described as "the key commercial adviser" on the proposed deal.

While the filings state that neither Kushner or Maffei are anticipated defendants in any proceedings, in the case of Kushner for instance, Uefa's lawyers say they are seeking subpoenas for "the production of documents and communications and for deposition testimony".

Although Kushner, who is the brother of US president Donald Trump's son-in-law, is yet to comment, some legal experts believe he could successfully challenge and block such a subpoena request by arguing that the details of the deal need to remain confidential to protect his business interests and future investments. Kushner has recently agreed a deal to buy basketball's Los Angeles Lakers for a record £9.3bn.

It is unclear how long this process could take, or whether Uefa will secure the evidence it needs to support its claim that the World Cup was deliberately undervalued at about £15bn. Nor is it clear whether it will ultimately follow through on its threat to lodge a criminal complaint in Switzerland.

How confident Uefa would be of criminal charges being brought is also highly uncertain. In 2002, in echoes of the current disunity, several Fifa executive committee members filed a criminal complaint against former president Sepp Blatter with a Zurich court, external. The public prosecutor took no action, while Blatter denied wrongdoing. Last year, a long-running attempt by the Swiss Attorney General's Office to prosecute Blatter and former Uefa president Michel Platini ended with both men being fully cleared of corruption charges.

"What Uefa have to show is that they have an arguable case for criminal proceedings to be brought against Infantino," says leading sports lawyer Nick de Marco KC.

"If they can show that…then they ought to be given disclosure of a lot of the documents."

When asked what he thought the chances were of the case eventually going to trial, De Marco said: "We're a long way off from that - the first stage is this disclosure application.

"My own view is that the likelihood of success in that, which is very important, is high, but then it's a question for the Swiss prosecutor, looking at that disclosure, to decide whether there is a case [and] that will take some time... but I think what we will likely see is disclosure of very interesting documents and more light shone onto this plan."

Perhaps aware of the challenges its legal action could face, Uefa has in the meantime pledged to "secure fundamental reform, restore proper limits on presidential authority and ensure that Fifa is once again governed as an institution - not around one individual", while demanding "a genuinely independent external review of FFE".

Given the support he retains in South America, Africa and parts of Asia, and how he has survived everything Uefa has thrown at him in recent weeks, many still expect Infantino to remain in power and seek re-election for a fourth term in the spring. Uefa has warned that, should he do so, it will "join forces with its partner confederations to ensure that member associations are offered a credible alternative - one committed to integrity, accountability, development and genuine institutional change".

But how likely is it that a unifying challenger will emerge? And how can the game avoid a repeat of such a crisis in future?

This video can not be played

Uefa 'will continue to fight' Infantino - Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister

"We have some clarity over the changes that are needed to modernise football governance and to make it run in a way that is accountable to its most important stakeholders," Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister told BBC Sport in Monaco.

"I think there are lots of credible candidates out there, but it has to be a candidate that can unite that standpoint and somebody who has the credentials and the credibility and the buy-in to really champion that agenda.

"We need to make the governance itself rooted on the principles that are so important like transparency and independence and critical challenge and due diligence.

"We knew this wouldn't be a simple process and we knew that change wouldn't happen overnight."

In October, Infantino will finally come face-to-face with some of his opponents at what could be a highly charged first Fifa Council meeting since the rebellion over FFE. The following month, presidential candidates must be nominated. Then, in March, an election is scheduled that, if contested by Infantino, could prove pivotal to the future direction of football.

Until then, the division and rancour that has engulfed the world's game in this remarkable drama of intrigue and power looks set to continue.

And right now, reunification seems hard to imagine.

Hundreds of migrants enter UK after 10-day lull

BBC News Fri, 28 Aug 2026 13:39:31 GMT

Nearly 500 migrants have arrived in the UK in one day, in the first boats to successfully cross the Channel in 10 days.

The seven vessels that made the crossing were the first since 17 August when 250 people arrived.

Dinghies arrived in British waters until late into the night on Thursday, with 494 people being brought into the Border Security Command compound in Dover, Kent.

The total number is down overall this year, according to BBC Verify analysis of government data.

Some 16,391 migrants have crossed the Channel so far, down 43% on the same time last year, and a 17% drop from the same point in 2024.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has said she will not be "complacent" about the falling numbers, and that there is "more we must do".

"That is why I have boosted enforcement on the French beaches and overseas and introduced new legislation to tackle the pull factors that draw people here through unsafe and illegal routes," she added.

World's youngest reigning traditional monarch dies aged 34

BBC News Fri, 28 Aug 2026 11:13:24 GMT

A traditional Ugandan ruler named as the world's youngest monarch has died aged 34, his prime minster announced.

Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV became king of Tooro in western Uganda at just three years old in 1995 after the death of his father.

The Tooro kingdom did not disclose the cause of King Oyo's death, but a Ugandan government minister was quoted in local media saying that he had been critically ill and was seeking treatment in the US.

Though Uganda is governed by an elected president and parliament, it has several traditional kingdoms which continue to have significant cultural influence despite not having political power.

Oyo, who Guinness World Records listed as the world's youngest reigning monarch, ruled over more than two million people. He was the 13th monarch of a kingdom that was founded in the early 19th Century.

Announcing his death, Tooro's Prime Minister Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki called his passing on Thursday an "immeasurable loss" to the royal family and the people of Tooro.

"I call upon all the people of Tooro to remain united, calm and prayerful during this profoundly difficult time," Akiiki said on Friday. "May His Majesty the King rest in eternal peace."

The Tooro Kingdom follows a hereditary system in selecting its monarch.

Oyo was not officially married, but Akiiki said "the continuity of the Crown is assured".

"His Majesty leaves behind a Prince as his heir, whose identity will be formally revealed at the appropriate time, in accordance with the traditions and customs of Tooro Kingdom," he explained.

When he became king in 1995 a regency, which included the queen mother, was established until Oyo turned 18 when there was an official coronation.

The young king was well respected by his people and according to a report in the Daily Monitor newspaper he promoted causes such as youth empowerment, education and climate conservation, as well as HIV/Aids awareness.

The country's largest and most influential traditional institution, the Buganda Kingdom, said it mourned with the people of Tooro following the death of their monarch, labelling him a valuable figure to Uganda.

Similarly, the Rwenzururu Kingdom also extended its condolences to "all those mourning this great loss", according to local media reports.

Others have also paid their respects to the late king.

The Federation of Uganda Football Associations, honoured King Oyo as a "true friend of the beautiful game", and announced a moment of silence before the kick-off of all matches until 4 September in memory of his "legacy, love, passion and contribution" to the sport.

Government minister Margaret Muhanga described the mood in the kingdom as "sombre... you can't see anyone smiling".

The king was "at the prime of his life", she said in a video shared on social media, "as young as he was, he had an impact on his kingdom".

Muhanga said they would be planting a million trees in his honour during the mourning period, and wants to ask the neighbouring districts in Tooro to do the same.

Uganadan musician Juliana Kanyomozi called it a "very dark day for Tooro", in an Instagram post. "Gone too soon. What a loss!!!!"

Meanwhile, pop star-turned-politician Bobi Wine, called for King Oyo's "soul to rest in eternal peace".

What we know after the big Grand Theft Auto 6 preview

BBC News Fri, 28 Aug 2026 11:04:11 GMT

After more than 18 months since the last official glimpse of Grand Theft Auto 6, developer Rockstar has shown fans a 26-minute preview of the upcoming blockbuster video game.

Its "extended look" debuted on Netflix, six hours before going live on YouTube, and was the first chance players have had to see detailed footage of the title in action.

The montage, with no commentary or explanatory captions, showed off improved graphics, detailed environments and a selection of car-chases and shoot-outs from the sequel.

The broadcast followed a week of unauthorised gameplay leaks, which the developer said it had been "heartbreaking" to see shared online.

After it got its chance to show the version of GTA 6 it wanted the world to see, here are some things we learned, and some things we still don't know.

The extended look spent a long time showcasing the relationship between protagonists Jason Duval and Lucia Camino, the couple at the centre of GTA 6's "Bonnie and Clyde" story.

In a preview published on website IGN, the developers said the characters' story - and the way it unfolds - can be affected by the player's actions, although they can "opt out" of developing the pair's bond if they want.

The Netflix preview didn't show this playing out in detail, but did show the ability to change control between the two characters at different points.

In one segment, Jason was seen lowering Lucia from a window as they escaped from a drug bust in a block of apartments.

A similar switching system was used in Grand Theft Auto 5, which had three playable main characters.

Praise for GTA 6's graphics was more or less universal, with characters displaying photorealistic faces and lifelike movements.

Fans were also impressed by the detailed locations on show, which included the interiors of apartments, rooftop bars and sleazy underground clubs.

The preview also showcased the various environments of Leonida, the fictional, Florida-inspired US state where GTA 6 is set.

Within Leonida, GTA 6 players can explore Vice City, an area inspired by Miami, which appeared in the hit 2002 game named after the city.

The range of different body shapes and sizes among background characters - something rarely seen in video games - was also highlighted by many players watching online.

Journalist Ryan McCaffrey said GTA 6 "might be the best-looking game I've ever seen".

The impressive visual fidelity has been attributed to the amount of time Rockstar has spent working on the game, and its budget, which is thought to be among the most expensive in video game history.

And according to reports, GTA 6's map is significantly larger than the playable area in Rockstar's previous games.

YouTuber TGG, who says he was invited to Rockstar North's headquarters in Edinburgh to see the game, says the developer told him the map was twice the size of GTA 5's map.

The company hasn't confirmed this officially.

While GTA 6 appears to break new ground in terms of visuals and scale, it is still, at its heart, a Grand Theft Auto game.

During the preview, viewers saw the armed heists, car chases and criminal underworld scenes that have become a trademark of the series.

Satirical swipes at US culture, darkly comic interactions between characters and a huge range of optional side activities were all present once again.

And Rockstar appears to have expanded on features it introduced in its last major release, 2018 hit Red Dead Redemption 2, such as an "honour" system that affects the player's reputation among other characters.

Fans of the series, which is estimated to have sold half a billion copies since it launched in 1997, will have been thrilled to see it.

Rockstar had already stated that GTA 6 will be a "single-player experience" on launch, leaving fans to assume a follow-up to the incredibly successful online element of its previous games would come later.

The Netflix preview was dedicated to showing off the story and gameplay, and was not necessarily expected to highlight any new multiplayer features.

Although the launch of the game on 19 November is widely expected to be the biggest of all time, the long-term success of GTA 6 will be judged on how well Rockstar converts players to any new online mode.

GTA online, which also launched after the release of GTA 5, remains one of the most-played games in the world, and is thought to have generated billions of dollars for Rockstar.

The previous game in the series, GTA 5, also broke records when it came out in 2013 and has sold more than 200 million copies since.

Two official trailers for the sixth game have almost 500 million combined views on YouTube, and the Netflix "extended look" on Thursday is being marketed as an event by the streaming service.

Next month the company is due to appear at an employment tribunal in Scotland to defend itself against claims it illegally sacked a group of ex-employees for trying to form a union.

It strongly denies the accusations, and says the workers were fired on the grounds of gross misconduct.

Who is Norway's new King Haakon VIII?

BBC News Fri, 28 Aug 2026 10:37:21 GMT

King Haakon VIII has inherited the Norwegian throne after the death of his father, Harald V. Many in Norway believe he has big shoes to fill.

King Harald was immensely popular with ordinary Norwegians, as shown by his consistent high polling and the outpouring of emotion in the lead-up to his death.

Haakon is the fourth king to head Norway's modern monarchy, since it was restored in 1905 after the country gained independence from Sweden.

Among his first duties as monarch, he led an extraordinary cabinet meeting where he announced his royal title and adopted his father's motto "Everything for Norway".

Many commentators believe he is well-placed to follow in his predecessors' footsteps.

As crown prince, Haakon worked closely with his father as he carried out his royal duties and in recent years was handed more responsibility, increasingly acting as regent while Harald was ill or absent.

"I am so lucky that Crown Prince Haakon is the one who will carry this forward," King Harald wrote of his son in his biography The King Tells.

Historian Trond Norén Isaksen tells the BBC that Haakon will be a different type of king to his father, but no less respected.

"King Harald... [was] very charismatic, he [had] a great sense of humour, which everyone appreciates, and Haakon is a bit more reserved, a bit more like his mother.

"But in recent years he has also become a bit more relaxed and opened up a bit and showed a bit more of his sense of humour... he has been pulling enormous weight for many years given his parents have become older and his wife has been ill."

Haakon is a great-great-great-grandson of Britain's Queen Victoria.

His daughter Ingrid Alexandra, 22, now becomes the crown princess and heir to the Norwegian throne.

Haakon was ahead of his older sister, Princess Märtha Louise, in the line of succession.

The constitution was changed in 1990 to give women the right to inherit the throne, so Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra is in line to be Norway's first female head of state since the 15th Century.

Haakon has become the king at a turbulent time for Norway's royal family.

The monarchy remains broadly popular among Norwegians and has been long praised for its modern outlook.

But in recent years it has been beset by scandal.

Only this year, Haakon's wife Mette-Marit, now Queen of Norway, has apologised for several years of ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and her son has been convicted of rape in a high-profile trial. Marius Borg Høiby, who was born from an earlier relationship, is appealing against the conviction.

Born in 1973, King Haakon is the youngest child of the late king and Queen Sonja.

By Haakon's own admission, he struggled at times to accept his royal status in his early years.

"Yes, I was a royal, but I did not want to talk about it... ​At school it made me anxious," he wrote in his 2023 autobiography, recalling his days in a state primary school in the 1980s.

He became crown prince in 1991 at the tender age of 17, following the death of his grandfather King Olav V.

Unusually for a royal, he was educated at local state schools before embarking upon a four-year-long naval career, graduating from the Norwegian Naval Academy in 1995.

He decided not to follow his father and grandfather to Oxford University, instead flying to California to enrol at the University of Berkeley, where he studied political science.

Soon after his return to Norway, Haakon met his now-wife Mette-Marit at a music festival in her home city of Kristiansand in 1999.

She was dubbed by the press as the Cinderella of Kristiansand - a reference to her humble beginnings.

"What we two found together was so strong that I could not let it go," the then-Crown Prince Haakon said of Mette-Marit ahead of their wedding in 2001.

But their relationship was not without controversy and there was a fierce public debate in Norway from the moment Haakon first announced they were dating.

Some commentators even warned at the time that their relationship could spell the end of the Norwegian monarchy, with comparisons being made to the infamous union between American divorcee Wallis Simpson and British King Edward VIII which led to his abdication in 1936.

Queen Mette-Marit was not the first commoner to marry into the Norwegian royal family - the late King Harald had already broken with tradition by marrying Queen Sonja three decades earlier.

She was, however, a single mother to a four-year-old child whose father had served time for a conviction of cocaine possession.

The royal couple's co-habitation in an Oslo flat had also drawn criticism from the conservative Lutheran Church of Norway - though polls from the time showed most ordinary Norwegians did not care about either.

What many Norwegians did question, though, was whether her former party lifestyle was one compatible with that of someone married to the future king.

In an emotional interview three days before their marriage, Mette-Marit publicly apologised for her "wild past" and condemned drug use after reports that drugs were taken at parties she attended in Oslo during the 1990s.

She did not say whether she had taken them herself.

It was seen as something of a turning point. She won the affection of ordinary Norwegians and for years has been seen as the embodiment of a modern monarchy capable of shaking up convention.

The couple have two children together, Ingrid and Prince Sverre Magnus.

In her new role as crown princess, she took up popular causes including support for people with HIV and promoting literacy.

Her diagnosis with pulmonary fibrosis in 2018 also led to widespread public sympathy.

Haakon has said Mette-Marit helped him come out of his shell and described her as an emotional counterweight to his analytical mind. "I am not very good socially," he wrote. "Mette is a natural talent. She can go into a room and get along with everyone."

But in recent times, Haakon's family has come under increasingly heavy public scrutiny and criticism.

Marius Borg Høiby's rape conviction hangs over the family. One of women was raped on Haakon's estate at Skaugum outside Oslo.

Høiby has always been treated as one of the family, although the royal house has repeatedly stressed he is not a royal.

Days before his trial began, documents were released revealing Mette-Marit's frequent contact with late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

She later apologised to King Harald and Queen Sonja for her three-year friendship with Epstein and admitted to "poor judgement", adding in a national TV interview that she wished she had never met him.

Several polls conducted earlier this year found nearly half of Norway's population felt the crown princess could not become queen, even though it was always bound to happen.

Two days after her son's trial came to an end, Mette-Marit received a lung transplant, eight years after her initial diagnosis.

Her doctors will not declare her stable until a year after the transplant, and the new king will face a difficult period of succession as he continues to support her.

Caroline Vagle, royal correspondent for Se og Hør magazine, says in regards to Epstein the most important thing the royal family can do is be "completely open about what actually happened, and not allow public speculation to take on a life of its own".

"But I also don't think we should overestimate the impact of one or two difficult cases," she says.

"What will ultimately matter is how the royal family handles them, and how Haakon and the next generation manage to build on the trust that Harald has earned over a lifetime."

Tove Taalesen, royal correspondent for Nettavisen, believes the scandals will be challenging but Haakon is "very much ready for the task".

"I'm sure that in the future he will be respected and loved, similar to King Haakon VII, King Olav V and also King Harald V."

Haakon's reign begins in the backdrop of these scandals, and how he navigates them might come to define his monarchy.
