This Indian pilgrim was about to enter Tibet for her dream tour - then her WhatsApp messages stopped

BBC News Fri, 28 Aug 2026 09:31:42 GMT

Early on Wednesday, Sudipto Bhattacharya received what would be the last messages from his wife.

She'd sent a picture of a departure stamp in her passport at 07:57 (02:27 GMT) - immigration at the Nepal border was done.

Six minutes later, at 08:03, she wrote: we are waiting to enter China. Then the messages stopped.

Subhrasree Chakraborty and the group she was travelling with had been waiting to cross into Tibet for the next stage of their pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, the sacred Himalayan home of Hindu god Shiva that Subhrasree had dreamed of visiting for years.

The 43-year-old is now among at least 290 Indians reported missing after deadly flash floods struck along Nepal's border with Tibet. Many of those unaccounted for were on the pilgrimage, which resumed last year after being disrupted by the pandemic and then by tensions between India and China. Thousands of Indians have been making their way to Mount Kailash for years.

Subhrasree was travelling without her family, as part of a group of about 30 people. A medical technologist working in critical care at a city hospital, she was used to emergencies. She knew CPR and intensive-care procedures and, according to her husband, was physically fit.

But none of that has brought her husband Sudipto Bhattacharya any closer to knowing what happened after that final message.

"After 08:03am, what happened? We don't know anything," he says.

Subhrasree had been looking forward to the journey for years.

The photographs she sent home from Kathmandu, taken just days before she went missing, capture something of that excitement.

In one, she stands in a blue tunic in the ornate courtyard of a temple, smiling gently at the camera. In others, she is dressed in red, posing by the ancient brick-and-carved-wood architecture of Kathmandu valley's historic Durbar Square.

She told her husband the countryside was beautiful.

"She was very excited," says Bhattacharya, a government officer. "This was her dream tour."

The journey had begun on Friday 21 August.

She took the Mithila Express from Kolkata and reached Raxaul on 22 August. From there she crossed into Birgunj and travelled by bus to Kathmandu, arriving that night.

She stayed in Kathmandu for three nights, sightseeing.

Then, on the morning of 25 August, the group left Kathmandu by bus for Syabrubesi, a small mountain settlement roughly 122km north of Kathmandu and a gateway to the trekking hub of Langtang region. The journey took almost 12 hours - and was not entirely a smooth one.

A landslide blocked their route for about four hours before the army cleared the road. But when Subhrasree spoke to her husband, she told him the skies were clear.

There was little to suggest what was coming.

"She kept saying the weather was good," he says. "She said it was rather warm, it was raining sometimes."

The next morning, 26 August, Subhrasree left her hotel shortly after 07:00.

Bhattacharya spoke to her on the phone, and the two continued messaging afterwards. Around an hour later, she told him the Nepal immigration formalities were complete and that the group was waiting to cross into Tibet.

After clearing Nepal immigration, pilgrims cross the border on foot to the Chinese immigration facility in Gyirong.

Bhattacharya believes his wife may have been inside, or close to, the Chinese immigration building when the disaster struck.

"I knew there would be connectivity issues on the Tibet side," he says. "So I waited for the next message."

At about 15:00, he saw reports of the floods in the media. He started calling pilgrims in her group. Nobody answered.

He tried the tour operator and then the two managers accompanying the group. Again, there was no answer.

The family has heard nothing from Subhrasree since.

"Have they been rescued? Was this group among those rescued in China?" Bhattacharya asks. "We want to know more."

He believes his wife and the others may already have crossed into Chinese territory before the floods struck. But he has received no confirmation of who made it across - or what happened to them afterwards.

"Please get me a list from the Chinese government," he says. "Missing, dead and rescued. We need an update."

Then comes the admission that captures the agony of those waiting at home: "What do I tell you? Sleepless nights, working on the phone."

For the family of 54-year-old Rina Banerjee, there is more uncertainty.

They do not even know which side of the border she was on when they lost contact.

Rina, an unmarried private tutor from Kolkata, was travelling alone with a tour operator as part of the same pilgrimage group.

Until then, her journey had appeared to be going smoothly. Her nephew, Dwaipayan Mukherjee, says the family had spoken to her over video calls while she was in Kathmandu.

"She was happy," he says. "She was doing a trip after a long time."

Rina was no stranger to mountains. She had travelled in the hills before and gone hiking with her family.

"She was quite fit," Mukherjee says. "We have gone hiking. We are used to going to the mountains."

She had told him about the landslide they encountered on the way the previous day. The group was stuck for about four hours, she had said.

The next morning, the tour operator sent a group photograph, which showed Rina outside the Nepal immigration centre.

Like Subhrasree, she had received her departure stamp, Mukherjee says. After that, silence.

"I don't know whether they crossed the border or not," Mukherjee says. "Whether they were on the Chinese side or the Nepal side, we are still wondering."

For Subhrasree, the two-week tour was to be her first pilgrimage, and a dream she had nurtured for years. Rina, too, had long wanted to make the journey and was no stranger to the mountains.

Both women shared what Bhattacharya calls a "wanderlust" - a love of travelling, discovering new places and, in their case, heading into the mountains.

Both had joined a group for the pilgrimage of a lifetime. Both appear to have cleared Nepal immigration, and both were believed to have crossed the border.

Their names now appear on the Nepal government's official list of 537 missing people. But that offers little clarity - their families still have no idea where they are or whether they are safe. The Kolkata-based tour operator says they have no information about the fate of the group yet.

For both families, the journey has ended with the same unanswered question: did the women make it across the border?

Reading and Leeds Festival unveils major overhaul, but will it draw in a new crowd?

BBC News Fri, 28 Aug 2026 06:33:21 GMT

Reading and Leeds Festival is unveiling what organisers say is the "biggest staging and arena overhaul" in its history this weekend.

Changes include revamping the look of some major stages, while other spaces, such as a campsite for over-21s, are being introduced for the first time.

Organisers Festival Republic say this will take the festival "firmly into its next evolution".

BBC Newsbeat has spoken with festival-goers and an artist to see whether they feel this shake-up will attract a wider demographic, as some say it has developed an image of attracting a younger crowd, putting off some older music fans.

It will also be the first time in 25 years that all headliners at the sister festivals are exclusively British and Irish acts, organisers say.

But others have questioned if some changes, particularly to stages dedicated to lesser-known acts, will still offer the same opportunities for up-and-coming artists from an array of backgrounds.

"None of my friends wanted to go [this year] because of the fact that there's so many 16 to 18-year-olds," Reggie Tanner says.

"They'd rather go to another festival where the demographic's a bit older."

The 20-year-old attended Reading Festival when he was age 16 and 17 as he says it was a "massive trend" which died down when he turned 18.

He's going again this year, mainly to catch Charli XCX, one of the six main stage headliners across the weekend.

Rapper Dave, singer-songwriter Raye, Irish rock band Fontaines DC, electronic duo Chase & Status and band Florence + The Machine are also topping the bill.

Tanner feels the diversity of the line-up and the addition of a new campsite for over-21s this year will "entice a lot of people from different age groups".

BBC Newsbeat understands there's been high demand for the new campsite and a dedicated "quiet zone", introduced in previous years but rebranded in 2026 as "The Oasis".

Tanner advises others who want to go but are worried about the perceptions around its demographic to "just do it".

"I think maybe you might feel a bit older, but that's just life," he adds.

Sasha Baylors and Ciara Hornsey, both 19, feel the stereotype that the festival attracts a younger crowd is "fair" but they "don't think that's a bad thing".

"It's very important to have places for young people to go to listen to music and discover new artists," says Hornsey, who is heading back to Reading Festival after attending last year.

Baylors, who last went when she was 17, says it is "not as rowdy as people say it is, it's not like some battle zone or anything".

College student Zara Hawkins, 17, agrees attending feels like a rite of passage for teenagers in the UK, and she is "really excited" for her first time at Leeds Festival.

She feels the dual sites make Reading and Leeds one of the more accessible festivals for younger music fans, who can head to whichever event is closest, and day tickets are available if you don't want to camp.

Hawkins plans to attend with a large friend group from her college, and says this will make her feel safer as "everyone does look after each other".

However, she feels the revamp and spread of acts across a host of genres will "attract a lot more people" this year.

In addition to the headliners, this year's line-up includes grime artist Skepta, pop singer Jade, Irish rap trio Kneecap, BBC Radio 1's Sound of 2026 winner Skye Newman and US rock band Geese.

As part of the staging shake-up, the main stage will now be called The Grid and mock-up images show a large walkway extending into the crowd.

Other new stages, such as "undercover immersive stage" The Gallery and "purpose-built" dance music area The Warehouse, claim to offer more of an experience than the traditional festival tent.

As part of the overhaul, the BBC Introducing stage, dedicated to highlighting new artists, has been axed.

Organisers say its replacement, The Canopy, will still host emerging musicians and "usher in a new chapter for new music".

But the line-up, which features the children of several high-profile celebrities, has led some people to nickname it "the nepo baby stage".

Among them is Cruz Beckham, the son of David and Victoria Beckham; Violet Grohl, daughter of Foo Fighters' Dave Grohl; Gene Gallagher, who fronts rock band Villanelle and is the son of Oasis' Liam Gallagher; and Moses Martin, the son of Chris Martin and Gwyneth Paltrow and lead singer of People I've Met.

Singer-songwriter Beth McCarthy tells Newsbeat she is "fuming" at the BBC Introducing stage being scrapped as she feels it is "such a foundation point of all festivals".

The 29-year-old is performing on the main stage at Reading and Leeds Festival this year, but last year she made her debut at Glastonbury Festival through the BBC Introducing stage.

"It's difficult to make your way into the festival circuit as an up-and-coming artist, particularly if you don't have a team around you yet or you're still building a fan base," she says.

"BBC Introducing was always the one way in for artists that weren't already established."

A Festival Republic spokesperson says they are "proud" of the work they've done with BBC Introducing over the years in "championing new British talent", but that the new stage will give them the "opportunity to showcase a broader range of new artists".

"We've also invested in a bigger stage, stronger production and an even better experience for both artists and festival-goers," they added.

Galapagos corals suggest climate change drives stronger El Niños

New Scientist August 27, 2026

A super El Niño that is gathering strength in the Pacific Ocean may have been made worse by climate change, according to new analysis of coral records that suggest El Niños have become more intense as global temperatures have climbed.

The impacts of El Niño – droughts, floods and storms – are already exacerbated by rising global temperatures, because a warmer atmosphere intensifies both rainfall and droughts.

But scientists have long struggled to untangle the effect of climate change on the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) cycle, which drives El Niño events. Part of the difficulty is that detailed observational records only began in the 1980s. A much longer timescale than that is needed to tease out a trend from natural variability.

Advertisement

The last-ditch plan to save coral reefs from utter destruction

Julia Cole at the University of Michigan and her colleagues hope corals can provide the answer. They collected living and dead corals from around the Galapagos Islands in the eastern Pacific ocean, where El Niños first develop.

They used uranium and thorium dating to identify the age of the corals, then analysed the chemistry of their skeletons to track changes to sea temperatures during their lifetime. In that way, they built a time series of sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific spanning the past 1000 years.

El Niño and La Niña events are measured by changes to sea surface temperatures in the Pacific, so by building this time series, Cole and her colleagues could track the fluctuating ENSO cycle through the centuries.

Free newsletter

“The chemistry of the coral skeleton preserves a record of the environment in which it grew, and certain aspects of the chemistry are especially sensitive to temperature changes,” says Cole.

The team found that, over the past 40 years, variability in the ENSO cycle has increased by 36.5 per cent compared with the pre-industrial period. This increase in variability has been driven largely by more intense El Niño events, the analysis found.

The corals collected by the team covered about half the 1000-year time period. Nevertheless, Cole is confident in the overall trend identified. “I think we show pretty clearly that the increase in variability in ENSO is tracking global temperature closely,” she says.

The findings add to an emerging body of evidence that suggests the ENSO cycle is changing in response to rising temperatures. “The evidence is better than 50-50 that climate change is affecting El Niño,” says Mark Cane at Columbia University in New York, whose own work used tree ring data to identify an increase in El Niño activity in recent years.

Michael McPhaden at the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) agrees. “If the current El Niño turns out to be as strong as we expect, that past decade will have witnessed three major El Niños – a sequence not seen before in the instrumental record dating back to the late 19th century,” he says. “It will add to the mounting evidence that climate change is amplifying the ENSO cycle… which is a concern considering the far-reaching global impacts that ENSO has on humans and natural systems.”

At first, we couldn’t see the whales themselves. As we pulled closer, it became increasingly obvious that Greg and his team had underestimated the number of whales. The plumes multiplied and spread, the slippery backs and blowholes of the humpback whales coming into view below them, until the ship was surrounded. There weren’t 20 whales or 40 whales, but hundreds, maybe even 1000. The captain cut the ship’s engines, and all we could hear was the splash of fins, the “poof” of whale breath, and the occasional “whoa, over there” from passengers and crew members.

We had travelled to Greenland with New Scientist Discovery Tours to see a total solar eclipse. Just four days earlier, the group, along with the entire crew and staff of our ship, the Sylvia Earle, had stood transfixed and in awe as the moon hid the face of the sun and the sky grew dark in the middle of the day. I thought that would be the most astonishing thing I’d see during the two-week voyage. I was wrong.

Advertisement

The most breathtaking photos of the total solar eclipse

Since about 2000, the population of baleen whales, which use a sort of natural sieve in their mouths to filter their food from the water, has exploded in eastern Greenland. “We know from the communities there that they never used to see all these baleen whales – maybe a minke whale once in a while, but never all these humpbacks and fin whales,” says Mads Peter Heide-Jørgensen, a researcher at the Greenland Institute of Natural Resources who studies the animal population of this region.

This is most likely happening because the ice that used to cover Greenland’s eastern coast, rendering it inaccessible to whales and ships alike, has receded significantly in the last few decades, while at the same time the warmer water in the area has produced a huge influx of the krill and small fish that make up baleen whales’ diets. This is obviously bad for many species of Arctic wildlife, whose habitats are rapidly shrinking, but for baleen whales, which winter in much warmer equatorial waters, it is like a magnet drawing them to feed.

Free newsletter

Heide-Jørgensen’s recent work has shown that the number of humpback whales in the region is up to about 4000, leading to feeding frenzies in which they, along with fin and minke whales, consume about 1 million tonnes of food during the four months they reside there each year.

That was precisely what we saw. As each whale neared the surface, it would first exhale into the sky, then turn on its side, opening its mouth to take in a huge draught of water. The entire front half of the whale went from a streamlined triangle shape to a bulging, rippling pouch of sea as it closed its maw. The next part of this so-called lunge-feeding behaviour happened underwater, where we couldn’t see it, but the water rushed out through the whale’s baleen, leaving the tiny creatures that constituted its lunch trapped inside.

In the end, we saw one last humpback whale fluke splash a few metres ahead of the ship, and then they were past us, the white patches on their fins glistening an otherworldly aquamarine through the water. We got under way again, stunned by what we had just witnessed, as they turned back into a copse of distant plumes and then disappeared.

When I finally wandered down towards lunch – how strange to follow such a profound experience of natural majesty with such a mundane one as a lunch buffet – every person I met was grinning and glassy-eyed, much as we had been in the moments after the eclipse. We didn’t know that we had seen as many as one-quarter of the humpback whales in the region, but we knew we had seen something special.

The expedition crew, with well over 100 years of experience among them sailing the polar regions, all said they had never seen anything like it. I spotted more than a few tears, and I may have shed some myself. And with events like this increasing, you can bet that I will be back, even without a solar eclipse to lure me north.

New Scientist August 28, 2026

Even top predators weren’t safe in Cambrian seas around 520 million years ago. An extraordinary fossil shows a healed wound where one predator took a bite out of the side of another.

“I would never have expected to see something like this preserved in the fossil record,” says Stephen Pates at University College London.

The predator with a bite taken out of it is called Amplectobelua symbrachiata, which belonged to a long-extinct group of strange arthropods known as the radiodonts that looked a bit like a cross between squid and lobsters. They had two vicious, grasping appendages on their heads for catching prey, and a line of swimming flaps protruding from their sides that decreased in size towards their rear.

Advertisement

Extraordinary ichthyosaur fossil shows its last meal was a pterosaur

They grew to nearly a metre long, which might be tiny compared with modern marine predators, but back in the Cambrian Period, it made them one of the biggest predators around.

The swimming flaps of radiodonts were softer than their grasping appendages, resulting in very few fossils of them. But a team recently found a single flap at a site in China called the Yu’anshan Formation, where soft tissues are exceptionally preserved.

It is recognisable as a radiodont flap because of a characteristic pattern of lines on its surface. If it was the largest swimming flap, the animal would have been at least 23 centimetres long. If it was one of the smaller flaps, it could have been much larger.

Subscriber-only newsletter

The researchers noticed an odd W-shaped feature on the edge of the flap – the kind of shape typically left when two fangs tear through flesh.

But is it really a bite wound? The researchers in China got in touch with Pates because he has studied similar injuries in trilobites. “You want to rule out that it’s been broken during the fossilisation process,” says Pates.

X-ray fluorescence mapping shows that the chemical composition of the W-shaped part is consistent with the rest of the fossil, which means it’s not an artefact caused by flaking. “This is telling us that this is likely a flap that was preserved like this, rather than altered later,” says Pates.

What’s more, there is a black band visible around the edges of the W-shape that appears to be a sign of healing. “In modern arthropods, you see this melanisation, this darkening around areas where they’re regrowing,” he says. “I think we can be fairly confident this happened while the animal was alive.”

It is an extraordinary find because only around 10 isolated radiodont flaps like this have ever been found, says Pates. “With more complete specimens, even if these wounds were there, you wouldn’t necessarily be able to see them.”

So, what took a chunk out of this ancient predator? The team can’t be sure, but it could have been another species of radiodont, or even a member of the same species, says Pates.

Palaeontologists have found new evidence that the early ancestors of amphibians, reptiles and mammals did not have a larval stage with external gills like modern frogs or salamanders

Hundreds of likely predation wounds have been found on trilobites, but their fossils are much more common because of their hard exoskeletons and because they survived until 250 million years ago, whereas radiodonts were all extinct by around 480 million years ago. Trilobites were also much smaller and nearer the bottom of the food chain.

“There have been other reports of healed injuries in Cambrian animals, though never in a radiodont,” says Joe Moysiuk at the Manitoba Museum in Canada. “With only one specimen, I don’t think we can rule out other potential causes.”

For instance, it’s not unusual for arthropods to suffer injuries while shedding an exoskeleton, and so this flap might have been damaged during moulting, says Moysiuk.

“You can’t rule it out, but it’s [a] balance of probabilities,” says Pates. For instance, a moulting wound is most likely to be a singular tear, whereas the W-shape points more towards a bite mark, he says. The location on the flap is also what would be expected if the radiodont was fleeing an attacker, whereas a moulting wound could occur anywhere on the animal’s body.

“For us, the best interpretation for this injury is a predation injury,” says Pates.

NASA’s huge Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is about to launch

New Scientist August 28, 2026

NASA’s next flagship space telescope is getting ready to launch. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, which will probe some of the cosmos’ most vexing mysteries, is set to take off from Cape Canaveral in Florida on 30 August.

This new observatory gets its name from NASA’s first chief of astronomy, who helped plan the Hubble Space Telescope and built the agency’s space astronomy programme. It and the previous major telescope to be launched, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), are designed to work together to investigate the universe in infrared-light wavelengths.

But while JWST was intended to probe deep into distant space with a relatively small field of view, Roman will take a broader, shallower view, capturing an area of the sky equivalent to the full moon in each observation.

Advertisement

Planned satellite launches could ruin Hubble Space Telescope images

Using its Wide Field Instrument, Roman will take images with the same resolution as the Hubble Space Telescope, but over an area of sky 100 times larger, making it 1000 times faster at gathering data than Hubble. This broad view is intended to allow Roman to map the distribution of dark matter across the universe and measure the effects of dark energy.

“The goal is not necessarily for Roman to take a picture of dark matter or dark energy, but to measure their effects with far greater precision,” said Kristen McQuinn at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Maryland, one of the science leads for the mission, in a statement. “That could help us understand what the universe is made of, how it developed and what may happen to it in the distant future.”

Subscriber-only newsletter

These broad surveys will also enable it to spot a huge variety of cosmic objects. JWST can then follow up on the most interesting of them to get deeper, more detailed data, or Hubble can observe them in a wider variety of wavelengths of light.

Over the course of its five-year primary mission, Roman is expected to observe about 12 per cent of the sky, unveiling the universe going back to just 2 billion years after the big bang. Space telescopes tend to have their missions extended – Hubble, for example, was only expected to last about 15 years and has now been operating for more than 36 years. This means Roman may well end up observing a much wider swathe of sky.

The observatory’s other scientific instrument is its coronagraph, designed to directly image planets orbiting other stars. By blocking the light from the stars themselves, it will allow the reflections of that light off any planets to shine through.

This will enable it to see planets that are 100 million times fainter than stars, far more than any existing space-based coronagraph can accomplish. Spotting all those planets will set the stage for NASA’s next proposed flagship space telescope, the Habitable Worlds Observatory.

If the launch goes smoothly, Roman should reach its final position at L2 – a gravitationally stable point about 1.5 million kilometres further from the sun than Earth – in about a month. It will then undergo another three months or so of instrument testing and calibration before beginning its science phase, so the first scientific observations are expected to begin around the start of 2027.

Fastest star ever spotted at the centre of our galaxy

New Scientist August 28, 2026

A star near the centre of the Milky Way is hurtling through its orbit with a peak speed of more than 8 per cent the speed of light, making it both the fastest star and the closest to a supermassive black hole that has ever been spotted. Named S301, this astonishing star could help us unravel the secrets of gravity.

Stefan Gillessen at the Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics in Germany and his colleagues found S301 using the Very Large Telescope in Chile. They have been watching it since 2023 to get enough data to pin down its orbit, and the results are unprecedented.

Everything from cells to stars to particles exists on the edge of chaos

At its closest approach, S301 is only about 1.8 billion kilometres from Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the centre of our galaxy. That’s just 12 times the distance between Earth and the sun, 10 times closer to Sagittarius A* than the previous record-holder. “If you were living on a planet around this star, the size of the black hole at the closest approach would appear similar to the full moon from Earth – it would be absolutely stunning,” says Gillessen.

Advertisement

Such a close pass by the black hole means that S301 spends part of its orbit in one of the most extreme gravitational environments in the universe. Next to a black hole, space-time stretches and warps. If a black hole is spinning, it should warp space-time even more, twisting it up in what is known as the frame-dragging effect.

“Earth does this as well, and we can measure with satellites around Earth that there is a very, very slight frame dragging from Earth’s rotation,” says Tuan Do at the University of California, Los Angeles, who wasn’t involved in the research. “This is doing the same thing, just with much different objects.”

Subscriber-only newsletter

Measuring Earth’s spin is relatively easy, but a black hole’s spin is much harder to determine because of its lack of a visible surface. The most precise way to measure it would be by measuring frame dragging, and S301 is the first star close enough to feel that effect.

“We drop a leaf in the wind and see how the air is moving by measuring that leaf,” says Gillessen. “A star is just the perfect leaf to drop to see the movement of space-time.”

Actually measuring the spin of Sagittarius A* using this method will probably take around a decade, he says, but that may speed up if we find more stars like it.

“With one star, it would take a while, but it would still be the best constraint on spin that we’ve ever had by far,” says Ziri Younsi at University College London. “If you can find another star that’s even closer, that’s better still. If you can find a population of these stars, then you’re in business.”

Gillessen and his team have several candidates for stars slightly further from the black hole than S301, but none yet that are closer, he says.

But when we finally do measure the spin of a black hole, it will be a crucial piece of the cosmic jigsaw. It will not only help us understand how black holes have contributed to the evolution of the universe, but will also provide a probe into the behaviour of gravity in extreme environments, which has proved extremely difficult to study.

“A black hole only has three measurable properties: a mass, a spin and possibly an electric charge. The mass was worth a Nobel prize in 2020, so, if you find the spin, you might expect a call from Stockholm in 20 years,” says Gillessen.

Where and when to see 2027’s ‘solar eclipse of the century’

New Scientist August 28, 2026

On 2 August 2027, the eclipse of a lifetime will pass across parts of northern Africa and south-west Asia. Totality, the period during which the moon covers the entire disc of the sun, will last for 6 minutes and 23 seconds in some areas, making this a profoundly special event. Eclipse chasers are already calling it the “eclipse of the century”.

Only one longer total solar eclipse has occurred in the 21st century, in 2009. A longer one won’t happen until 2114. The most recent eclipse, on 12 August 2026, had a maximum totality of 2 minutes and 18 seconds.

Total solar eclipses occur thanks to a cosmic coincidence: the sun is both about 400 times wider than the moon and about 400 times more distant, so they appear almost exactly the same size in the sky. The differences in the length of totality are because of the geometry of Earth’s orbit around the sun and the moon’s orbit around Earth: when the moon is at its closest, or the sun at its most distant, it takes the moon a little longer to pass across the sun. Based on those orbits, the longest a total eclipse could possibly last is 7 minutes and 32 seconds.

Advertisement

The most breathtaking photos of the total solar eclipse

With 2027’s eclipse getting so close to that maximum, researchers and tourists alike will be flocking to the path of totality to witness the cosmic spectacle. Cities under the path of totality include Luxor in Egypt, Tangiers in Morocco and Cádiz in Spain, and hotels in those areas are already reporting huge numbers of bookings nearly a year in advance. These areas also have a very low likelihood of clouds obscuring the eclipse, making it even more tantalising. Much of Africa, Europe and Asia will experience a partial solar eclipse, with the moon only impinging on the edge of the sun instead of blotting out the whole thing.

Anywhere along the eclipse’s path, totality will occur in the late morning or early afternoon, when the sun will be nearly directly overhead. When the sky goes dark, several planets will be visible, including Mercury, which is usually impossible to view with the naked eye because of its proximity to the sun.

For scientists, eclipses like this one present a perfect opportunity to observe the faint outermost layer of the sun, called the corona. Most of the time, the corona is hidden in the glare of the sun’s disc, but during totality it suddenly becomes visible in shimmering strands beyond the area blocked out by the moon.

The corona is more than 150 times hotter than the surface of the sun, and researchers have been trying to understand why for decades. It is also strangely patchy, making the mystery even more puzzling. While there are scientific instruments, called coronagraphs, that block out the sun’s disc to study the corona, the area blocked during a natural eclipse is much tighter against the sun, allowing us to observe the closest-in areas of the corona, which could be crucial to understanding it.

The scientists hope that, by researching this puggle and other echidnas, we will finally be able to understand some fundamental questions about the evolution of pregnancy in mammals.

The short-beaked echidna (Tachyglossus aculeatus), also known as the spiny anteater, has proved to be an extremely difficult species to breed in captivity. In spite of numerous attempts, a dedicated research colony had never been successfully established, though several zoos and wildlife sanctuaries have bred the species.

Now, Oliver Griffith at Macquarie University in Sydney and his team are successfully rearing a puggle, which is thought to be the first in the world born at a university. Advertisement

T. aculeatus is one of only five known species of monotremes, a group of mammals that lay eggs. The others are three different species of echidna in New Guinea and the platypus (Ornithorhynchus anatinus). Most researchers believe monotremes are an ancient mammalian lineage that predate placentals.

Studying the chemical composition of echidna eggs may reveal how different they are to those of reptiles, which could give clues on when mammals and reptiles diverged, says Griffith. “We’ll look at eggshell proteins in the echidna and compare that to eggshell proteins in reptiles and try to work out: do they have the same origin or did they evolve independently?”

Five females and four males are in captivity at Macquarie University. In early August, Griffith and his colleagues noticed that the puggle’s mother, named Kootear, had stopped eating and moving for around 10 days, a sign that birth is imminent. Pregnant echidnas move their egg into a pouch, where it incubates while the female is fasting and immobilised.

“We had an inkling that she may have laid an egg,” says Griffith. “So, three weeks ago, we looked into her pouch and we found what was a very tiny, almost jelly-bean-sized baby that had hatched only a couple of days before.”

A week later, the team checked the pouch again and found the puggle had surged in size. “It had grown a crazy amount actually, and it was surprising to see it so much bigger in just seven days,” says Griffith.

When it was checked for the third time, the researchers anaesthetised Kootear so the puggle could be briefly removed. They found it weighed 36 grams and was starting to look like an echidna, albeit one without any spines or fur.

“Before this point, you couldn’t obviously see it was an echidna – you might confuse it with a platypus puggle or, maybe even, just because it’s a pink thing, you might think it was a kangaroo baby,” says Griffith. “But today you could really see the shape of an echidna – the beak, the feet, everything.”

Echidnas can live for more than 50 years in captivity. The university’s echidnas are unlikely to ever be released into the wild. “This is a long-term research programme,” says Griffith. “I’ve set this up to be sort of a career’s worth of research, and this puggle may well outlive me.”

Einstein thought time dilation was both real and not – he was right

New Scientist August 28, 2026

The passage of time often seems like the most malleable thing in the world. A minute may feel much longer when you’re asked to hold a plank position in a workout class, and an hour may fly by when you’re chatting with a friend. In these cases, your perception of time is altered. But real, physical time dilation also happens. According to Albert Einstein’s special theory of relativity, clocks that are closer to Earth’s centre of gravity, say at sea level, tick more slowly than those at the top of a mountain. A similar slowing happens when a clock is physically travelling extremely fast.

Why banishing irrational numbers could trigger a revolution in quantum theory

Undeniably, this sounds bizarre, but decades’ worth of experiments haven’t managed to disprove it. Yet in what exact sense time dilation is real – and what it means for a physical effect to be real at all – has inspired philosophical debates ever since Einstein first formulated his theory in 1905.

In fact, in June, at the Foundations of Physics conference in Irvine, California, I heard Marco Giovanelli discuss how time dilation is both real and apparent at once. It sounds paradoxical, but when I called Giovanelli, who is a historian of philosophy and science at the University of Turin in Italy, to talk through it, I started to understand that it reflects the facets of our physical world that Einstein’s work first uncovered.

Advertisement

For Einstein, it was all about rods and clocks, explains Giovanelli. Suppose that you and a friend each had an identical clock and a metre-long rod. You stand still, while your friend gets into an incredibly fast spaceship and sets off on a journey. Compared with yours, their clock will tick less quickly and their rod will contract in size. If you want to know by how much, Einstein’s got your back: he worked out those calculations more than a century ago. If you happen to have a second friend who has a slightly slower spaceship and their own clock-and-rod set, the same trick will work again, except that their clock will slow and their rod contract a little less than your speedier friend. Finally, if you also acquire a spaceship and catch up with either of your friends, your clocks will start to tick at the same rate again, and your metre-long rods will again look the same length.

To discuss these effects, physicists use the language of “inertial frames”, similar to comparing a room at rest, or a rest frame, with a spaceship travelling at a constant speed, or a moving frame. In your individual frames, you and your friends can each establish a coordinate system, the familiar grid of width, depth and height. Your coordinate systems will match when you are all at rest or when your spaceships move side by side at the same speed.

When one of you moves more quickly, though, special relativity shows that their grid will deform, contracting in the direction of motion. It is this detail that bothered Einstein’s contemporaries. It seemed that the change in the rod length was uncomfortably intertwined with changes in the coordinate system used to situate it. But an effect that is a function of a coordinate system cannot possibly be real, critics argued. Ultimately, coordinate systems themselves are of dubious reality. They seem to simply be tools that we humans made up to help us organise our theories and observations of the physical world.

Does gravity create reality? A shocking path to a theory of everything

In 1911, physicist Vladimir Varićak argued that the rod’s length contraction “is only a psychological and not a physical fact, i. e., the body has not really undergone any change”. Giovanelli recounts another anecdote where, in the 1970s, physicist John Stewart Bell surveyed his colleagues at the CERN particle physics laboratory about whether length contraction could break a thread suspended between two spaceships accelerating at exactly the same rate. Most physicists said the thread wouldn’t break, endorsing the idea that nothing physically changes about the atoms in the thread. Could they have possibly been wrong? This made my head spin.

I will admit to having always been a rather terrible student of relativity, only learning it just well enough to pass my preliminary exams in graduate school. However, I’m certain I was previously taught that relativistic time dilation and length contraction are unquestionably real. We know they are, from experience in everyday life. The precise clocks on GPS satellites tick at different rates than those on Earth. This is partly because they move quickly and partly because of the gravitational effects explained by Einstein in his general theory of relativity. For GPS to be accurate, the difference in ticks must be corrected for. Failing to do so would have very real consequences, like ending up in someone’s backyard when I try to use my phone to visit a new café or bookstore. But here’s the crucial thing: the clocks on GPS satellites derive their precision from leveraging quantum control over atoms rather than some macroscopic clock gears, so it feels especially egregious to suggest that time dilation does, well, nothing to an atom.

Einstein himself was thinking about this, too, Giovanelli tells me. In fact, an atomic effect was at the centre of a 1906 debate he had with Johannes Stark, a physicist who was awarded the Nobel prize for discovering how electromagnetic fields can affect the energy states of atoms. Stark was studying fast-moving charged atoms and Einstein recognised that these experiments may display the transverse Doppler effect – in the same way that a siren changes pitch as it approaches you due to a shift in the frequency of its sound waves, a similar effect can happen due to time dilation. It is a distinct prediction of special relativity, an effect that doesn’t exist in other theories, says Giovanelli.

For the standard Doppler effect, you know that you could cancel it out by driving after the police car and that what is happening isn’t due to something changing inside the car’s speaker. The same question reared its head for the transverse Doppler effect. “Stark really thought, kind of naively but naturally, that something is going on in the atom,” says Giovanelli – in our analogy, the speaker in the car would be physically changing. Einstein rejected this. He posited that all the atoms remain the same and that their inner workings are unaffected by motion. Time dilation was the only explanation. Seemingly apparent, here it was confronted with a real, empirical test.

Ironically, when the transverse Doppler effect was experimentally verified in 1938, one of the two physicists involved was Herbert Ives, who never accepted special relativity. Ives thought that he had found signatures of the “luminiferous aether”, a hypothetical substance that some researchers thought permeated the universe and provided one preferred, true reference frame. A preponderance of other experimental evidence, much of it obtained even prior to Ives’s work, completely ruled out this option, and special relativity became the only game in town. For all the clamouring about the oddity of an effect related to an observer’s perspective, one that many physicists wanted to dismiss, time dilation withstood the test of time. Over the ensuing decades, ever-increasingly precise atomic clocks have never uncovered any evidence that something more “real” could be happening.

As far as Giovanelli is concerned, what happened was not so much a dispute over physics, but rather a run-in between physics and philosophy. Underneath the sticky question of whether time dilation is real hides another, even stickier philosophical one: what does it mean to be real?

Einstein killed the aether. Now the idea is back to save relativity

“At a certain point, you cannot avoid it,” says Giovanelli. “And so, Einstein was forced to address the question philosophically. OK, really, let’s define: ‘apparent’ means disappears for the co-moving observer, ‘real’ means empirically testable.” In some sense, the situation ought to never have become that complicated, he says. Scientific theories provide testable hypotheses – it is what they are designed for – and special relativity has passed every test we’ve put it to. What more could you ask from a theory?

Well, it’s hard to understand from an intuitive point of view, says Giovanelli. Einstein even had his own questions, primarily about how certain he could really be that two clocks, or two atoms being used as clocks, could be reliably identical. The advent of quantum physics offered some assurances, but Einstein had his qualms with quantum theory and spent time worrying about it way beyond how it applies to rods and clocks. But he never questioned the empirical reality of time dilation and length contraction, says Giovanelli.

As we talked, I wondered whether for me, like Einstein’s critics, it was my notable lack of relativistic intuition that made time dilation so hard to grasp. It may have been easier to accept that when atoms within a clock or a rod move at a certain speed, some as-yet-unknown mechanism physically changes them, leading to time dilation and length contraction. Instead, I have to grapple with there really being no such thing as absolute time.

Being a student of modern physics, however, I am not necessarily surprised by this somewhat frustrating duel between the words “apparent” and “real”. I gained my intuition about the behaviour of physical objects by interacting with mundane things like pens, oranges and soccer balls, never anything extremely small or cold, nor anything incredibly fast. Quantum theory, which governs all things tiny and chilled, taught me that I can’t always expect just one thing about an object to be unambiguously true at once. In fact, quantum objects can exist in states akin to clouds of probability that contain completely contradictory options. Absolute precision and absolute certainty are simply off the table. Special relativity may be teaching me a similar lesson about time.

The daring idea that time is an illusion and how we could prove it

Read an extract from Chanda Prescod-Weinstein’s The Edge of Space-Time

New Scientist August 28, 2026

sε wo werε fi na wosan kɔfa a, yεnkyi

it is not incorrect to go back and get what you forgot

Advertisement

—Akan proverb

We are called to go back and get the history of space-time. And who am I to argue with the ancestors?

Even so, I do. Science in this society is often done for the wrong rea­sons, I find myself telling them. And they remind me that because it’s my job to study the origin and evolution of the universe and every­thing inside it, I know there is a location in space-time where the uni­verse became transparent to light: the first place where light could fly free. The ancestors insist: This is a story that I have learned so I could tell it to others. To do cosmology—to study the beginning and evolu­tion of space, time, and matter—is to be a griot, a keeper of stories and history. To do cosmology is to go back and get the beginning, to map out the future.

So: Quite nearly at the beginning, the universe said let there be light. And particles of light—photons—all of them traveling at the speed of light, the fastest in the universe, couldn’t get very far. They were stuck in a plasma stew where they constantly bumped into par­ticles, especially electrons, which swallowed their energy and spat it out in the form of new photons and other particles.

Humanity has only been aware of this cosmic light for eighty-two years. It has been there almost since the beginning of everything and has been traveling for nearly 14 billion years. It was there when the universe was cool enough for atoms to form. It was with the sun when it was just a cloud of gas, and it was there when the sun’s hydrogen ignited with fusion, turning the sun into a star. It was there when the leftovers from the gas cloud condensed into planet Earth. And it was there when carbon-based life forms evolved into apes.

Free newsletter

This light is a cosmic edge: We cannot look past it because at any time earlier than that, the photons were trapped, unable to get out. And this edge is a reminder that physics is a way of gaining deep insight into the universe, one we can add to the variety of overlapping forms of knowing that we have long used. To understand this bound­ary, and how we have come to know about it, is to deepen our rela­tionship with ourselves and the universe around us in a very specific and beautiful way. We should embrace it, for ourselves, and for future generations, because it is our history—and who are we to argue with the ancestors?

…

The book you are reading is about the queer, poetic wonder that is our universe and what we gain when we look at it from the margins. It is my version of what historian Aimé Dafon Sègla calls cosmovi­sions, a response to the question of why we should bother trying to get beyond the edges of human knowledge about the physical universe. The Edge of Space-Time is part of a larger tradition that includes not just scientists but also artists. People like jazz percussionist, artist, and technologist Milford Graves, who used percussion, sound, and observations of praying mantises and plant growth to understand a phenomenon he termed “cosmic energy.” Graves, a maker working in a long tradition of Black artists, was not formally trained as a scien­tist, and “cosmic energy” sounds a little like mystic talk. But when I listened to him describe his ideas in the documentary Milford Graves Full Mantis, I heard a familiar sensibility about how matter is linked with and through space-time, a relationship that takes center stage in this book.

As a set of knowledges and techniques, physics provides a path­way toward answering the same questions Graves asked about the fundamental nature of our cosmos and the relationship between matter, energy, and space-time. It allows us to specify in great detail the relationship between photons and the plants in Graves’s garden which transformed the photons into living particles. It is another entry point to what plant biologist and Black feminist theorist of intersectionality in science Beronda L. Montgomery calls lessons from plants.

When it’s at its best, physics is a kind of poetry, a story about the cosmos that is made from metaphors—and a producer of metaphors in its own right. We often analyze the world through metaphor, and I believe that seeing the universe through the perspective offered by physics strengthens our ability to understand what work metaphors are doing on us and how we might wield them. It is in this sense that physics works on us like poetry: a perspective on the world that provides insights not available to us elsewhere. This helps us under­stand why we should bother with it. We should bother with physics because it is, in part, how we as a species learn to use our minds. We should learn and teach poetry, physics, algebra, and other abstract ideas because they train us to think in symbolic and figurative terms. The same goes for calculus and quantum mechanics. And if we can­not learn to think in and through the abstract and the symbolic, then we are pliable. We are sitting ducks for the fascists and authoritarians who will use us for their ends, and their ends are ultimately catastro­phe for the rest of us. That’s always been true, and it always will be.

In a world where genocides (plural) can be live-streamed and still continue unabated, it is hard to imagine that society could be oth­erwise when what is broken about it feels so total and, in the case of the families shattered and lives lost, so final. I don’t think cosmology by itself can save the world. Even so, I believe in the ways that people experience a connection to the cosmos as nourishing. And I believe in preparing for the better world that is coming.

This is an extract from The Edge of Space-Time by Chanda Prescod-Weinstein (Canongate Books), the September read for the New Scientist Book Club. Sign up for the club here, and join the discussion on Discord here.

‘Thinking about the edges of space-time can help build a better world’

New Scientist August 28, 2026

If I could go back in time and tell my younger self something about life as a theoretical physicist, I might say: mind the gap between what’s exciting about physics and what the job actually is. My new book, The Edge of Space-Time, was born in part out of thinking about the physical questions that get pushed to the margins in professional physics. Big-picture questions like, what is the material nature of space? What is a quantum theory of time? It is very difficult to build a professional life working on these questions – even as books tout them as the most exciting ones in the universe.

I was recruited into the world of physics by the Errol Morris documentary about Stephen Hawking, A Brief History of Time. Eventually, I read Hawking’s book of the same name and my impression of a working life in physics was that, for the most part, physicists think big thoughts about wonders of the universe every day.

Free newsletter

Today, I’m a tenured professor of physics at a major research institution, and a lot of my job is sending emails about bureaucratic things, like asking whether anyone can tell me the policy that is governing changes that the university is making to my grant. On a good day, I get to have conversations about science with the postdoctoral fellows I employ in my research group – but that’s not every day. And in either case, the kind of research that we can get grant funding to do is quite limited. The sort of work Hawking did on the nature of time is financially out of reach for most physicists, a situation that is getting worse as the UK and the US both slash and burn basic science budgets.

Advertisement

The Edge of Space-Time was born in this gap between what we say science is and the reality of living it. I began it at a moment of transition. I had just been awarded tenure, which, in the US, historically has meant my position is permanent, and I am free to research whatever interests me without worrying about being fired. At the moment my tenure became official, I was thinking about what I had given up to get there, the strategic choices I had made.

Why dark matter is still one of the biggest open problems in science

I gave up working on quantum gravity, for example, both because of racism I experienced as a PhD student and because the job prospects weren’t good. I never took a class where we were asked to think deeply about time, space and the fundamental nature of space-time. Mostly, I learned to calculate and pursue questions that were broadly agreeable to the physics community, like understanding the nature of dark matter. And while I think these questions are important and interesting, they live at a kind of margin that physicists are pushed to by economic and social forces that determine which questions we can be paid to pursue and which we won’t be.

When I began working on the book in 2023, I was in the midst of a five-year stint working in US science policy, alongside colleagues from around the world (mostly the UK, Europe and Canada). As I learned more about the politics of science at the government level, it became clear to me that particle physics and cosmology were in trouble. Politicians were no longer sold on the fundamental importance of our research and didn’t see how it was beneficial to the capitalist economy or the military, which historically is how that support has been rationalised. The cultural arguments – that a well-cultured civilisation does things like try to understand the universe – didn’t seem impactful at all. And the general public, struggling with climate change and economies that don’t serve the 99 per cent, couldn’t see how we had anything to add.

You can’t put a price on the sense of awe particle physics inspires

I could see that we were about to be on the margins in a new way. And so The Edge of Space-Time became not just a return to my roots and the big-picture questions that once drove me, it also became a plea: don’t let me be the last of my kind. The cuts that are being made to science in the UK and the US right now seem like a political problem that is easily remedied, but it is more complicated than that. Even one year where there is a gap in funding means we haemorrhage workers who may never return. As those researchers leave, they take with them knowledge. Because the sciences work through apprenticeship, if there is no senior instructor to pass on knowledge, it doesn’t matter if there is money and an apprentice waiting in the wings.

With The Edge of Space-Time, I take readers on a journey through huge questions, like why does my favourite physics experiment foist the structures of quantum physics on us? And will we ever know what space-time really is, or is it always just going to be a useful mathematical construct that allows us to calculate motion in environments where gravity plays a significant role, like near black holes?

While thinking through the physics, I also try to make the case for why any healthy democracy needs people who live at the edge of what is known and what is unknown – the keepers of these cosmic stories that have fascinated humans for millennia. I make the case that, like poetry, physics gives us a viewpoint on the universe that we need because it is our ancestral inheritance. I also argue that spending time with what feels strange about physics can help prepare us to better reckon with difficult political questions.

Given the crises we face – genocides, climate change, attacks on transgender people – we need our critical faculties now more than ever. Thinking a bit about the various edges of space-time, like black holes and cosmic event horizons, can help us build the better world we need.

Heavy rain across the top of the country could cause flash flooding and make driving difficult, so anyone planning to go out should do so now “before things get worse”, a MetService meteorologist says.

“There’s a possibility of some flash flooding since we are expecting some significant accumulation … something like 70 to 100 millimetres of rain in those areas [and] ... there’s a possibility of some localised downpours which might result in surface flooding, even difficulty in driving in those conditions", meteorologist Samkelo Magwela said.

“The rain will start being more persistent from early afternoon or late morning, but in terms of downpours, it will be just in those localised areas. So it won’t be heavy all the time ... if anybody is planning to go out, I think it’s better to rush now before things get worse.”

Heavy rain warnings have this morning been upgraded to Orange level for much of the top of the country, as a “big swirling mass of rain” descends on the upper North Island.

Auckland, including Great Barrier Island, is under a 17-hour heavy rain warning from 9am today, with up to 100mm forecast and “possibly more in localised downpours”, MetService said.

“Peak rates of 15 to 25 mm/h, but possible 25 to 40 mm/hr in downpours mainly from this evening.”

Those in Coromandel Peninsula, Bay of Plenty and Gisborne/Tairawhiti north of Ruatoria have also been warned to expect heavy rain over a 17-hour period from later this morning until early tomorrow morning.

A heavy rain warning already in place for Northland continues to late tonight, MetService said.

Those areas have been told to expect up to 100mm of rain, possibly more in localised areas, with areas east of Whakatāne likely to be the wettest spots in Bay of Plenty.

A heavy rain watch for Waikato north of Hamilton runs from noon today until early tomorrow morning.

And in the deep south forecast strong winds have prompted MetService to issue a watch for southern areas of Southland and Clutha from 9am tomorrow to noon Monday.

A combination of weather systems is behind the wet weekend.

MetService meteorologist Katie Lyons said “some complex weather” was expected this weekend up north, with the front that caused severe conditions in the South Island this week moving up the country.

“We’ve got a low that’s sitting north of Northland and that’s got a couple of features, a couple of rain bands within it - one of which was the front that we saw move over the South Island [on Thursday] and is making its way on to the lower North Island now.

“The other rain band that is associated with this low is approaching from the north … and these two rain bands actually kind of merge over the North Island and create a big swirling mass of rain over the upper North Island.”

The rain bands are set to move on in the early hours of Sunday, leading to more settled weather for the North Island for the rest of the weekend, Lyons said.

“We’ve got some showers in the lower north on Sunday but, overall, it’s not too bad.”

The weekend brings a welcome reprieve for parts of the South Island that have been battered by days of heavy snow and rain, which has caused flooding, slips and road closures.

“For the most part that wintry blast is really done and I guess we’re looking at more spring-like weather this weekend over the South Island.

“Those in northern Otago up through Canterbury and Marlborough will have a pretty nice weekend overall, albeit a bit windy perhaps.”

Temperatures are set to be slightly warmer than average this weekend, with a few places on the east coast of the North Island cracking the 20s as spring approaches.

It’ll be 21C and partly cloudy in Napier tomorrow, and the rain should clear early in Gisborne, where a high of 20C is forecast.

Freeze, fight or flight: How mental skills coaches help teams like the All Blacks get back in the game

New Zealand Herald August 28, 2026

New Zealand high-performance athletes and team players benefit from mental skills coaching from sports psychologists such as Gilbert Enoka.

The All Blacks might have won the opening Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry test against the Springboks last weekend but mental skills coach Gilbert Enoka will need to make sure the players have their heads in the game for the next three. Jane Phare looks at why mental skills coaching is an essential part of a winning formula, and why it can be used in everyday life.

Watch closely during a Blues game and you just might notice the team’s big lock Cameron Christie doing something a little odd. He knocks his wrists together.

Former All Black Dan Carter used to whack himself on the leg. It’s a technique highly trained sportspeople use to bring themselves back to the moment, focus on the now, not what was. The idea is to forget about what went wrong on the field or court, or board or council meeting, and concentrate on what needs to happen next.

Christie, 22, who also plays for North Harbour, has come up through the ranks since leaving Ōrewa College, playing in age-grade rugby and the New Zealand Under-20s. Throughout that journey, he’s had access to sports psychologists and is now a firm believer in the power of the mind.

He’s picked up “bits of gold”, he says, and added them to his toolbox to cope with pressure and perform better on the field.

Christie’s taken inspiration from role models like Sam Whitelock, Carter and, in particular, English rugby legend Jonny Wilkinson, who worked extensively with a mind coach and a psychiatrist throughout his career to visualise success and handle pressure.

Like Carter, Christie uses a physical reset to bring himself back to the present, to stop thinking about a mistake or a play that went wrong and focus on what to do next.

“So I just tap my wrists together from over the top and then underneath. It just kind of brings you back to where your feet are.”

On Instagram, Carter talks about going into a state of “red head”, an unhelpful mindset when the brain is locked into a mistake that happened minutes ago. Mental skills coaching helps players to focus, get back into a calm “blue” state and get on with the game.

Carter describes three types of reaction in a state of red head – freeze, fight or flight – and how he would react when under pressure as playmaker for the All Blacks.

“I would freeze, I would go quiet. My teammates are looking at me going, ‘well, what’s the move, what’s the call?’ And I was like, ‘man, I’m still thinking about that mistake I made sort of 10 minutes ago’.”

Whereas his teammate Ma’a Nonu would go into a state of fight when things went wrong, Carter says.

“Like he was trying to take out the opponents, he was yelling at the referee, he was yelling at his teammates, he was trying to shoulder charge or physically trying to fight the opposition.”

The third reaction is flight, a state of mind where players “just want to get the hell out of there”.

Players might want to get substituted off or, in a work situation, people might call in sick.

“You just don’t want to be in that moment.”

Recognising that “red head” state early and having the tools to get out of it is the key, Carter says.

“If I made a mistake, I would whack myself on my leg ... recognising that I had made a mistake or recognising that I’d frozen and it’s like, right, now, next task, what do I need to do right now in this moment? And just catch the ball, just communicate to my half, whatever it was, that would get me back into the present and on task in that moment and I’m back in the state of blue.”

Auckland sports psychologist and mental skills coach Iain Saunders, a former police officer, uses a “win-win” model: what’s important now and what’s important next. The idea is not to ruminate on the past, things that can’t be changed, he says.

“It’s making sure that you’re living in the moment.”

Saunders, who has a masters degree in psychology, draws on years of experience with the Armed Offenders Squad and assessing candidates for New Zealand’s elite special tactics group to make sure they are the right fit under pressure. At the same time, he worked part-time as a sports psychologist, leaving the police two years ago to become a fulltime mental skills coach.

He’s worked with the Blues, Auckland Rugby, the Black Ferns and Pulse Netball and also has business and career clients who need help to manage stress and get past setbacks. Saunders says the same techniques apply both in professional sport and in everyday life and business.

Part of his job is to create the right culture, an environment that allows athletes, or people in business, to perform at their best.

Team members need to be connected by a common purpose and understand the team’s direction and values. There needs to be a clear vision about what they, and the team, need to do. And they need to know how to manage relationships, how to lead, how to be a good communicator and how to achieve goals together.

Saunders prefers creating an optimistic environment rather than teaching positive psychology.

“So if you’re in a game of rugby and you’re 20 behind after 10 minutes, there’s nothing positive about that, but you’ve got to be optimistic, right?”

Working with Pulse Netball, he gets the players to work on moving forward.

“It’s like a belief system.”

“The last centre pass in a game of netball has absolutely no bearing on how the next centre pass will go unless you allow it to occupy a part of your brain where you’re thinking about it. And then that makes you slower, it makes you more cluttered in your head.”

Forget the last goal, he’ll tell players.

“We don’t even want you to know what the score is really. It just doesn’t affect how much effort or how much skill you apply to the next centre pass. It’s got nothing to do with it.”

Don’t worry about the things you can’t change; concentrate on the next play, he tells them.

Christie says his mental skills are “a work in progress”, that he still catches himself ruminating over a mistake he’s made which distracts his focus.

“I want to be really instinctive when I’m on the field so I want to have an absence of [that] thought.”

He uses the physical reset method, the wrist tapping, but also uses visualisation and repeats “power phrases” in his head like “I back myself” to counter negative thoughts.

Learning those mental-skills techniques has become increasingly important in team sports, he says.

“It’s massive. I put a huge importance on it.”

So do his teammates.

“In the warm-up you’ll see boys meditating, potentially visualising ... ”

The goal is to quieten down the inner critic, or thoughts that the day’s performance will fall short.

“So then the innate skill you have within you can come out and you can just play freely.”

Christie says he uses the same techniques to get back into the “blue” mode of calmness in his personal life.

“[I can] use those techniques to get back into that state where I can make clear and rational decisions, where you can communicate and lead better.“

Former All Blacks captain Sean Fitzpatrick, currently in South Africa for the Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry tour, says mental skills coaching by specialists wasn’t available in his day.

“So we basically learned through experience how to handle pressure. Whereas now it’s absolutely paramount because it’s the one thing that you can do to make a difference without the opposition knowing what you’re doing, how you prepare.”

The best-prepared team usually win, he says.

“So we used to just drum that into ourselves, ‘We need to prepare, prepare, prepare’, put pressure on each other and that was our mental coaching. We didn’t have a Gilbert Enoka telling us how to prepare. We just learned.”

The same pressures happen off the field in business, careers and family life, he says. Preparation is the key whether it’s to be the best golfer in the world or successful in business.

Fitzpatrick is chairman of the Laureus Sport for Good Foundation, a London-based global charity that raises millions to support sport-based projects for under-privileged youth around the world.

“It teaches you so many values, resilience, dealing with failure, getting on with a team, getting on with people.”

Saunders says back in the Fitzpatrick era and the early rugby sevens tournaments, it was more about surviving the training to create resilient individuals. Rugby clubs had a larger pool of talent from which to choose, because so many youngsters were playing the game back then.

“They could afford that attritional sort of selection of the fittest approach. But we’re probably trying to be a bit more broad than that now and realise there’s a scarcity of good athletes.”

Gilbert Enoka has been incredibly successful helping athletes to perform at a high level by creating an environment in which they can thrive and understanding what individuals need, Saunders says.

“He’s fairly famous for that.”

That builds confidence and trust, enabling people to stay calm in the face of big decisions.

A stress response, getting in the red, makes thinking foggy.

“That’s true of life as it is of sport,” Saunders says.

Getting out of that state and into a calm head space might mean taking some breaths, repeating a phrase or doing a physical movement.

“A common one in sport is just counting things you can see just to get you out of your head and pay attention to the external environment.”

In rugby, he says, stressed players are often told to just move.

“When you start moving, take five steps, it forces your brain to navigate within the game and then you’re back into the environment.”

Jane Phare is a senior journalist based in Auckland. Her roles at the Herald have included assistant editor of NZ Herald, editor of the Weekend Herald, founding editor of Viva, features editor and deputy print editor.

Rotorua cannabis raids: Court documents allege Vietnamese gang money laundering

New Zealand Herald August 28, 2026

One of the sophisticated grow houses busted in Auckland last year that was run by Vietnamese organised criminal gangs.

Dirty money from Vietnamese-run cannabis hothouses is being laundered through construction, beauty and hospitality businesses, court documents relating to Rotorua drug raids say.

Most people arrested as part of a police operation targeting Vietnamese organised crime gangs operating out of Rotorua have now been deported in exchange for their cannabis charges being dropped.

The 10-month national police operation raided homes in Auckland late last week, arresting the man they allege is the “kingpin”.

Court documents were released this week to the Rotorua Daily Post that detail the local growers’ involvement in the syndicate and the exploitation of migrants.

Police raided 14 houses in Rotorua at the end of July and found $6.5 million worth of cannabis growing hydroponically in homes.

Detective Inspector Lindsay Pilbrow said at the time that, in some cases, the homes were “packed to the brim” with cannabis plants.

Fourteen people were charged with cultivating cannabis and other related charges.

Three of those facing cultivating cannabis charges appeared in the Rotorua District Court this week.

Crown solicitor Amanda Gordon told Judge Joanne Wickliffe the charges against the accused, as was the case with many of the others charged, would be dismissed once they were deported.

The summary of facts documents said the syndicates were operating in “an ever-increasing landscape” in New Zealand.

The documents said the Vietnamese syndicates established businesses in industries such as construction, beauty and hospitality to launder their criminal proceeds.

Profits obtained through the supply of cannabis were filtered through legitimate businesses, frequently owned or linked to other Vietnamese gang syndicate members.

The Vietnamese gangs’ linked businesses are used to sponsor visas to bring Vietnamese workers to New Zealand.

The summaries said some of the workers believed they were travelling to New Zealand for legitimate employment and entered into significant debt to do so, leaving them vulnerable to exploitation.

The summaries said the Vietnamese gangs operated the same way around the world – buying leases in residential areas and using the houses for the sole purpose of cultivating cannabis.

They have been known to pay above-market rents to secure tenancy agreements and use fake or stolen passports for identification purposes, the summaries said.

The Vietnamese gangs use a hierarchical system where those at the top of the operations typically isolate themselves from criminal activity and are therefore difficult to identify, the police summaries said.

Low-level syndicate members, including the 14 arrested in Rotorua, were responsible for running the cannabis grow houses and day-to-day care of crops, the documents stated.

The summaries said these “crop sitters” or “gardeners” tend to be caught by authorities.

Their jobs include maintaining the crops at one or more cannabis grow houses. They don’t necessarily live at the houses but might stay overnight occasionally.

The summaries said crop sitters or gardeners were often illegally in New Zealand, and some had been “trafficked” for the sole purpose of working for the Vietnamese gangs.

The Rotorua Organised Crime Unit ran Operation Harvey between October last year and July.

It targeted local Vietnamese gang members by analysing their cellphones and financial records, and in some cases people were under surveillance or had their vehicles tracked by police.

The operation ended with raids at the properties on July 28.

In one of the cases before the courts this week, the man was a Vietnamese national in New Zealand on an expired visa.

The summary of his case said the man lived at a house on Miller St. While the house wasn’t being used to cultivate cannabis, this property and another on Ruihi St were used as “safe houses”, where members of the syndicate would meet.

The man was under police surveillance and was seen at Bunnings Rotorua buying equipment used for cultivating cannabis, the summary said.

It said that when police raided his home, the equipment and other items, including shades, lamps, transformers, cables and socket boards, were found in a shed.

In a bedroom, officers found 40lbs (18.1kg) of cannabis head material packaged in 1lb vacuum-sealed bags, it said.

According to the Massey University New Zealand Drug Trends Survey, a pound (448g) of illegal cannabis in New Zealand this year was priced at just over $2500, meaning the cannabis found at this man’s house would have been valued at more than $100,000.

In another case in court this week, a charged man had sought refugee status.

Throughout the operation, detectives had watched him come and go at an Otonga Rd property, the summary said.

When police raided the house, they found a sophisticated cannabis cultivation set-up and 174 plants, the summary said.

Police also raided the Ruihi St “safe house” and found several syndicate members there.

Police found five large bags of good-quality cannabis heads. The combined weight was 13kg, or 30lbs (about $75,000 worth of cannabis according to the drug trends survey).

A woman, described in court documents as the wife of the man who lived at Miller St, has also been deported. She was charged with possession of cannabis for supply after being found at the house when police raided it on July 28.

The summary said she told police she “doesn’t go into that room” and didn’t know anything about the cannabis.

The summary said electricity at the Otonga Rd property had been stolen from the mains supply by bypassing the electricity meter. This resulted in unmetered power being supplied to the property.

The summary said the unlawful diversion of electricity presented an “inherent and substantial risk of fire, electrocution and damage to the property”.

Operation Blackout, led by the National Organised Crime Group, raided 19 properties in Auckland – including Flat Bush, Howick, Sylvia Park, Wiri and Massey – at the end of last week and arrested 12 people.

Police said in a statement this week that Immigration New Zealand and New Zealand Customs supported them.

Police said the operation had provided “unprecedented insight” into the sophisticated criminal operation based out of Auckland suburbs.

Detective Senior Sergeant John Brunton said the investigation went beyond suburban cannabis grow house operations.

Brunton said a 36-year-old Flat Bush man, who police allege is the kingpin of the operation, faces six charges.

During search warrants in Auckland, police seized about $1.25 million worth of cannabis and $80,000 in cash.

Several large bags of MDMA pills were also seized.

So far, the nationwide 10-month operation had seized more than five tonnes of cannabis at more than 50 rental properties.

The statement said 11 Vietnamese nationals, acting as crop-sitters, had been deported. Five others remain in New Zealand, pending prosecution.

Kelly Makiha is a senior journalist who has reported for the Rotorua Daily Post for more than 25 years, covering mainly police, court, human interest and social issues.
