Why New Zealand’s shameful legacy of shoddy and leaky building is not over yet

New Zealand Herald August 28, 2026

Back in the ’80s and ’90s, it was dubbed the leaky homes crisis. Decades later, experts predict another wave of multibillion-dollar heartbreak is coming, leaving behind a trail of misery and financial ruin. Jane Phare investigates why substandard homes and apartments are still being built, who is to blame, what needs to change and what home buyers should watch for.

Nearly 20 years ago, as a journalist with the Herald on Sunday, I interviewed Aucklander John Gray about leaky homes. Back then, he was an Air New Zealand pilot who, during his time off, advocated for the distressed owners of properties from which there was no way out.

Their homes – built between the late 1980s and the early 2000s – were rotting from the inside out. And there was no cavalry coming to fix the problem. One apartment owner had already taken his own life; others were on suicide watch.

Roll forward to 2026, and Gray is still a pilot, still advocating for home owners trapped in a nightmare of rot and decay, and I’m still a journalist writing about the same subject.

“It’s neverending,” he says. “It’s very sad, really.”

What’s worrying is that now he’s dealing with the distressed owners of new homes, multiplexes and apartments, some of the properties barely five or 10 years old.

Back in 2006, Gray and colleague Roger Levie co-founded the Home Owners and Buyers Association (Hobanz), never dreaming they’d still be battling the same issues two decades later.

Both had first-hand experience of owning leaky apartments and dealing with body corporates and owners who either couldn’t agree on what to do or couldn’t afford to fix the problem.

Since then, the pair have advocated for thousands of distressed property owners, lobbied successive governments, talked endlessly with council officials, done media interviews and made a documentary series called A Living Hell: Apartment Disasters. But little has changed.

Ticking time bombs are everywhere; the number of defective apartment blocks and multiplex units in New Zealand is too numerous to list. The quotes to fix them reach eye-watering levels.

Now Gray is dealing with appalling examples of new builds that he knows, at a glance, will fuel a shameful legacy of defective construction that will leave thousands of homeowners in despair in the future.

At times he’s overwhelmed by the number of emails in his inbox, mostly pleas for help from desperate home owners. He’s still dealing with the “long tail” of rot from the era of monolithic cladding and untreated timber framing, decay that took longer to show up in some parts of the country.

Banks won’t lend on properties with weathertight issues.

But now there is a new wave of problems showing up in some, not all, modern-day construction. Quite simply, Gray says, they are defective and they will leak.

“In a lot of these cases we see, it’s not a whoopsy, it’s not a mistake, it’s a wilful decision to build something with timber where there should be steel. Or ‘let’s remove a supporting pillar in the carpark because we can get more cars in’.”

Settlements, if owners can corner those responsible, are usually cloaked in confidentiality clauses so reputations go untarnished.

“And so there are no consequences for them and they go out and do it again.”

Gray warns buyers to look beyond the oak floors and designer kitchens. Instead, pay attention to the outside, he says. Even better, pay for a pre-purchase property inspection report from a qualified surveyor.

And therein lies one of the problems. A professional report is likely to cost $1500 to $2000, and if home buyers miss out on several properties at auction, the cost of those reports adds up.

The risk is that buyers will skip the report, or get a cut-price version from an “expert” who lacks qualifications and experience.

“For the most part, the vast majority of pre-purchase inspectors are not competent and are uninsured and are ripping people off.”

Dr Dirk Stahlhut, director of property and building consultancy Prendos New Zealand, agrees. He says even though he and his colleagues have had years of training to become chartered and registered building surveyors, anyone can call themselves a building surveyor or inspector. There’s no requirement for a licence or formal qualification.

The Herald asked the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) if the Government had plans to license pre-purchase inspections. The answer was no. In a statement, the ministry said it was aware of complaints but it regarded pre-purchase inspections as private arrangements between consumers and service providers.

Gray says the “cowboys” in the industry are hard to catch. He knows of one Auckland inspector who has no assets to his name, no indemnity insurance, doesn’t turn up to mediation meetings, doesn’t comply with disclosure requirements and “gives the middle finger to the law courts”.

He uses an example of a disastrous leaky house sale in an affluent area of the eastern suburbs which resulted in two sets of victims: the couple who were forced to take legal action and the elderly original owner who had to sell her property to pay for the mediated settlement.

The couple bought the property based on a report done by an unqualified building inspector, who escaped having to share in the reparation.

“Lots of photos and not much substance,” Gray says of his report. In reality, the house wasn’t fit for sale.

“It was rotten. I could put my finger through it.”

The Herald was contacted earlier this year by a man distressed about defects in his new home which was built by a reputable home building company north of Auckland.

The home is part of a new subdivision with several houses built by the same company. It received a Code Compliance Certificate (CCC) from Auckland Council and yet still has a list of issues needing to be fixed, including a non-consented culvert giving access to the owner’s garage.

The Herald has viewed a property inspection report commissioned by the home owner that lists defects including non-compliant waterproofing issues, gaps between weatherboards and window frames, missing structural components, poor workmanship and water pooling in the spouting.

The Herald has chosen not to name the man, aged 33, or the company involved. He says the building company has sent builders to his home several times to try to rectify the problems.

“But why not do it right the first time?” he wants to know.

Stahlhut, too, says Prendos is seeing problems with properties built by home-building companies from Invercargill to north of Auckland.

Gray’s not surprised. This year he agreed to take a first look at a new terrace house in Te Atatū before the young woman buyer got a pre-purchase inspection.

At first glance, he knew what he was looking at.

“It was a leaker from 20 metres away.”

Inside, the home was beautifully presented, but outside, the metal cladding was buckled with gaps between joins. Gray sent photos to Auckland Council after learning that an inspector had passed the property’s CCC.

The estate agent had assured the woman that the property had a 10-year warranty (under the Building Act 2004). But home owners still need to be able to fund civil legal action, Gray says, and they need to be able to pin down the developer and builder.

Building companies can strip a company of assets, “put it on a shelf” and start a different company to get around the “Phoenix rule”. Or they put assets in one company and another company, without assets, “hires” from the first company.

“People are getting legal advice on this, which just really sickens me.”

Gray is the first to admit there’s no easy fix. Chris Penk – now stripped of his Building and Construction portfolio and replaced by Simon Watts – had a go. He introduced the Building Amendment Bill last month, wanting a fairer liability system to ensure those responsible for botched or shoddy work paid their fair share of compensation.

Currently, under the joint and several liability model, local councils often end up as “the last man standing” and ratepayers are left footing the bill for millions of dollars in reparation.

The new bill would introduce a proportionate liability model so that those responsible for mistakes or poor work will be forced to share in the cost. The bill also requires:

Gray says the bill doesn’t go far enough. For a start, a fine of $20,000 is not nearly enough, not when some of the botched developments are costing owners millions of dollars to put right.

And he has doubts about the one-year and 10-year defect periods. Many of the cases he’s dealing with now relate to properties that are older than 10 years.

There’s little doubt that to date the reparation burden has fallen largely on local authorities. Before amalgamation, Auckland City Council paid $333.1 million between 2000 and 2009.

Between 2011 and 2025, Auckland Council paid out a staggering $735.4m. The largest amount was $125m paid in 2019. Not included are millions of dollars in legal fees, and staff time, a cost likely to put the amount well over $1 billion.

And the problem’s not going away any time soon. Poor standards show up in the council’s building inspection figures for the past 12 months. Just over 37% of residential buildings failed their final inspections and 36.4% of commercial final inspections failed.

It’s a crisis that has collectively cost the country billions of dollars, including the repair of leaky schools, hospital buildings and retirement villages.

Eastcliffe Retirement Village in Ōrākei is a case in point. Built in the early 2000s, the structure was plagued with weathertight issues from the start. Residents gradually had to move out and now the whole development will be knocked down and replaced with a $700m complex.

Apart from the distress to the residents, Gray says, think of the waste: resources, labour and the amount of demolished material going into landfill. New Zealand should be building sound new houses, not constantly repairing or demolishing defective ones.

He’s aware of an upmarket apartment complex near Auckland’s downtown waterfront that’s less than five years old and already showing defects. Owners will be faced with millions of dollars in maintenance costs within the next few years.

Both Gray and Levie are convinced the industry needs far tighter regulation. Rather than “tinker around the edges” of the Building Act, Gray says, the Government should consider adopting a ready-made piece of legislation devised by global think tank the International Centre for Building Quality, spearheaded by New Zealand barrister Kim Lovegrove, that promotes best practices in building codes, construction laws and regulations. And it includes hefty penalties for both civil and criminal charges.

Otherwise, New Zealand home owners will continue to be plagued by issues that will ruin their lives. Gray points to one of the country’s worst leaky building disasters, the St Lukes Garden Apartments in Auckland, built between 15 and 23 years ago, and now facing a staggering repair bill of more than $240m divided between 243 owners.

Ratepayers in Wellington, Christchurch, Tauranga and the Queenstown-Lakes District have also been saddled with millions of dollars in compensation for defective buildings and homes.

So why is the problem not going away? Gray says take your pick: not enough regulation and licensing in the industry; not high enough penalties to force “cowboys” out of the mix; incompetent and unqualified pre-purchase building inspectors; buildings constructed to minimum standards; shortcuts taken to meet cut-price contracts; not enough qualified, and preferably independent, oversight on big projects.

MBIE sent a lengthy statement to the Herald, pointing out changes in the proposed Building Amendment Bill, which is not expected to become law until 2028. Home warranty providers will be required to report the number of claims received and the types of defects to MBIE which will provide valuable information about standards in the industry, the statement said.

Although MBIE does not record the number of defective residential units built in the past decade, “concerns about building quality and accountability are among the factors informing ongoing building system reforms”, it said.

The ministry did not directly answer a question from the Herald as to whether it considered the Building Act 2004 and the New Zealand Building Code provided adequate protection for the homeowner against defective builds. It said “ ... no regulatory system can completely prevent defective building work from occurring”.

MBIE says it is also exploring further improvements across building and construction trades and professions, including whether supervision, competency and accountability settings are appropriate to support high-quality building work.

“These reforms will also make it harder for poor performers and ‘cowboy’ operators to remain in the market.”

Insurers and home warranty providers would assess risk before providing cover, meaning builders and developers with poor track records would likely face greater scrutiny, higher costs, or difficulty obtaining coverage.

Levie, who is Hobanz’s CEO (Gray is voluntary), spends much of his time working with the body corporates and owners of defective apartment blocks. He sees first-hand the intolerable toll that rotting and leaky apartments have on owners who have no money to fight or fix, and still have mortgages and body-corporate levies to pay.

Because of high building costs, architects are designing to a minimum standard, not a robust standard, he says. The required long-term maintenance plans aren’t submitted by developers at the time of completion because that would put body corporate fees up.

“They are trying to sell units and keep fees down.”

The result is poorly designed buildings with no consideration of maintenance.

“Very new buildings are failing all over the place.”

As one professional building manager says about owning an apartment in a defective building, “You’re one email away from financial disaster.”

Levie has witnessed some appalling behaviour by body corporate committee members that includes trying to push responsibility for leaky decks back on individual owners; hiding documents about the issues because they don’t want the building to get a bad reputation; and whoever finds out first selling up before the problems become common knowledge.

Stahlhut says in a tight economy, many jobs are won by the lowest bid. That means corners are cut to meet the budget and the hired manpower may not be adequately trained or experienced. In some cases, it comes down to what a builder can get away with.

His team sees it all: cavities not installed properly, blocked drainage paths, missing or inadequate flashings, basic mistakes that will trap moisture.

“Rather than actually doing it right first time and maybe even targeting excellence.”

New builds are still being signed off with CCC that he knows will cause issues in the future. He’d like to see that change with an increased emphasis on good training and education to improve the industry.

Although the industry is no longer using untreated framing timber, treated timber only buys people a little more time. Eventually, he says, that too will rot.

“It’s just a repeat history, really, of the leaky building crisis.”

Jane Phare is a senior journalist based in Auckland. Her roles at the Herald have included assistant editor of NZ Herald, editor of the Weekend Herald, founding editor of Viva, features editor and deputy print editor.

Wairarapa whānau, Rotorua farmers among 2026 Freshwater Champions

New Zealand Herald August 28, 2026

The Lake Rotorua Farming Community was named the Established Catchment Champion for its long-term contribution to improving water quality in the Lake Rotorua catchment.

Five individuals and groups from around New Zealand have been named the 2026 Freshwater Champions in recognition of their efforts to improve the health of rivers, lakes, wetlands and estuaries.

The winners were announced at the Freshwater Champions Forum in Nelson on Friday.

The awards are run by the Cawthron Institute with support from NZ Landcare Trust.

More than 60 nominations were received from across Aotearoa New Zealand, with nominees including individuals, whānau, iwi, landowners and community groups to improve the health of freshwater ecosystems.

The 2026 Freshwater Champions are:

The Riddiford Whānau received the Individual/Family Actions Award for their work through the Ruamāhanga Farm Foundation in South Wairarapa.

Founded in 2021, the foundation is restoring an eight-hectare wetland and riparian forest system through native planting, freshwater monitoring and community involvement.

The Mana Moana Three Lakes collaboration received the Te Ao Māori Award for bringing together the Whakakī Lake Trust, Wairewa Rūnaka, and Lake Ōmāpere Trust to restore and protect the mauri of their culturally significant lakes.

The project is developing freshwater management solutions across three regions, grounded in both mātauranga Māori and environmental science.

The Engagement Award was presented to Sam Ludden for his contribution to freshwater restoration, environmental education and cultural leadership across Wairarapa.

Ludden uses art, storytelling, ceramics, and restoration activities to connect people with freshwater issues, while mentoring others and advocating for iwi perspectives.

The Arapārera Community Catchment Society received the Early Impact Award for its community-led response to the 2023 floods and Cyclone Gabrielle.

Working across an 8800ha catchment that flows into the Kaipara Harbour, the society has planted more than 3000 native trees, undertaken fish and eDNA monitoring, completed freshwater mussel surveys, and installed water quality monitoring equipment.

The Lake Rotorua Farming Community, represented by the Lake Rotorua Primary Producers Collective and Te Arawa Arataua, was named the Established Catchment Champion for its long-term contribution to improving water quality in the Lake Rotorua catchment.

Since 2005, the community has worked alongside iwi, scientists, councils and community groups to reduce nutrient losses and improve land management practices to improve the water quality of Lake Rotorua.

Achievements include more than 6600 hectares of lower nutrient-leaching land use through the Lake Rotorua Incentives Scheme, retirement of vulnerable land from grazing, wetland restoration, waterway fencing, native planting and full compliance with catchment nutrient management rules.

Monitoring shows the catchment is now operating below the 2027 nitrogen reduction target set in the Bay of Plenty Regional Natural Resources Plan.

Freshwater Champions assessors commended the community’s collective approach, which has shifted relationships from conflict to collaboration, supported science-based decision-making, and delivered measurable environmental improvement.

The farming community’s commitment to collaboration and long-term environmental stewardship has been central to reducing nutrient losses and supporting the lake’s restoration.

The Lake Rotorua Farming Community are represented by the Lake Rotorua Primary Producers Collective and Te Arawa Arataua.

A Special Recognition Award in Māori Engagement was presented to Dr Te Kīpa Kēpa Brian Morgan.

Through the development of the pioneering Mauri Model and mauri0meter, he has created practical tools that help iwi, councils and communities assess freshwater health in ways that reflect both cultural and environmental values.

Lead assessor and Cawthron Institute Group Manager of Freshwater Ecosystems, Dr Roger Young, said the quality and diversity of nominations reflect the growing commitment to freshwater restoration across the country.

“Communities are facing increasing pressure on freshwater resources, and these champions demonstrate the impact that local action can have,” he said.

“Their work shows how people can come together to improve freshwater outcomes in ways that are both practical and enduring.”

Its ambition is to advance the sustainable use of marine and freshwater resources and deliver lasting benefits for the environment, the economy and communities.

Black Caps wife’s cancer treatment complete: ‘Sarah is officially done with leukaemia’

New Zealand Herald August 28, 2026

Sarah and Blair Tickner at the 13th Stag on Thursday. Photo / Doug Laing

After two years and five months fighting cancer, Sarah Tickner has finished her leukaemia treatment.

Now Tickner, a Hastings cafe owner and wife of Black Cap Blair Tickner, is ready for her next battle – helping others facing a similar fight.

“I encourage anyone to reach out if they need advice,” she said on Thursday, at the Mitre 10 Sport’s Park’s 13th Stag cafe she runs with Blair.

“There is value in the cancer community, and it’s all added value to my community,” she said.

On Thursday, the Tickners decided to thank friends and family who have supported her by giving away her version of Italian coffee and cocoa dessert tiramisu at the cafe.

“Sarah is officially done with leukaemia,” said the general invitation on the cafe’s social media page. “Bugger off, cancer.”

Tickner said she still has a job protecting herself against any relapse of the leukaemia.

It was first diagnosed in 2024, after arriving with 8-month-old daughter Florence in England for her husband’s county cricket season.

She underwent eight months of chemotherapy, and was home for Christmas.

By August last year she had been in remission for about 12 months.

Her latest blood tests have established she’s in the clear.

A gym bunny, she can start ticking off some more goals, with Hyrox fitness racing in November, comprising eight 1km runs with functional exercise stops at fitness stations along the way.

But rule out a marathon.

“I don’t like long runs,” she said.

“I am pretty lucky - I had a pretty good diagnosis from the get-go,” she said.

She emphasises a big part of the fight has been attitude, research and eating the right nutrients.

Still requiring occasional checks – more monthly than daily, she said: “Food is medicine”.

Besides, she wants to be a strong mum.

Her husband Blair said he was stunned by the number of people facing the plight, and is now well aware of the battles they’ve all faced.

“Sarah’s been very diligent,” he said, as another customer appeared with well wishes at the cafe. “There have been hard days, but she’s always been positive.”

Doug Laing is a Hawke’s Bay Today reporter, based in Napier. He has had more than four decades covering news events and issues in Hawke’s Bay.

Japan-bound Magpies and Hurricanes star loosie Devan Flanders opens up on his ‘why’

New Zealand Herald August 28, 2026

Devan Flanders was in white-hot form before signing a three-year deal with Japan’s Urayasu D-Rocks – a move that potentially cost him an All Blacks call-up. The 27-year-old Hurricanes and Magpies barnstorming loosie talks to Hawke’s Bay Today deputy editor Mark Story about his “why”.

Given your stellar season for the Hurricanes, a new All Blacks coach and pending world cup, the timing of your move surprised many fans.

This decision was extremely hard, and we went back and forwards over it many times. I suppose the final part of that is knowing that we only have a short period of our lives playing rugby. All it takes is one injury, and our career can be over. I feel as if I have been playing very similarly over the past few years and have given the All Blacks a big enough crack. But it is also a business, and when the time was right for my fiancée and me, we made the decision to head offshore.

As a local player, your native Hawke’s Bay Magpies and Hurricanes provenance has been a big part of your “why”. What do you tap into in Japan, given you can no longer draw from this well?

These two clubs have been a huge part of my life and have contributed a lot to the person I am today. They’ll always hold a strong place in my heart, and I’ll continue to follow and support them. Although, my ‘why’ has always been my family and future family. So, moving to Japan, I’ll take that same mindset with me. D-Rocks will also become my family, so I’ll be doing everything I can to have a positive influence on the team.

If you and your fiancée Mariah decide to stay long enough in Japan, and the stars align, can you see yourself in the Brave Blossoms’ national jersey?

Yeah, playing for Japan is definitely on the cards if I’m still performing at a high level in five years.

What’s your most savoured memory in a Magpies jersey?

It has to be when we won the Ranfurly Shield back off Wellington in 2023. The way the shield became such a big part of our team, and having that date saved on our calendar all year, then winning it back, is definitely up there.

Devan Flanders time-travels back and visits his 10-year-old self. What piece of advice would he give?

To believe in myself. That all your wildest dreams can be achieved but you’re the only person who can do that. There’ll be a lot of outside noise telling you to do this and that, but as long as you focus on yourself you’ll get to where you want to be.

The last Google search before Stewart Pledger-Davies died: ‘He wanted help’

New Zealand Herald August 28, 2026

Sister Kayley Newton (left) and mother Joanna Newton hold a photo of Stewart Pledger-Davies, who died in January. Photo / Rafaella Melo

The last Google search a Napier man made before he died in January was “rehab centres near me”.

While his cause of death is yet to be determined by the coroner, his family believe it was accidental.

Stewart Pledger-Davies was later found near his mother Joanna Newton’s home before dying that Sunday morning.

His grieving family allege shortcomings including addiction treatment and care, and emergency services responses.

The 32-year-old’s family is inviting the community to a fish and chip gathering on the beach outside the Surf Club on Marine Parade to commemorate his death with the wider community at 2pm on Sunday.

Sister Kayley Newton, who was close to her brother, is organising the event.

She said she wanted to bring together people affected and remind them they were not alone.

Kayley hoped the event would challenge addiction stigma.

“They are someone’s family member,” she said.

“My brother was my idol.”

Months after his death this year, she said his absence still did not feel real.

“I’m still waiting to see him come out of his room, but he’s just not there anymore.”

The case is before the coroner, and his cause of death has not yet been determined.

His family say there were failures across addiction treatment, mental health care, Corrections and the emergency response on the night he died.

They believe he might still be alive today had those failures not occurred.

In early January, Pledger-Davies knocked on Joanna’s door, struggling with a years-long methamphetamine addiction and saying he wanted help.

Joanna agreed he could stay, on the condition he engaged with rehabilitation.

She told Hawke’s Bay Today she called addiction services repeatedly and sought help.

At some stage, Pledger-Davies searched for where to find a rehabilitation centre.

On Friday, January 23, Joanna said she was still desperately trying to secure a place for her son in residential rehabilitation.

Two days later, on January 25, he was dead.

“He wanted help,” Kayley said.

“Unfortunately, that night became his last night.”

Pledger-Davies had struggled with methamphetamine for years and had several convictions that resulted in periods under Corrections supervision.

Joanna Newton said meth was increasingly affecting her son’s mental health by late last year.

However, Joanna said she was told there was “no room” for him to get care under the Hawke’s Bay public health system.

“The moments of wanting support are so rare, the window is so small,” she said.

“If there was somewhere I could have taken him when he said, ‘I need help,’ ... we wouldn’t be in this situation.”

Pledger-Davies was under Corrections supervision and Joanna said drug and alcohol counselling and treatment had been expected as part of his rehabilitation.

“It just never happened. No one pushed him to do it.”

A Corrections spokesperson said that from December 2025, Pledger-Davies was subject to Intensive Supervision with special conditions, and had previously been subject to multiple community-based sentences.

They said Corrections was limited in the information it could provide as Pledger-Davies’ death was before the coroner.

Director of communities, partnerships and pathways Glenn Morrison said alcohol or drug services required the person’s consent, motivation and ongoing commitment.

“If the Coroner finds there were any shortcomings by Corrections, we will absolutely address these and act on any recommendations if appropriate.”

David Warrington, Health New Zealand Hawke’s Bay group director of operations, said the organisation could not comment on Pledger-Davies’ care while his death was before the coroner, but was open to meeting with his family about their concerns.

He recognised people with addiction often needed rapid access to support when motivated to seek help.

He said the region “consistently meets the national target” for timely access to specialist mental health and addiction services.

Joanna was home at her Milton Rd house on the Friday night, unaware her son was in distress at a property on the same street.

She claimed a resident found Pledger-Davies shortly before midnight and called 111, but police did not arrive for nearly two hours.

Officers asked for an ambulance, but one was not immediately available, so they put him in a police vehicle and went to the hospital, she said.

Joanna claimed she was told he stopped breathing on the way, and police stopped to perform CPR, temporarily restoring a heartbeat.

She said she was uncertain what happened from this point, but was told of her son’s death about 5am that morning.

Hato Hone St John also cited the coronial inquiry as a reason it was inappropriate to comment.

Acting Hawke’s Bay police area commander Inspector Andy Sloan said a complaint Joanna lodged about the police response was being assessed.

Taumarunui mother Lisa Gailey faces breast cancer as daughter fights brain tumour

New Zealand Herald August 28, 2026

Lisa Gailey (left) with her 17-year-old daughter, Tayler Gailey. Photo / Givealittle

A Kiwi mother who has spent more than 15 years supporting her daughter through a lifelong health battle is now facing a fight of her own.

Lisa Gailey, 40, found out she had stage 3 HER2-positive breast cancer via her Manage My Health app as she rode the bus home to Taumarunui last month.

She had just spent five weeks at Auckland’s Starship Children’s Hospital caring for her 17-year-old daughter, Tayler, who was fighting a tumour in her brainstem.

The mother of four told the Herald managing two cancer journeys at once had become “absolutely nightmarish”.

“Sometimes my phone rings 10 times a day and that’s all I do,” she said.

“I now have to ask them, ‘Which cancer are you calling about?’”

Gailey also said she felt a strong sense of guilt knowing her own prognosis was far better than Tayler’s.

“It’s just the lesser of the two evils,” she said.

“I feel quite guilty that there’s treatment for me and not for Tay.”

While her own cancer was “fast-growing”, Gailey said doctors expected it to respond well to treatment.

But she said the timing of her diagnosis left her feeling as though precious time with Tayler was being taken away.

“I don’t really feel anything other than annoyed at the inconvenience and the timing, like, what kind of timing is that?” she said.

“It makes me feel like I’m being robbed of time, whatever time Tay has left.”

Tayler had already defied the odds after being diagnosed with a terminal brain tumour as a toddler and given just nine months to live.

After 15 years of stable cancer, another tumour was discovered deep within her brainstem in February.

Gailey told the Herald in June that Tayler had lived with “a lot of radiation injury”, including mobility and cognitive difficulties, speech impediments, multiple surgeries, and a hip replacement.

She has since undergone radiation and suffered a series of complications, including pneumonia, a collapsed lung and blood clots in her lungs.

Tayler is now home but requires significant assistance, including a wheelchair and hoist.

Gailey said Tayler was worried about what her mother’s cancer treatment would mean for her.

“I thought she might feel not so alone in her own situation ... but she’s worried, I think.

“She’s said things like, ‘But you know that I need you all the time when I’m like this’.

“I think her fear is more not being with me ... having to leave her for a day or two to go and have treatment.”

Gailey’s treatment plan involves four months of chemotherapy, followed by surgery and radiation, then another six months of chemotherapy.

“Tayler’s lost so much and I know she’s frustrated, she’s sad.

“It takes a lot to actually get her to smile, which is devastating because she always had this big smile on her face.”

Despite everything the family is facing, Gailey said their home was not defined by sadness.

“The story sounds really, really sad, and it is, but, on a day-to-day basis, Tayler’s still got all her faculties, she still is hilarious.

“Everything we do, we cope by humour.”

Funds raised through the family’s Givealittle page will help support both Lisa and Tayler through treatment, including travel, accommodation, fuel, meals and lost income.

Your ultimate guide to Opportunity Party – as Qiulae Wong eyes potential balance-of-power role

New Zealand Herald August 28, 2026

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong has had a meteoric rise. Photo / Mark Mitchell

The Opportunity Party has reinvented itself so successfully over the past year it could decide which party holds power in 10 weeks. Audrey Young and Chris Knox explore the people and policies behind the party – and provide a tax calculator showing what its land tax could mean for you.

Since becoming a political leader last November, Qiulae Wong has taken the Opportunity Party from virtually nowhere to “kingmaker” for a National-led or Labour-led Government.

Not that she likes that term, or suggests the party might hold the balance of power, despite polls showing it could do so in what is looking like a close election on November 7.

She likes to think of the party as a potential “circuit-breaker”.

Wong indicates Opportunity would seek influence over different areas, depending on the party it was negotiating with and that party’s perceived weaknesses.

“If it is National, we’re going to want to have more influence over some of the environmental policies, for example,” she tells the Weekend Herald.

And if it were Labour?

“I think the other part ... that we’re very strong on is our things like competition and innovation. So commerce, consumer affairs, energy is really important to us as well,” she says.

“In a Labour-Greens Government, the role that we play there is really making sure that the solutions that are being put on the table work for business and are going to drive good, strong, economic outcomes for New Zealand. So we might want to have more of an influence there.”

Notwithstanding that National has ruled out working with Opportunity and Labour has not, she is adamant that the Opportunity Party does not have a preference.

“We’re neutral and happy to go either way.”

She says it would negotiate in good faith to the end with whichever party got the largest vote.

There would be no parallel negotiations of the type New Zealand First conducted with National and Labour in 1996 and 2017.

“We would take it as far as we can and give them the opportunity to meet our bottom lines and come to an agreement that we’re happy with,” she says.

“But if it feels like ... we can’t get there or it’s not achievable, that’s when we would go to the second-largest party.”

Opportunity plans to set out its non-negotiable bottom lines closer to the election but has already set one: it would not be part of a Government in which Winston Peters was Foreign Minister.

It made its decision after Peters’ comment in Parliament to Chinese-born Green MP Lawrence Xu-Nan, telling him to go back to where he came from.

“We felt that those remarks were racist, and it’s not tenable to have a Foreign Minister that makes comments like that and the fact that it’s not been the first time that he’s made those kinds of comments. We can’t support a Government with him in that role.”

But other than that proviso so far, the party would genuinely try to find common ground with any party, including New Zealand First.

“It’s no secret that New Zealand First has probably the least in common with how we view the world and what we’re trying to achieve, but in saying that, there are a few things that they talk about around supermarket competition and energy market competition where we also feel very passionately.

“So there are potentially areas that we could work with them on.”

Wong’s discussion about its approach to Government is not idle speculation. A fourth consecutive major poll this week, RNZ-Reid Research, put Opportunity over the 5% threshold for gaining seats in Parliament and holding the balance of power with six MPs if the poll were translated to an election result.

Pollsters Talbot Mills have tracked where the party’s supporters are coming from in terms of how they voted at the last election and, while they are necessarily numerically small, about a third come from the left and about a third from the right. A quarter supported the party last election.

It has been a meteoric rise for Wong and Opportunity.

When the party advertised for a leader a year ago, it looked like a publicity stunt for a party that had failed under three leaders, founder Gareth Morgan, Geoff Simmons and Raf Manji, in three successive elections at 2.4%, 1.5% and 2.2% respectively.

Wong was not a party member, although she was on its mailing list and saw the ad that way. She was working for consulting firm KPMG advising on sustainable business.

Wong lived in Britain for nine years and returned to New Zealand in 2022 with her husband, Grant, an IT and cybersecurity specialist. He was originally from Palmerston North, but they met through friends at a Jack Garratt concert at the Hammersmith Apollo.

She says she voted Opportunity in 2023. She has previously voted Labour, National, Māori Party and Greens, and joined the Greens for a year after returning.

She decided the Green brand of activism wasn’t for her and favoured what she calls a more pragmatic approach to make gains on environmental issues.

She dislikes “tribal politics” and the view that no good ideas can come from the other side “and painting them as the enemy”.

“We should be trying to embrace the fact that we all have different perspectives, and there can be valuable ideas to come from right across the political spectrum,” she says.

“If we keep shutting people down just because they come from a different ideology, I think that divide just gets bigger and bigger, and it’s harder and harder to drive long-term solutions.”

Wong made Opportunity’s shortlist of four candidates who were put through selection interviews, mock media interviews, and town hall meetings with party members.

The selection panel recommended her appointment to the board, and she was announced in November.

Former Labour Cabinet minister Iain Lees-Galloway, who was sacked by Jacinda Ardern in 2020 for a relationship with a staffer in one of his agencies, was part of the selection team.

He has been the Opportunity Party general manager since January, having joined in 2024.

Daniel Eb is also part of the core group reinventing the party. He also applied for the leader’s role and was offered the deputy leader role. He is the son of communications guru Deborah Pead and set up his own communications company with a rural bent. Until recently, he was the party’s lead communications and press officer but has handed that role to Lees-Galloway as he steps up campaigning.

He is standing in Kaipara Ki Mahurangi, the electorate held by former Cabinet minister Chris Penk, who was sacked for disloyalty to Prime Minister Christopher Luxon this month.

The party’s most controversial policy is its radical tax policy, which includes a universal citizens’ income of $19,400 annually and a 1.75% land tax that would lower land values.

It would advantage low – and middle-income earners but disadvantage many pensioners, farmers, landlords, and Kiwis returning from abroad – see below for details and a calculator showing whether you would be worse or better off.

It is a variation on a policy originally proposed in 2016 by founder Gareth Morgan, who proposed taxing all productive assets, including the family home, at a deemed minimum rate of return.

Another controversial part of Opportunity’s proposals is an estimated $1.7 billion in public service efficiency savings, on top of those already planned by the Government, which has been slammed by the Public Service Association.

But it is debatable whether the policies are attracting the support or whether Wong is a fresh face in the political marketplace.

Qiulae Wong and her husband have two daughters aged 5 and 2 and live in Mt Albert, the electorate she is standing in, which is held by Labour’s Helen White with a majority of 18 votes.

Wong was born in Fiji and raised in Epsom and One Tree Hill, attending Epsom Normal Primary School and Diocesan School for Girls from Year 4. She is the youngest of three.

She has a law degree and BA from the University of Auckland but wasn’t a political activist there.

She says she did not have a political upbringing. But it is woven into her life story. Her grandparents fled China after the Japanese occupation in World War II and before the communists took charge in 1949. They ended up in Fiji, where her grandfather set up a bottling business and became Mayor of Lautoka.

Her parents, who met at university, had been in Fiji to help with the business and she was born there in 1988. But given the instability around the military coups, they returned to New Zealand, where they eventually split up.

“I feel like I had a very fortunate childhood and upbringing,” says Wong. “Very multicultural and diverse, given the half-Chinese family who are all based in Auckland as well.”

Her mother is lawyer Margaret Malcolm, a former long-serving chief executive of the Auckland District Law Society when Judith Collins was president. Malcolm became one of Collins’ most trusted senior advisers when she was Justice Minister and was with her on the famous trip to China and dinner with Oravida, over which Collins faced conflict-of-interest allegations.

“My mum was a lawyer, so we never shied away from having conversations about politics,” says Wong. “I wouldn’t say that we were talking about political parties or anything, but about issues of the day and social justice.”

The party’s charter in its constitution sets out what it describes as its vision, purpose, values, principles and objects.

For example, its vision is “for an Aotearoa New Zealand in which individuals, our society, and our environment thrive together”. Its purpose is “to enact policy that affords every Kiwi equal opportunity to pursue their potential in ways that are socially, economically, and environmentally sustainable”.

Its values are truthfulness, ingenuity, equality and efficacy. Members are to be guided by four principles including “follow evidence over ideology” and “prioritise long-term outcomes over short-lived wins”.

It also aims to “honour Te Tiriti o Waitangi as the foundation upon which any fair and equitable future is to be built”.

Like many of Opportunity’s candidates, it is not simple to categorise the jobs Wong has done. Her career has covered work such as human rights and disability advocacy, ethical fashion, and helping businesses lower carbon emissions. When Winston Peters describes Opportunity as a party of consultants, he is not entirely wrong.

Its leading six candidates all have university degrees. Four were born abroad, though most were educated and raised in New Zealand.

Those top six candidates were announced in late July.

1. Qiulae Wong, Mt Albert

Aged 38. Leader since November. Born in Fiji and raised and educated in Auckland. Returned in 2022 from nine years living in Britain. Degree in law and politics. Worked in business sustainability and climate. Party spokeswoman on finance, economy, commerce, energy, community and voluntary sector, and national security.

2. Daniel Eb, Kaipara ki Mahurangi

Deputy leader. Born in South Africa, came to New Zealand aged 8. A communications expert with a special interest in regenerative food and farming systems. Set up the open day farm project Open Farms. Party spokesman on agriculture, forestry, Customs, Police, Corrections, foreign affairs, defence and trade.

3. Jessica Hammond, Wellington North

A public servant born and raised in Wellington. Has specialised during her career in transport infrastructure, health and disability and Māori development policies. The most experienced of the candidates, having previously stood in Ōhāriu in 2017, 2020 and 2023. Unsuccessfully stood for the leadership in 2020. Has been an advocate for kids with allergies. Revealed she was treated this year for breast cancer. The party’s spokeswoman on health, social development, employment, public services, children, seniors.

4. Kayla Kingdon-Bebb, Wellington Bays

CE of conservation group WWF with a special interest in oceans and fisheries, Treaty law and resource management. Born and educated in Canada. Gained a PhD in land economy at Cambridge University. Former public servant in the Department of Conservation (DoC) and the Ministry for the Environment. Worked on He Puapua, the controversial report commissioned by the Government to respond to the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. The party’s spokeswoman on climate change, conservation, environment, oceans and fisheries.

5. Eden Skipper, Christchurch Central

Research assistant at Canterbury University in alternative economic futures. Works in environmental restoration and indigenous development. BSc in statistics from Canterbury. Born and raised on Banks Peninsula and is active at his marae. Has worked for the Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) as an adviser in Māori capability. Party spokesman on Māori development, Treaty of Waitangi negotiations, statistics, and youth.

6. Jodie Kuntzsch, Nelson

An entrepreneur with a background in seafood and aquaculture, she led the set-up of Moananui, a collaboration of organisations centred on oceans and the blue economy. She arrived in New Zealand from Midwest America 23 years ago on a working holiday and stayed to work as an aquaculture analyst at MPI. Party spokeswoman on science, research, technology; immigration; state-owned enterprises.

As is evident from their backgrounds, the party’s top candidates lean heavily towards environmentalism, sustainability and social justice, more common to the left than the right.

Heavily redistributive tax policy is usually associated with the left of politics. Asked if there were any National policies she supported, Wong cited its compulsory KiwiSaver policy and expansion of paid parental leave. Asked if there were any Green policies she disagreed with, she cited its Kiwipower policy, setting up a Government-owned entity costing $1b over four years to be responsible for firming power required in dry years.

At a recent public meeting in Wellington, the tax policy was of major interest and concern. Hammond suggested it should not be seen as left wing because of positive comments that former National and Act leader Don Brash had made about the citizens’ income, also known as a universal basic income (UBI).

Brash told the Herald that he spoke at an Opportunity Party meeting several years ago.

“I noted that a UBI had been proposed by writers on both the left and the right as a way of dealing with the very high effective marginal tax rate faced by people looking to get off a benefit.

“When I was leader of the National Party, Lockwood Smith and I both spent quite a bit of time trying to work out how to deal with that problem. There were beneficiaries in New Zealand at that time facing an effective marginal tax rate of above 90%, and it was hardly surprising therefore that they were not inclined to leave a benefit.”

He said he probably mentioned in his speech that a writer like Charles Murray, on the political right in the United States, had written a book favouring a universal benefit income.

However, Brash said he did not have a view on Opportunity’s current policy proposals and had not looked into them.

Economist Cameron Bagrie says the party was on “both sides”, left and right, because of the redistributive nature of the tax.

“They are being perceived as far left because of the tax policy, but if you look at what they’re saying in regard to competition policy, that’s more right.”

The party wants to augment the powers of the Commerce Commission to allow companies to be broken up where competition has failed.

The likes of OECD and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) have called for a land tax for some time – “those are hardly what you’d call hard left organisations. But because it is being used to redistribute, it has more of a left connotation.”

That said, there was no way the land tax and universal basic income would be a starter with either National or Labour and both parties have ruled it out.

He also believed that despite Luxon ruling out working with Opportunity, he would do so if needed to stay in Government.

“You can bet your bottom dollar he would … If he needs them to get back in, he will pick up the phone,” Bagrie said.

Former Act chief of staff Andrew Ketels made the same point in a recent Herald column after Luxon ruled out working with Opportunity, citing its tax policy.

Ketels said Luxon had robbed Opportunity of its “strategic ambiguity” but made the best decision to avoid National voters switching to Opportunity.

“If Opportunity is the kingmaker after the election, National will need to talk to it. It won’t be able to face its supporters and tell them it couldn’t because Opportunity is too left-wing a party. National voters won’t accept that.”

Wong had a bruising encounter on Q+A recently about the tax policy and in particular how much worse off Kiwis returning from abroad would be compared with other taxpayers if they had been away for more than five years and did not qualify for the citizen’s income.

It prompted former Labour Prime Minister Helen Clark to tweet that the interview had been “a train wreck” and Wong’s defence of the land tax, higher tax and job cuts in the public sector had been “fantasy posing as policy”.

“I was surprised and a bit disappointed, to be honest,” Wong tells the Herald.

“I wouldn’t have thought she’d play into that left-right tribal politics, but it felt like she was trying to put us down in order to protect Labour, potentially. That’s how I read it.”

Wong may be even more disappointed with Clark’s follow-up remarks to the Herald this week.

When asked if she thought Opportunity was left-wing, right-wing or neither, Clark said: “I call them the Opportunistic Party.

“I mean, it’s kind of ‘see a niche and play to it’.”

She did not suggest the party emulated New Zealand First policies but said it reminded her of the way its leader, Winston Peters, played to different niches over the years.

“At the beginning it was superannuitants in the 90s, then it became anti-immigrants, chuck in a bit of anti-Treaty, then it was anti-vax. It’s sort of opportunistic.”

Clark believed the reason Opportunity was resonating now was that Peters had removed himself as a centrist.

“I think it’s the sole reason, because no one’s taken any notice of them before.

“When Winston positioned himself as a bit more centrist, there wasn’t room for that. But he’s gone off to the fringes so they’re seeing there could be an opportunity to be the man and the woman in the middle as it were.”

The attraction of the party to different niches is not dissimilar to Cameron Bagrie’s observation that Opportunity is like a latter-day Rob’s Mob of the 1970s, when blue-collar workers normally aligned with Labour jumped ship and went with Sir Robert Muldoon.

“I think there’s a whole lot of disillusioned groups around New Zealand at the moment that are mini-replicas of Rob’s Mob,” says Bagrie.

“They’re not the same group; there’s different groups, but it’s the same basic philosophy.”

The centrepiece of Opportunity’s policy platform is a radical overhaul of the New Zealand tax system. Its three-pronged “Tax Reset” consists of a land tax, a citizens’ income, and compulsory KiwiSaver.

The proposed citizens’ income is an annual payment of $19,400 to almost every New Zealander aged 18 and over. This would replace benefits like jobseeker, student allowances, and superannuation. Superannuitants would get a top-up, bringing the citizens’ income in line with current NZ super payments.

Combined with Opportunity’s higher tax brackets, this would mean anyone earning $65,883 would effectively pay no income tax – their taxes of $19,400 would be equal to the citizens’ income.

Anyone earning less than $65,883 will receive more in citizens’ income than they pay in income tax. Anyone earning more will pay more than they receive.

The proposed tax bracket changes and savings wouldn’t cover the entire cost of the citizens’ income. The balance would come from Opportunity’s proposed land tax.

The land tax would be based solely on land value. An empty plot worth $1 million and a million-dollar section with six townhouses would both attract the same land tax.

Urban land would be taxed at 1.75% of its value each year while rural land would face a 0.5% tax. Opportunity estimates this new tax would raise $24b a year.

If you don’t own land, you’ll always be better off under Opportunity’s proposed “Tax Reset”. But if you own land, the picture is quite different.

For an individual, land worth $650,000 is roughly the break-even point. The point where the tax bracket changes, citizens’ income and land tax all cancel each other out, and there is no change in the amount of tax paid.

An individual with land worth less than $650,000 will pay less tax under Opportunity’s proposal than they do now. Someone with land worth more will pay more tax than currently.

The Herald has estimated the average per-property land tax for each of the 64 general electorates.

Epsom – as the electorate with the highest average residential land values – would have the highest residential land taxes.

The Māngere electorate, home to the airport and large blocks of urban-adjacent rural land, would have the highest average land tax for business and rural properties.

The inclusion of Waiheke in the Auckland Central electorate lands it in third place in the rural land tax ranking – just above Rangitata.

Sophie and Simon are a working couple living in Avondale with two children, aged 9 and 13, in their own home valued at $1.4m ($800,00 land value). Sophie is a nurse, earning about $105,000 a year, and Simon works for an IT company on a salary of $155,000. They also own a rental unit in Onehunga valued at $750,000 (land value $400,000).

At present, they pay $65,555 income tax combined.

Under Opportunity, combined they would pay $16,845 more in income tax, $14,000 in land tax on their home and $7000 in land tax on their rental unit, but together would receive $38,800 in a citizen’s income.

Overall, they would be better off by $955 a year.

Lynette is a working sole parent living in Christchurch with two children, aged 11 and 15, and pays a mortgage on a house valued at $750,000 (land value $400,000). Lynette earns $125,000 annually as a senior physiotherapist.

At present, she pays $31,128 in income tax and does not receive Working for Families.

Under Opportunity, she would pay $8372 more in income tax. She would pay $7000 in land tax and receive $19,400 in citizens’ income.

Overall, she would be better off by $4027 a year.

Mitch and Meg run an 850ha beef and sheep farm in Hawke’s Bay. Their three children are adults and have left home. Their farm is valued at $11m, and their income fluctuates. They have had a great year with income of $280,000, but it is usually a lot less.

At present, they pay $72,155 in tax. Under Opportunity, they would pay income tax of $105,400 and a land value tax (0.5% on rural land) of $55,000 (which could be deferred) but would also receive citizens’ income of $38,800 a year.

Overall, they would be worse off by $33,245 a year.

Lindsay and Moana are a working couple who rent a house in Hamilton for $670 a week and are looking to buy their first home. They have three children, aged 2, 5 and 8. Moana earns $45,000 working part-time in a rest-home kitchen and Lindsay earns $75,000 as a builder’s labourer.

At present, they pay $21,504 in income tax.

Under the Opportunity tax plan, they would pay $35,100 in income tax but receive $38,800 in a citizen’s income.

Overall, they would be better off by $24,204 a year.

Wiremu is a pensioner aged 75 living alone in the Hutt Valley in a unit valued at $630,000 (land value $360,000). He receives $555.15 net weekly in New Zealand superannuation.

Under Opportunity, he would continue to receive that amount each week, comprising citizens’ income and a superannuitant top-up to ensure the current payment does not drop.

He would also pay $6300 each year in a 1.75% land tax, which could be deferred until it is sold.

Overall, he would be worse off by $6300 a year.

Kim and Lee are a Kiwi couple who have recently returned from living in Britain for seven years. They have twins, aged 4, and Kim landed a job as an insurance executive paying $175,000 annually.

They have bought a house on the North Shore worth $1.7m (land value $1m).

At present, Kim pays tax of $47,628. Under Opportunity, the income tax bill would increase to $56,500, and they would pay land value tax of $17,500 annually.

If they had been living in New Zealand for the previous five years, they would receive $38,800 in citizens’ income and be $12,428 better off annually overall.

But they would not be eligible for the citizens’ income. Until they had lived in New Zealand for five continuous years, they would be worse off by $26,372 a year.

Opportunity’s citizens’ income would replace most benefits, and the party proposes to simplify – and in many cases expand – the remaining benefits.

Opportunity proposes replacing Working for Families, paid parental leave payments, and Best Start with tax-free child support incomes.

A couple would receive $18,250 for their first child in its first year, $13,750 in its second and third years and then $7750 a year until the child is 18. Payments for second and subsequent children are $1000 a year less than the first-child payments.

Sole parents would receive an additional annual $9500 allowance.

Unlike the citizens’ income, child support payments would decrease with family income. Every dollar a family earn over $50,000 would result in a 10c reduction in the payment.

A couple earning $50,000 would receive the full $18,250 in the year their first child was born. A couple on the average household income of $140,000 would receive $9250 for their first child’s first year.

Opportunity estimates its approach to the remaining benefits would cost about $15.6b – roughly double the $7.3b cost of the benefits they are replacing. The difference in cost would come from the land tax.

The party’s tax policy has a companion transition policy attached, stipulating that it would take two years to develop in detail and a further 10 years to implement in phases.

Wong has made it clear in numerous interviews that its tax policy would not be a bottom line.

“I think we also have to be realistic and pragmatic about how we might get there.

“And as a new party coming into Parliament for the first time, I think ... it’s naive of us to say we can walk in and do tax reform overnight.”

But being able to advance its tax agenda from inside Parliament would be a good win for the party.

Policies already announced include:

Some of the party’s big policies have not yet been announced, including health, education, crime, housing, climate change and Treaty of Waitangi.

Wong says the policies have been developed, but the party is waiting until closer to the election to reveal them.

The party will not have any foreign affairs and defence policy.

Wong: “As a small party outside of Parliament, we do have to be mindful of the resources and time that we do have and focus our efforts on the policy areas where we’ve got expertise and ... feel that we can make the biggest difference.”

The party will not have a developed policy on gene editing either. Under Simmons’ leadership, it backed liberalisation of laws similar to Australia and slammed GE Free New Zealand as scaremongers who did not or would not understand science. This year, Opportunity opposed the Gene Technology Bill, which is based on Australian law but sits stalled on Parliament’s order paper without sufficient support to proceed. Wong says the party has listened to the concerns of organic farmers. It wants the policy developed by citizens’ assemblies.

Party policy is developed by a policy committee appointed by the party board. Under the party constitution, the committee has complete independence and does not require policy approval from the board or a general meeting of members, although any member can propose a policy.

The rules go further and state: “The board, other officers, and members of the party are expressly prohibited from interfering with the development of policy by the policy committee.”

Unusually, members of the policy committee do not have to be party members, although Wong says they all are. She said the rule about interference was to ensure policy was based on evidence and there was no undue influence on policy development from stakeholders or donors.

Wong and Jessica Hammond are on the four-person policy committee, but Wong won’t name the others, saying they are public servants and need to remain anonymous.

Another unusual aspect of the constitution gives the board power to override a caucus decision with a 75% majority if it believes a caucus decision would prejudice the charter. But the rule is set to be changed at a general meeting on September 20 on the board’s recommendation.

According to the party’s website, the board is chaired by Penny Fairbrother, a senior adviser at the Greater Wellington Regional Council. Other members are Darren Savage, who works in the public health sector in Hamilton and is a freelance commercial financial sector adviser; Scott Pollok, a patent attorney in Auckland with a background in mechanical engineering; Dan Thurston Crow of Taranaki who chairs the environmental NGO Sustainable Taranaki and stood for the party in 2017 and 2020; and Alan Wilderland, a founder of music software company Serato Audio Research, employing more than 160 people in Auckland.

Last year Opportunity declared $179,000 in donations while National received $6.28m, Act $2.45m, Labour $2.40m, Green $1.85m, NZ First $1.36m and Te Pāti Māori $142,000.

Slightly under half, $86,000, of Opportunity’s donations came from donations of less than $5000 while two large donors accounted for most of the rest. Its mix of small and large donations was similar to other parties’; NZ First received the lowest portion of small donations – 31% – with Labour having the largest at 63%.

We won’t know the total raised by each party until after the election, but can get a sense of their progress because large donations must be declared as they are received. The Electoral Commission also publishes quarterly figures on “protected” donations.

So far this year National has declared $2.25m, Act $1.81m, Labour $708,000, NZ First $630,000, Opportunity $561,000, Green $343,000 and Te Pāti Māori $114,000.

Opportunity donations have certainly picked up this year, but they are a long way off the $2.34m the party received in 2017.

The party has a few major donors. The biggest is Opportunity board member and one of the founders and owners of Serato Audio Research, Alan Wilderland. Wilderland has donated $271,160 to the party – $230,000 directly and $41,160 via a company he owns.

Phillip Mills, founder of Les Mills International and Brian Cartmell, a US tech entrepreneur now based in Queenstown, have both donated $100,000. Ian Kuperus, a tax lawyer, has donated $87,600.

This year Mills has also donated $150,000 to the Green Party and $150,000 to Labour. Cartmell has donated $200,000 to Act, $204,999 to NZ First and $201,994 to National.

Opportunity has also received $70,000 in donations protected from disclosure – second only to National’s $316,160 in protected donations.

Jem Cassar-Daley had to be bribed to sing with her famous dad – but not any more

Sydney Morning Herald August 29, 2026

The singer, daughter of country music icon Troy, has become one of Australia’s sharpest indie-pop songwriters.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

When Jem Cassar-Daley was little, she and her family would pile into the car at their Brisbane home and make the three-ish-hour drive south to her Nan’s place near Grafton.

When they neared the massive Clarence River as it splits the land at Harwood, just inland from Yamba, her parents would tell her to roll the windows down and breathe in the smell of cane sugar as it wafted from the factory on the riverbank. It’s a core, treasured memory, one the Gumbaynggirr and Bundjalung songwriter immortalised in her gently melancholy 2024 single, Big Container.

She can still see and smell it in her memory now, as we sit at a dark marble table in Sydney’s Ace Hotel to discuss her debut album, tattoos used to come off in the pool. “You could see all the smoke coming out, and we’d smell it, and it was so beautiful,” she smiles, buoyed that as a Northern Rivers person, I picked up on the reference to the famous local landmark.

“I love that you know that,” she says with a laugh. “Driving down the M1 on holidays is still so vivid in my mind.”

Jem didn’t have to go far to find famous Northern Rivers landmarks. Troy, her dad, is one of Grafton’s most famous sons: a beloved country artist who has been releasing albums and touring the country longer than Jem has been alive. He and her mum, singer and radio broadcaster Laurel Edwards, brought up Jem and her brother Clay in Brisbane in a house bursting with music. Growing up, Jem didn’t really have any idea her parents were different from her friends’ parents – except for the singing.

“I just always thought that all families sang together. My friends would be like, ‘Oh, you guys sing?’. I’d say, ‘Well, don’t you all sing at home?’,” Cassar-Daley laughs, mock exasperated. “Like, I genuinely thought it was just so normal because it’s all we did. It took me a while to realise that not everyone did that.”

She started scribbling down songs before she was a teenager, recording them with a mic that was lying around the house for Troy to use for demos. “I think one of the first songs I wrote was Why Is It So Windy Today? That’s a famous one in our house,” she remembers. “I’ll have to find the recording … and I still ask that today, why is it so windy? What’s going on?”

Singing at home? Wonderful. Singing on stage with her dad? Not so much. Jem recalls another clear memory of clinging to her dad’s leg while he was on stage in Tamworth, terrified of the crowd and the bright lights. “Dad said we’d go get ice cream after,” she says. “I basically had to be bribed.”

That couldn’t be further from the truth now. Over the past five years, Cassar-Daley has steadily asserted herself as one of Australia’s sharpest indie-pop songwriters. She’s released a fistful of popular singles, chief among them being King of Disappointment in 2023 – a piercing kiss-off about being ghosted – and last year’s yearning Kiss Me Like You’re Leaving.

She’s got a whole heap of touring under her belt, including a recent headline show in the Sydney Opera House’s intimate Utzon Room (some fireworks blasted from Vivid Sydney boats behind her during the set, which added a certain unplanned specialness to the occasion). She’s also collected a few awards along the way, including song of the year for King of Disappointment at the Queensland Music Awards; last year, she earned a place on the Brisbane Walk of Fame and was named the QMA Indigenous artist of the year.

From the outside, it might seem like Jem’s professional music career was pre-destined, but that wasn’t necessarily the case. She started a Bachelor of Arts degree at university in 2020, “hell-bent” on trying something else and “doing everything right by the book”. That lasted about a month, she recalls with a laugh. “I was like, ‘I’m gonna just put this on hold for a minute and just go play some shows and do what I want to do, and I can always come back to it.’ I ended up going on the road with my Dad … It was like 80 shows in a year.”

With her attention turned fully to music, Cassar-Daley spent the next few years diligently chipping away at tracks, travelling to the UK and Nashville for writing and recording sessions. In 2022, she released her debut EP I Don’t Know Who To Call, featuring the single Changes and a devastating cover of I Just Don’t Think I’ll Ever Get Over You – written by one of her favourite songwriters, Colin Hay. While all that was happening, she packed up and moved away from her beloved Brissy, spending a bit of time in Melbourne before settling in Sydney earlier this year.

Tattoos used to come off in the pool gets its name from a moment when Jem was 21, when she jumped in the pool and realised her brand-new ink wouldn’t come off, no matter how hard she scrubbed. And like that scene of the sugar factory in Big Container, Cassar-Daley’s songs are lifted from the page by these clear and expressive scenes.

While she credits Hay and Joni Mitchell as some of her biggest influences, you can also trace the threads back to more recent pop powerhouses like Phoebe Bridgers and Taylor Swift. The characters in Cassar-Daley’s world are vividly drawn – whether they’re sleeping on the couch in the other room after a fight, or dreaming of wedding dresses after a breakup, or scrolling through Instagram obsessing over a new partner’s ex-girlfriend.

Sometimes these characters are Jem, but other times (like on Speak Now) she writes from a friend’s perspective about having to call off a relationship before it gets to the altar. The push and pull of love and the people enmeshed in it is tattoos’ chief concern, most beautifully on the sorrowful and resigned Into Sunsets.

Cassar-Daley knows people will draw connections between her and her father – but this is a source of pride, not anxiety. “I have always idolised my dad as a musician,” she says. “It’s been such a massive inspiration for me. He’s always told me to just do my own thing and stay true to myself and write what I wanted to write and not worry about anything else. That’s been a really important message that I’ve carried from my dad of just trying to be true to myself as much as I can throughout my writing process and who I am.”

There was a moment early on in her career when she considered dropping the recognisable last name, but that thought didn’t last for long. “There was a thought of just going by Jem,” she says. “But I was like, ‘Look, there’s four of us, probably, in the world’. I don’t know if we know of any other Cassar-Daleys! It just felt right, it just feels like me.”

Jem Cassar-Daley’s debut album tattoos used to come off in the pool is out now. Her national tour includes shows at Melbourne’s Northcote Social Club on September 19, Sydney’s Lansdowne Hotel on September 25, and Brisbane’s The Brightside on September 26.
