After the parades and plaudits: How the tide turned for ‘steel saviour’ Sanjeev Gupta

Sydney Morning Herald August 29, 2026

The billionaire was given a hero’s welcome for saving Whyalla and the planet – but all was not what it seemed.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Sanjeev Gupta is a puzzle. He is certainly a world-class salesman. On that let’s all agree. It is how he managed to borrow so much money, how he came to be a billionaire and how he persuaded so many decent people to share his vision.

But surprisingly, the silver-tongued steel tycoon is no brash fairground spruiker. He is a shy man, an introvert: quiet and softly spoken. Picture a besuited Dr Evil in the Austin Powers comedy movies and you’ll get a fair idea of what he looks like. Although Gupta, of course, was promising to save the world and not destroy it.

Naturally, he loved money and expensive toys. But those who observed him from up close believed he was driven by a craving for attention and the thrill of the deal. He was an outsider who wanted to be on the inside and be accepted into the Establishment.

The people who liked him said he was smart, generous, likeable, loyal and sincere. Some even called him a visionary. But many saw a less attractive side. One former executive described him to me as “the most selfish man I’ve ever met”. A second who knew him well branded him a narcissist. A third said he wouldn’t believe anything that came out of his mouth. Yet all agreed he had world-class charm, if he chose to turn it on.

So what do we know of his formative years? Before the luxury homes in London, Sydney and Dubai? Before the private plane and helicopter, a yacht in every port and a slew of offshore companies and trusts to keep his baubles safe? Before he was hailed as the “Saviour of Steel” for rescuing South Australia’s famous Whyalla steelworks. Before all of it – the worldwide business empire built on billions of dollars of Other People’s Money, and the disaster waiting to happen north of Adelaide?

Sanjeev Gupta was born in India in 1971 and spent his childhood in the Punjab, in the industrial city of Ludhiana, often known as the Manchester of India. His father, Parduman (“PK”) Gupta, was a self-made man who left school at 11 and started out selling nuts and bolts before making his fortune manufacturing Victor bicycles in India and trading commodities in Nigeria.

Gupta was the third of four children, who, according to his big sister Anjali, was always trying to prove himself. “You know, he sometimes needed more attention,” she told the BBC in 2016, “but he was very driven, very ambitious … He was a very quiet child, and he wouldn’t want to talk to people.”

On Anjali’s account, Gupta was wilful and determined. At the age of 11, he convinced his seven-year-old brother to run away from their exclusive boarding school at Shimla in the Himalayas, which they hated, and catch a bus back home, six hours away. “They gave us a shock of our life because they had to check into a hotel overnight,” his sister recalled.

Four years later, as Sanjeev was turning 15, he persuaded his father to send him to one of England’s most expensive boarding schools, St Edmund’s Canterbury, where his elder brother Raj was already a student. Coming into fifth form when most of his classmates had already chosen their friends, he was younger than most and was small, chubby, quiet and shy.

“He wasn’t bullied but he was certainly teased,” says one old schoolmate, who is now a successful businessman. “He had a bit of an accent. One boy called him De Gupita Singh and would chant the name at him, laughing.”

At the start, Gupta was homesick and missed his mum and dad. He slept in a big, cold, chapel-like dorm with 50 other boys, one of whom recalls the 15-year-old crying in his sleep. And while life at St Edmund’s wasn’t quite as brutal as Rugby School in that famous Victorian novel, Tom Brown’s Schooldays, it was certainly a tougher environment than would be tolerated today. Sixth formers would come into the dorm during the night and “lamppost” the beds, tipping them up on their ends with the occupant inside. Another random punishment was the Boko, a painful knuckle to the head. And a third was the “yellow card”, which obliged a boy to report 10 times a day to prefects, so they could check that the victim’s shirt, tie and uniform were in perfect order.

Gupta survived this thoroughly British institution but didn’t leave much of a mark. He never scored a mention in the school magazine, was not in any teams, had no interest in sports and was certainly not in the cool group or in-crowd.

But he was smart enough for his classmates to plagiarise his homework. And his tuck box remains famous to this day. It was full of goodies like cold tandoori chicken that Gupta could sometimes be persuaded – or perhaps pressured – to give away.

What does that tell you? Was he being kind and generous by doling out these treats? Was he trying to buy friends? Or was he just being stood over by the bigger, stronger boys? Perhaps this was young Gupta’s Rosebud moment: the key to understanding what drives him on.

For 20 years after his stint in school, Gupta made a fortune trading commodities in London and Dubai. Then in 2013, he started four years of frenzied buying, acquiring almost two dozen ailing steelworks and aluminium smelters in Britain, Europe, the United States and Australia that had been pushed to the brink of bankruptcy by cheap Chinese steel flooding the world market.

Everywhere he went he was hailed as the “Saviour of Steel”. Politicians loved him, as did the workers whose jobs he was saving. In 2017, he set his sights on the steelworks at Whyalla. It was in the hands of administrators and in danger of closing for good. There, in the industrial town on the Spencer Gulf, he received a hero’s welcome.

Dressed in a dark blue three-piece suit in 30-degree heat, Sanjeev Gupta was piped up Whyalla’s main street by a bagpiper in a kilt, at the head of a parade of politicians and steelworkers waving flags. It was no wonder they loved him. He was saving not only thousands of jobs, but the very town that he said had “adopted” him. He even called the place his “spiritual home”.

That September 2017 night there was a party for the steelworkers and staff down on the foreshore, with Indian dancing and a huge fireworks display – the biggest Whyalla could remember. Gupta and his kids were right in the thick of it all, as was his wife, Nicola, who was happily bumming cigarettes off the locals.

Natalie Hyde, whose partner Shane Karger was then an Australian Workers’ Union delegate at the steelworks, was impressed. “They seemed down-to-earth and real,” she told me. “We were hearing he had saved the Scottish steel plants, and everyone was encouraged to see him as a white knight.”

Gupta was so impressed by the warm reception that he said he would buy a house in the town: one of many promises he would ultimately fail to keep. Yet he did go some way to keeping his word, because he also announced he would now abandon his mansions in Wales and Dubai and move his family to Sydney to set up a home. He had brought Nicola and the children with him to Australia to enjoy a four-week holiday and had broken the news on the plane that they would not be going back.

“She looked at me like I was joking,” he later told The Australian, “but she knew I wasn’t. She rallied everyone to persuade me otherwise, but of course I won, as I always do.”

His arrival in Australia’s harbour city caused a stir in the business community and in Sydney’s status-conscious eastern suburbs, where many were keen to befriend the British business guru. As his profile rose, he threw generous parties for politicians, stockbrokers and B-list celebrities, with pink champagne on tap and invitations to “Meet the Guptas”. A garden party under white marquees, arranged at a moment’s notice to celebrate Harry and Meghan’s royal wedding, had then-prime minister Malcolm Turnbull among the guests. Another, reportedly, had a sit-down dinner for 200 revellers.

But the parties were by no means his only extravagance. A few days before Christmas 2017, Sanjeev bought Maya, a 30-metre motor yacht, in time to host a New Year’s Eve party on the water. With teak decks, wenge flooring, a mirrored stateroom and aft cockpit bar, it was a stunning boat with a $5 million price tag.

Only later would it emerge that his big boat was owned through an Isle of Man company called GFG Marine and registered in Jersey, effectively paid for by the good folk of Whyalla, with the bill picked up by the company that owned the steelworks, OneSteel Manufacturing.

Gupta spent the next seven years building this house of cards while promising to transform Whyalla – to make it a world leader in low-emission “green steel”. He would build a “mega” steelworks, 10 times the size of the existing plant, powered by Australia’s largest solar farm. He would scrap the ancient coal-fired blast furnace and install an electric arc furnace, plus a direct reduction iron plant using “green” hydrogen.

Instead, he siphoned hundreds of millions of dollars out of his Australian businesses and pushed suppliers to the brink of bankruptcy. It finally caught up with him in 2025, as his worldwide steelmaking empire imploded under the weight of billions of dollars of debts. Gupta was left desperately shuffling money between his private companies in an attempt to keep his creditors at bay, all the while declaring that -everything would turn out fine. But everyone had stopped believing.

With his dreams in ruins and his promises unfulfilled, the good folk of Whyalla were left wishing they had never set eyes on him. With hundreds of millions of dollars owed to creditors and local businesses pushed into bankruptcy, Gupta’s employees, suppliers and political backers told him, bluntly: “Pay up or piss off.”

He was kicked out of Whyalla by the South Australian government, and almost all his companies around the world went bust, leaving debts of around $8 billion. And it was not just Australia giving him the bum’s rush; the Whyalla story was playing out in a dozen different theatres in a dozen different countries, with the plot always the same: angry creditors, broken promises, shattered dreams and employees fearing for their future.

The fast-talking entrepreneur, however, is still rich, and free, and has based his family in Sydney. But his world-class charm, infectious optimism and remarkable ability to inspire his followers – if they even still exist – are no longer enough.

Investigators are pursuing him worldwide. Gupta is being investigated by the corporate cops in at least four countries – the United Kingdom, France, Romania and Australia – for possible crimes that include, as Britain’s Serious Fraud Office put it, “Suspected fraud, fraudulent trading and money-laundering in relation to the financing and conduct of the business of companies within the Gupta Family Group …”

Perhaps the biggest question left to answer now is, “How did he lead the world on such a merry dance for so long?”

This is an edited extract from The Big Steal: How Steel Tycoon Sanjeev Gupta Fooled Australia and the World, by Paul Barry (Allen & Unwin, $37), out August 25.

More than a bridge: Remembering Brisbane’s 2001 Goodwill Games

Sydney Morning Herald August 29, 2026

It cost $30 million and left only a footbridge, but the 2001 Goodwill Games – 25 years ago today – permanently altered Brisbane’s global footprint.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

A stepping stone, or second-rate sideshow. The Brisbane 2001 Goodwill Games could be remembered in several ways, perhaps none as enduring as the pedestrian bridge that bears its name.

Friday marked a quarter-century since of the Goodwill Games opening ceremony at the Brisbane Entertainment Centre, with competition starting 25 years ago on Saturday.

Created by recently departed media mogul Ted Turner in 1986 after the Cold War-era Moscow 1980 and Los Angeles 1984 Olympic boycotts, the Goodwill Games were designed to bring elite athletes from rival nations together and promote international goodwill.

Unlike other competitions, the event offered substantial prize money – about $US10 million by the time Brisbane came around – and sought to provide a politically neutral stage.

The Queensland government spent $30 million in 1997 to attract the Goodwill Games, beating Shanghai, Guangzhou, Hong Kong, Cape Town, Osaka, Rio de Janeiro and Buenos Aires.

Brisbane would become the first, and ultimately the last, host outside the United States and Russia.

Then-premier Peter Beattie says it was part of a broader strategy to elevate Brisbane’s international profile.

“For us, it was a step-stone of using sport to attract major events to Queensland,” he says.

“We had a major event strategy designed to not just attract the world’s attention, but to put Brisbane on the world map.”

Quite literally, as 2001 Goodwill Games chief executive Campbell Rose recalls.

“It seems a bit trivial, but the fact was that Brisbane didn’t exist on the CNN weather map. Melbourne did, Sydney did, but Brisbane didn’t,” he says.

“Well, since the Goodwill Games, Brisbane’s been on the CNN weather map.”

Having the network’s owner behind the Games helped, but Beattie says Turner’s involvement meant far more than map placement.

“Ted Turner was a billionaire. Obviously, business people came with him and we were looking to get money invested into Queensland,” he says.

“Australia’s problem is that we are short of cash. We don’t have a lot of capital, so you’ve got to find imaginative ways to attract people to come.”

The Goodwill Games attracted potential investors from the world’s largest markets. The USA. China. Japan. Germany. And of course, Russia.

As Rose says: “It projected Brisbane right into those markets with pinpoint accuracy.”

Held less than a year after Sydney 2000, Australia was basking in the post-Olympic glow when Turner’s circus rolled into town.

Rose, a Melburnian who was poached from the city’s major events office, says Sydney 2000’s shadow loomed large, and the Goodwill Games attracted its share of sceptics.

“You would get things like, ‘Is it a second-rate event for a second-rate city?’” he says.

“There was that cloud of Sydney being a hard act to follow and, yes, it was a hard act to follow, but we did a couple of key things.

“We developed an outstanding cultural festival called Paint the Town Red. We lit the Story Bridge and staged events across the city throughout the Games, which really resonated with the Brisbane population.

“The other key thing we did, very successfully, was that the Goodwill Games was all about having the best 10 or so athletes in every discipline compete.”

Investment, tourism and putting-on-the-map aside, the Goodwill Games were an elite sporting competition and that invitation-only format set them apart from the Olympics.

No qualifiers, no Eric the Eels.

Instead, there was Ian Thorpe. Michael Johnson. The since-disgraced Marion Jones.

And two-time Sydney 2000 Olympic gold medallist Grant Hackett.

“What was really cool about [the Goodwill Games] was the good rivalries that came out of that Olympic Games,” Hackett says.

“Like we saw the men’s 4x100 freestyle relay when Michael Klim broke the world record and Thorpey brought that home. We also saw Peter van den Hoogenband beat Thorpey in the 200-metre freestyle, and there was going to be another rematch of that race less than 12 months later.”

While his Goodwill medals might not take the same pride of place in his trophy cabinet as the Olympic golds, Hackett still remembers the Goodwill Games fondly.

“It didn’t come with the pressure of like a World Championships, or an Olympic Games, or Commonwealth Games – it was one of these major international meets where you could really enjoy it and enjoy other events,” he says.

“It just had more of a relaxed feeling about it.”

Gold Coast native Hackett, along with US track superstar Johnson, was an official Goodwill Games ambassador.

“Michael Johnson was a hero growing up, wearing his gold shoes, and I got to jump in the car with him and drive around and do a few things and get to know him really well.

“The Goodwill Games probably was not a meet that you would have put up on your goal list when you’re a teenager, but once you’re in the sport representing your country, you want to be doing all the meets like that.”

Another home-town hero coming back to Brisbane with Olympic gold was beach volleyballer Natalie Cook – one of Brisbane 2032’s most enthusiastic cheerleaders.

Beach volleyball was held at the South Bank Piazza – a unique experience for Cook and her teammate, Kerri Pottharst.

“It was very intimate, with a roof as well, and small – I think it held about 5000 maximum, with people bumped in around the edges,” she says.

“I enjoyed the crowd being so close. There was security, but it wasn’t as restrictive as an Olympic Games, so people could get closer to the action.”

Hackett also loved that aspect of the Goodwill Games.

“Natalie’s right – there was a lot more interaction with fans and other sports, and it just felt easier. We could roam free a little bit,” he says.

But those relaxed days ended about 50 hours after the Goodwill Games’ September 9 closing ceremony, when 19 men boarded flights in the US armed with box cutters.

Everybody knows how that story ended.

“I didn’t even feel like I noticed [the security] in Sydney. But then when I went to Athens [in 2004], it was like there was military every 100 meters around the fence,” Hackett says.

“But that [freedom] was the best part of the Goodwill Games and I think Brisbane can use that moving forward [to 2032] – to make it fun, make it interactive, put the big screens up at the parks and in and around the city.

“Create an atmosphere so everyone is inspired – and I think the Goodwill Games did that in Brisbane in 2001.”

For all the star power, television reach and economic impact, the Goodwill Games have faded somewhat from Brisbane’s collective memory.

When chronicling Brisbane’s “coming of age”, two events typically enter the conversation – the 1982 Commonwealth Games and World Expo ’88.

So why aren’t the Goodwill Games mentioned in the same breath?

For a start, the Goodwill Bridge connecting South Bank and Gardens Point is the only enduring piece of infrastructure associated with the 2001 Games. They did not leave a stadium, arena or sporting precinct, unlike what is planned for Brisbane 2032.

The 1982 Commonwealth Games, meanwhile, left Rose a major stadium and aquatic centre.

“We could not have done it without the infrastructure that had been built for the Commonwealth Games,” he says.

Rose says the fact Brisbane hosted the last Goodwill Games meant it no longer has the continuity – or the currency – of an Olympics or Commonwealth Games.

“It’s a travesty that it didn’t continue,” he says.

“There’s no doubt that the significance of it, the impact, the benefits it brought got lost.”

Rose says the Games’ demise came as a surprise, especially given Brisbane 2001’s $26 million operating surplus.

“It was the most financially viable and profitable of all the Goodwill Games,” he says.

Cook says the Goodwill Games could have continued to have a presence on the international sporting calendar – and be a trailblazer for athletes’ pay.

“The Goodwill Games could have been an accelerator of invite-only potential commercial return for an athlete and start to be celebrated that way – look at the way tennis players get an appearance fee before they even enter the tournament,” she says.

“That was where the Goodwill Games could have built its relevance.”

Although the Goodwill Games were orders of magnitude smaller than the upcoming Olympic and Paralympic Games, Beattie says 2032 organisers could still learn a lot from them.

“Firstly, ignore the whingers and the knockers – they don’t understand how investment works, where the jobs come from. They don’t understand the importance of tourism and investment,” he says.

“Then, focus on delivery – make sure you do things as quickly as you possibly can.

“And finally, take people with you … Have a long-term strategy, share the problems with the public, and tell them: this is what we’re doing, these are the challenges, but this is what we’re doing about it, so they understand what they are.

“In the end, you have to take people with you.”

‘The bots just botting each other’: In the world of jobseeking, an absurd future is upon us

Sydney Morning Herald August 29, 2026

AI tools are becoming increasingly common in the hiring process – for both employers and jobseekers. Their benefits are being widely debated, but they do highlight a truth about the power of human relationships.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

You’re fast asleep, snoring, dreaming happily that you’ve quit work, you’re somewhere warm, siestas, great books, cocktails at sunset. Suddenly though, something jolts you awake. Good morning, reality! Now you remember. Reality is that you’re unemployed and your redundancy dollars are going down while your living costs go up. Buying groceries brings on anxiety attacks. Ahead again today: drudgery, scanning jobs ads, LinkedIn to Seek and back again, writing new cover letters, tweaking your résumé, sending out a fresh round of applications to add to the dozens you’ve submitted over months. Coffee. Despair. Coffee.

But then you remember something else: your personal AI job-hunting agent – I’ll call “her” Mavis – has been busy since before dawn. Think of Mavis as a PA: While you were dreaming of sunset cocktails, Mavis scraped job boards for newly posted career opportunities deeply aligned with your unique experience, skills and proven track record, dug into your digital files to pull up your résumé and cover-letter template, then tailored them for each fresh application. Relax, go out and grab a coffee (if you can afford to); when you’re ready, Mavis’s work on your behalf will be waiting in your inbox, ready for you to check over and send off.

Don’t take for granted, though, that a human being will be sitting in an office somewhere waiting to read your application.

Mavis, meet Bob.

Bob is going to take care of things at the employer’s end. Bob, as I’m going to call “him”, is one of a growing number of AI recruitment tools.

Bob and its peers don’t, as we understand the term, actually read. Nevertheless, they can make decisions about job applications and act upon those decisions on behalf of hiring managers and recruiters.

These tools, variously described as chatbots, AI agents or AI co-pilots (an “AI companion and hiring hero” is how one recruitment AI company cheerily describes its product), can, among their many superpowers, shortlist candidates and advance them to the next step in the process – or, simply, click, bingo, eliminate them. It’s not cold, it’s not brutal, it’s just business (and no, AI did not write that sentence, I did!).

If the human beings that Bob rejects are lucky, it has also been configured to send out an automated “thanks but no thanks” reply to their applications. If they’re lucky. “I used to think that the agony of waiting for a yes/no response was bad,” one jobseeker tells me, “but now I know that receiving an automated AI rejection to the application you spent two hours carefully crafting – literally 30 seconds after submitting it – is truly soul-destroying. Like, WTF – could it not just pause and pretend?”

“Applicant tracking systems” (ATS), which collect and sort job applications and track candidates through the stages of a hiring process, have been around for more than a decade, largely in a clunky supporting role to human HR staff. Increasingly, however, employers are adopting more sophisticated AI-powered recruitment tools, which take on tasks once performed by human recruiters. These more “intelligent” tools can drive and connect almost every step in the hiring process, from researching, analysing and shortlisting candidates and identifying potential applicants beyond those who have applied directly, to conducting preliminary screening “robo-interviews” and psychometric tests, carrying out background and reference checks, answering applicants’ questions and scheduling interviews.

This dehumanised combat zone is not the future, it is now. About 80 per cent of Australian companies report using AI technology at moderate or higher levels in recruitment, according to the 2025 Australian Responsible AI Index. The World Economic Forum put the figure in March 2025 at 90 per cent of companies worldwide.

In the opposite corner, fighting fire with fire, many if not most job-hunters now use generative AI systems such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini to draft and/or cross-check job applications. But in tacit recognition that the hiring process has become too machine-mediated for ordinary humans to negotiate unaided, the savviest of jobseekers, especially in the tech sphere, are pioneering new ways to navigate the employment market. They’re using what’s called “agentic AI” to build personal AI job-hunting agents like Mavis to automate multiple elements of the dismal process.

In my research for this article, I come across Abhijay Arora Vuyyuru, a San Francisco-based AI specialist employed by Alphabet, owners of Google, which wants to “democratise access to career knowledge”. Via a WhatsApp call, he describes to me how such an agent can start looking for and applying for jobs early every morning while the jobseeker hits the snooze button. He thinks that, within five years, every jobseeker will have one. “It most probably would be talking to an AI recruitment agent of the company – they’d exchange notes.”

I chat with a friend, a senior HR leader, and tell her that I’m working on a story about job-hunting in the age of AI. She sighs. “Recruitment will become the bots just botting each other soon, little robots yelling at each other,” she says.

I first wrote about job-hunting for Good Weekend in 2023. Then, the overwhelming story I heard was that older jobseekers face issues including ageism, income security, under-employment and a soul-eroding sense of irrelevance. None of that has changed. Only now, there is a pile-on of new factors. As the employment market starts to wobble, Ever more sophisticated AI-powered recruitment systems are contributing to the challenges and stress all job-hunters experience, not just older ones. As New York Magazine noted in an article earlier this year, “The job search has become a humiliation ritual.”

Recruiter Stephen Coldicutt says the automation process has left many candidates lost and demoralised. “It can be heartless,” says Coldicutt, associate director of Sydney-based The Safe Step, which specialises in the health, safety and environment sphere.

And recruiters widely acknowledge that the systems can make poor decisions: algorithms can determine an excellent candidate is not a sufficiently close match for a role and eliminate them before he or she has a chance to get near a human. Anna Whitlam, CEO of WhitlamCo executive search and advisory firm in Melbourne, offers the example of a senior corporate affairs leader, “a no-brainer candidate”, who applied for a job but was immediately rejected by an automated system. “Time and time again what you will hear is a senior candidate not even getting an interview,” Whitlam says.

Jobseekers have long talked about the “ATS black hole” – applications that disappear into the ether, applicants left forever wondering where they went wrong. But there are deeper concerns: experts are sounding the alarm about what happens when one of life’s most pivotal processes is increasingly controlled by opaque systems few people understand.

Amanda Bowler realised when she was 40 that her arms weren’t going to let her keep working as a hairdresser until she retired and, in 2018, she started a psychology degree. “I really love people and the mind and behaviour and how it all works,” Bowler says via Zoom from the granny flat behind a friend’s house in the central Victorian town of Trentham, where she’s living temporarily. Unprompted, another friend of Bowler’s tells me that she’s “one of the most energetic, driven, resilient, adaptable, vibrant, empathetic, generous and smart women I know”.

Bowler finished her honours year in psychology last year. Before embarking on the postgraduate study required for clinical practice, she decided to test the job market for roles that might put her degree to use in areas including aged care, research and program delivery, hospital administration, disability support and child protection casework. She estimates that over the past six months she has submitted 50 job applications. “Basically, crickets. I have not had one face-to-face interview.”

Bowler would like to think that she made the right decision to go back to study, but frequently feels she’s on a path to nowhere. “I’m willing to work hard. I have 30 years of business management and ownership behind me and build rapport with nearly everyone I meet. I keep thinking that surely organisations will see my transferable skills! I just need someone to look outside the box and see that I have so much to offer; I just need an opportunity to talk to a real person.”

Bowler is 48. She has a HECS debt of about $44,000, a meagre super balance and nowhere permanent to call home. While she looks for work, she’s surviving on friends’ love, loyal hairdressing clients and Airbnb cleaning work. “I have watched as her bubble, which she desperately tries to keep inflated, has started to shrivel,” Bowler’s friend tells me.

In such a dehumanising job market, there will be casualties: the technologically unsophisticated, the anxious, the sensitive or the timid struggle. Older workers who pre-date the LinkedIn-buzzword-optimised, keyword-dense professional identity frequently find themselves in unwanted early retirement or the driver’s seat of an Uber. And AI systems are not generally friendly towards people who have had varied career and life experiences and built a wide array of skills rather than a specific, highly honed few that can be encapsulated in corporate-speak, or those like Bowler, who might be trying to launch into a new industry. “If organisations are using AI to screen the first volume of applications, and are looking for keywords, I am the square peg in a round hole,” says Bowler.

Think of it as a giant game of word-matching: AI recruitment systems scan at a granular level for keyword and terminology matches between a position description and an applicant’s experience. If, for example, a job ad for an aged-care worker asks for someone with experience in “case management”, “holistic health plans” and “person-centred care”, and an applicant like Bowler describes broadly similar experience using different language, a human recruiter reading her application might recognise her aptitude for the role. But the AI system has no imagination, no interest in nuance and debatable judgment. Bowler’s application is likely to be screened out because she has not used precise keywords and terminology.

“The person who’s the absolute diamond in the rough is sitting ranked number 221, they’re never going to get seen,” says John Baker, a former executive search leader who now coaches senior jobseekers. “I don’t think AI is at a point where it would identify that person.”

Recruiters can also instruct the systems to prioritise candidates who have one particular credential or experience in a particular niche or sector and downgrade those who don’t. For example, a car company looking for a CFO could tell an AI recruitment system that it is only interested in people who have worked for Toyota and Subaru; someone who might match every other requirement for the role but who has only worked at Hyundai won’t get a look in. Such is the opacity of the AI systems that applicants will never know why. Transparency has always been limited in the job application process but at least in the past, decisions were made by humans and potentially explainable.

“It’s really hard to get a handle on how [the AI systems] are being used because everyone uses them differently, even if they use the same tool, it might be operating the process in a different way,” says Dr Natalie Sheard, a lawyer and postdoctoral fellow at the University of Melbourne, whose research has included extensive interviews with employers. “They might configure it in a different way to suit their organisation. It’s really complicated technology. What came out of my research was that employers didn’t know how these systems worked. The recruiters themselves could work it day to day, but they might not understand the technology.”

The AI effect overlays the issues that have always faced job-hunters – including common discourtesy. Claudia*, 42, is living with her mother in Tasmania and working in an unstable government role while looking for senior roles to match her international marketing experience. She tells me that she has applied for more than 100 jobs over the past two years – with some breaks for sanity. “I just hit a wall last year – I was really angry from the rejection; I just thought, ‘This cannot be happening.’ ” Last year, Claudia had a 2am interview scheduled for a position with a “scrappy” overseas company. “I got online, made sure I was made up and looked alert and alive and, at that ungodly hour, the person didn’t join the call – for a job I didn’t even want!”

Others face ageism and the searing issue of finding relevance and meaning in life when there’s no job to provide it. Cameron McDonald, 63, has not been able to find work since his position as a senior business development specialist with a Canberra consultancy was made redundant in 2022. He says he wasn’t actively chasing work, but when he was approached via his LinkedIn profile to put his hat in the ring for a handful of roles, he submitted applications. He got through to the interview stage for two of the positions but was eventually eliminated. McDonald blames ageism. “The people who got the job, I could see, were 10 to 15 years younger than me,” he says. “It didn’t make me feel too good; the most upsetting thing was the fact that I knew that I had a hell of a lot to offer.”

Although financially secure enough not to work, McDonald thought a little pocket money might be handy and, in late 2025, he applied for a service position at Bunnings. He reached the second stage – a recorded one-way video interview, often called a robo-interview. These increasingly common, torturous sessions require candidates to talk to their blank screen recording video responses to a series of questions, with the footage later reviewed by recruiters, AI software or both. One jobseeker tells me that he felt he always looked flustered during the interviews as his eyes were forced to dart between the question and his computer’s camera.

“I do not agree with them,” says Sydney recruiter Stephen Coldicutt. “I don’t think it’s great for the candidate at all, they don’t allow people to be natural.”

Certainly for McDonald, it was an awkward experience. “I didn’t do very well at all, obviously, because I didn’t get through; I felt uncomfortable.” He knows he was enormously over-qualified for the job but still, he was “pissed off”. He says he hates to sound like an “old fart” but he looks around his local Bunnings and “Gen Z people, they look like they are asleep”.

His issues might or might not have had anything to do with the AI hiring process, but experts worry that automated systems make it harder to detect and challenge existing forms of discrimination. The opacity of the technology is a “massive problem”, says Sheard. “The headline is – there are serious risks of discrimination when employers use AI in hiring. You could put anything into that back end: you could put in that you don’t want a woman, or you don’t want anyone over a certain age.” Sheard points out a US discrimination lawsuit where a company had to pay out $US365,000 [about $515,000] in 2023 after configuring its AI to reject women 55 or over and men 60 or over.

And in what Sheard says is an important new study, researchers at the Stanford Digital Economy Lab have found evidence that when large numbers of employers use the same AI hiring systems, the same algorithms can produce repeated outcomes and biases across the labour market, potentially disadvantaging the same kinds of candidates across multiple employers.

Vendors of AI hiring technology counter that the problem is not AI itself but how it is designed and deployed, and that human recruiters can bring their own prejudices to the hiring process. I ask Elle Green, Asia-Pacific head of marketing for the AI hiring platform SmartRecruiters, which is used by organisations including Qantas and the NSW government, about embedded biases in the technology. “That is a definite concern,” Green says. “It’s an area that we certainly haven’t solved for yet as an industry.”

But she adds that not all AI hiring processes are equal; “good AI”, she says, should be transparent and can be trained to remove bias. “Hiring managers are often the blocker when it comes to ageism, for example.”

Green adds that good AI systems offer employers a range of benefits, including attracting a “broader, better-match” candidate pool and speeding up high-volume and repetitive parts of the hiring process such as sorting a large array of applicants and coordinating interviews, allowing recruiters and managers to spend more time on interviews and decision-making: “It’s actually uplifting the recruiter’s human, softer skills.” She also says that well-designed AI systems can go beyond simple keyword matching to identify a candidate’s transferable and related skills – “inferred skills” – that a recruiter scanning a résumé might overlook.

Antony Nardone, founder and director of FourQuarters Recruitment, says the company is using AI as much as possible to make processes more efficient, particularly those related to sorting and filtering candidates. “What we’re also seeing is our clients are investing heavily in using AI tools.” Processes that once took days, he says, can now be completed in minutes.

But AI is a double-edged sword. Recruiters face a new challenge: determining the authenticity of applicants, Nardone says. “It’s harder to distinguish because our candidates are utilising AI themselves for their own applications. AI is still not the perfect tool … it still requires the human element.”

When I ask Phoebe* during our Zoom conversation how she’s feeling about her job search, she pauses to hold back tears, then turns her head away from her screen. She’s swallowing tears. “I promised myself I wouldn’t cry when I was talking to you,” she says. “But it’s really hard to keep going. I won’t lie, you just feel like such a loser.” Since her role as a senior corporate affairs leader for a major multinational company was made redundant at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, Perth-based Phoebe, 53, has found herself in a similar situation to that facing Claudia in Tasmania: she has not been able to find a role to match her international experience and seniority. She has held several roles in the years since, including as the head of an industry association, and now as a corporate affairs consultant, but has earned less than half her previous salary.

Phoebe does a quick count for me while I wait; she lifts her head from a spreadsheet and says she has applied for more than 50 roles since 2023 and had nine interviews. Frequently she doesn’t get a response to her applications, niente, nada, the “ATS black hole”. She applied for a role with the major AI company Anthropic. She received no response. The AI company that can’t get its AI right to send a courteous AI reply.

Phoebe has concluded that the AI systems screen her out early because of her substantial experience and salary expectations and the fact that she has applied for roles in industries other than the one in which she has mostly worked. In such applications, it’s harder for her to include all the keywords listed in job ads. She shrugs: “I thought my skill set was industry-agnostic.”

In any case, wearily resigned to the process, Phoebe uses the mainstream generative AI tool Gemini to help with her applications. “I use it as a thought-starter, or like my study buddy – I ask it loads of questions, like, ‘What are the main challenges in this sector’ or ‘Who are the main stakeholders across this industry?’ ” She also uses AI to tailor her master résumé to specific roles, identify gaps and match keywords between the position description and her application. Aware of AI’s fallibility, she fact-checks anything it feeds her and spends considerable time writing cover letters. It’s an approach that recruiter Stephen Coldicutt would applaud. He believes candidates should do 90 per cent of the work themselves, especially on cover letters which should, he says, “be telling a story”.

Phoebe’s approach might help her stand out amid what recruiters describe as a deluge of AI-written applications; LinkedIn data shows that since late 2022, Australian applicants per role have nearly doubled. “It’s a sea of sameness, you see the same résumé produced by Claude or ChatGPT a hundred thousand times a day, using the same language and listing the same skills,” says Rob Dunderdale, former KPMG Australia head of talent attraction.

But AI specialist Abhijay Arora Vuyyuru does not believe the future of job-hunting lies in ever greater torrents of applications written by Claude or ChatGPT washing into recruiters’ inboxes. Instead, it’s something else altogether.

Enter Mavis, your personal AI job-hunting agent.

“The shift we are seeing is from just a simple prompt that you’d give to ChatGPT to something more complicated where you’re creating an automation that runs at a given time,” says Vuyyuru, who works on AI products at Alphabet-owned YouTube. He became interested in how a job search could be assisted with agentic AI – systems that can plan, act and use tools with some autonomy – after graduating in 2022 from Harvard Business School into what he describes as a “brutal” job market. Frustrated by the time he spent applying for internships, out of curiosity he later built a personal job-hunting agent which can work across a range of job-hunting tasks, from scraping job boards to tailoring résumés.

“I didn’t want anybody else going through that pain,” says Vuyyuru, who writes a Substack newsletter, AI Action Letter and has more than 600,000 followers on Instagram. While initially Vuyyuru imagined his audience was people with sophisticated tech skills, off-the-shelf software including workflow and data-gathering tools are increasingly opening up automation to everyone – “no coding background required”. He believes that, within the next few years, those looking for work who don’t have a personal AI agent will be at a disadvantage because people who do “will be so much more proficient in applying for jobs”.

But Vuyyuru’s predictions don’t stop there. “AI agents are going to be everywhere; it’ll be an interesting space.” He says communication between employers’ AI agents and job-seekers’ AI agents will be “big”.

An absurd future is upon us. Think of it as a case of “I’ll get my AI agent to talk to your AI agent.”

Matt* comes on to my computer screen with a broad smile on his face. I tell him that he looks like he just got a call to say he got the job (he didn’t). “Every day is a wonderful opportunity to meet or exceed customer expectations while delivering outstanding value,” he says. I do a double take, then realise he’s poking fun at management speak.

Until late last year when Brisbane-based Matt, 51, stepped away from work to devote time to his neurodivergent daughter, he had spent nearly two decades in executive positions as an operations expert across a range of companies. He embarked on the process of returning to the workforce about three months ago. The experience, he says, has been “horrible”.

Matt’s big smile fades. He has applied for about 200 jobs and, in some cases, had AI rejections to applications within 30 seconds of submitting them; he’s had to provide his date of birth and refused to do robo-interviews and been ghosted by recruiters. He has developed some strong opinions about younger members of the recruitment industry. “Their understanding is really single- or two-dimensional at best,” he says. “They go, ‘Oh, we spoke to the client and the client said they want XYZ, do you have XYZ on your CV?’ If you don’t have XYZ and you’re not matchy-matchy, you’re not the right person.”

Matt says he can pay the bills for several more months, but the story is more loaded than that. “Financially it’s not bad; it’s the mental stability and … [thinking], ‘I’m not meeting my commitment to my family,’ and that’s really screwing with my psyche.” His wife works but tensions are emerging between them. “As a bloke you’re supposed to be the provider, you’re supposed to be looking after your family,” he says. “It has been quite challenging to the point of like, sometimes it feels better if I’m not here … I’ll just twitch the car off the cliff.”

His comment is a grave reminder of the humanity at the heart of job-seeking. Life stressors run alongside the process, emotions run high, important life decisions go on hold, things go nowhere. One woman I speak to for this story, a lawyer who has been searching for a new job for nearly a year, wants to try to get pregnant. She turns 40 later this year, she can see the clock, but she and her husband’s credit cards are maxed out. Any idea of a baby is on hold. Claudia in Tasmania is increasingly fearful for her government job – “major downsizing” is coming. She would like to buy her own home but her ongoing uncertainty around employment means she can’t even consider it. “It’s definitely not how I thought my life would be,” she says.

Natalie Sheard, the University of Melbourne academic, has interviewed a number of jobseekers for her research. “It brings up a lot of emotions in people,” she says. “It’s like you’re being excluded from society. I think someone actually said, ‘I just want to participate in society, I want to contribute.’ ”

The creeping encroachment of increasingly powerful AI recruitment systems adds a new layer of agony. All this brisk, automated efficiency, hundreds or thousands of human hopefuls sorted, filed, rejected, processed. … There will be a price to pay, on both a societal and individual level.

Ironically, all the job-hunters I’ve interviewed who are dealing with AI recruitment systems say that relationships, human contact, lie at the heart of their work – why they love it, why they’re good at it. “The way I operate, relationships are at the core,” Matt tells me. Amanda Bowler, who as a hairdresser spent her days listening to her clients’ stories with kindness and empathy (who hasn’t poured their heart out to their hairdresser?); Phoebe, whose corporate affairs work relies on her ability to form relationships and collaborate with stakeholders to solve problems or advance opportunities.

Each of them just wants the chance to be seen and heard. Hello! Look over here! I’m here! Listen to what I can tell you! In this new automated job market, that seems almost impossible.

If there is a small shaft of light, it’s that the experts I speak to tell me that the more AI systems are used, the more humans will be needed. For a start, recruiters and career coaches agree that intense networking with other human beings, the a-coffee-date-a-week approach, is still the best way to get a job. “Self-advocacy and personalising your approach to a job search is actually quite a game-changer and takes you out of being part of the mass application pool,” says Jannine Fraser, group CEO of Melbourne-headquartered career transition and coaching specialist Directioneering. Fraser says that if a job-hunter has been out genuinely connecting with people – industry contacts, potential employers, recruiters – they might already have met someone in some position of influence before any job hits the market. “You’ve already had a conversation.”

Conversely, as AI makes it easier for people to misrepresent themselves in their job hunt, humans in positions of authority will be needed to identify the authentic candidates. “This may sound a little bit counter-intuitive, but human relationships will become more and more important,” Abhijay Arora Vuyyuru says. “I would think that a lot of hiring is going to happen in person; a lot of these AI systems are getting so good that [an employer] would want to test whether a person is actually able to think for themselves or has just leveraged AI for their application.”

Rob Dunderdale adds: “If we’ve got AI producing the CV and AI marking the CV, everybody’s going to come out with a five-star rating.” How, he asks, do recruiters and hirers work out where the top talent is, who has the experience a company wants rather than just an AI-manufactured résumé?

Dunderdale is one of many who believes the answer might partly lie in even further AI advances – more precise, more insightful tools that can assess candidates fairly and transparently against an organisation’s values, overlaying a human’s core skills and the transferability of those skills, how they like to work and, even, good grief, who they are as a human. ”I would love to see death to the CV. I think the CV now has had its day,” Dunderdale says. “It’s telling me what you’ve done in the past. It’s not telling me anything about your values, it’s not telling me anything about your potential. It’s not telling me anything about your core skills and the skills that are adjacent to those skills.”

Just before I’m due to submit this article, I get an email from Amanda Bowler. Finally, she found someone to really see her, see past her résumé. Her application made it through to the second round of a process for a role in child protection. A video interview with a human being followed. “I was offered a position,” she wrote. “After all the hard work looking for a career path, something finally came. I was so excited! But then, incredibly, I heard that I’ve been offered a Commonwealth Supported Place! It will save me so much money. … I turned the job down and I’m going back to uni to do my masters.”

*Some names have been changed.

Lifeline: 13 11 14.

Police arrest seven more men in aftermath of deadly A66 crash

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 22:00:46 GMT

Cleveland police say a total of 24 people arrested in investigation after crash that killed two officers

Seven more men have been arrested as part of an operation tackling alleged organised crime after the head-on crash on the A66 that resulted in seven deaths, Cleveland police have said.

Officers said four men, aged 21, 25, 35 and 40, were being held on suspicion of criminal damage with intent to endanger life after a vehicle crashed into a house in Steele Crescent, Middlesbrough.

They were also being questioned over alleged arson after a caravan was set alight in Atlee Road on Wednesday morning, and over a drug offence.

The force said the men were in a vehicle when they were stopped by police in Kingsley Road in Grangetown on Thursday night.

Class A drugs were seized, officers confirmed.

The three other men arrested were a 23-year-old man, on suspicion of threats to kill, a 42-year-old on suspicion of threats to kill and possession of criminal property, and a 30-year-old on suspicion of possession of criminal property.

All three have been released on conditional bail.

It brings the total number of people arrested since the crash to 24.

Earlier on Friday, detectives confirmed they were not linking a house fire that killed a seven-year-old girl and her aunt to the A66 crash, which left two police officers and five young men dead.

Hundreds of extra police officers have been drafted in to support officers after a series of incidents in the Middlesbrough and County Durham area.

Inquests have been formally opened into the deaths of the seven people in the crash in the early hours of 22 August. The two police officers who died were PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38.

The Teesside area coroner, Paul Appleton, said that there was a collision at South Bank between a police vehicle and a Volkswagen Passat.

He said the provisional cause of death for Blades was head and neck injuries and for Clough was neck injuries.

Later, inquests were opened and adjourned into the deaths of the Passat occupants, named as Cole Worthy and Theo Rae, both 17, Makai Saddington, 18, and 23-year-olds Michael Robert Cahill and Jacob Matusiak.

Police initially arrested 17 people after the crash, which followed a police pursuit, as part of an investigation into alleged organised crime.

Cleveland police assistant chief constable Wayne Fox said of the latest arrests: “This latest disruptive activity now brings the total number of arrests to 24 since the investigation commenced.

“Several suspects arrested throughout the course of this week have been charged with serious offences and a number of offenders have been recalled to prison.”

On Friday, Cleveland police said Kai Inico, who was arrested on Monday on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group, had been charged with possession with intent to supply a class B drug.

The force said four other people arrested on Monday had been bailed – a 16-year-old boy and 18-year-old man arrested on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group, a 55-year-old man arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender, and a 23-year-old man arrested on suspicion of threats to kill.

Earlier this week, two other people were charged with offences and appeared in court.

Meanwhile, two men have been arrested on suspicion of murder in connection with the fire which killed Natalie McDonald, 34, and seven-year-old Valentina Foster, as well as injuring four others, in Grangetown.

Matt Storey, the police and crime commissioner for Cleveland, said on Friday: “After what has been the most tragic week in its history, I want to extend my heartfelt thanks to local residents for the outpouring of love and support they have shown to Cleveland police.

“My thoughts remain with the family, friends and colleagues of PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough. They will be remembered as selfless, professional and courageous police officers, dedicated to serving their communities.”

Large fire near Wembley Stadium disrupts tube and rail services

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 21:47:05 GMT

About 125 firefighters tackle blaze at Neasden waste facility as nearby Amazon warehouse is evacuated

A large fire has broken out at a waste facility close to Wembley Stadium in north-west London, disrupting tube and train lines in the area.

Twenty fire engines and about 125 firefighters were sent to tackle the blaze at a mixed-waste facility on an industrial estate in Neasden, less than a mile from the venue.

There was no service on the entire Metropolitan line, which runs close to the blaze, and no service between Wembley Park and West Hampstead on the Jubilee line, with severe delays on the rest of the line, Transport for London said.

Rail services into London Marylebone were also disrupted.

A nearby Amazon warehouse, separate from the industrial unit involved, has been evacuated, according to PA Media.

A London fire brigade assistant commissioner, Andy Pennick, said: “The brigade was called at 11.36[am] to reports of a fire on Hannah Close, Neasden. Upon arrival, firefighters were met by a well-developed fire involving a waste transfer facility.

“Recognising the scale of the fire, the initial officer in attendance immediately requested 20 fire engines be mobilised to the scene.

“An industrial unit, approximately 100 metres by 150 metres, was alight. At the height of the fire around 125 firefighters were in attendance.”

Pennick added: “This is a protracted incident that will see crews on scene for the remainder of the day as they work to fully extinguish the fire.”

LFB earlier said that the blaze was under control by about 5pm. Its cause was not yet known and was under investigation, the LFB added.

St Helens playoff hopes hang by a thread after thrashing by Leeds

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 21:20:18 GMT

St Helens 6-34 Leeds

Rhinos return to top of table after running in six tries

If you needed any further proof that Super League’s two most successful sides are travelling in opposite directions in 2026, this was about as conclusive as it can get.

There are two very different fates awaiting Leeds and St Helens in three weeks or so. The Rhinos will now almost certainly be resting before a Super League playoff semi-final, having earned a bye through the opening week of the playoffs by virtue of a top-two finish. They are still favourites to end the regular season on top after this latest impressive victory.

But Saints, barring a late miraculous run of results involving themselves and the teams around them, will be resting and preparing for 2027, with their 60-year record of making the end-of-season playoffs coming to a screeching halt. After back-to-back wins in the past fortnight, you wondered if this was the night that St Helens could really make people sit up and take notice.

Win here, and they would not only dent Leeds’ chances of the League Leaders’ Shield, but they would put themselves right back in the mix for the top six. Instead, what we saw was an 80 minutes very much played out to the form of 2026 as a whole. Rhinos were impressive, Jake Connor was sensational yet again, and Saints disappointed.

With two rounds to go, Leeds can now look ahead to what is effectively a decider for top spot next Saturday against Wigan. St Helens, in all probability, have to win their last two games and win them well to stand any chance of making the playoffs. This season has presented enough evidence to suggest they simply will not be able to do that.

They huffed and puffed all evening to little avail and, when the big moments arrived, Leeds handed out a lesson in how to attack with the precision and style befitting of a team that will be in the mix for the Grand Final. St Helens, ultimately, are a team not good enough to be mentioned in the same breath.

Connor pulled strings to devastating effect, as he has done all year. It would be a travesty at this stage if, after being overlooked for last year’s Ashes, he is left out of the travelling squad for this autumn’s World Cup. He was hugely influential in Leeds moving into a commanding 18-0 lead by the break, and Rhinos did not relent after half-time, nor did their talisman.

It was Connor’s inch-perfect pass for Chris Hankinson that broke the deadlock and while Saints survived a 10-minute period with Daniel Suluka-Fifita in the sin-bin, that period took the wind from their sails. Leeds then took full advantage as the hosts wilted with half-time approaching, scoring twice in six minutes.

Cameron Smith produced a sublime solo effort to double Leeds’ advantage before Connor again produced the decisive pass, this time for Harry Newman to score. Saints simply had to score first after half-time, but their attacking prowess in key moments failed them. That meant that Leeds were able to respond through Ryan Hall’s try to make it 22-0 and kill it as a contest.

Jack Welsby at least ensured Saints would not fail to score on home soil when he broke from deep to touch down, but normal service was soon resumed. The hosts knocked on from the following set after Welsby’s try, with a kick from Connor – who else – being grounded by the Rhinos captain, Ash Handley.

Connor’s boot then caused mayhem among the St Helens defence again to allow his half-back partner, Brodie Croft, to score his 28th try of the season. That made it 34-6 but by then, the home support had already begun to filter away. Their season is ebbing away and is almost over, but in truth, Leeds’ may just be beginning.

Milo Yiannopoulos, a far-right political commentator, detained by ICE

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 21:13:39 GMT

A former editor of Breitbart News, Yiannopoulos has also served as an intern for Marjorie Taylor Greene

Milo Yiannopoulos, a far-right British political commentator, was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Louisiana, according to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

In a statement on Friday, a DHS spokesperson said that Yiannopoulos was arrested on Thursday at the Louis Armstrong New Orleans international airport (MSY). The spokesperson said Yiannopoulos “legally entered the country” in May 2019, but that “he chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws”.

The spokesperson said Yiannopoulos was issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge on 22 July, “after failing to show up for his immigration hearing”.

“He will remain in ICE custody pending removal,” the spokesperson added. “This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport.”

As of Friday afternoon, Yiannopoulos is listed in ICE’s online detainee database as being in “ICE Custody”. The database states that he was born in the United Kingdom, but it does not disclose any additional details, including where he is being held.

The statement comes as multiple outlets reported on Friday that Yiannopoulos had been detained in Louisiana. Fox News reported that Yiannopoulos is currently detained in Alexandria, Lousiana.

Yiannopoulos, a former editor of Breitbart News, previously served as an intern for Marjorie Taylor Greene, a former US representative, in 2022, and also worked on the 2024 White House campaign of Ye, formerly known as Kanye West. It is unclear why Yiannopoulos might have been in Louisiana, but Ye is scheduled to perform in New Orleans on Friday night.

Last year, in posts on social media, Yiannopoulos had been supportive of immigration enforcement in the US.

“California needs ICE checkpoints at supermarket entrances, gas stations, strip malls, intersections and government buildings, with on the spot deportation for anyone who can’t prove they are in the US legally,” he wrote in a social media post in June 2025.

On social media on Friday, Laura Loomer, the far-right activist and ally of Donald Trump, claimed credit for Yiannopoulos’s detention and wrote that she had previously reported him to ICE.

The Rainmaker review – please don’t hurt your eyes trying to find anything good in this legal drama

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 21:00:08 GMT

From dialogue so hokey it could be printed on a tea towel to mind-numbing storylines – how can a glossy take on John Grisham’s novel about a fiery law graduate be so tedious?

The Rainmaker was once merely an average film about lawyers starring Matt Damon. Now, thanks to the magic of television, it’s a below-average series about lawyers starring a man who looks like Matt Damon. This is one Milo Callaghan, whose jawline suggests a certain mettle, but whose acting suggests much woe. Or at least a fitful unease with the role in which he finds himself. Accordingly, he drifts around this 10-part John Grisham adaptation with the air of a man who has forgotten what he came into the courtroom for, certain only that whatever it was, it was not a drama that compels him to say things like: “Ah just wanna be a lawyer.”

Callaghan plays Rudy Baylor, an ambitious South Carolina law graduate with a social conscience and a thirst for justice. Rudy wants to make a difference but dammit if his fiery temper don’t keep conspirin’ to screw up his plans. The huffing greenhorn is even late for his first day at prestigious law firm Tinley Britt, having spent the morning hurling his mom’s lunkish boyfriend around the garden (“You think ah’m gonna let you keep leechin’ off ma mother? Gnyaaarrr!”).

Insouciant new boss Leo F Drummond (Mad Men’s John Slattery) promptly fires the sod. “I am the punishment of God,” he drawls, gliding around the boardroom like a shaved eagle on castors. “If you had not committed great sins, God would not have sent a punishment like me upon you.” A smirk. “Genghis Khan. Warrior. Would’ve made a great litigator.”

Alas, this is the sort of programme that equates tea-towel quotations with gravitas, and we must endure several more such guffstorms as the series progresses. (Or rather, as the series goes on. “Progresses” feels too optimistic a term for a drama that features the line, “This kid’s got balls.”)

Unlike the 1995 novel from which it takes (some of) its characters and (fewer of) its themes, The Rainmaker is a startlingly uncomplicated affair. This is not the type of legal drama in which characters harbour tortuous secrets and plots contort themselves into unexpected shapes. This is not The Good Fight, or Suits, or Damages, or even Boston Legal, the sporadically magnificent mid-00s comedy-drama in which an empurpled William Shatner puffed and rumbled like the world’s cheeriest internal organ. Instead, it’s a straightforwardly soapy affair, a glossy show-and-tell in which linear storytelling is soundtracked by incessant MOR country-rock and characters are introduced with lines such as: “You’re Wilfred Keeley, CEO of Great Benefit Hospital Systems, one of Tinley Britt’s most important clients!”

The plot? If we must. Having been booted out of Tinley Britt, Baylor washes up at a one-horse personal injury firm operating out of an abandoned taco joint. Here he finds sassy maverick Joceyln “Bruiser” Stone (Lana Parrilla), who does her bit for feminism by hoisting her bosom nostrilwards and refusing to pay Baylor a living wage. His first case? An unlawful death suit that will offer the hothead a chance to subject The Man to the full force of his pleated chinos. Unfortunately, it will also pit him against both his former boss and his lawyer girlfriend (“What happens when Leo finds out my boyfriend is suing his prize client?!”) – but them’s the judicial breaks, kid. And so forth.

It’s peculiar, in this day and age, to find a series so wilfully devoid of depth, authenticity and nuance. So much so that you may find yourself initially denying The Rainmaker’s pounding simplicity, assuming that if you squint for long enough, interesting things will start to appear, emerging as if from a magic eye picture composed solely of gavels and shouting. But no. It’s tedious. Baylor’s boohoo backstory is revealed in the first few minutes (his brother died before he could fulfil his dream of bein’ a lawyer) and everything from motivation to the identity of the baddies is spelled out in 800pt HOPE YOU’RE GETTING ALL THIS AT THE BACK typeface.

Will Baylor stop punchin’ and start litigatin’? And thus, in turn, start livin’? The answer is yawnin’ in the wind.

The Rainmaker is available on ITVX in the UK, Peacock in the US and Stan in Australia

Cherki and Haaland double up in Manchester City cruise at Crystal Palace

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 20:59:41 GMT

All who attend the Rayan Cherki show know the ticket comes with a guarantee of entertainment. Enzo Maresca, a manager famed for his obsessive positional control, does not need to put limits on the Manchester City wizard. Cherki has to feel free and he was at his creative best against Crystal Palace, who were in this game before City’s creative heartbeat took it away from them in the second half.

It has been a fine start to the former Lyon player’s second year in England. Cherki was inspired against Bournemouth last week, coming off the bench to spark City’s fightback from 1-0 down with two assists, and this was better. The Frenchman scored twice and the first, a little prod with the outside of his left foot after a mazy run, left you wondering if you have seen something like it before.

Palace, stuck on zero points despite fleeting signs of encouragement in Pierre Sage’s first two outings, had no answer to Cherki’s magic. He is an irrepressible talent and a deep thinker. Listening to the post-match plaudits, Cherki smiled, shrugged and said his performance in the first half was “so shit”. Maresca, though, had a different view.

“His performance for me was very good, not because of the two goals, but the way he worked off the ball,” City’s manager said. “He has to press. His game was complete. He loves football. We know how good he is. We know the quality he has.”

Cherki was not alone in starring for City. Phil Foden impressed and Erling Haaland, who is up and running for the season, grabbed an emphatic double in a performance strong enough to make Maresca think his post-Pep team have moved on from their Community Shield debacle. “We struggled the first five, 10 minutes, because we were pressing in the wrong way,” the Italian said. “After that we were in control.”

A challenge for Maresca is working with an incomplete midfield following the exits of Rodri and Bernardo Silva. Ayyoub Bouaddi has arrived from Lille, £86m an eye-catching fee for an 18-year-old after his exploits for Morocco at the World Cup, but there is room for one more. Enzo Fernández, desperate to leave Chelsea, is the top target before Tuesday’s deadline.

Not that anyone is going to argue that City are short on midfield options. Maresca, ever the tinkerer, shuffled the pack again. The experiment with Marc Guéhi in the engine room was discontinued, allowing him to slot into central defence against his old side. The £116m Elliot Anderson was the sole pivot, Nico O’Reilly pushed high in a 4-1-4-1 system and Josko Gvardiol inverted from left-back, much like Marc Cucurella in Maresca’s Chelsea side.

There are subtle tweaks to the Guardiola template, though some things never change. City led through a familiar source in the 17th minute, Antoine Semenyo crossing from the left and Haaland finding space to loop a clever header over Dean Henderson.

The defending was poor from Palace, who have had an uncertain summer. They were arranged in familiar fashion, Sage sticking with Oliver Glasner’s 3-4-2-1, but some key faces have gone and others were missing.

Jørgen Strand Larsen led the line in the absence of the wantaway Jean-Philippe Mateta, who may be out for four weeks. Ismaïla Sarr, keen to join Galatasaray, was unavailable and Daniel Muñoz was on the bench amid suggestions of interest from Nottingham Forest. Frailties were inevitable. The defence has lost Maxence Lacroix, sold to Chelsea. Anderson, Semenyo and Foden had chances before half-time. “You saw how we want to play until the 65th minute,” Sage said. “We trust in our process.”

Sage likes to play on the front foot. Adam Wharton, subject of a failed enquiry from City recently, swept a ball through for Eddie Nketiah to test Gianluigi Donnarumma in the second minute. Daichi Kamada went close and Tyrick Mitchell fluffed a header after more enterprising play from Wharton.

Palace lacked incision, Nketiah missing again early in the second half. City pressed, O’Reilly and Foden hustling Kamada. Foden advanced and Cherki took over. The Frenchman danced in from the left, danger rising as he wriggled into the area. A host of Palace defenders were thrown off balance, unable to live with Cherki’s footwork and close control. Expect the unexpected. Cherki floated past Jaydee Canvot and held off Chris Richards. For a moment the ball seemed stuck under his feet but he used Takehiro Tomiyasu as a shield and unveiled a finish that was less poke and more dab, Henderson rooted to the spot as the ball rolled tantalisingly over the line.

Palace quickly grabbed a lifeline, Yéremy Pino’s free-kick hitting the woodwork and bouncing in off Donarumma for an own goal, but Cherki was in his element. He scored again in the 59th minute, a fierce shot from 20 yards deceiving Henderson after flicking off Richards.

City sent Bouaddi on for his debut, Anderson withdrawn. They wanted more. Foden, catching the eye in front of Thomas Tuchel, released Haaland. The Norwegian, who has scored in all six of his league games against Palace, was never going to miss.

Spencer Jones: Dogs review – barking comic sniffs out community through canines

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 19:00:05 GMT

Pleasance Dome, EdinburghBehind this grab-bag of papier-mache heads and walkies banter lies a celebration of simply talking to one another

First came Ricky Gervais’s cynical cats; now here are Spencer Jones’s optimistic Dogs. One was tawdry, the other couldn’t be sweeter, as the prop-comic delivers this hymn to the canine-human relationship. Like much of Jones’s work, it’s a grab-bag, as he circles seemingly at random between character comedy in papier-mache heads, loop-pedal nonsense and dopey dog-walking business with an animatronic mutt. Not all of it is dog-related. And yet, it adds up to something winning, as Jones leads his four-legged friends towards a closing message about social cohesion in acrimonious times – and how our pets can help.

It begins as a chat with the audience about their animals, with Jones poshing it up in character as a snobby dog-walker. One strand of the show, taking as its motto the question “Aren’t humans weird?”, functions as a gleeful anthropology of dog owners. They carry bags of poo by their sides. They lose control of their hounds, and in that panic reveal their true selves. Their armoury includes something resembling a ladle – cueing, apropos of nothing, a very funny sequence in which Jones, in horsey false teeth, samples soup supposedly cooked by his audience.

And crucially, they talk to one another – which might just save us, says Jones, in a homily bolted on to the end of his show. Coming from this performer, who radiates innocent idealism even at 50, you might even believe it. And if not, there’s still the pleasure of an hour spent celebrating the inner child, and spirit of play, in all of us. Highlights here, as Jones bounds way beyond the limits of his theme, include the tale of a brutal parental separation as seen through the eyes of an unwitting kid, and a chat between two blokes competing to suspend the most ash from the end of their ciggies.

There are arguably too many instances when Jones displays then abandons an idea (“I haven’t got any material for that …”) rather than develops it. I accepted that, finally, as part of the bricolage appeal of this very charming hour, a scrapbook full of wonky images of dogs, their owners and much else besides.
