‘The flood took everything I have’: survivors grieve for relatives and homes swept away in Nepal

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 18:22:00 GMT

Army helicopters ferry survivors from inaccessible areas to a camp at a barracks in Bidur

The three women sat together in the army tent and wept. They cried out for their sons, their husbands, their homes. As flash floods coursed through the Himalayan mountains on Wednesday morning, a monstrous black wave took everything from them.

More than 1,900 people are missing and at least 579 are dead after part ⁠of a glacier crashed on to the valley floor in the Langtang national park. Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian

More than 1,900 people are missing and at least 579 are dead after part ⁠of a glacier crashed on to the valley floor in the Langtang national park. Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian

Keep scrolling

As a melting glacier high up in the Himalayas between Tibet and Nepal splintered and crashed into the valley below, it set off a deadly cascade of water, mud and debris down the Bhote Koshi River. The impact of the glacier collapse was so strong that experts initially reported it as an earthquake. The Nepali village homes that lined the riverbank and clung to the mountainside stood little chance.

The glacier impact set off a deadly cascade along the Bhote Khoshi River. Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian

The glacier impact set off a deadly cascade along the Bhote Khoshi River. Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian

Keep scrolling

Sangke Dolma Tamang, 61, had been cheerily cooking snacks in her village of Mailung in the Rasuwa district when the floods came without warning. The whole family ran uphill for safety, but as she grabbed for her husband, he slipped from her grip and was washed into the dark, fast-moving waters.

“Others tried to pull him to safety, but the flood swept him away,” she said, tears rolling down her weathered cheeks. There was, she said, nothing left of her village now. She had spent a night sheltering on higher ground, until an army helicopter arrived and brought to her safety at the barracks. Her son too was missing since the disaster, and she waited anxiously for any news.

“Now I have nothing left to live for,” said Tamang. “The whole house is gone. We couldn’t salvage anything.”

Two days after the disaster, at least 579 people have been confirmed dead and more than 1,900 are still missing, the numbers rising by the day. Many in Nepal fear that the true scale of the disaster has yet to emerge, as the worst-hit areas in districts such as Rusawa are only accessible by helicopter. The situation remains even more opaque in Tibet, which is under tight Chinese media control. Though it was at the centre of the disaster, Chinese authorities insist only five people there have died.

In the army barracks in the town of Bidur, where Nepal’s rescue efforts were being coordinated, helicopters carrying those rescued from flooded areas continued to arrive every few minutes, while others carrying vital supplies of food and clean water flew out and high up into the mountains.

On Friday morning, ground rescue efforts were halted over fears that the river levels were rising once again. But the Nepali army spokesperson, Brig Gen Raja Ram Basnet, said the helicopter rescues would continue for as long as people were missing. He accepted that the death toll was hard to calculate. “Right now, our focus is mostly on finding the living,” he said.

Among those recently brought to safety was 60-year-old Murali Maiya Tamang, who had been in Rusawa and was found hanging in a tree. As the flash floods came down the valley, she had watched as her house was washed clean away. She convulsed with tears as she waited desperately for news of her son, who was in their village when the floods struck and has been missing since.

Rescuers found Murali Maiya Tamang, 60, hanging in a tree after her house was washed away. Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian

Rescuers found Murali Maiya Tamang, 60, hanging in a tree after her house was washed away. Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian

Keep scrolling

“My husband had already died in Nepal’s 2015 earthquake,” she said. “Now this flood has taken away the only son I had left. I am all alone now. What is the point of living now?”

Many in the barracks waited of news of their fathers, brothers and husbands who had been working on vast hydroelectric projects along the Bhote Koshi River, many of which were washed away and the tunnels filled with mud. On Friday, footage showed rescuers pulling some workers to safety from within the tunnels.

A few miles from the army barracks stood the remains of the town of Bidur, on the banks of the Trishuli River. It was one of the last towns to be hit by the flash floods, but it took just a few minutes for it to be reduced to mangled debris. The ruins of a bank, a government office and an ATM booth stood still half submerged in mud. Rescuers said there were bodies buried inside, but it was still too dangerous and the terrain too unstable to collect them.

On Friday afternoon, Nepal’s newly elected home minister, Sudan Gurung, surveyed the damage. “It is so sad to see such a heavy loss of human lives,” he told the Guardian. “Our priority right now is rescuing people. We are searching for everyone who is still missing, assuming that they are all alive. We are searching for everyone, whether they are Nepali citizens or international nationals.”

Dozens of local people made attempts to return to the site of their homes, in a bid to collect any remnant of their lives. Most just found a deep abyss of mud. Picking through the deep mud and devastation of the town, Ashok Chaurasia, a shopkeeper, said he had heard the terrifying roar of the water before he saw it. The dark muddy waters already snapped at his heels as they ran uphill for safety, a bridge over the river collapsing behind them. He survived by just 20 seconds, clinging on to the wall of a monastery for dear life. His nephew and his sister-in-law were not so lucky.

Yet even as he blessed his survival, he wept at his losses. “We had a three-storey house here, and now there isn’t even a single brick left,” he said. “Nothing can be seen. We have nothing to eat or wear. The flood took everything I have.”

Olé for Robinson as England take firm control of Lord’s Test against Pakistan

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 18:06:46 GMT

Second Test, day two: England 290 & 81-3; Pakistan 110

Ollie Robinson takes 4 for 11; Jofra Archer picks up three

Joe Root did not want the England captaincy when it started to be floated earlier this summer. After performing the role as a stand-in for the suspended Ben Stokes against New Zealand at the Oval, his father, Matt, asked about a full-time return as a hypothetical and has since said this was met with a “no”.

Root was apparently then swayed by the impending arrival of Stephen Fleming as head coach, with the pair speaking regularly before roles were finally locked down. But watching this one-sided second day against Pakistan at Lord’s – and, indeed, the one-sided series opener at Headingley – one wonders whether being handed the keys to this pace attack was just as much of a clincher.

This has clearly been a stressful week for Root, with the needless Brydon Carse affair dominating the buildup and serving as an early reminder about the curve balls a Test captain can face. As per his old man, Root spent “four hours” on the phone last Sunday dealing with the fallout when he was meant to be relaxing at a family lunch. He was still thoroughly unhappy about it at his pre-match press conference two days later which, given his usual cheery disposition, said plenty.

All that anger appeared to melt away at Lord’s on Friday, however, when, with 290 first-innings runs on the board after some tailend swish in the morning, Root’s attack unstitched Pakistan’s gun-shy batting lineup once more. Ollie Robinson claimed a remarkable four for 11 from 13 overs, Jofra Archer three for 26 from 11.2. The visitors were bowled out for 110 to ship a 180-run deficit – with England stretching this to 261, three wickets down, before bad light brought stumps.

There is a danger of getting carried away, of course, with Pakistan a struggling Test side and a calf injury sustained by Imam-ul-Haq on day one leaving only nine wickets to claim. The only real positive on the green side of the ledger was the 21-year-old opener Azan Awais holding firm for just shy of three hours while his colleagues folded inside 38 overs. The left-hander eventually holed out off Robinson for 46 once a diplodocus tail had begun but showed guts against Archer’s pace.

Yet for all that at times it was fish-in-a-barrel stuff – ideal bowling conditions thanks to cloud cover and a pitch that, while slow, offered nip – it feels reasonable to say that better teams could well have struggled also. Jimmy Anderson and Stuart Broad may have ridden off into the sunset – their portrait now greets dismissed batters on their way back into the pavilion – but a potent new attack is forming.

Plenty went back to the 14.1 overs that England sent down before lunch. With Root marshalling things from his new position at mid-off (or occasionally joining the catchers) it was a straitjacket of line bowling by Robinson from the Nursery End, allied with the heat of Archer from the other. Crucially, there was next to no let-up when Gus Atkinson and Josh Tongue eventually slid in to replace them.

Tongue’s removal of Abdullah Shafique brought about the interval and Pakistan, 16 for two after an hour-long ordeal, had gone the square root of nowhere. Archer had earlier nicked off the footwork-devoid Shan Masood and repeatedly breached the 90mph mark. Jamie Smith also continued his promising summer with the gloves, be it stood up to Robinson or back deeper for the quicker men.

Buoyed by a career-best unbeaten 30 in the morning, Tongue resumed things in the afternoon and made light work of Babar Azam when an ambitious drive flew into the cordon on eight. Though Tongue then started to leak runs by trying to entice further repeats, Root was simply able to whistle for the refreshed Robinson to shut things down with another stifling burst of 76mph wobblers.

Having conceded only seven runs from his initial six-over spell, Robinson’s next set of seven cost a mere four and sent as many batters on their way. Saud Shakeel and Mohammad Rizwan were both caged in by Smith’s proximity behind the stumps and trapped lbw after smart reviews from Root. And two balls before Awais fell in search of his half-century, Khurram Shahzad poked to slip.

Interspersed was the sight of Archer castling Ali Usman and Mohammad Abbas, with Atkinson the one bowler left wicketless. This may in part be down to a change of role this summer, with Atkinson having been elbowed out of new ball duties. Still, his 45 from No 8, and the early stand of 47 alongside Tongue, meant the quietest member of Root’s quartet still had something to be chipper about.

The value of those runs increased early in England’s second innings when Ben Duckett chipped Shahzad to mid-off for one and Jordan Cox, lbw for eight, handed Shahzad a second. But alongside Emilio Gay, who battled to 30 not out, Root settled things down to take England close to a first series win for 18 months.

Beyond the annoyance of Carse, Root’s chief issue is a growing pattern of falling over the ball and being pinned lbw. It happened again on 26 inside the final hour of the day, with Mohammad Ali the man to strike. But with the lead already looking plenty for his hungry attack to work with, this was far from a knockout blow.

Dads and dudes: the two style clans that dominate menswear

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 18:03:37 GMT

The ‘dad’ look favours straight lines and muted colours, while ‘dudes’ prefer baggier clothes with adornments

There is a competition going on at the US Open this week and it’s not the one involving rackets and balls. Instead, leading men who are not entered into this year’s draw are serving looks rather than aces.

Tennis legend Roger Federer took to the court on Tuesday in navy blue polo shirt and shorts, navy blue sweatbands and navy blue socks. The cuts were trim and the top was tucked in. The young Spanish player Carlos Alcaraz wore a Nike vest, untucked and the colour of Ribena, maroon shorts, and trainers that looked like a sweetshop counter.

The players represent two style clans that are dominating current menswear: the dads and the dudes. If you’re not sure what side of the sartorial net they’re on, here’s a quick form guide. Novak Djokovic, Taylor Fritz and Félix Auger-Aliassime are all “dads”, while Arthur Fils and Andre Agassi are “dudes”.

Away from baselines and backhands, David Beckham in his slim, sometimes three-piece suits, actor Theo James, in real life as well as in Netflix series The Gentleman, the second series of which will land next week, Idris Elba and Andy Burnham are all prime examples of “dads”.

Dudes, meanwhile, include Brad Pitt, who appears on the cover of September’s Esquire in a red shirt with hot-pink neckerchief, Adam Sandler in chaotic ensembles, and men across Britain.

The “dad” look, which has nothing to do with paternal status, is summed up by straight, tight lines, on the whole more muted colours and embellishment for practicality’s sake – a carefully placed sweatband for a tennis player, a pair of neat little cufflinks on a suit. What it is not, says men’s fashion editor Hikmat Mohammed, “is just your dad who wears normcore. It’s an elevated dad … they wear Ralph Lauren, they wear Brunello Cucinelli, they wear Loro Piana.” Or, if thousand-pound price tags aren’t in reach, they wear Cos and Arket.

Mohammed cites Mark Zuckerberg in caramel-hued cashmere on the Prada front row earlier this year as “dad”. But it’s trickled down to the latest John Lewis menswear lookbook, which is full of sensible overcoats, cashmere cardigans and argyle knits. According to Jacqui Markham, fashion creative director, “a lot of what we’re calling ‘dad style’ is really just great menswear fundamentals rediscovered, after a few years of fashion having moved so fast in the other direction.” Searches for “elevated wardrobe staples” have increased significantly this season, she says – “polo shirts with proper collars, chinos that actually fit, the perfect cut blazer”. Plus “sales of tailoring are up 17% so far this year, making it one of our fastest-growing menswear categories right now.” In high fashion, one of the biggest recent menswear launches also offers up dad style in spades: the luxury label Toteme’s first foray into men’s clothes.

Dudes wear things baggier, have adornments for adornment’s sake – a backwards cap or a chunky chain. It’s an atmosphere that has seen the late Bill Oddie hailed a style icon. But the patron saint of the style is the aforementioned Sandler, who in 2019 was declared a fashion icon for his unapologetic “grocery-run look” by Vogue writer Liana Satenstein.

Influences on the “dude” look include Justin Bieber and his brand Skylrk, which launched last year and sells baggy hoodies and baggy shorts. “It’s more street wear. It’s more relaxed, it’s more fun, it’s more colourful,” says Mohammed. “They have more camouflage. It’s, like, Chrome Hearts,” he says, referring to the LA brand beloved of Timothée Chalamet (in his current iteration: a “dude”). “The ‘dude’ maybe not stoner, but they’ll take a gummy here and there.”

The rise of the so-called “schlub hub” – men who dress as slobs relative to their maximalist, often very on-social media partners – shows that neither does marital status (Bieber, who became a meme for his hoodie and Crocs, worn alongside his wife in a red evening dress, is the prime example). While it can be about age, it’s not about age: “dudes” Pitt and Bieber are 62 and 32 respectively. Luca Guadagnino-favoured actor Drew Starkey (a “dad”) is 32. According to Ben Hewitt, brand director at men’s tailoring brand Hawes & Curtis: “The real shift towards ‘dad style’ is no longer generational, it’s about intentional dressing, whether dressing for the working week or downtime.”

Sign up to Fashion Statement

Style, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solved

after newsletter promotion

It isn’t, of course, a binary: Harry Styles, whose 30-show run at Madison Square Garden began this week, wears “dad”-style togs but with a “dude” energy (see the cut of his suits, the billowing white shirts), plus “dude”-style togs with “dad” energy (see short-shorts with sensible loafers). JFK Jr, who recently re-dominated the zeitgeist thanks to Love Story, was both. For Hikmat Mohammed, who says he is more dude in summer, “dad” in winter: “JFK Jr out of hours was dude but when he was working that was ‘dad’.”

Why are these style camps so prevalent now? The march of the dad has been happening for a while: in 2019 the New York Times Style Magazine heralded “The Unstoppable Rise of the Zaddy,” meaning an older man with impeccable style. Mohammed thinks it could be a recession indicator: “People just want a full look that’s clear and really sharp,” he says. It is also a case of the slower menswear cycle playing out: “I feel like finally the quiet luxury that womenswear had is finally catching up to men.”

Plus, actual dads became a menswear inspiration. As the writer Jason Diamond wrote in The Cut this week: “Just a few years ago, there was the idea of a stereotypical dad look that usually included denim shorts, New Balance sneakers, wearing socks with sandals, and higher-rise, more-relaxed jeans. Then, in one of the oddest cases of cultural appropriation, style-conscious and young people started borrowing those looks and making them their own.”

For dudes, it helps that menswear in recent years has become more interesting in general, and men, from Colman Domingo to your colleagues, have perhaps felt more comfortable to experiment. The perfect example is Daniel Craig, known as a sharp-suited, small-c conservative dresser (“dad”), he caused a stir with a run of chaotic styling in tandem with becoming the face of Loewe, then under JW Anderson, in 2024. He became fully dude.

But who feels comfortable – and who is able – to dress like a dude is complicated. There’s a privilege to being able to present so baggily. Plus, “it’s more expensive to dress ‘dude’,” says Mohammed. Dude-style streetwear can take a lot of searching for, and can cost far more than a shirt and chinos, especially some of the rare, vintage stuff, which “[has] almost become memorabilia. It’s like having a blue chip painting in your house.” It’s not, says Mohammed, “like a grey suit [that] you can buy in Reiss or M&S.”

Drumcree ruling raises fears of sectarian confrontation in Northern Ireland

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 17:11:03 GMT

High court quashes latest restriction on Orange Order march, reigniting political row over Garvaghy Road

The boiling cauldron known as Drumcree that used to scald and torment Northern Ireland each summer gradually cooled two decades ago, leaving it as a name for the history books.

Instead of pitched battles between Orangemen and police around the parish church near Portadown in County Armagh, and the murderous sectarian violence they triggered across the region, gave way to a de facto truce.

The Orange Order still wished to march down Garvaghy Road in the run-up to 12 July celebrations – a route opposed by the mainly Catholic residents – but its members no longer tried to storm lines of police who dug trenches and erected barbed wire to stop them.

Fury dwindled after 1998, when the mayhem threatened the nascent Good Friday agreement, and the Orangemen settled for annual peaceful, ritualised protests.

However, a court ruling this week ignited a political row over Drumcree and raised the spectre of renewed confrontation next July.

On Tuesday, the high court in Belfast quashed the latest in a series of determinations that have prevented the march from proceeding down Garvaghy Road since 1998. The commission accepted that its decision-making process had been flawed. Billy Gamble, one of six commissioners, resigned.

Unionist parties hailed the ruling as an overdue comeuppance for a statutory body that adjudicates on contentious marches. Gavin Robinson, the Democratic Unionist party leader, said: “The outcome of the legal challenge is a totemic victory, which has laid bare why confidence in the Parades Commission has collapsed within the unionist community.”

Nationalist politicians, in contrast, expressed foreboding.

Michelle O’Neill, the Sinn Féin first minister, visited Garvaghy Road and said residents feared a return to the violence of the 1990s. “Does anybody really want to see those days? This community certainly doesn’t. I certainly do not want to see those days visited upon us and I think the question here is: for the leaders of unionism, why do they want us to revisit those dark days?”

The dispute centres on the legitimacy and workings of the Parades Commission. It adjudicates on thousands of marches each year and is credited with a dramatic reduction in parade-related disorder, but unionists have long alleged bias.

The Orange Order accused the commission of a “copy and paste” response in refusing applications and of overlooking the order’s willingness to engage with communities that oppose certain marches.

Last month, a Portadown Orangeman launched a legal challenge over the most recent decision on Drumcree, which led to Mr Justice McAlinden ruling that the commission had not followed procedure.

He said: “Public administration must have the confidence of the public and that means that when errors are made, when shortcuts are taken, when sloppy procedures are manifest, those issues come to the public knowledge and appropriate corrections are made within that administrative body to ensure that such behaviour does not occur again.”

Unionist leaders want all the commissioners to resign, but the chair, Evelyn Collins, vowed to stay and fix the problems. “We will work hard to regain the trust of all sections of the community,” she said.

Chris Bryant, the secretary of state for Northern Ireland, said the commission “simply can’t function” without respect from all communities. On a visit to Belfast, Andy Burnham, the prime minister, declined to say whether commissioners should quit and called for “a calm and a measured” response.

The Orange Order signalled it would return to court if the commission rejected an application to march down Garvaghy Road next year. Analysts said Northern Ireland assembly elections next year might tempt some nationalist and unionist parties to exploit the issue.

Residents told reporters they dreaded any return to the chaos of the 1990s.

The Portadown branch, known as the Vatican of Orangeism, said it was ready to engage in mediation. Breandán Mac Cionnaith of the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition said marches through the mainly Catholic neighbourhood “finished” in 1998 and “will not be repeated”.

Russia ‘losing 6,000 more troops in Ukraine each month than it can recruit’

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 17:05:02 GMT

Moscow recruits an estimated 1,000 people a day but western officials say it cannot keep up with casualty level

Russia is losing about 6,000 more troops in Ukraine each month than it can recruit, western officials have said.

While Russia is still acquiring new battlefield recruits at speed, with an estimated rate of 1,000 a day, in the last two months even this has not been sufficient to replace those killed or injured.

“We estimate that the gap between the number of people Russia is losing to casualties and the number they’re being able to recruit is around 6,000 a month at the moment,” one western official said.

“Putin’s response to this has been to escalate himself and to target civilian infrastructure and civilians in Ukraine, firing over 360 missiles since early July and exploiting Kyiv’s shortage of defence against ballistic missiles. It’s clear that Moscow intends to try and break Ukrainian morale by destroying its energy infrastructure this winter.”

Such tactics are in part because Putin has limited options for overcoming the huge losses on the battlefield with more recruitment.

Western officials believe further mobilisation would be a big risk both politically and economically, saying the last such event, in autumn 2022, saw about a million – often highly skilled – Russians leave the country, with less than half returning.

It is also unclear whether the Russian military could absorb the several hundred thousand new recruits which would result, given a lack of equipment and officers.

Ukraine has repeatedly attacked Russian targets connected to oil, creating fuel shortages, but has appealed repeatedly for more help from allies, both with offensive missiles and defence systems.

Andy Burnham visited Kyiv on his first overseas trip as prime minister this week. He told Volodymyr Zelenskyy that the UK would give Ukraine previously classified information on the British-manufactured components for long-range cruise missiles.

Burnham has also urged the international community to do more to protect Ukraine against Russian attacks, particularly with more US-made Patriot interceptor missiles. He is expected to make this argument at next month’s UN general assembly in New York.

In response, Russia has made repeated threats of retaliation, including talk of attacks on UK military targets both inside and outside Ukraine.

The western officials said that while the threat from Russia remained very real, the situation had not changed, and the assessment was that “Putin absolutely wants to avoid a direct confrontation with Nato”.

One official said: “We are seeing a continuation of hostile rhetoric and various accusations against the UK. This is absolutely consistent with longstanding Russian military doctrine, which is to use rhetoric to both exploit fears in adversaries and to influence decision-making. So this is not a new phenomenon.”

Officials say Russia still has the capability to target the UK, with cyberattacks or physical attacks on civilian targets by proxies, for example on factories or warehouses. Last year, six men were jailed for their involvement in an attack ordered by Russia against a warehouse in east London housing aid to Ukraine.

But officials said their assessment was that Putin would limit any such action to avoid more direct conflict with Nato.

Putin’s overall aim in Ukraine, western officials believe, is to maintain a campaign of attrition, hoping that support from Ukraine’s allies will ebb away, particularly if governments are spooked by public alarm over Russian threats.

Such threats should be seen, one official said, as attempts to create a “fractured and more vulnerable Europe”.

Another said: “It’s important to keep in mind that this is not new. Russia has invoked the threat of the possible use of nuclear weapons numerous times in recent years to try to scare us into ending support for Ukraine.”

New heart attack definition promises better care for women

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 17:00:03 GMT

Leading cardiovascular health groups reclassify overlooked causes and introduce sex-specific diagnostic thresholds

Doctors have agreed the world’s first universal definition of a heart attack, paving the way for millions of women to finally receive better treatment after decades of being “deprioritised”.

In one of the biggest procedural shake-ups in a generation, the world’s four leading cardiovascular health groups have signed off on new guidance for healthcare professionals when seeing suspected heart attack patients.

Historically, some less common forms of heart attack, which evidence shows typically affect women far more than men, have been coded as less important, with treatment and care often worse as a result.

Until now, experts said, women had been getting less effective treatments, which did not always target the specific cause of their heart attack and could even make them more unwell.

Now the world’s top cardiologists have promised a “revolution” in care after agreeing the biggest overhaul of how heart attacks are defined and diagnosed in decades, in part to reduce the often deadly delays afflicting women.

The landmark agreement was announced in Munich on the opening day of the annual congress of the European Society of Cardiology (ESC), the world’s largest heart conference.

The new guidance will upgrade three types of attack that are up to 10 times more common in women and often caused by childbirth, exercise and emotional stress.

The most serious cases, previously known as “type 1” and now classed as “primary” heart attacks, had previously prioritised those caused by a clot blocking blood flow to the heart.

However, the types of attacks more common in women involve reduced blood flow for other reasons, such as a tear or tightening of arteries, and are more likely to be missed or not treated as urgently, with delays to care.

The new guidelines will also reduce the threshold for any type of heart attack to be diagnosed in women based upon the levels of a protein called troponin in their blood.

Until now, women had been expected to reach the same threshold as men for troponin – which is released when the heart is injured and damaged – to get a diagnosis.

Speaking to reporters in Munich, Prof Bryan Williams, the chief scientific and medical officer of the British Heart Foundation, Britain’s biggest heart charity, said: “This is a landmark moment, a radical shift in how we define and diagnose heart attacks worldwide which will transform people’s care.

“For decades, women have missed out on accurate diagnoses and treatment. This focus on finding less common causes of heart attacks, which predominantly affect women, should help to change that. It could be life-changing for huge numbers of women in the UK and worldwide.”

Crucially, the new streamlined heart attack categories will also help patients to fully understand the cause of their heart attack and what comes next, Williams said.

The three types of heart attacks that have been upgraded – and which mostly affect women – are coronary artery spasm, coronary embolism, and spontaneous coronary artery dissection (Scad).

The first involves the tightening of the artery, which can deprive the heart muscle of blood and oxygen and cause a heart attack, and can be caused by emotional stress, exercise or extreme cold.

The second is where a blood clot or fatty deposit travels to a coronary artery and causes a blockage.

And the third is caused by a tear in the coronary artery, which occurs in women at least 80% of the time and often happens during or soon after pregnancy.

Prof Nicholas Mills, a cardiologist at the University of Edinburgh who led the international taskforce of doctors that agreed the new guidelines, said it was “the first time that we’ve had a truly global approach to aligning how we diagnose what is probably the most important diagnosis there is”.

“It kills so many people, and we’ve never got everyone together around the world to agree how we’re going to describe it, classify it, explain it to our patients,” he said.

“Our job now is to implement this as widely as possible. It’s just as relevant for the UK as it is for any other country around the world. It is a revolution. It’s going to make care better for patients.”

Mills said there had been “unintended systematic bias against women”, including by using the key blood test for diagnosing heart attacks at an average level, which picks up all men but misses some women.

“This is used for all types of heart attack in every emergency department in the world, and we want to make sure that it’s used correctly,” he said.

The new guidelines, published in the European Heart Journal, were drawn up by the world’s four leading cardiovascular health groups: the ESC, the American College of Cardiology, the American Heart Association and the World Heart Federation.

The Guardian climate pledge 2026

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 17:00:03 GMT

Each year, the Guardian reaffirms its commitment to the environment – both in our reporting and how we operate as a business. From critical tipping points to war in Iran, this is how the last 12 months have looked

Support the Guardian’s environment coverage

The Guardian climate forum 2026

Today marks the end of the Guardian’s annual climate support campaign. Each year, during the campaign, we remind our audience about the Guardian’s role in covering the threats to our planet and the importance of independent journalism in telling that story. Our climate pledge is a reminder of the environmental values we place at the heart of our reporting and our organisation.

Since our 2025 climate pledge, the world has experienced extreme levels of heat as well as extreme forms of denial and abdication in the face of the climate crisis. But, across the world, there have also been inspiring efforts to tackle it.

This update reflects how the Guardian has remained steadfast in exposing those who have tried to block or reverse the transition to a clean energy world, as well as highlighting the efforts of those who have been bravely confronting the greatest challenge of our time.

In the past three weeks, more than 30,000 Guardian readers have supported our backed our annual climate support campaign. If you believe in the power of independent journalism, please consider joining them today.

The Guardian’s commitment to agenda-setting climate journalism has become even more crucial this year as other news outlets have scaled back their own climate coverage. While the news cycle continues to be dominated by conflict, division and the abuses of autocrats, we have worked tirelessly to keep the health of the planet firmly on the public agenda.

We have highlighted how the climate emergency has pitted the interests of billionaires against the wellbeing of billions of ordinary people. For example, our journalists have been reporting extensively on the environmental impact of the AI revolution, revealing how the race to build giant datacentres has been driving up big tech’s carbon emissions – as well as how US tech giants lobbied the EU to hide the environmental toll of their datacentres.

The Guardian has also examined how the oil crisis triggered by the war on Iran has helped a coalition of business interests, rightwing populists and media outlets to ramp up their attacks on net zero goals. We revealed that major oil companies made £93bn in profits in three months following the start of the conflict.

As the climate emergency has increasingly become part of the culture wars, we have countered dangerous and widespread disinformation – from myths about the cost of clean energy to its impact on jobs and the economy. We have also highlighted how the transition to green energy can make countries more resilient.

The Guardian’s independence from corporate interests means we have been able to speak truthfully and plainly while the statements from climate sceptics have become ever more contorted. While the northern hemisphere has been scorched this summer by the most severe and widespread heatwave on record, some of those who have long denied the crisis have suggested we now embrace the devastation. Guardian journalists have reported on how the world’s most powerful climate denier, Donald Trump, has continued reneging on the US’s international climate commitments and undermining federal climate regulations. We have examined how the US president has been pouring taxpayer money into his crusade against clean energy and also into boosting coal.

If it feels as if tackling the climate crisis has been eclipsed by climate culture wars, disinformation and toxic discourse, our journalists have continued to shine a light on the remarkable progress being made in some places and the possibility for positive change. For instance, we have looked at countries, such as Spain, that have embraced renewables and are benefiting from lower utility prices. We have reported on how Australia has pioneered a revolution in home renewables and battery use, providing inspiration for the rest of the world. And we captured people’s imaginations about what is possible by covering how Paris is building a gigantic cooling machine using river water from the Seine. As some countries forge ahead with the transition to a clean energy world while those in hock to fossil fuels try to turn back the clock, we have also examined the implications for the shifting geopolitical balance of power.

Our daily reporting on climate impacts and extreme weather events has drawn on the Guardian’s network of correspondents around the world and our genuinely global outlook.

We have reported on the toll the warming climate is having on gig workers in India, as well as how the closure of schools across the country means working mothers have been bearing the brunt of the climate crisis, either forced to stay at home or switch jobs.

With Europe heating up twice as fast as other continents, Guardian reporters spoke to locals and tourists about their experiences of this year’s heatwaves. We also reported on the experiences of those on the frontline tackling the effects of extreme heat, speaking to firefighters about how the scale of this year’s wildfires has forced them to make incredibly difficult choices. Our reporters also highlighted the impact on other people providing essential services in dangerous levels of heat, such as nurses, teachers and bus drivers.

As wildfires raged across Europe and North America, another impact of climate breakdown has been the unprecedented rains in other parts of the world. We reported on the extreme flooding and typhoons across Asia, from Taiwan to Afghanistan. We reported on how floods in Nigeria have been inducing “climate anxiety” that can trap people in a sense of anticipation and dread, and we explained how the floods across west Africa have been supercharged by global heating, displacing thousands of people.

We have continued to remind our audience how the poorest suffer most from the climate catastrophe – while rightwing populists continue to claim that action on climate is merely an elite concern.

Guardian journalists have also highlighted the consequences for the natural environment, for example travelling 100 miles along the Danube to witness how drought has devastated the EU’s longest river.

Our coverage of the natural world and precious wildlife has highlighted how other species we share this planet with have also experienced the catastrophic consequences of the year’s extreme weather.

Given such far-reaching impacts of the climate emergency, Guardian journalists have written about how a more just and equitable world is possible, for instance by amplifying a new report by Thomas Piketty and others at the World Inequality Lab, as well as the work of influential economists and social thinkers such as Mariana Mazzucato.

Meanwhile, our ongoing The Alternatives series has highlighted the practical work being undertaken by local communities and political parties coming up with low-carbon ways of living.

And we looked at how communities are developing ways to prepare for the effects of climate change, such as a Colombian neighbourhood that has been adopting tree nurseries and rainwater harvesting.

By encompassing these practical initiatives and everyday human stories alongside the macro perspectives and analysis of geopolitical shifts, our climate coverage has sought to inspire people by showing what is possible at both a global and local level.

As climate records continue to be broken, we reported on new data that illustrates how planetary conditions are changing rapidly.

This year we have closely monitored the scale and impact of the devastating back-to-back summer heatwaves in the northern hemisphere – including in Europe, where such extreme weather would have been impossible without the climate crisis, and in the US, which saw its hottest-ever month in July.

We are closely tracking and explaining the impact of the fast-developing El Niño event too,, forecast to be the biggest in a century and which is already intensifying a spike in ocean temperatures. Our reporting has also highlighted critical changes linked to climate breakdown, including ocean currents, Arctic ice levels, Antarctic temperatures and the Earth’s energy balance, alongside other important tipping points such as the loss of permafrost.

Since 2020, our company’s greenhouse gas emissions have reduced by 48%, meaning we remain well positioned to achieve our target of a 67% reduction by 2030. Our emissions decreased by 9% during the 2024/2025 reporting period, and we are continuing to make headway in reducing the footprint of our print operations, which still represent the largest share of our overall emissions (64%).

Lowering our emissions remains a key priority, and our progress over the last year will be included in our sustainability report published in the autumn.

The Guardian has refused advertising from all fossil fuel-extractive companies since January 2020. The Guardian is supported by the Scott Trust and the returns from its endowment fund. The fund’s environmental strategy is focused on contributing to a reduction of emissions in the real world and to protecting nature and biodiversity. The fund has made significant investments supporting the transition to a net zero economy and environmental solutions, with around £150m invested in areas ranging from renewable energy to decreasing emissions in manufacturing and industrial processes. Additionally, the fund has made a commitment to invest at least 3% of its value in natural capital and biodiversity solutions.

We believe transparency is the key to tackling the climate crisis. By sharing our data, our successes and our challenges, we can be part of the global movement to make businesses accountable for their climate and nature impacts. As part of this commitment, we continue to hold ourselves accountable to B Corporation standards, which recognises companies who meet the highest levels of environmental and social performance and public transparency.

We will be publishing our annual company emissions data in the autumn, explaining what drives our emissions and where they have risen and fallen.

We have started the process of estimating our emissions from generative AI usage. We hope to report on this next year.

We have undertaken our B Corp recertification in line with the new standards introduced by B Lab in 2026. We will find out our result later this year.

We have participated in advertising industry working groups that published a methodological framework that aims to capture the emissions impact of digital and print advertising.

We open ourselves up to scrutiny by independent third parties, such as the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) and B Corp, so they can assess the robustness of our targets and our internal policies.

Cole Palmer is a unicorn in this world inventing moments of pure footballing pleasure

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 16:59:43 GMT

Much like Central Cee, the Chelsea attacker is a distinct presence and right now is perhaps the only truly creative English player out there

This week Central Cee launched his new Premier League song, called The Team. It owes its existence to a youth-centred, fist-bumping corporate tie-in with Coca-Cola, the press release for which appears to have involved a man in golf-casual clothing frowning at his computer screen for half an hour before typing “cool urban street words, what are?” into the AI search box, then nipping off for a quick brain-bowl strategy lunch with Roger from the Bluesky Synergy hub.

The song is really good, because Central Cee is really good. He’s super-smart with words, funny and snappy, but also surprisingly tender and raw.

And yes, this is an oh-no-dad’s-talking-about-rap moment. You can just scroll down if you like. The whole thing moves on to Cole Palmer very quickly, why he’s both the best English footballer and very easy to love currently, for various reasons.

Central Cee is a significant figure, perhaps the biggest British recording artist right now. He’s also oddly raw and fearless in the things he says, in a way that feels distinct from the standard, mannered modern person, and which has got him into trouble at least once.

A few years back there was a furore when Central Cee decided to speak out against sexual prejudice. This sounds as if it should just be fine. Except, Central Cee’s call for tolerance was expressed via a lyric in the song Doja. And that lyric was: “How can I be homophobic? My bitch is gay.”

Hmm. Problems there. What Central Cee is saying here, what Central Cee has done while appearing to express a progressive sensibility, is to introduce an entirely new tier of … Basically what he’s saying is: how can I be homophobic? I’m far too busy being sexist.

This caused understandable offence. The b-word is demeaning and cheap, whatever your intentions. Don’t say it. Find better words. To his credit, Central Cee was very good at explaining and apologising, open to other views, while also seeming genuinely non-judgmental of other people regardless of difference or identity, with the exception, of course, of wastemen, mugs and snitches.

He seems to have been forgiven now. More than that, he’s startlingly successful, the most streamed British rap artist of all time. Young people respond to him hungrily. He seems adaptive, fitted to the modern world. In the Coke video he looks blankly into the lens, gives you everything and nothing, risky but also weirdly fearless.

What does this have to do with Cole Palmer, and the surge of heartfelt Palmer-love across all platforms this week after his brilliant performance against Fulham on Monday?

First, Palmer is good friends with Central Cee. He even turned up at the launch of the Coke song just before Chelsea’s Premier League opener. And Palmer really was sensational at Craven Cottage, twirling about between the defensive lines, all perfect touch and interesting angles.

The reaction was significant too. Everyone went wild for this. In particular passionate football men of a certain age went wild. This boy is gold, this boy gets people off their seats, the man in the TalkSport video chair growled, speaking from the gut and the spleen, coming off less like a piece of football analysis, more like a man offering a brave, husky funeral elegy for a very loyal family dog.

This passion does have an edge to it. It is a mark of how hungry we are for something different, a counterpoint to the dominance of systems football, that despite being entirely academy-coded Palmer still seems to be a unicorn in this world.

For the middle-aged proper football man he can look like a flicker of the pre-digital memory, football in the time of maverick authenticity, an age of mud, of landlines, of not wearing a seat belt, of smoking in pubs, of the casually discarded woodland porn mag, of Barry Davies shouting: “Oh, it’s magnificent and can’t they just taste it” while mods throw darts at each other in the background, because old fun is the best fun.

This is, of course, both deluded and incorrect, because football encourages such feelings and because many middle-aged men are already both of these things. But Palmer is genuinely unusual in the modern game. He turns up in strange spaces, finds gullies and currents in between those static pegs.

Right now he is perhaps the only truly creative English player out there, in the sense of inventing the game in front of him, dishing up in those moments the pure pleasure of a story being told in real time.

He even looks a little unusual in an era of hyper‑athletes. Palmer is light and mobile. He can turn with balletic grace. But he also has that gangly, mischievous physicality, like a very clever cartoon alpaca has worked out how to put on a royal blue football kit and run around occasionally doing amusing celebrations.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

From here Palmer will benefit from having a very good club manager who gets his position. At Bayer Leverkusen Xabi Alonso designed an entire team around getting the best out of Florian Wirtz, the “free electron” in the structure.

Beyond this, Palmer is clearly the player the national team should have been configured around after Euro 2024. It made some logical sense not to pick him for the World Cup, because merit and fitness are also important. But Thomas Tuchel simply has to play Palmer, Jude Bellingham and Harry Kane together now, even if you have to pack the team with cement sacks and tins of beans to make it work, because this is just incredibly hot, and there is literally no other point in playing these games.

But it isn’t just the football. Palmer is also just weirdly likable. There is a temptation to cast him as a Lego-haired blank, some kind of urban idiot savant, a human being made entirely from white bread, energy drinks and discarded phone cases. But he’s clearly very smart, and also very modern in his own way.

This is another element of the Palmer persona. He looks unbothered, wry and oddly gentle. But the blankness is a thing, a way of being in the middle of all that glare. Palmer gives you nothing to bite on, no gaps in the armour. He even seems weirdly post-race, or just non-race, some kind of bowl-headed omni-man.

It is both an attitude and a shield of sorts. There’s a thing young people do on the internet, known as Nonchalance. This is all about projecting indifference and impassive facial expressions, appearing comically unbothered while chaotic things happen around you. In the picture with Central Cee at the Coke thing they’re both doing it, staring blankly into the camera open but also closed.

Palmer seems to do this naturally. He will sit with his legs crossed while a group of angry men have an on-pitch brawl nearby. He will have the sense of raw dramatic irony to look genuinely amused on the live TV feed as the referee stands right in the middle of the Chelsea huddle, one of the most comically weird sub-moments of the modern age.

There is a theory nonchalance is a political attitude, a response by the post-Gen-Z demographic to the challenge of making the world you find less incoherent, less intrusive on your space, a blank against the constant wall of noise, dogma and ideological boilerplate hurled your way.

Even the way Palmer plays has a kind of shrug about it, an existential creativity, making up your own patterns, making the world small, you-sized, following the lines in front of you.

One of the best bits of Monday night’s game was his interview after. Sky’s reporter Emma Saunders asked Palmer: “How ready are you for this season?” His response was: “Did you not watch the game?” – which from some old‑school, spam-faced football man might have sounded a bit weird, a bit off on power dynamic, a bit man-woman.

But it really wasn’t that at all. Palmer was already laughing. Saunders laughed back. And it was just a nice moment, banter-stuff, mate-chat, playing the game in front of you. English football has such an interesting figure here, not just a brilliant footballer, but a distinct presence, a way of existing in the middle of all that heat. Let’s try not to break him this time.

The Guardian view on political donations: Labour should curb the power of big money

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 16:56:00 GMT

Before becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham favoured a £500,000 donations cap. In office, he’s backing away. That is a mistake

On the campaign trail in Makerfield, Andy Burnham told a democracy activist that he favoured a political donations cap of around £500,000 and wanted it reduced over time. His government is now resisting amendments that would move in precisely that direction. Mr Burnham was right in May. He is wrong now. It is difficult to argue that restricting a single person to giving half a million pounds a year to a political party would damage democracy. Such a cap would only affect the mega-rich. Reducing the cap would force parties to wean themselves off the present regime that allows the rich too much say.

There are two contra arguments swilling around Labour. The first is that there should be room for wealthy, progressive donors – whose cash helps rebut claims that Labour is in the pocket of the trade unions. The second is the warning from unions that a cap could undermine their ability to contribute to the Labour party.

Neither of these arguments holds much water. Whatever benefit Labour might derive from rich friends is dwarfed by the wider damage caused by parties being bankrolled by a few rich individuals. Mr Burnham has registered £345,000 of donations over the past year, including £164,000 from billionaire Lord Sainsbury. In comparison, Thai-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne gave Reform UK a single £9m donation in August 2025 – a sum which exceeds the £8m in trade union donations that Labour will get this year.

The timing makes Labour’s retreat baffling. This newspaper’s revelation of Nigel Farage’s undisclosed £5m gift from Mr Harborne in 2024 has turned big money in politics from an abstract concern into a live issue. Reform’s support has fallen markedly in recent months.

Mr Burnham could recover the situation by backing amendments from two Labour MPs. Stella Creasy’s changes, which have cross-party support, start with a £500,000 cap – Mr Burnham’s own figure – before reducing it, while allowing parliament to alter the level. She proposes to exclude trade union political funds, recognising that money aggregated from thousands of members differs fundamentally from a donation controlled by a single billionaire or company. The former represents many individual contributions; the latter concentrated economic power. Unions warn that a cap might restrict their political activity. But Ms Creasy explicitly protects their member-funded campaigning cash. Opponents should explain why that safeguard is inadequate.

Anneliese Dodds, a former Labour cabinet minister, asks the right question: if ministers believe the growth of big money in politics is a risk, why retain the Conservatives’ sharply increased election spending limits? A donations cap limits how much concentrated private wealth can enter party politics; lower expenditure limits reduce how much money parties need to raise in the first place.

Instead of backing these measures, tabled as amendments to the representation of the people bill at next week’s report stage vote, ministers are pressing ahead with elaborate rules governing where political money comes from and how it reaches parties. Yet this year’s Rycroft review, which ministers are responding to, urged parliament, “if it wishes to restore confidence in the political process and to keep big money out of UK politics”, to consider spending limits. Given the scandals of recent years, it is astonishing that Labour is declining to regulate how much political influence any single wealthy donor can purchase.

The Guardian view on the loan of the Bayeux tapestry: a manifestation of soft power

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 16:55:09 GMT

The British Museum’s landmark cultural exchange is a symbol of post-Brexit rapprochement between Britain and France

“Harold Rex interfectus est”: King Harold is killed. As every British schoolchild knows, the Bayeux tapestry depicts a turning point in the history of these islands: defeat at the Battle of Hastings in 1066, which would lead to the ascent of William the Conqueror to the English throne. Its return to the UK for the first time in nearly 1,000 years is being hailed as a hugely historic moment in its own right. The loan of the tapestry (technically an embroidery of wool on linen) to the British Museum in exchange for UK treasures from Sutton Hoo is the ultimate manifestation of soft power – a 70-metre symbol of post-Brexit Anglo-French rapprochement in comic-strip form.

Ticket sales for the exhibition, which opens on 10 September, were the biggest in a single day in the museum’s history, with online queues of 80,000. Radio 4 is devoting a day of special broadcasts to mark the arrival of the tapestry, including a new drama with verse from the poet laureate Simon Armitage. The museum’s videos explaining this tale of ambition, friendship, betrayal and revenge are fittingly narrated by Traitors presenter Claudia Winkleman. Norman-mania is here.

“It probably took more years to deliver this project than all the Brexit talks,” Emmanuel Macron joked in a speech to the British parliament last year. To the list of 623 men, 190 horses, 35 dogs and only three women depicted on the tapestry, one might add a 21st-century British king, a French president, and three British prime ministers who have helped to bring it here – not to mention the millions of pounds it has cost.

Two previous attempts – one for Queen Elizabeth’s coronation in 1953 and another in 1966 – failed. It would not have succeeded this time if the tapestry had not needed to be moved for renovations to the Bayeux Museum in Normandy. Many curators and restorers still believed the risks of bringing it to London were too great. The late David Hockney called the transferral “madness”. One of his final works, the 90-metre iPad frieze A Year in Normandie, on display this summer at the Serpentine gallery in London, was testament to his lifelong fascination with the tapestry. An online petition against the move attracted nearly 80,000 signatures. However, political will won.

From poetry to parody – from Tennyson’s 1876 epic verse drama Harold to an episode of The Simpsons – the tapestry has enjoyed a rich cultural afterlife. But its message has always been political. Napoleon and the Nazis recognised its potential as a propaganda tool. In 2014 Nigel Farage, then leader of Ukip, sported a Bayeux tapestry silk tie during the Rochester byelection, as a reminder of “the last time we were invaded and taken over”. The tie sold out in 24 hours.

In these fractured times, the enduring appeal of this 11th-century artefact speaks of a need for a national story. The Bayeux tapestry is a devastatingly human saga. With war raging in Europe, this medieval masterpiece is a reminder of conflict’s brutality, human suffering and the importance of collaboration between countries. The tapestry will return to France for the 1,000th anniversary of William the Conqueror’s birth next year. According to Philippe Bélaval, Mr Macron’s former culture adviser: “Such a loan will only happen once and never again.” This is truly a once-in-a millennium event. Hopefully, its success will pave the way for equally ambitious cultural exchanges in the future. Vive l’entente cordiale!

Infallible style: Pope Leo appears in Vanity Fair’s ranks of most fashionable

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 16:44:53 GMT

Pontiff, who has caught the eye in trainers and a baseball cap, praised for taking dress to ‘heavenly heights’

For the first time in a decade, Vanity Fair has released a best-dressed list. Featuring 70 names, the list ranks the most fashionable people in the world in 2026. The lineup includes the usual suspects spanning Hollywood actors and global pop stars but nestled among the Hollywood stars is an unexpected entrant. Pope Leo XIV.

The 70-year-old head of the Catholic church has been praised by the magazine for taking papal style “to heavenly heights”. His most memorable look? A simple white cassock styled with a pair of Nike trainers.

Vanity Fair’s style correspondent José Criales-Unzueta, who worked on compiling the list, said he and the team were impressed by the “innate Americanness” of the way the pope dressed.

The Chicago-born pontiff has carved out a style niche and garnered a loyal fashion following with his enthusiasm for both bespoke vestments and vintage fashion accessories. Alongside trainers, he prefers simple black oxford shoes to the traditional red papal slippers.

He wears a discontinued Swiss-made quartz watch, carries his own battered briefcase and in June 2025 popped a White Sox baseball cap over his papal cap for a general audience in St Peter’s Square. For more formal occasions, he turns to the Italian designer Filippo Sorcinelli, who also created liturgical vestments for the previous popes Benedict XVI and Francis.

The Catholic church, with its long mastery of symbolism and optics, is experiencing an uptick driven by gen Z. For Leo, being featured in a publication that its global editorial director, Mark Guiducci, has described as a “magazine about personalities” and that feels “like the pantheon” works well with the papacy’s own aim to position itself as a modern power.

“The world’s embrace of this pope has been stunning to me,” said Robert Orsi, a professor of religious studies at Northwestern University in Illinois. Orsi pointed to Leo’s criticism of AI and calls for peace as also speaking to gen Z.

Carol Richardson, a professor of early modern art history at the University of Edinburgh, said the pope, who has his own Instagram account, would be aware of his inclusion on the list. “He and the people surrounding him are very savvy,” she said. “The majority will think it’s fun. They will like the fact it has been noticed how busy he is, that he has to wear trainers to run around in. That he is working.”

From Christian Lacroix ecclesiastical riffing in the 80s and the Met’s Heavenly Bodies exhibition in 2018 to crucifixes and depictions of Christ on the most recent catwalks, the papacy has long fascinated fashion. Criales-Unzueta says its appeal lies in its vastness. “There is so much to take in and so much to find inspiration in.”

The pontiff is listed in Vanity Fair’s “originals” division, a category of individuals commended by the magazine for being “the most outlandish and innovative dressers” with “a singular point of view”. Others on the list include the film-maker Spike Lee and the singers Björk and Rosalía.

Criales-Unzueta described the list as “an opportunity to showcase the way fashion and style are deeply embedded in culture and society” and that “style, good style, is a practice that is not reserved for celebrities or their stylists”.

When Leo was first spotted last May wearing Nike trainers in a still from Leone a Roma, a Vatican-produced documentary that retraces his time in Rome before he became pope, the image instantly went viral. Many people mistook it as fake. It was compared to the AI-generated image of Pope Francis wearing an oversized Balenciaga puffer jacket, which has since been described as “the first real mass-level AI misinformation case”. Criales-Unzueta said that was the moment Leo became “a talking point in and outside of fashion”. Trainer fans were quick to identify Leo’s Nikes as a discontinued retro tennis-style shoe that was first sold in the 70s. “What a papal flex,” declared Esquire, while some online users were quick to christen his style as “holy drip”.

By the end of last year, Leo found himself featured alongside A$AP Rocky and Bad Bunny in Vogue’s best-dressed list, while the New York Times named him as one of its 67 Most Stylish People of 2025.

Orsi said he had been thinking about what the trainers symbolised. “A sportiness? A familiarity with track and field, basketball courts, running?” he pondered. For him it was “a lightness on his feet, a readiness to move quickly to where he is needed the most”, he said. “They signal that he is approachable, like a good coach, and also humble.”

Salmonella cases in UK likely to rise until source of outbreak is found

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 16:42:32 GMT

Experts say imported eggs served in cafes and restaurants may be behind hundreds of infections and one death

Salmonella cases in the UK are expected to rise until the common source is identified, something that is notoriously difficult to establish, experts have warned.

There have been 474 confirmed cases and one death linked to the current outbreak, according to the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), with the latest investigations suggesting it is associated with eating imported eggs in cafes and restaurants.

About 1.6bn eggs are imported to the UK every year, according to the British Egg Industry Council, with the number having risen 60% since 2021.

The link to eggs consumed outside of the home is consistent with imported eggs commonly being used in catering, according to Paul Wigley, a professor of animal microbial ecosystems at the University of Bristol.

Wigley said: “Bought in bulk these eggs are cheaper than UK lion mark eggs and so can end up being used in schools and nursing homes along with cafes, restaurants and takeaways. The eggs may be mixed batches from different batches, but the clustering of cases suggests there may be a single source.”

He added: “As far as controls and the future, it’s difficult to judge, though identification of the source would help in being able to put specific controls on a producer or country in place. Avoiding runny eggs outside the home, unless lion mark eggs, is perhaps the only step an individual can make.”

Although previous salmonella outbreaks in the UK have been linked to eggs imported from European countries such as Poland, the current source of this outbreak has yet to be identified. For some experts, this makes the current surge in cases particularly worrying.

Prof Chris Elliott of the school of biological sciences at Queen’s University Belfast, said: “All we have been told is that the likelihood is that it’s been imported.

“There is a huge amount of difficulty in tracing the origins of something like this, particularly when it’s food service. Within the UK’s retail industry, they really know their supply chains extremely well. But with food service, less so.”

He added that the number of cases would keep rising until the source was identified, which could take “not days, but weeks”.

Elliott added: “My expectation is those numbers will continue to rise until they can not only track the source, but right back to the country of production. It is fiendishly difficult to track the source of a food and ingredient, so I certainly wouldn’t be critical of the agencies. They’re under immense pressure, and the worst thing that can happen is that they feel pressurised to say that it came from Poland or it came from Romania when they’re not 100% sure about that.”

Prof Brad Spiller, the head of medical microbiology at Cardiff University, said the fact that this particular outbreak was linked to a common source was “probably the most concerning aspect” of the cases.

He said: “It is only once we have a better idea of which countries are involved, we can begin to track back the source.

“This is how they identified that both of the previous outbreaks seen in recent years that were happening simultaneously, and were both linked back to Poland as the source of that. I think until they identify the source, the source won’t naturally stop.”

Prof Mark Stevens, the chair of microbial pathogenesis at the University of Edinburgh, added that the outbreak was also unusual because cases were occurring at the same time, whereas salmonella cases across the UK were usually more spread out.

He said: “This is obviously a real challenge for the health protection agencies because they have to now identify that source and try to restrict its entry into the food system.

“It is of concern to have an outbreak of this size. There are thousands of salmonella cases each year, but rarely are they on this scale where hundreds of people are being infected by a common strain.”

Stevens added: “I think until we really understand the source of these infections, it’s possible that we’ll continue to see more of them.”

Shaky Sabalenka and wide-open men’s draw set stage for US Open drama

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 16:39:37 GMT

Defending champion arrives at Flushing Meadows in poor form and with a host of challengers looking to usurp her

Under any normal circumstances Aryna Sabalenka would not have lost her third-round match at the Cincinnati Open last week. For all of her unforced errors, indecisiveness and the obvious tension surrounding her tennis, the world No 1 had led the unheralded Sára Bejlek 5-1 in the first set tie-break and then 4-1 in set two. She gave herself more than enough chances to close out a comfortable win.

Instead Sabalenka returns to New York trying to find a path through her greatest crisis since she first reached No 1 in the rankings more than three years ago. That straight-sets loss in Cincinnati extended a mediocre 17-7 record dating back to the beginning of April during which she has not reached a final. She has just one more chance to turn her fortunes around as she tries to claim her first grand slam title of the year at the US Open, the tournament she has won on the last two occasions.

Such is the competition at the top of women’s tennis, her rivals are congregating at her front door. Elena Rybakina begins this tournament sitting at No 1 in the live standings and in control of her own destiny. Sabalenka must win the title to have any hope of retaining the top ranking, but Rybakina will become the new No 1 regardless of all other results if she reaches the semi-finals. Should either Coco Gauff or Jessica Pegula win the title and Rybakina fails to make the semi-finals, they would take top spot. This additional pressure could further add to Sabalenka’s woes, but perhaps, after 97 consecutive weeks as the undisputed best player in the world, this is exactly what she needs.

There are other unanswered questions. Rybakina’s physical condition is uncertain after she was forced to retire from her quarter-final against Iga Swiatek last week due to a leg injury. A year after she spent this lead-in week to the US Open changing her service action, and parts of her matches in tears, Gauff has rebuilt confidence in her serve and the 2023 champion produced some of her best tennis during her Cincinnati Open title run. Fresh from her own success in Toronto, the 2022 US Open champion Swiatek looks similarly rejuvenated after struggling badly with anxiety and nerves in many matches this year. Pegula, a finalist in Cincinnati having defeated Swiatek, remains as consistent as ever and will put pressure on her rivals.

The strength at the top of women’s game is reflected in the fact that every player inside the top 11 currently holds a WTA 1000 title or above. They have each shown that they are capable of winning the biggest tournaments in the world.

Things could hardly be more different in the men’s draw. As was the case when he exited the French Open in round two, Jannik Sinner’s withdrawal from the US Open with a knee injury has cracked this tournament wide open. Carlos Alcaraz is clearly capable of greatness whenever he enters the court, but the prospect of him launching a serious challenge in his first event back after a four-month layoff due to a right wrist injury and only a few weeks of training seems fanciful. Although he has never been the strongest doubles player, Alcaraz’s rustiness and the caution with which he hit his serve in the mixed doubles competition alongside Serena Williams only reinforced this sentiment.

It was Alexander Zverev who took advantage of the void in Paris to win his first grand slam title and, as the top seed, he is high on the list of contenders again. The two biggest winners in the weeks leading up to the US Open, Montreal and Cincinnati champions Ben Shelton and Arthur Fils, are young players who have long viewed themselves as worthy of competing for major titles. Such is the cruelty of the draw, the close friends have been drawn to face each other in the fourth round.

Otherwise, just about everyone is in with a shot. The French Open finalist Flavio Cobolli continues to play some of the best tennis of his career, reaching the semi-final in Cincinnati. The rise of 19-year-old Rafael Jódar, who was ranked No 369 this time last year, continues unabated. A group of US players, including Taylor Fritz, Frances Tiafoe, Learner Tien and Brandon Nakashima have found their best form at the right time. Félix Auger-Aliassime, the third seed, will try to replicate the immense level he demonstrated on these courts last year on his run to the semi-final.

Perhaps the most interesting question of all is where Novak Djokovic will land over the next few weeks. Had any of the grand slam tournaments been this wide open in 2025, he would have been heavily favoured to become the oldest champion in history. But a year is an eternity at Djokovic’s advanced age. He has continued to put himself in contention at the grand slams, reaching the Australian Open final and Wimbledon semi-final, but he also has to manage a constant stream of physical problems that only worsen over the course of a fortnight. However, these are not normal circumstances, and he is far from a normal tennis player, so the pursuit of grand slam No 25 is still alive in New York.

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 16:23:00 GMT

Norway in mourning after death of King Harald

‘It’s only a small thing in the bigger picture’

The Norwegian Andreas Leknessund launched a successful solo attack on ⁠the final climb to the summit finish of Aramón Valdelinares to win stage ⁠seven of the ⁠Vuelta ​a España, ahead of his Uno-X Mobility teammate and compatriot Tobias Johannessen on a day ⁠when their country mourned the death of King Harald.

Leknessund made his move from ⁠a five-rider breakaway 7.5km from the finish at ​the end of the ‌149.8km ride from ‌Vall d’Alba, and pulled away to win his first ‌Grand Tour stage on his Vuelta debut.

“It’s been a special day for the team and also for the whole of Norway,” Leknessund said. “Obviously it’s only a small thing in the bigger picture but still, it ‌makes the day more special.” A minute’s silence was held for King Harald before the stage began in Vall d’Alba, and the Uno-X Mobility team wore black armbands as a mark of respect.

“I didn’t expect it to be this emotional, but for sure there’s so much feelings around this,” Leknessund added. “I’ve ​been fighting really hard, and it means a ‌lot.”

Johannessen came in 34sec behind, having left the Belgian Wout van ​Aert in his wake close to the finish, with the Visma-Lease a Bike rider having to settle for third after he had made the initial attack from the ⁠off and spent most of the day out in ​front with ​Leknessund.

Tadej Pogacar, winner of ​three stages already, was happy to sit ​back in ‌the peloton before ​pulling away ​from his general classification rivals approaching the summit to gain more seconds. The Slovene now leads Spaniard Enric Mas by 3min 50sec.

Van Aert and Leknessund got away early and were joined by ‌another three riders, Johannessen, Eddie Dunbar (Pinarello Q36.5) and Alexey Lutsenko (NSN) coming to the top of the first of five climbs.

The leaders worked together, building a substantial gap and at the foot of the ​final climb the five were one minute ahead of a chasing group of 13 riders with the peloton out of the running with less than 10km to the finish.

Leknessund was the first to try to get away, and when nobody followed he was able to claim his stage win at last, having finished runner-up three times at this year’s Giro d’Italia.

“I said ⁠to Andreas that he should try to go early and then we check if the ​other guys are willing to work together,” ​Johannessen said. “That’s what you always dream about ​when you try to be two guys in the breakaway and you can play it ​like this. I think we ‌played it perfectly.

“A special ​day with what is ​happening back home in Norway so we are super proud.”

Felix Gall, fifth overall, tried to get away from Pogacar, but the Slovene responded and in the end gained 16sec on his closest rival Mas, with Pogacar’s compatriot Primoz Roglic a further minute behind in third.

Stage eight on Saturday is a flat 176.4km route from Pucol to Xeraco.
