An $18bn settlement – and Zuckerberg barely blinked. The tech titans must be stripped of their power, and soon

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 16:10:15 GMT

Those who said Meta harms children struck a blow, but the ability of big tech to gouge profits and cause harm is barely diminished. That’s the battle to come

Follow the money. If you want to know how the tech giant Meta really feels about the $18bn it agreed to fork out to end a landmark lawsuit against it – an outcome widely hailed as a victory for campaigners – just look at its share price. It didn’t go down when word came on Wednesday that Meta had settled with the 29 US states that had argued that the company’s Facebook and Instagram platforms harmed children. On the contrary, Meta stock went up, initially surging by 5%, before levelling out at a gain of just over 1.25%. There could be no clearer proof that the money men reckon Meta dodged a bullet.

To be sure, there was plenty to hearten those who have long believed that social media damages teenagers especially, whether by exposing them to content they shouldn’t see or by sapping their self-esteem, offering them filters that show how much prettier they would look if they had cosmetic surgery or giving them a metric of their popularity – and unpopularity – in the form of a running tally of “likes” and views.

For one thing, $18bn is a lot of money. For another, Meta has agreed to a series of changes in the way young people use their platforms. There’ll be a two-hour daily cap on use; restricted access during the night and the school day; likes will not be shown automatically and assorted safety and parental supervision measures will no longer be opt-in extras but the default standard. You can see why Lori Schott of Colorado, who believes the content her daughter encountered on Instagram played a part in her suicide aged 18, declared Wednesday to be “a good day”.

But look closer and you see that, for Meta, $18bn is not exactly a bank-breaking sum. It amounts to less than a month’s revenue. And it has 10 years to pay it out: the monthly payments could come out of petty cash. What’s more, nearly a third of that sum is contingent on Meta’s rivals YouTube and TikTok agreeing to the same restrictions. All told, the financial penalty is less than a tenth of the $200bn the 29 states were seeking, and a tiny fraction of the $1.4tn the company told the court it feared it would have to cough up. No wonder Meta’s shareholders were doing fist bumps on Wednesday.

Beyond the money, Meta will be thankful it has escaped a court ruling against it, a legal verdict on the behaviour detailed so compellingly in the California courtroom in the first week of the trial before it was abruptly halted. Jurors heard from the former Meta safety engineer Arturo Béjar, who spoke of his own teenage daughter’s experience on Instagram – how she received unwanted sexual advances, crude misogynistic insults and photos of male genitalia on the platform – and of a survey he had conducted that found 51% of teen users had had bad or harmful experiences on Instagram within the previous seven days, and that content was taken down only 0.02% of the time. Béjar reported his findings to Mark Zuckerberg directly, but got no reply. As Béjar told me when we spoke on Thursday: “They knew that harm to kids was happening, but they were telling the world it wasn’t.” Under Wednesday’s settlement, Meta hasn’t even made an admission of liability.

As for the new restrictions, anyone who has seen a teenager on a computer or phone will have little confidence that they won’t find a way around them. If they do, then, according to this week’s deal, Meta will not be accountable. And crucially, says Béjar, it is Meta itself that still gets to define what constitutes harm.

No less frustrating, these new terms apply inside the US only, even though Meta’s reach, and its capacity to do damage, is global. As the gagged former Facebook employee Sarah Wynn-Williams described in her riveting book Careless People, the company was assiduous in hunting for new users in those overseas territories with few legal safeguards. There’s a parallel here with the tobacco industry: long after the US and Europe had cracked down on cigarettes, big tobacco was energetically selling into developing countries that had not yet put up their defences.

Above all, this week’s settlement addresses only the safety of children, despite the copious evidence of danger to adults, whether in the form of addiction or exposure to toxic misinformation. The danger lies not in this or that specific feature, but rather in the fundamental business model of social media: namely, tracking and surveilling individuals online, using the data gathered to construct a profile, which is then sold to advertisers eager to target potential consumers with extraordinary precision.

It’s this model that keeps users hooked, scrolling for hour after hour, as they are served content aimed directly at their interests and anxieties. As Ravi Naik, the lawyer who acts for Wynn-Williams and others, told me: “The algorithm preys on you.” The trouble with this latest settlement, he explains, is that “it reaches the features of Meta’s platforms but not the engine that drives them. The recommendation algorithm is untouched.”

What, then, can be done? For Béjar, the answer is to approach social media as a public health crisis, akin to the road traffic accidents that led to mandatory safety belts in cars (and not only for children). Governments need to say that any company involved in this crisis has to be involved in tackling it. And no one should fall for the line that the nature of the internet is such that it cannot be subject to meaningful regulation. When the music industry objected to copyright infringements online, incentives were swiftly arranged to fix the problem. As Béjar so damningly puts it: “A song has more protection than a kid.”

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

There are ample other precedents that can serve as guides to action, though none of them will please the titans of big tech. For decades, they have avoided being viewed as publishers, liable for what appears on their platforms. Nor do they want to be treated like carmakers, responsible for product safety. And they don’t like being likened to cigarette firms, selling a product they know is dangerous. Perhaps policymakers need to make a new comparison.

More than a century ago, when Standard Oil’s de facto monopoly was deemed harmful to consumers, it was broken up by order of the US supreme court into 34 smaller companies. Meta operates like a monopoly, with users feeling they can’t move, because all their friends and contacts are on the same few platforms. “Meta knowingly exploit this and refuse to make changes to their platforms that they know would deliver safer user experiences,” Damian Collins, a former chair of the UK parliamentary committee that oversees the digital realm, told me. If users could move their data and contacts over to new services, giving them more options, “break-up would work”.

This week’s settlement has been a disappointment to those longing to see the tech giants finally brought to heel, found guilty by courts and made to pay for it with costs too big to ignore. For now, Meta has swerved judgment day. But that day must surely come.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

Brighton appoint Arturo Ruiz as head coach following exit of Dario Vidosic

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 16:00:54 GMT

Ruiz led Real Sociedad to Champions League qualifying

Vidosic frontrunner to take over NWSL side Angel City

Brighton have confirmed the appointment of Arturo Ruiz from Real Sociedad as a replacement head coach for Dario Vidosic.

The Women’s Super League club have acted quickly to replace Vidosic, whose departure was confirmed earlier on Friday, just over a week before the start of the new Women’s Super League campaign. Vidosic is understood to be the leading candidate for the head coach role at the NWSL side Angel City and although Brighton are disappointed to lose the Croatia-born Australian, they are understood to be very happy to be able to bring in Ruiz on a three-year deal, subject to a work permit being finalised.

Ruiz led Sociedad to third in Liga F last season and into the qualifying rounds for the Women’s Champions League, where they are trailing Chelsea 5-2 on aggregate after Wednesday night’s first leg in London. “We are delighted to welcome Arturo to the club. During our recruitment process, he quickly stood out,” said Zoe Johnson, Brighton’s women’s and girls’ managing director. “He has a proven track record of developing teams and individuals. We have confidence in his ability to continue to drive this team forward, and he will have our full support as we make our final preparations for the start of the new WSL season.”

Writing on Instagram on Friday, Ruiz said: “I would have liked my farewell to both the team and the fans to have been different, but circumstances didn’t allow it. Thank you from the bottom of my heart to all the players and colleagues at the club, who have treated me so well. Together we’ve experienced something spectacular, which will leave a lasting memory for each and every one of us.”

Vidosic has been in charge of Brighton for two years and led them to their first Wembley appearance in May’s Women’s FA Cup final. The departure of the 39-year-old, which was first reported by the Daily Telegraph, is understood to have surprised many members of Brighton’s squad.

“We would like to thank Dario for his contribution over the past two years. During his time with the club, he led us to our highest-ever WSL finish and our first Women’s FA Cup final,” said Johnson. “We are naturally disappointed but respect his decision to pursue a new challenge and wish him every success for the future. Our priority now is recruiting our new head coach and continuing our preparation ahead of the start of the Women’s Super League season next weekend.”

Vidosic, a former Australia midfielder who has also managed Melbourne City Women, said: “I have loved my time at the Albion and am proud of what we have achieved together. Leaving has been a difficult decision, but I believe it is the right time for me and my family to begin a new chapter. I would like to thank the players, staff and supporters for their support throughout my time at the club and wish everyone associated with Albion every success.”

Angel City have been led by their interim head coach, Leif Smerud, the former Crystal Palace manager, since June’s departure of Alexander Straus. Sources close to Angel City have said the club are very happy with Smerud leading the team for the rest of this season. The Los Angeles-based team are ninth, two points off the playoffs.

‘This place might look bad but it’s not’: fear and hope in Middlesbrough community after week of violence

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 15:57:07 GMT

Nine people have died in events police had linked to organised crime in an area shaped by deprivation and fading opportunities, but there is light, say residents

“This place might look bad but it’s not, the people are good people,” said one woman before turning to her young daughter and asking: “Is this place bad?” The girl shakes her head vigorously.

It’s a difficult thing to say given the week’s events in Grangetown and South Bank on Teesside.

Around the corner is the burned-out shell of a house that was deliberately set on fire on Wednesday, killing Natalie McDonald, 34, and her seven-year-old niece Valentina Foster. Metres away is the A66 where, less than a mile away on Saturday, a head-on crash killed seven people, including two police officers.

Cleveland police had linked the crash to organised crime and initially said they could not rule out it also being connected to the house fire, but on Friday said there was no link.

The news will be of no surprise to neighbours and well-wishers who this week gathered sombrely opposite the house in Birchington Avenue, Grangetown. They had already said there was no link.

“It’s smackheads. That’s the problem round here,” said one neighbour.

John Kirton, the brother of McDonald, told reporters: “My sister was not involved with anything to do with gangs, or the [crash on the] A66.

“That’s what makes this so senseless. People think they can do whatever they like. There’s some terrible people in the world and now my sister and Valentina have gone.”

People, all reluctant to give their names, said the community was a tight-knit one. “Everyone looks out for each other,” said one woman.

But they also agreed that there was a big problem with gangs of boys and young men involved in drug dealing and other crimes.

People felt trapped in their own homes, afraid to go to the shops, said the Middlesbrough and Thornaby East MP, Andy McDonald. He called it a form of “terrorism”.

Jonathan Brash, the MP for Hartlepool, said communities felt organised crime was “embedded”.

There have been nine deaths and other possibly gang-related local crimes including a knife attack and the ramming of an empty house. On Thursday evening, video was shared on social media showing cars being torched at a vigil for one of the men who died in the A66 crash. It was in Haswell, County Durham, 20 miles north of the crash site.

The events of the last week have clearly left a community shellshocked and in need of help, fearful of what might happen next.

Alec Brown, the leader of Redcar and Cleveland council, said authorities were working “tirelessly” to ensure people feel safe. About 200 extra police from other forces have been drafted in and some could be seen arriving at Cleveland’s police headquarters on Friday morning.

The extra police are coming from the Northumbria, Durham, Humberside and North, South and West Yorkshire forces as well as the National Crime Agency. The hope is that a show of strength can dampen tensions and reassure the area.

Anna Turley, the MP for Redcar, said on Friday that not every incident police attended was connected to the investigation into organised crime.

“I think it’s really important to get across the fact that these incidents are not all linked,” she said. “It could feel that way at the moment because of the national spotlight on us, but unfortunately, we know we’ve had a high level of crime, and in this area for a long time now, these are incidents, sadly, that we see all the time.”

Terry Chapman is not from Grangetown, but was “born and raised” on a different Middlesbrough council estate.

He didn’t quite know why he had come to the site of the house blaze, but felt he had to. “I know these areas, they are like where I’m from,” he said. “We have problems but when things happen like this … it’s just hard to believe. It’s really horrendous and scary.”

Chapman said criminal gangsters were the minority. “The vast majority of people, including in places like Grangetown, are absolutely fantastic people.

“They may not have a lot. Some do. Some are managing and some are barely managing. But fundamentally, the majority of people are decent and they’re law-abiding. The trouble is that the small minority seem to have a bigger influence in places like this and it’s gone unchecked for years.”

Grangetown and South Bank are clearly deprived, rundown areas. There are small terraces of shops, many shut, and no obvious centre.

It’s also striking how few pubs there are. One former pub, the Magnet – which hosted early gigs for the Grangetown-born comedian Roy Chubby Brown – is now a branch of Heron Foods.

Saturday’s collision took place on the A66 between Church Lane and Normanby Road. Police had been pursuing a VW Passat with five young men in it for seven minutes before it turned on to the dual carriageway, against the flow of traffic. The pursuit was aborted. Ten seconds later the Passat crashed into a police car. Everyone died at the scene, including the police officers Matthew Blades and Tom Clough.

On the corner of Church Lane and the A66 a retired steelworker is looking desperately at the bouquets left for the PCs.

He’s called Joe. “I better not give you my surname, because of the lunatics …”

The former steelworks, where most people in the area worked, was literally on the other side of the road, Joe said. “I could be out of work and back home in 10 minutes.”

He is close to tears at what has happened in his community this week. “The problem is the police don’t have the resources. There used to be a station in South Bank, there used to be a station in Eston. Now there’s no police here and they [the criminal gangs] are doing whatever they like with drugs passing from one to another. They’ve got away with it for years.”

It’s also true that the problems in this part of Teesside are not isolated. Countless other places everywhere, not just the UK, have major problems with gangs and organised crime. You can watch versions of the problem on TV whenever you want, whether it’s Naples, Baltimore or Liverpool.

It’s easy to see places like Grangetown and South Bank as postcards for forgotten England, places tabloids sometimes say are controlled by feral gangs. But scratch the surface and there is light.

In South Bank on Normanby Road, near the A66 junction, is a community gallery set up by the Iraqi artist and Teesside University graduate Azad Karim Mohammed.

The Saabat Gallery is a great place, currently showing and selling the work of the local artists Rita Readman and David Watson.

The gallery’s coordinator, Nathaniel McGovern, has been there five years. “Everyone is warm and welcoming round here,” he said. “People are happy to help and it’s a close community.

“It has been a mad week for everyone round here but you get nice people and bad people everywhere, don’t you? I’d say this area’s got more nice people than bad.”

Russ Abbot: a class act, on stage and off

Readers respond to Simon Hattenstone’s interview with the retired actor and comedian

Simon Hattenstone’s wonderful interview with Russ Abbot (‘In 1984, I worked 363 days’: how Russ Abbot soared to success – then walked away, 24 August) brought back a treasured story that leaves my family eternally grateful to him.

During the summer of 2010, we travelled from Scotland on holiday, staying in Windsor, and attended Oliver! at the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane. When the show ended late at night, I had to set off on a 30-minute walk just to retrieve our car.

With my wife in a broken-down electric wheelchair and our two daughters, aged just eight and six, beside her, they faced a long, vulnerable wait on the pavement. Making matters worse, I then got caught in a central London driving nightmare, desperately trying to navigate back to them with a broken satnav, no map, and no knowledge of the city streets.

When Russ walked out of the stage door, he didn’t just pass by. Seeing my stranded family and my young daughters deeply distressed, he stayed and went to work comforting them, running through multiple Fagin monologues right there on the street. The girls were so completely sidetracked that they forgot anything was amiss. They were absolutely buzzing to meet “Fagin”, and it became an overriding memory they talked about all night. He turned a stressful situation into pure magic.

Our evening was saved not only by Russ’s incredible warmth, but also by the extraordinary humanity of two Polish doormen from a nightclub across the street. They rushed over to assist, letting my children stay warm in the back of one of their family cars until I finally found my way back.

To my family, the man who stepped out of the Drury Lane stage door that night was a true class act, both on and off the stage. Philip ShowellHamilton, South Lanarkshire

Simon Hattenstone’s interview with Russ Abbot took me straight back to our living room in the early 1980s – Saturday evening, dinner over, and all of us settling into that post-dinner golden hour of family television.

Russ always seemed such a happy chap, and his humour was wonderfully infectious. I can still hear my dear mother’s uncontrollable laughter one evening in particular as he launched into a gloriously over-the-top Bruce Forsyth, complete with cries of “higher! Higher!”

More than 40 years on, the memory still makes me smile. Thank you, Simon, for taking me back to that very happy time and place. And to Russ and his wife, Trish, after 60 years together, may the laughter continue. Noel HineyDublin, Ireland

Reading the Russ Abbot interview reminded me of a time when Saturday afternoon telly into the early evening would be a gathering force for our family.

Wrestling and Big Daddy and the latest American show like The A-Team or Airwolf, followed by gameshows hosted by the big comedian of the time and then the sketch comedy series. It didn’t matter if it was a repeat such as The Two Ronnies or Russ Abbot’s Madhouse.

Strict timings were adhered to and tea worked around a Radio Times-driven schedule – that, or you mastered the recording settings on your VCR.

Something’s been lost in an era where each of us has an individual screen and streaming services, meaning we can watch as and when we like. My father had the remote, and dictated the narrative on the box, but at least we were all in the same room at the same time, laughing simultaneously.

It’s never as good as you remember – but I do miss it. Lovely article. David Howes Hebden Bridge, West Yorkshire

Protect fossils from hammer-wielding tourists

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 15:31:20 GMT

Jill White responds to an editorial calling for fossils to be given legally protected national-treasure status

I write this while sitting on Charmouth beach in Dorset with my required reading of the Saturday Guardian, as I do regularly. Your editorial (The Guardian view on the export of fossils: they deserve national treasure status, 21 August) produced a hollow laugh as – this being the centre of fossil hunting on the Jurassic Coast – I am surrounded by armies of hammer-wielding tourists busy smashing the daylights out of any rock available around them. The vast majority have no idea which stone types are likely to bear fossils and don’t report any finds even if they are lucky. Others take carrier bags full of stones back to their cars.

Thus, we have no idea what fossils are being lost to the record every single day here, and so I completely support the suggestion of giving them legal protection. Of course, amateur collecting has a valuable place in unearthing important fossil finds, but only if they are shared and documented. The Charmouth Heritage Coast Centre valiantly tries to educate and inform visitors, but sadly these will inevitably be the minority.

Charmouth is a key part of the designated Jurassic Coast world heritage site, but I can’t think of any others where visitors are allowed, or even encouraged, to bring or rent hammers to wreck the protected features and/or remove them from the site unrecorded. If we want to protect our fossil heritage for future generations to study, we could make a start by regulating this geological vandalism. Jill WhiteMusbury, Devon

Choking is sold to teens as a safe sexual practice. The research says it never is

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 15:00:04 GMT

More and more young people are engaging in sexual strangulation. But experts say there’s no safe pressure – and we have to start talking to teenagers about it

When touching someone’s throat, it can only take the pressure of a handshake to cause serious injury, unconsciousness or death. These injuries, which include brain damage and stroke, are often internal and invisible, showing up days or even months after the initial incident occurred. Experts say many who participate in sexual choking are not aware of the risks.

Choking or sexual strangulation is common among young people, says Prof Heather Douglas of the Melbourne Law School. In a 2024 survey of 4,702 Australians aged between 18 and 35, she and her research team found that 57% reported ever having experienced sexual strangulation; 51% reported ever having strangled a partner and 43.9% reported participating in both.

A police investigation into the death of a 16-year-old girl in Sydney, who is believed to have become unconscious as a result of asphyxiation during sexual intercourse, has brought the practice to national attention again this week.

Douglas says their survey found gender differences in prevalence rates. Young women were more likely to report having been strangled (61%) and young men were more likely to report strangling a partner (59%). Among trans and gender-diverse young people the rates were even higher, with 78% reporting ever having been strangled and 74% reporting ever having strangled someone else. Many had positive perceptions of the act – believing it was safe and led to more enjoyable sex. “I don’t think that a lot of young people know how dangerous it is,” Douglas says.

There have been similar findings globally. Dr Debby Herbenick is the world’s leading researcher on sexual choking.

When Herbenick conducted her first nationally representative survey asking about sexual choking in the United States a decade ago, “the data came back and I was just floored,” she says. Only a small percentage of adults in midlife and beyond reported being choked, but for those aged 18-39, “more than a third of them had reported being choked during sex”.

The issue “felt really urgent”, says Herbenick, who is director of Indiana University’s Center for Sexual Health Promotion. When she spoke to her students about it, “they were like, ‘Oh no, it’s OK. We’re all doing the same thing.’

“I think what bothered me about it, and worried me, was I felt like they weren’t making informed choices. They were making choices, but they weren’t informed.”

In Australia, when choking results in serious harm, the laws are straightforward. Every state and territory has specific assault laws around strangulation. “Injuries or a strangulation that causes death or really serious harm can’t be consented to,” Douglas says.

But the fact that many young people believe choking is low-risk and enjoyable is a vexed public health issue.

When Women’s Health New South Wales was funded to improve workforce capacity to respond to strangulation, they ran headlong into this problem. Jackie McMillan, a senior project officer, says: “When we started that work, we realised that we couldn’t do that without also talking about sexual choking.”

Physically, strangulation and sexual choking carry the same risks, but “they’re slightly different conversations,” McMillan says.

“If people are calling what they’re doing ‘sexual choking’, it’s because they’re making a distinction between what they see as a consensual sexual practice about freedom of sexual expression, and something that is violence. And if you start in with a language of violence, you often lose those people … They’re not interested in what you have to say. They turn off because they think that what you’re talking about is not what they’re doing.”

Herbenick agrees. “Our research here is very clear that we need to be using the word ‘choking’,” she says. “If people think about what they’re doing as choking, and you call it strangulation, they think, ‘oh, well, I’m not strangling or being strangled. I’m doing choking and choking is safe’.”

When Herbenick has asked young people to describe how they choke in detail, overwhelmingly they describe applying pressure to the neck, and list symptoms like dizziness, seeing stars and shortness of breath. “And so certainly anyone in those buckets has some evidence of doing what we would call strangulation,” she says.

Herbenick’s research includes a partnership with neuroscientists, testing for brain changes in women who have been choked. While there is a large body of evidence about the neurological effects of strangulation in domestic violence contexts, because the subjective experience of choking can be so different, “in some ways I felt like we had to start from scratch,” she says.

For instance, in domestic violence contexts, there is strong evidence that repeat strangulation has more pronounced neurological effects. “But when you look at those multiple versus single strangulation studies, multiple is often like two or three or four times, right? But then if you look at sexual choking, people are often choked, in our studies, an average of 25 times – but sometimes 50 or 100 or 200 or 500 times, because it’s become such a common thing that people do.”

Observations of women who frequently participate in choking and recently participated in choking both suggested it can cause brain injury.

But data on effective public health messaging is still nascent.

Herbenick’s team tried educational messages around the health implications of sexual choking, the importance of receiving specific consent for choking, and messages about the potential legal consequences if an injury occurs. While they found “all three message types were very well received by young adults”, for women, “only the health and consent messages were especially effective” in changing their intentions around choking.

For men to change their intentions, “they needed to know about potential legal consequences in the event of injury or death,” Herbenick says. “It was tough to see, because of course we would like to think that knowing that something could be harmful for somebody’s health would be enough to make a lot of people change their behaviour.” That finding persisted regardless of whether men were choking or being choked.

All the experts who spoke to the Guardian agreed that widespread and robust sexual education that engages specifically with choking is a vital first step in preventing catastrophic health outcomes.

But school systems are not prepared to engage in this level of sexual education, and young people’s information environment, especially on social media, is flooded with misinformation.

“There are some sex educators … who claim that there are safe ways to choke. And there’s just a lot of regular people out there making TikTok videos claiming there are safe ways to choke,” says Herbenick.

“Pornography is one piece of it,” she adds. “Social media is one piece of it. Anyone whose kids are reading fan fiction or … dark romance novels is almost certainly coming across choking.”

On social media, it is often referred to lightheartedly as a “hand necklace” or through memes like “Choke me daddy”.

There are no circumstances under which exerting pressure on the soft tissue of someone’s neck is safe; and when drugs or alcohol are involved, the practice becomes even riskier. But this information is not easy to find. McMillan created a website, It Left No Marks, to help combat this void. “We had to build it because it wasn’t there,” she says.

Wellington-based criminology academic Dr Samantha Keene says the tragic death of UK woman Grace Millane in New Zealand in 2020 “put conversations about rough sex and sexual choking or sexual strangulation on the public agenda”. But lately, she says, it has fallen off the radar.

“We know that sexual choking and sexual strangulation is eroticised in a whole range of media … yet we aren’t addressing that in sexual and relationships education.”

“What we know works is having an evidence-based approach,” she says. That means “meeting people where they are” in a non-judgmental way, by giving them access to information that outlines the range of risks associated with this form of sexual practice.

Meeting young people where they are is not a comfortable conversation, Herbenick says. “A lot of parents are thinking, ‘How am I living in a world where I’m supposed to be talking about strangulation during sex, with my … 13-year-old, 15-year-old?’

“I don’t know, but I can tell you that in our studies, when we ask college students how old they were when they first learned about choking, on average the age is 15. Which means that about half of them are learning about it younger than 15.”

McMillan says it takes “endorsement” to deliver this kind of education.

“That’s endorsement from parents. That’s endorsement from the school. That’s endorsement from the principals. We can’t leave teachers out there alone to discuss websites that they can’t even go to without there being a panic,” she says.

“How can we get teachers to talk about pornography if they can’t even visit the sites that the kids are on? We’ve created an impossible situation.”

International research has found that many of the young people who engaged in choking felt some degree of pressure from their partner, or their wider social environment, to do so. “So there’s questions around whether that is true consent, if we say it’s truly free and voluntary,” Douglas says.

Beyond understanding the consequences physically and legally, “what we need to do is make sure that people are skilled up with the things they need to redirect sexual activities to something else they might find pleasurable,” McMillan says.

“And also that particularly young women know sex is meant to be pleasurable. So if you’re not having fun, don’t do that bit.”

Four men admit destroying Jewish community ambulances in Golders Green

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 14:30:28 GMT

Prosecutors allege men were deliberately targeting Jewish community when four vehicles were set ablaze in March

Four men have pleaded guilty to destroying four Jewish community ambulances in an arson attack causing about £1m of damage.

Hamza ⁠Iqbal, 20, Rehan Khan, 19, and Judex Atshatshi and Saif Ali, both 18, admitted to a charge of destroying or damaging property being reckless whether life would be endangered.

Atshatshi, Khan and Iqbal entered their pleas by video link from Wandsworth and Pentonville jails, with Ali in the dock of the Old Bailey on Friday.

Four ambulances belonging to the Jewish volunteer emergency service Hatzola were set on fire on the morning of 23 March while they were parked near a synagogue in Golders Green, an area of north London that has a large Jewish community. Prosecutors said the attack caused about £1m of damage.

The prosecutor, Leo Seelig, suggested the incident had a “terrorist connection” although no mention was made in court of potential proxies working for Iran.

Previously, counter-terror police had looked into the possible involvement of Iranian proxies in the Jewish ambulance arson, as well as other attacks on Jewish sites in London. Most have been claimed online by Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamia, the Islamic Movement of the Companions of the Right.

However, in April, Iran’s embassy in the UK said it “categorically rejects” allegations of involvement in “violent activities or incidents in the United Kingdom”.

Three of the defendants were said to have set fire to the fully stocked vehicles while a fourth waited in a blue Toyota Avensis. The resulting blaze caused gas canisters inside the ambulances to explode and nearby flats and a synagogue were also damaged by the fire.

The four men were arrested after an investigation by counter-terrorism police.

On his arrest on 1 April, Ali threw his mobile phone out of the window, the court was previously told. The defendant, then aged 17, had been in contact with someone in February with a view to buying a blue Toyota Avensis and had researched online the cost of ambulances.

The prosecution had alleged Ali went on to source the Toyota that was used in the attack, with WhatsApp messages between him and a co-defendant relating to the purchase.

Prosecutors have said they believe the incident was a targeted attack against the Jewish community.

Hatzola is a Jewish charity established in 1979 and run by volunteers, providing free medical transportation and emergency response to Jewish and non-Jewish people in north London.

As well as the ambulances, said to have cost between £240,000 and £250,000 each, four electrical charging stations and cables costing about £5,000 each were also damaged.

Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb ordered pre-sentence reports for Iqbal and Khan, from Leyton, east London, Atshatshi, from Dagenham, east London, and Ali, of dual British-Pakistani nationality, from Walthamstow.

Remanding them in custody, the senior judge said their sentencing would take place in the spring of 2027 at the conclusion of a separate trial.

At the same hearing, a fifth defendant, Subhan Ahmed, 18, from Walthamstow, pleaded not guilty to a charge of assisting an offender.

Ahmed, who is alleged to have helped to get rid of the car used in the attack, will go on trial at the Old Bailey on 27 January next year.

Andy Burnham says he will not vote on assisted dying bill to avoid swaying debate

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 14:30:01 GMT

Exclusive: PM also warns his ministers against trying to influence vote when bill returns to Commons next month

Andy Burnham has told Labour MPs that he will not cast a vote when the assisted dying bill returns to the Commons next month, to avoid influencing the debate.

While supporters of the measure welcomed his move, No 10 officials said the prime minister had no wish to affect the process in either direction, and was just doing what he thought was best to allow MPs to reach their own collective view.

In a separate letter to his ministers on Friday, Burnham warned them against trying to influence the process. When an earlier version of the bill was before parliament, Wes Streeting, the then health secretary who now holds the defence brief, voiced worries about its impact on the NHS.

An original version of the private member’s bill to permit assisted dying in limited circumstances in England and Wales, led by the Labour MP Kim Leadbeater, ran out of time in the last parliament after peers tabled 1,200 amendments.

Another Labour MP, Lauren Edwards, who came second in May’s new ballot for private members’ bills, has tabled a near-identical version to allow adults with less than six months to live to apply for an assisted death, subject to the approval of two doctors and an expert panel.

It has its second reading in the Commons – the first opportunity MPs get to vote on a bill – on 11 September.

Keir Starmer voted for Leadbeater’s bill as prime minister on its second and third readings, while otherwise remaining neutral on an issue seen as a matter of conscience, and where parties gave their MPs a free vote. In his letter to MPs, Burnham said he was taking a different approach.

“The government remains neutral on the question of assisted dying and on the passage of the bill,” he said, stating it was “vital that every view is respected”.

Burnham wrote: “There is no single right position and I have deep respect for MPs on all sides, and the expertise they bring to this debate.”

Saying he had his “own personal views on the issue”, Burnham went on: “However, I am also clear that this is a matter for parliament to decide and my role, as the prime minister, will be to lead a government that implements the will of parliament in this area – whether that is to change the law or not.

“I also do not want to unduly influence the debate as prime minister and for every colleague to know it is a genuinely free vote. For these reasons, I have taken the decision that it is most appropriate for me not to vote at second reading.”

As the Greater Manchester mayor, Burnham previously said he supported the idea in principle. But in July, he said it would be “very challenging” to introduce the change before palliative care and social care were improved.

Supporters of the bill argue that, with a proposed implementation period of up to four years, there is time for this to happen.

In his letter to ministers, Burnham confirmed that, as is the convention for issues involving conscience, collective responsibility would be again set aside, with frontbenchers free to vote or abstain as they wanted.

MPs should be “able to reach those conclusions without feeling that the government is seeking to influence the debate”, he wrote, adding: “At the dispatch box, I ask that ministers reiterate that this is a question for parliament, on which the official government position is to remain neutral, with the same approach taken outside parliament when dealing with all forms of media, including social media.

“Of course, ministers do not need to resile from their previously stated views when directly asked about them and can correspond with constituents about their previous position, but they should avoid being part of the public debate, and should not express views about the implications of the bill for their department’s responsibilities.”

When he was health secretary under Starmer, Streeting used a message to constituents to express doubts about whether the NHS could afford to establish an assisted dying service given other budgetary pressures.

Edwards said: “Andy Burnham is absolutely right to say that people’s personal experiences around terminal illness lie at the heart of the debate and I welcome his view that everyone’s views should be treated with dignity and respect. That is certainly the approach I will be taking and I look forward to what will be a very important debate in two weeks’ time.”

Sarah Wootton, the chief executive of the campaign group Dignity in Dying, said: “We welcome the prime minister reaffirming the government’s neutrality and requesting that ministers do not attempt to influence the debate.

“More and more countries are introducing choice at the end of life. France has just legalised assisted dying. This week Australia completed the set; every single state and territory offers dying people this choice. The will of the public is settled. The will of the Commons is clear, and parts of the British Isles have already moved. On 11 September, MPs must finish what they started.”

King Harald V of Norway obituary

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 14:07:11 GMT

Monarch who opened up the Norwegian royal family and its palaces to the public, and married a commoner despite his father’s opposition

King Harald V of Norway, who has died aged 89, Europe’s oldest serving monarch, was the country’s third king since it regained independence in 1905 following the dissolution of its union with Sweden. Although he ceased to be head of the Lutheran state church in 2012 and subsequently lost his constitutional status as “holy” six years later, he did exhibit the Scandinavian moderation, stoicism and genial approachability that led a newspaper to name him Norway’s person of the year in 2017.

The first Norwegian king to be born in the country since 1370, Harald was also related to both the Swedish and the British royal families. His parents were Crown Prince Olav, who was king as Olav V between 1957 and 1991, and his wife, Princess Märtha, a member of the Swedish royal dynasty. His grandparents were King Haakon VII, the first king of the independent country, who reigned for 52 years from 1905, and his wife, Queen Maud, daughter of Britain’s Edward VII. The family roots are Danish – from the Glücksburg dynasty – as were those of the Duke of Edinburgh and the former Greek royal family. The mixed heritage made him sympathetic to refugees: “It is not easy to say where we come from. Home is where the heart is,” he said.

He was Queen Elizabeth II’s second cousin and a knight of the garter. At the time of his birth, Harald was 16th in line to the British throne, though he had fallen in the rankings to around 80th in more recent years. Confusingly, he was not the fifth Harald to rule his country, but the sixth – the 10th-century Harald Bluetooth generally not being assigned a number in the list of Norwegian kings. The king never attracted a picturesque title as did some of his Viking predecessors – such as Bluetooth, Harald Fairhair and Harald Hardrada, who tried to seize the English throne a few weeks before the Norman invasion in 1066 and was killed at the battle of Stamford Bridge.

Harald himself was only three at the time of the Nazi invasion of Norway in 1940, and he and his mother and two older sisters, Ragnhild and Astrid, initially fled to Sweden, which, trying to maintain its neutrality while accommodating the Germans’ attack on their neighbour, was reluctant to let them in. It is alleged that the royal party was initially turned back at the border, and allowed to proceed only when the driver of their car threatened to ram it through the border post. Within three months, Harald, his sisters and mother had escaped to the US. They spent the war years in Washington DC and Harald thereafter spoke English with a slight American accent.

Meanwhile, Harald’s grandfather and father escaped to England, where they led a government in exile. Famously Haakon, turning up at the BBC to make a broadcast to his people, was asked by a receptionist: “Where did you say you were king of, dear?”

Following the liberation of Norway at the end of the war, the family was reunited and Harald was enrolled first at a state primary and then at Oslo cathedral school. From there he studied at Oslo University and the Norwegian military academy, before following in his father’s footsteps to read history, economics and politics at Balliol College, Oxford, where he also rowed for the college. A keen competitive yachtsman, he and his crews represented Norway at successive Olympics in Tokyo in 1964, Mexico City in 1968 and Munich in 1972, and won world championship medals through the 1980s and a European championship gold medal in 2005.

If this was a conventional career, much less so was his determination to marry a commoner, Sonja Haraldsen, a shop assistant who was the daughter of an Oslo textile manufacturer, whom he had met at a sailing party in 1959. The friendship was kept secret for several years, partly because of Olav’s reluctance to have the heir to the throne marry someone who was not royal. In the end, Harald forced the issue by declaring to his father that if he was not allowed to marry her he would not marry anyone, thus bringing an end to the dynasty. The couple married in 1968.

Harald was sworn in as king automatically following Olav’s death in January 1991. Although lacking his father’s easy bonhomie, the king attempted successfully – and popularly – to open up the institution and its palace and estates more freely to the public. The Norwegian monarch’s duties are similar to those in Britain, with non-exercised executive power, and all official acts having to be endorsed by the governing council of state, equivalent to a British cabinet. The Norwegian parliament constitutionally debates whether to continue the monarchy every four years, and earlier this year, despite controversies concerning the royal family, voted in favour of its continuation by 141 to 26.

The greatest crisis in the country’s modern history occurred on 22 July 2011 when the domestic terrorist Anders Behring Breivik murdered 77 people, mainly at a young socialists’ holiday camp on Utøya island. The king attracted public praise in the wake of the tragedy, when he met bereaved relatives and called for national solidarity and mutual support. He was seen to weep at the memorial service for the victims.

Harald was treated for bladder cancer in 2003, contracted Covid, had a pacemaker fitted in 2024 and was being treated for the blood disorder haemolytic anaemia.

He is survived by Sonja and their children, Princess Märtha Louise and Prince Haakon, whose wife, Mette-Marit (nee Tjessem-Høiby), was obliged to apologise in February this year for email exchanges with the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, in which her name was mentioned nearly 1,000 times. The king said that she had not broken any law. Mette-Marit’s son by a previous relationship, Marius, was jailed for four years in June following convictions for two rapes and drug offences.

Haakon succeeds Harald as King Haakon VIII and will adopt the monarchy’s traditional motto: “All for Norway”.

Reading and Leeds have dropped BBC Introducing for a new ‘nepo baby stage’. Where does it leave DIY artists?

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 14:00:01 GMT

As R&L replace the BBC’s unsigned artists stage with one filled with rock scions and a Simon Cowell boyband, many are decrying disappearing opportunities for grassroots acts

This year’s Reading and Leeds festival lineups are a testament to the catholic tastes of a generation who have little regard for musical tribalism or the concept of genre: brash pop stars rub up against drum’n’bass acts, underground rappers, meat-and-potatoes indie bands and much more.

What at least 70% of those acts have in common, however, is that early on in their careers they were supported by the BBC’s Introducing scheme, a combination of regional and national radio shows playing music submitted by unsigned artists and festival stages that platform them. For almost 20 years, a BBC Introducing stage has been a core part of Reading and Leeds – until it was scrapped last month.

“It’s a loss,” says Juliette Jackson, of the Mercury-nominated indie band the Big Moon, who played the stage in 2015, a year after forming. “It was a really big deal to play that as a new band with no money. It’s huge when you’re starting out – it gives you an opportunity and puts you on a platform.”

Over the years, major British artists including Ed Sheeran, Charli xcx, the 1975 and Sam Fender started their careers with support from the initiative, which has few of the barriers to entry of the traditional music industry. Regional DJs suggest local acts for festival slots, with final decisions made by a wider BBC team.

Reading and Leeds organisers Festival Republic did not respond to detailed questions from the Guardian about why it had pulled the plug on an unsuspecting BBC, who were already planning their 2026 lineup. It has been replaced by the Canopy stage, billed as a “home for new and breaking acts”. In a public statement, Festival Republic claimed it offers greater opportunity: “Previously, only artists who had been selected by the BBC were qualified to play the Introducing Stage – now, we are able to open up this important platform to a much wider pool of emerging talent and book any new music artist for the stage.”

But that so-called “wider pool” has come under scrutiny. Fans have been highlighting the connections behind many of the acts booked for the stage, such as Violet Grohl (daughter of Dave Grohl), Cruz Beckham (son of Victoria and David) and Villanelle frontman Gene Gallagher (son of Liam). The boyband December 10 are already signed to a label after they formed on Simon Cowell’s Netflix series The Next Act.

It has led some to nickname the Canopy “the nepo baby stage”, and prompted coverage in Private Eye. In an Instagram post, music industry commentator the Secret DJ decried “nepotism and the rising use of famous names over new talent [that] is rapidly destroying the arts”.

In a general statement provided to the Guardian, Festival Republic said their booking policy for the stage is “open to emerging artists from all backgrounds and at different stages of development. Artists may be independent or signed and may have come through a variety of routes into the industry.”

BBC Introducing editor Kelly Betts told the Guardian: “We will miss being at Reading and Leeds for this year. Programming decisions for that stage are made by the festival organisers, so it’s not really for me to comment on how they choose to curate it.”

Jason Carter, who founded BBC Introducing in 2007 and was responsible for forging the relationships with festivals to put on live events, said he was “disappointed to hear [the news] and sad to see it no longer there” but that he “can see both sides”, adding that the industry has changed and “there’s a lot more ways today to access new music that the festival probably wants the opportunity to feed off”.

Ex-BBC Introducing presenter Tom Robinson said that while “the beauty of BBC introducing was that you needed no inside access”, it could still occasionally be an “arcane” process. It was also not immune from someone in the industry “having a whisper in the ear of somebody, and an act that a record company was supporting would mysteriously appear on the BBC Introducing stage. But on the whole, it worked, and it was great.”

Get music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every week

after newsletter promotion

But with Glastonbury having a fallow year this year – and with it their BBC Introducing stage – it’s an extra blow for young artists. “Reading and Leeds is a big moment in our calendar,” says Jess Iszatt, who hosts BBC Radio 1’s Introducing show. “Because it’s got such a young audience, it’s a really important one, and it means there’s less opportunity for the artists that we share each week on the show. It’s really sad and it feels like the end of an era.”

BBC Introducing is far from finished – it has just announced a full month of live events in 10 cities across the country in November, has recently expanded into the US, and continues to host stages at other festivals. But the sole grassroots pipeline to a major UK event has now been closed off. “When we talk about the successes of it, it [the decision] doesn’t make sense to me,” says Iszatt.

As for accusations of the new model favouring already well-established artists, Robinson prefers to see this as an opportunity rather than a threat. “Let the nepo babies go and do their nepo baby thing. If they make shit music, it’ll still be shit music. If they make great music, they deserve to succeed, but let’s not worry about them.”

Instead, he thinks it’s time to go back to celebrating the core purpose of Introducing. “At a time when we’re getting shat on from a great height by multinational streaming giants, I think the grassroots is the future,” he says. “And I’m hopeful that Introducing will carry on supporting gobsmacking talent and helping them find a wider audience.”

“I don’t know how they’ve booked their stage,” Iszatt says of Reading and Leeds’ Canopy offering, “but I do know how we book ours. And that would have been committing to supporting artists regardless of their means and wanting to make sure that it would be diverse in every aspect. Because that’s fair.”

All Blacks brace for Bok-lash as Erasmus adds late fly-half plot twist

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 12:35:16 GMT

Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu’s inclusion may be a classic piece of misdirection from South Africa in their must-win match against New Zealand

On the face of it, South Africa have been beset by disruption before their most significant match since the successful defence of their World Cup title. Rassie Erasmus had sought to lean further on the Springboks’ set-piece strengths by selecting Handré Pollard at fly-half for the second Test against New Zealand in Cape Town, suggesting a narrow gameplan. A return to the tried and tested. A reliance on what he knows best. Then came news of the “niggle”.

Out goes Pollard, who, according to the Friday morning bulletin, suffered said niggle in training on Wednesday and failed a fitness test 24 hours before the match, and back comes the far more adventurous Sacha Feinberg‑Mngomezulu into the No 10 jersey. Feinberg‑Mngomezulu struggled in last week’s 33-16 defeat at Ellis Park, as he did on his comeback from injury against Argentina earlier this month, but the 24-year-old has a skill set that has marked him out as a future global star.

Sign up to The Breakdown

The latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewed

after newsletter promotion

The upshot is that South Africa head to the Mother City for their must-win match against the All Blacks with a completely different type of fly-half. Pollard is experienced, reliable from the tee and, as Erasmus said this week, has delivered “under extreme pressure” time and again for the Springboks. His nerveless goal-kicking guided them to the 2023 World Cup title and, in what are forecast to be wet conditions, South Africa’s initial approach seemed clear. As Erasmus had said when reflecting on his side’s game management in the first Test, “we made a lot of stupid calls. Three points is two less than five [for a try]. Handré is a guy that has always done it for us”.

In turn, it is a fair conclusion to reach that the approach changes somewhat with the introduction of Feinberg-Mngomezulu, while the return of Cheslin Kolbe, who has replaced Kurt-Lee Arendse in the starting XV as of Friday, is significant because he will assume goal‑kicking duties.

It does not take much looking on social media, however, to find the conspiracy theorists spouting what, truth be told, most of us are wondering – was this a classic piece of misdirection from Erasmus? Was it the plan all along? The fact that Erasmus has previous further fuels that particular fire, as does the convenience of recalling Kolbe to kick at goal, but Pollard’s selection did make a degree of sense.

In the 2023 World Cup semi-final against England, Erasmus hooked Manie Libbok after half an hour, sending on Pollard to steer the Boks home. When the chips are down, Pollard is the Springboks’ go-to move. As the 1995 World Cup-winning captain, Joel Stransky, says: “Handré brings maturity and stability, and an ability to close the game off. I think there’s a bit of a message in that saying we might just go back to what we used to do best and maybe not the running game.”

New Zealand have clearly been preparing to face Pollard, and the type of gameplan he would carry out, and as a result will have to adapt on the hoof. But to what extent can the same be said for the Springboks? Injuries, of course, happen and South Africa are not the first side to possess a variety of options at fly-half. But the significance here is that his particular selection speaks to the identity of the Springboks just a year out from their tilt at a third straight World Cup title.

Do they intend to try to defend it with the set-piece-heavy gameplan that has served them so well or, with Feinberg-Mngomezulu running the show, to do so with more creativity and imagination? It is to South Africa’s credit that hitherto in the World Cup cycle, they have looked a side perfectly equipped to do both. But when the “extreme pressure” comes on, which way will they turn? Erasmus has been forced to change tack at the 11th hour. On the face of it.

The All Blacks, for their part, will try to shut out the noise. They are walking tall after ending South Africa’s run of 12 straight victories and the penny has dropped that, whoever is playing at fly-half for the Springboks, the scrum contest will be pivotal in Cape Town. Such was South Africa’s profligacy in the New Zealand 22 last week, the All Blacks ran out comfortable winners despite conceding six scrum penalties in a barrage by the Boks. That they were able to turn the tide, winning a crucial scrum penalty of their own near their own line, and achieve relative parity thereafter was key to their victory; Dave Rennie wasted little time in flagging concerns this week over South African tactics.

“Scrum-wise, we’ve spoken with World Rugby around a couple of issues from our point of view, and so we think – scrum-wise – we’ll be a lot better,” Rennie said. “That was massive for them last week. We think if they’re forced to scrum square and not allowed to step sidewards and walk around us, then we’ll be able to stay in front and we’ll be able to get the footie going off that.”

As pre-match comments go, they are about as predictable as a late Springboks team change but, with rain expected, the close-quarters battle will be the most significant aspect of the match on Saturday. Having lost 43-10 in Wellington last year, a week after edging home in Auckland, the All Blacks know the Bok-lash is coming.

‘I want to be seen as a bloody good trainer’: Gihan Arnolda’s journey from sleeping rough to beating Britain’s top stables

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 12:16:54 GMT

Former jockey reflects on remarkable story from overcoming hardship to breaking barriers as the first trainer of black or Asian heritage at Flat racing’s HQ

“It’s just unbelievable, isn’t it?” Gihan Arnolda says as he reflects on his first three months as a trainer: five winners from 33 runners, £50,000 prize money banked and a string that is, according to the much-respected Timeform operation’s “run to form” statistic, outperforming every other Flat yard in Britain.

But it could equally apply to the story of Arnolda’s journey from the east end of London to Cadland Cottage Stables at the bottom of Warren Hill in Newmarket. He was the first trainer of black or Asian heritage in Flat racing’s HQ when he received his licence earlier this year, and that is just one among a host of unlikely firsts and Sliding-Doors moments along the way.

It is safe to assume that he is also the first trainer to have slept rough on the streets of east London as a teenager.

“My mum and dad are Sri Lankan and Portuguese background,” Arnolda explains. “My mother passed away of leukaemia when I was very young. My dad was off the rails, really. [From 12 years of age] I used to run away and I was just living on the streets for weeks at a time.

“I was stealing from shops to live, not that I was that person but I had no other way of living. I remember living in people’s gardens and I couldn’t see any way out, and then you’re on the verge of the gang stuff. I could easily have gone down a very, very different path, because people I knew at that stage have gone down very different paths.”

The starting point for Arnolda’s escape from the downward spiral was unexpectedly close to home after a confrontation with his father.

“I went next door to a neighbour and they said whatever happens, we’re going to back you and try to foster you.

“I didn’t believe it really, and obviously the police came and I got taken back into care, but literally a year later that English family fostered me. I went from a rough school in east London to going to Wimbledon College. It was amazing. I got all my GCSEs, six As, four Bs, and went on to a law course at college.”

By this point, though, an alternative plan had already started to form in Arnolda’s mind thanks to his Saturday routine of watching racing on TV with his foster dad.

At 18, he applied for the foundation course at the British Racing School in Newmarket, and sat on a racehorse for the first time on day one. Less than nine months later, in July 1998, his fifth ride in public, Knave’s Ash, squeezed home by a short head in an apprentice handicap at Thirsk.

Arnolda had more than 200 rides and rode five more winners over the next decade, but he struggled to shake off the lingering effects of his tough early years.

“I went on to be a jockey but I really struggled mentally when I went into the big, wide world, and I couldn’t really focus on being a jockey. It’s really tough [to leave the care system], you’re kind of let go. You’re 18, but you’re not a normal 18-year-old that has had that guided upbringing.”

A broken pelvis in 2009 ended his riding career, by which point he had become “disillusioned” with racing. JETS – the retraining scheme for ex-jockeys – helped him to enrol to retrain as a chef. After a spell with the Michelin-starred Andrew Pern in Yorkshire, he moved to Gordon Ramsay’s Maze in London.

Five years on from his injury, though, racing was back on his mind. “I just felt like I had missed something in racing,” he says. “In 2014, I got offered a job at Godolphin with Charlie Appleby, then moved to Chris Wall and then Roger Varian, and I learned so much off them. They were my biggest mentors, and then I moved from assistant at Roger’s to [the Derby-winning trainer] Peter Chapple-Hyam, and he was a massive help too.”

Even with a dozen years of experience behind him, however, training in his own right still felt like a step too far from his East End roots.

“People were saying to me: ‘You’ve got so much knowledge, you’re such a horseman,’ and I’d say: ‘Yeah, well, there’s no chance of training,’ because I didn’t see anyone else like myself training. It’s normally handed down, or people have a massive connection in racing. I thought, I’ll just rattle around as an assistant.”

But an opening appeared when an owner with Denis Quinn, the previous licence holder at Cadland Cottage Stables, offered to support him, and Arnolda seized his chance.

“I’ve got that will to win, and the drive and the work ethic as well,” he says. “I’ve started with my partner [Charlotte] and we have two small children, so it’s a family thing and we’ve got friends that work with us as well, and it’s just slowly growing.

“I’ve got orders for six or seven yearlings at the [autumn] sales and I feel like having two-year-olds will add another string to the bow. Our aim was 10 winners by the end of the year, so we’re halfway there already, fingers crossed.”

Damascus Steel was Arnolda’s first winner, at the 11th attempt, in a handicap at Goodwood in mid-June. The six-year-old grey gelding followed up in a race at Epsom a month later and will attempt to take his trainer a step closer to his target on Monday in the Amateurs’ Derby, one of the feature events of the bank holiday programme.

Arnolda’s blossoming future as a Newmarket trainer is the focus now. “I love the heritage thing, don’t get me wrong,” Arnolda says. “But I want to be seen as just a bloody good trainer, and put it out there that you can have a really horrible start in life, but if you work twice as hard, you can actually get somewhere.”

Recent winners of the Solario Stakes have a mixed record in the top three-year-old events a year later, as three – including Masar, the 2018 Derby winner – went on to record Group One wins, but for several more this Group Three prize was as good as it got. Today’s latest renewal, though, looks unusually strong on paper, with three unbeaten colts at the top of the market.

Charlie Appleby’s Rock Montreal, a 1m gns (£1.05m) yearling, was highly impressive on debut at Yarmouth this month, while Sonic Angel is two-from-two in all‑weather novice events. The pick of the field, though, could be William Muir & Chris Grassick’s Breacher (3.30), a comfortable winner on debut at Salisbury in June from a stable whose juveniles find plenty for a run. He is bred to relish middle-distances next year so Sandown’s stiff seven furlongs looks sure to suit.

Goodwood 1.25 Rhythm Of My Heart will appreciate this step up to a mile after a promising run into a three-length second on debut at Kempton this month.

Sandown 1.40 Charlie Appleby’s Flower Show is a definite “lurker” on debut for a stable with a four-in-10 strike rate with its two‑year-olds this year, but John and Thady Gosden’s Thi Qar, second amid greenness first time up, is the one to beat on what little form there is.

‘I don’t care if I look good’: French heartthrob Louis Garrel on fashion, fatherhood and his radically dorky new role

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 12:00:57 GMT

The star has long been French cinema’s favourite tousle-haired Adonis, which makes his latest performance – as a schlubby, stay-at-home dad – all the more surprising. ‘I appreciate people laughing at me,’ he says

‘Even though I’ve been working in film for over 20 years, I still have this desire to look beautiful on screen,” says Louis Garrel, on a video call from his bed inside a boat off the coast of Corsica. The French film star is lying on his stomach, occasionally kicking up his bare legs, ruffling his curls and running the nail of his thumb over his moustache. I think the person he sees on the laptop screen in front of him is me, but I am pretty certain he is flirting with his own reflection.

The attraction between the Paris-born 43-year-old and the camera tends to be reciprocal. Long of limb, tousled of hair and chiselled of nose, Garrel has spent a career on screen as French cinema’s favourite Adonis – the man film-makers turn to when they need an erotic wrecking ball to smash up bourgeois twosomes and turn them into quivering menages a trois.

His breakout role in 2003 was as a priapic student revolutionary who inserts himself in the sexual bond between his twin sister (Eva Green) and a visiting American student (Michael Pitt) in Bernardo Bertolucci’s The Dreamers. Since then, he’s been reliably effective as smouldering sexpots whose intense stare cuts across dancefloors – bewitching two friends in Canadian director Xavier Dolan’s 2010 film Heartbeats, enticing Angelina Jolie into a fling in high-fashion drama Couture, or hawkishly pouncing on the poor Yves Saint Laurent in the 2014 biopic Saint Laurent, where he played Karl Lagerfeld’s dandy companion Jacques de Bascher. “I fight against it because I know that good actors don’t care about looking good,” he excuses himself. “But I’m not such a good actor.”

That is false modesty of the highest order. He hails from a dynasty of actor-film-makers that includes his mother Brigitte Sy, father (and ex-lover of Velvet Underground singer Nico) Philippe Garrel and grandfather Maurice Garrel, on whose advice he applied to and graduated from Paris’s prestigious Conservatoire drama school. On screen, he has not just impersonated dreamboats but also Alfred Dreyfus, King Louis XIII, Robespierre and Jean-Luc Godard. And in his latest film, Garrel does something that only good actors can do: to play magnificently against type.

In the comedy Just an Illusion, he is Yves, a former executive at a kitchen appliance firm who has recently lost his job but can’t bring himself to tell his family. Befitting the film’s 80s suburban Paris setting, Garrel’s hair here is bouffy rather than tousled, the moustache more Ron Burgundy than The Leopard-era Alain Delon. He wears a billowing beige trenchcoat that makes him look as befuddled as Monsieur Hulot, the comical everyman in the films of Jacques Tati.

In one scene, Yves is flicking through a magazine on the living room sofa while their apartment block’s caretaker Monsieur Berger (Pierre Lottin) shows Yves’ wife Sandrine (Camille Cottin, of Call My Agent fame) how to use her new desktop computer. As the mulleted Berger places his tattooed paw over Sandrine’s hand to guide the cursor, she giggles in delight. “If you go like this, Sandrine, it jerks.” “It jerks off all over the place,” she coos back. Yves, startled by echoes of the frisson that has long vanished from his marriage, rushes to put out the sparks and shows Berger the door. If reducing France’s go-to libertine to an anxiety-ridden gooseberry isn’t a feat of acting, what is?

“When I was very young, a director told me that on screen you have to be like a gorilla,” Garrel says. “You have to be intense and fascinating to watch, but have absolutely no idea of yourself. When I’m playing a character like this one, I can do less, you know, modelling. I don’t care if I look good, and most of the time you are better on screen when you don’t care.”

A hit upon its French release this spring, Just an Illusion is directed by film-making duo Éric Toledano and Olivier Nakache, who have been a major guarantee of box office success since Untouchable, about the relationship between a wealthy quadriplegic and his home helper. Like that predecessor, their new film’s comedy is of the non-inflammatory kind, its emotional timbre unashamedly sentimental. But along the way, it processes some surprisingly big political themes, including Franco-German reconciliation, the 1870 Crémieux Decree that granted French citizenship to Algerian Jews, the rise of the Front National and the anti-racism concerts that were organised in response. There is also the question of how a frustrated stay-at-home husband copes with a spouse embarking on a career. When Sandrine passes her computing exam and gets an executive-level job, Yves sheds tears of joy with her.

“What strikes me when I watch modern movies these days is that everybody gets divorced or separated and couples never live together from the beginning to the end,” says Garrel, who separated last year from his wife of eight years, the actor and model Laetitia Casta. “This movie portrays one man and one woman who stay together without separating, which would have been bourgeois in the 1970s but now feels very punk.”

The protagonist of Just an Illusion is not Yves but his younger son, 12-year-old Vincent (Simon Boublil), who has fallen hopelessly in love with a girl in his class. Vincent has caring parents, but the film’s central message is that at some point every generation has to tell the previous one to eff off, as well-meaning as they may be. I wonder how that message resonated with Garrel, given his profession is in keeping with family traditions? Has he ever told his parents to eff off? He answers in a way only someone whose family tree is mapped out on IMDb can. “Of course I love Pasolini, of course I love Godard, of course I love Truffaut. But I want to get inspired by films that don’t show at the Cinémathèque Française. Like Lethal Weapon. That is one of my favourite movies, I don’t care.” OK, but has he ever told his parents to do one? “It’s a small rebellion, I know, but that’s maybe my way to say fuck off.”

Sign up to The Guide

Get our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every Friday

after newsletter promotion

Just an Illusion is the 62nd film Garrel has acted in and his first role that really interrogates fatherhood. In real life, he has a five-year-old son from his relationship to Casta, and an 18-year-old adopted daughter, Oumy Bruni Garrel, from a previous relationship with Valeria Bruni Tedeschi, sister of the former first lady of France, Carla Bruni. Oumy has starred in some films, but Garrel seems sanguine about the fact that the acting dynasty that shares his name may come to an end with his children. “She [Oumy] is a very talented actor, she has a gift. But I recently asked her, do you really want to become an actress? And she told me no, no, no, I don’t want that. So next year she’s going to study anthropology, sociology and philosophy. I’m very proud of that.” Did he discourage her? “She doesn’t need discouraging, because she’s seen the kind of life that we have.”

Seeing yourself through the eyes of your own children might make it harder to still be in love with yourself the way you were as a young man. But for an actor, it also makes it easier to not care, and act like a gorilla. Garrel seems to be developing a taste for it. Later this year, he will play the lead in It Will Happen Tonight, the new work by Nanni Moretti, one of Europe’s great comic film-makers.

“I’m 43 years old, and the moments that I appreciate the most as an actor now are when I’m in a screening room and I hear people laughing at me,” Garrel says. “It’s terrible. But this is what I’m waiting for.”

Just an Illusion is out in UK and Irish cinemas on 11 September.
