Dolly Parton was the polar opposite of our bullying president

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 12:00:56 GMT

Terrified of being seen as a loser, Donald Trump is nonsensically lashing out – even against our old friend Canada

I’m still grieving Dolly Parton. I never met her and always wanted to. She was almost exactly my age and my height and had values I deeply admired. Her death leaves a hole in the firmament.

Which brings me to the person whose values are as far from Dolly Parton’s as any human could possibly be and still claim to be human. I’m referring, of course, to the current occupant of the Oval Office.

“I knew her a little bit,” Trump boasted about Parton on Glenn Beck’s radio show. “She really liked me, I will tell you!” at which Beck laughed out loud.

Trump has become mad as a hatter. Loonier than looney tunes. Totally nuts. An enraged, engorged child who’s frightened to death of being seen as a loser.

He’s losing his war in Iran – the war he decided to start without consulting Congress, without even telling the American people his goal or exit strategy.

Now he’s trapped there – with a stronger and more extreme group in control of Iran than before his attack, probably more intent on making a nuclear bomb, blocking the strait of Hormuz (it was open before Trump attacked), causing oil prices to rise again.

His current attempt to stop other countries from dealing with Iran is a bad joke. Iran is becoming the dominant power in the Gulf, having demonstrated its ability to damage the oil and gas infrastructure of its neighbors.

Besides, China can supply almost everything Iran needs and has a strong incentive to do so.

So – now clearly revealed as a loser – what does Trump do? Like any bully, he lashes out.

If the courts won’t allow him to put his name on the Kennedy Center, he’ll demolish it. If they say he doesn’t have authority to build his ballroom, he’ll fight to build it anyway.

If his blue paint on the reflecting pool is peeling and the green algae are back and his US attorney won’t prosecute “vandals” for causing the problem, he’ll stick to his story and blame vandals anyway.

It’s all going so badly for Trump that his lizard brain is compelled to show he can bully someone. So who does Trump choose? Our old neighbor and friend Canada, who has always gone along with whatever the American colossus ever wanted.

Trump imposed 50% tariffs on all cars, trucks, auto parts and steel coming from Canada.

Why? Because, he says: “Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years. On Trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with. They feel entitled, and yet, WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US!”

In other words, we’re in a trade war with Canada because, well, Trump wants one. A trade war with Canada probably seemed easier to win than a hot war with Iran. And he had to save face somehow, right?

Even though the supreme court found his attempt to use emergency powers for his last round of tariffs to be unconstitutional, he’s now using the Hawley-Smoot Tariff Act of 1930 – which, not incidentally, worsened the Great Depression.

But maybe a trade war with Canada won’t be all that easy to win. Canada has now retaliated with its own tariffs of up to 50% against about 700 American products.

As the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, noted on Saturday: “Last spring, I warned that America is trying to break us so they can own us, and I promised that will never, ever happen. We are keeping that promise.”

Carney is now a hero in Canada with approval ratings in the 60s, while Trump’s have sunk to the low 30s.

Humiliation upon humiliation for the man who can’t stand to be humiliated.

It gets worse by the day.

Netanyahu has rejected Trump’s plan for Gaza. Congressional Republicans are blasting him for increasing imports of ground beef.

Universities are rejecting his latest directives. ABC has sued his regime for threatening its broadcast licenses.

Even the bond market won’t be cowed. It’s in open revolt against his bonkers fiscal policies.

Thank goodness for him that Darline Graham won South Carolina’s special election Republican runoff to replace her brother. Trump had made her race all about himself – of course – telling supporters that her opponents were “only fighting Darline because they want me to lose”.

I’m sure that’s what he’s telling himself about his many losses and humiliations – that they’re all due to his opponents plotting and scheming against him.

(Hopefully, he’s about to lose Congress, too.)

That’s an easier story for Trump to accept than the truth: that his carefully cultivated aura of invincibility has just about disappeared.

The would-be emperor has no clothes. Almost everybody now sees the thin-skinned, peevish, petty, incompetent, corrupt, naked infant who’s been parading around in presidential garb.

And they’re not going to obey him any more.

Dolly Parton was a huge winner, bless her soul. Trump is the biggest loser on the planet.

Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich. substack. com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK

Bigmouth strums again: was Andy Burnham’s Smiths jam in Kyiv the perfect soundtrack to a Britain in freefall?

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 11:00:57 GMT

The UK prime minister clearly still adores the band. Perhaps he’s attracted to songs about sham justice and murderous meat factories, shot through with nihilism and exquisite despair

As an origin story, Andy Burnham: Smiths Fan has a lot going for it. It’s plainly authentic: he can name the time he saw them live (Salford University, Queen Is Dead tour, 1986). A cynical young man in a hurry might fake that now, but not back when he first said it, in 2013. Asked by Labour Uncut for his desert island tracks during his 2010 leadership bid, three of the eight were sung by Morrissey (two Smiths singles and one off Viva Hate), which is superfan territory.

That’s a softball exercise to endear yourself to Labour members; you have eight chances to hit every base, and to blow three lives on an artist who had already, by then, been dabbling in nationalism for 18 years (we’ll come back to this) was dicey and brave. You’ll recall that Burnham did not win that election. If you were an enemy state, amassing this hinterland for an asset, you’d have basically done a really good job.

In the business of projecting a human being, through a miasma of talking points and half-answers, it’s more important that the passion be genuine than that it hit the right cultural and social touch points, but in the late 90s and early 00s, the Smiths hit those too. Bear in mind that they’d already been split for a full decade by the time Tony Blair came into power and Burnham first appeared in parliament, so they already signalled a bygone youth, rather than: “I am a cool dude who still goes clubbing to this day.”

But the Smiths’ body of work has a worldview and it’s explicitly political: the lyrics describe a nation in permanent decline, its justice a sham, its education a meat factory, its meat factories (obviously) murder, its subjects shot through with nihilism and exquisite despair. People who called the Smiths miserablist were wilfully ignoring what they actually sounded like, which was the opposite of despair, a kind of penetrating vivacity that obliterated the greyness its words described.

It was funny, ironic, complicated and even its counterculturalism was knowingly passé, declinist. There was so much in there about the queen – and who really cared about the royals by the mid-80s? It had a defiant intellectualism and prefigured the 90s spirit in which everything was infinitely interpretable, and to be contradictory was a sign you were alive.

In that sense, Burnham’s fandom encapsulated the long 90s pretty well. You didn’t have to be literally left behind to be alienated by modernity. You could just vibe left-behindness. When Burnham jammed Rusholme Ruffians on guitar in Kyiv on Monday, there was something plangently nostalgic about it – not for 1985, when the song was released, but for the turn of this century, when we could all be lonely yet not alone, where death wishes were routinely expressed but also a metaphor for whatever you liked, where fairgrounds were empty but also full. It was the era when history was over, when ideological differences had collapsed; and while that turned out not to be true, it did allow in a spirit of openness and intellectual experiment that was extremely rich.

It was the kind of attitude that would now be derided as “metropolitan elitist” and Burnham noticed that pretty early, caveating in an interview in 2015, during his second leadership bid, that he went off the Smiths in his mid-20s when he decided that they were “for people who almost want to make themselves slightly superior: ‘I’m into the Smiths and I look down on people who listen to Level 42’”. That, too, was a little risky, since this was the musical love of his life, and he was suddenly prepared to throw them under the bus just to gate off the possibility that Level 42 fans might vote for Liz Kendall. You’ll remember that he did not win that leadership election either, and nobody voted for Kendall, except, conceivably, Level 42 fans (she got 4.5%).

Two things complicated the picture further. First, Morrissey’s own politics. By 1992, he was lyrically and performatively flirting with a nativism that is now, unavoidably, Islamophobia (in 2017, he expressed support for Anne Marie Waters, a name now lost to public life, then a Tommy Robinson ally and proponent of Great Replacement theory). Burnham has addressed, in pretty weak terms, the fact that he and Morrissey no longer see eye to eye, but that probably does it.

Morrissey’s politics were ugly from the start of his solo career – the lyrics of Bengali in Platforms are honestly stomach-churning – but the Smiths were never just him (as a judge famously determined in 1996, ruling in favour of Mike Joyce on the matter of royalty-sharing, calling Morrissey “devious”). It seems unlikely to me that even Johnny Marr, (the late) Andy Rourke and Joyce could tell what Morrissey would later become, when they were making that work in the 80s, let alone any of the fans.

Second, in 2006, David Cameron just marched in and vandalised everything, choosing This Charming Man on Desert Island Discs, describing listening to the Smiths at Eton. It tested the proposition – we can all be as alienated as each other – to destruction, and with the most insulting imaginable song: “Why pamper life’s complexity / When the leather runs smooth on the passenger seat?” can function as so much, but it cannot work as karaoke for the guy in the seat.

Marr and Morrissey both publicly forbade him from liking the Smiths, which I guess may have mollified true fans such as Burnham but did nothing to head off Cameron’s callow, low-affect, “I’d like to capture all the wealth but also join in your economic alienation, it looks meaningless and kinda fun” politics, and their ruinous effect on the nation.

At the age Burnham is now – 56 – there’s no going back. He’ll die a Smiths fan. He may as well enjoy it. Judging by his Kyiv jam and his July “I left the north again / I travelled south again” video on socials, quoting Is It Really So Strange?, it looks like he is.

The Home Office must not be allowed to bury the spycops inquiry

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 11:00:56 GMT

Doreen Lawrence and other victims of police surveillance have waited decades for justice. Delays and expense due to Met intransigence are no excuse to deny them that

In June 2013 Peter Francis, a former Metropolitan police officer, broke a 20-year silence about the role he had played in surveilling the family of Stephen Lawrence in a documentary jointly made by the Guardian and Channel 4’s Dispatches programme. Two years later, thanks in part to the programme, the Home Office established an undercover policing inquiry, commonly known as the spycops public inquiry, to shed light on the scale of surveillance of activists and trade unionists. That inquiry is now under threat.

Francis had served in the Special Demonstration Squad (SDS), a Met unit founded in 1968 whose officers lived for years at a time inside political and campaigning organisations under false names.

In the months after Stephen Lawrence’s murder in 1993 Francis had been deployed to pose as an anti-racist campaigner. His superiors pressed him to find “dirt” that could be used against the Lawrence family and their supporters. Stephen’s mother, Doreen, told the Guardian and Channel 4 that nothing she had heard since her son died had topped the revelation that police had been spying on her while she grieved. She had always suspected the police were watching. She never had proof.

The Lawrences were not an isolated case. Justice campaigns and trade unionists across the country were also monitored.

At least 139 officers adopted fake names, pretending to be political activists, to spy on people between 1968 and at least 2010. Dozens of anti-racist campaigners, family members of victims of police violence and leftwing activists have been surveilled by police.

Suresh Grover, whose Monitoring Group stood behind many of these victims of police surveillance, has told the inquiry that the suspicion directed at Black campaigners was rooted in racist stereotyping. Complaints from Black communities were treated as a public order threat in a way that identical complaints from others were not.

The government has justified the consultation they launched on 16 July into the future of the inquiry on the grounds that it has gone on for more than 11 years and cost £137m. The figures are accurate but their explanation is missing.

Applications for anonymity and restriction orders, the vast majority sought by police officers, have slowed down this inquiry. Litigation over cover names, and a persistent unwillingness among former officers and their commanders to say what they did has also hampered the process. The Met, which ran the SDS, made the inquiry slow and expensive. The same government department that funded and served the squad now cites the inquiry’s slowness and expense as reasons to cut it short.

Despite a push to wind up the inquiry, it is still producing revelations about the conduct of England’s police forces. Just last year, it revealed that an undercover officer, James Thomson, who had deceived two women into intimate relationships, was suspected of fabricating an elaborate plot to link an anti-foxhunting activist to a gun that he told managers the activist intended to collect in France.

Before the inquiry, Thomson’s managers admitted that in order to protect the SDS, nothing was done either about his intimate relationship with women he was surveilling or his possible fabrication of evidence. The unit, it seemed, trumped almost anything.

The inquiry also exposed numerous instances in which managers appeared to have knowledge of undercover officers having had sexual relationships that continued long after undercover deployments ended, in one case even after the announcement of the inquiry.

Another shocking discovery from the inquiry is that the Met spent £2.5m hiding an officer – John Dines – from his former lover, going as far as to relocate him from New Zealand to Australia for that purpose.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

For the spycops scandal to be possible courts had to be misled. Officers were arrested alongside activists, appeared in court under false names and in some cases gave evidence under them without the court being told.

Surveillance was not limited to political activists and victims of racist violence. The Met’s own investigation concluded that special branch and the security services fed material to construction companies that blacklisted more than 3,000 workers suspected of being members of trade unions.

More instances of misconduct may come to light in the future, which is all the more reason to keep the inquiry running. The consultation is scheduled to end on 20 September, but there is still time to write to the Home Office to make sure that the government knows your views.

An inquiry that was set up because the state spied on the parents of a murdered child should not be closed down because the state has heard enough about itself. Doreen Lawrence has been told for 33 years that the truth is coming if she will wait just a little longer. She – and other victims of spying – have waited long enough. The inquiry should finish the job it was given.

Imran Khan KC is a practising solicitor

Nepal-Tibet flood: this is the cost of not acting in the face of the climate crisis

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 10:56:29 GMT

Nepalis and Tibetans must not pay the price – with their lives, livelihoods and money meant for education and health – for global heating caused by wealthy states

Sunil Acharya is an international climate policy and just transition specialist based in Kathmandu, Nepal

As a Nepali citizen working on international climate policy for more than a decade, it is difficult to look at the harrowing images coming out of the catastrophic flash flood that thundered down valleys in Nepal, sweeping down the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers, and not feel angry.

Not just because of the destruction, but because it comes after years of warnings from scientists and civil society that a rapidly warming planet would make disasters more frequent, more intense and harder to predict. This is what the cost of delaying global climate action looks like.

On 26 August, a wall of ice, water, rock and mud tore through communities, destroying homes, markets, bridges, roads and hydropower infrastructure in Nepal and Tibet. Hundreds of people were killed and many more remain missing. The devastation came with terrifying speed. For people living along the rivers and the tourists trekking in the hills, there was little time between the hazard emerging high in the mountains and destruction reaching the valleys below.

The immediate questions are rightly being asked about what happened and whether people could have been warned. Nepal needs stronger early warning systems, better monitoring of glaciers and unstable slopes, cross-border communication between Nepal and Tibet and greater investment in preparedness.

But Nepal’s flash floods expose something more fundamental: the problem is not the absence of a warning system – it is a climate crisis that is producing hazards that behave differently from those the systems were designed to detect.

The warning system in the high-mountain Bhotekoshi valley illustrates the problem. The sudden, debris-laden flood destroyed upstream hydrological stations before they could register a rising water level and trigger an alert. The system was designed to detect a more gradual rise in water levels. This flood arrived as a massive surge of rock, mud and water, destroying the very instruments meant to detect it.

Preliminary assessments indicate that a large glacial collapse triggered an ice-rock avalanche and debris flow, temporarily blocking the river before a massive surge travelled downstream. The precise sequence is still being investigated. Whatever the final scientific explanation, the event shows how quickly hazards can cascade in a warming mountain environment.

By the time authorities received information about the flood and warnings were sent downstream, communities closest to the source had virtually no time to respond. The monitoring infrastructure did not simply fail to communicate the warning. It was destroyed before it could see the flood coming. That distinction matters. An early warning system designed around yesterday’s floods can be dangerously inadequate for tomorrow’s extremes.

This does not make early warning futile. It means we need to be honest about its limits. A warning is useful only if there is time to act. It cannot stop a mountain of ice and rock from collapsing. It cannot protect infrastructure in an increasingly hazardous corridor. And it cannot bring back a home, a hydropower station or a livelihood once it has disappeared.

Adaptation has limits, too. For years, Nepal and other vulnerable countries have been ramping up efforts to adapt: by strengthening infrastructure, improving preparedness, and protecting livelihoods – but often without financial support from the countries that historically contributed most to the climate crisis through historical emissions.

Nepal needs much greater international support for adaptation: early warning, mountain monitoring, climate science, anticipatory action, resilient infrastructure and disaster preparedness. Because Himalayan hazards originate beyond national borders, this must also include stronger cross-border cooperation and timely sharing of information.

The Nepal Himalaya is changing rapidly. Glaciers are retreating, while warming is altering the conditions in which glaciers, permafrost and mountain slopes remain stable. The climate in which these hazards occur is changing, and continued warming will make an already difficult risk landscape harder to manage. That is why the global response cannot stop at adaptation.

The first task must be to stop making the crisis worse. The countries that benefited most from decades of fossil fuel-driven growth have a particular responsibility to cut emissions rapidly. They also have far greater resources to do so. A just transition away from coal, oil and gas towards renewable energy is therefore a matter of global justice.

The fossil-fuel industry cannot be separated from this conversation. Companies have made enormous profits extracting and selling the fuels that have driven global heating, while communities on the climate frontline are being asked to prepare for increasingly destructive impacts with far fewer resources. Even rapid mitigation cannot undo the warming already baked into the climate system or immediately reverse changes already taking place in the Himalaya.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

There is also a lesson for Nepal. It should not copy the economic model that created the climate crisis and call it development. We have an opportunity to build something different: an economy that puts people, livelihoods and ecological resilience before extraction.

The second task requires historical polluter states to pay for loss and damages. Nepal has contributed less than 0.1% of historical global greenhouse gas emissions. Its per-capita emissions remain among the lowest in the world. Yet we are increasingly paying for a crisis we did almost nothing to create. There is something profoundly unfair about this.

The cost of such an event is not an abstract figure in a post-disaster risk assessment. It is the lives of people killed by the flood; a hydropower station that took years to build and disappeared in minutes; livelihoods; public money that must now be spent on recovery instead of health and education.

Nepal and other vulnerable countries have repeatedly called on developed countries for compensation. The country should not be forced to borrow to recover from disasters to which it contributed so little. Nor should its scarce domestic resources repeatedly be diverted to repair damage caused by emissions of the global north.

Loss and damage finance must therefore be additional to existing official development assistance, adaptation and mitigation finance. It needs to be accessible and predominantly grant-based. But it cannot substitute for mitigation. No amount of compensation will be enough if the world continues to burn fossil fuels at the scale it does today. No adaptation programme can keep pace indefinitely with a climate that becomes more dangerous every year.

The people living along the Bhotekoshi river did not choose a warming Himalaya. They did not choose the fossil-fuel economy that drove most of the warming. However, with enough support, they can prepare better and build more resilient livelihoods. Sadly, they cannot adapt their way out of every disaster. This is why loss and damage finance is not charity – it is an obligation to people already paying the price.

Sunil Acharya is an international climate policy and just transition specialist based in Kathmandu, Nepal

Digested week: Is there anything sadder than the end of summer?

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 10:11:48 GMT

Plus, views from the Cotswolds of Harry and Meghan’s return, and the embarrassing anachronism that is Ali G

Is there anything sadder than the end of summer? As schools go back next week and parents rely on the boosting effect of a return to routine, we look around for other ways to soften the blow. A few things this year that might make it easier: the need for rain ensures that the advent of autumn is slightly less depressing than usual; people with attic conversions in which you could bake a muffin over the summer will be able to use them again; and if you happen to be a woman of 50 or thereabouts, the fresher weather is ... a relief.

Still, looking down the barrel of dark nights and the slow descent towards Christmas clenches the spirit and I find myself pining for the very recent past. I think of this as micro-nostalgia, a form of self-indulgence that, in this case, involves looping back in my mind to the first days of summer when it was all still ahead of us. There should be a word for this particular and intense kind of yearning, which might be described as: a wistfulness for past anticipation based on the certainty of future nostalgia. Even the Germans might struggle to find a compound to cover it.

Distraction comes in the form of the back-to-school shop, which, stupidly, I think will be nice to do the old-fashioned way. And so we take our actual bodies to an actual shopping centre, walk around for five hours, visit 700 shops, buy two lip glosses and some stick-on nails, then come home and order the entire back-to-school haul online. So much for nostalgia.

At the National Theatre in London for a production of the musical Pride, which has been making people weep since it first opened in Cardiff in March, and London in June, and will, presumably, continue to do so when it transfers to the Bridge Theatre in Southwark this winter. I was ready with tissues but managed to hold on – just – despite the show’s absolute best efforts to take me down.

If you know the story, which chronicles the solidarity between striking Welsh miners and gay activists in the mid-1980s, you’ll understand the show’s potential for poignancy. The stage production is, if anything, even more moving than the 2014 film. Part of this is because it leans slightly more heavily than the film into the Aids story. Towards the end of the show, Pride uses a trope popularised in recent times by Madonna, who, during her Celebration tour in 2023, sang Live to Tell while images flashed up on screens of all her old cohorts from the 80s who had died of Aids, and everyone in the audience lost it. The recently shuttered Broadway show, Cats: Jellicle Ball, which celebrates the 80s drag queens of Harlem, did a similar thing to stunning effect.

And it’s not spoiling anything to say that Pride uses a similar method to flay the audience into a final state of sniffing, gulping and hiccuping disintegration as fallen heroes come up on screens in black and white – captured in a youth made more glorious by its horrifically truncated end.

Harry and Meghan fly back into Britain after six years in the US, and the world’s media is treated to the opinion of British people stopped on the street for their thoughts. It always strikes me how much better prepared the average American is when called on by a passing TV hack to offer a spontaneous view. This was particularly in evidence this week as passers-by in Nashville were asked about Dolly Parton and were, by and large, effortlessly fluent, while those in the Cotswolds, where the not-quite-royal couple are reported to be moving, were required to say something sensible about them. (There was a lot of shifty body language, sliding eye contact and “made their bed and lie in it” sort of commentary, all of which made me feel very fond of my people.)

Meanwhile, the Daily Mail dug up the term “praetorian guard”, and raised, with relish, the prospect of the two brothers running rival courts, while the New York Times speculated on William’s “silence” since his brother’s return. Which raised the question: feud or otherwise, what did anyone actually expect the Prince of Wales to say?

Pushback against the forthcoming Ali G movie, Ali G: Who Iz I?, gathers force in the form of a petition – 35,000 signatures and counting – to keep the film out of cinemas on the basis that, under not very subtle cover of satire, it reinforces racist stereotypes. On the other hand, it may be the case that no petitions are necessary if Sacha Baron Cohen’s 20-year-old vehicle strikes modern audiences as an embarrassing anachronism that is as bafflingly bad as it is crashingly unfunny.

Early indications aren’t good. You might have seen Baron Cohen in character earlier this year, towing a camera crew to Centre Court at Wimbledon and contriving to get himself thrown out. Dressed in a white tracksuit with a marijuana leaf insignia that turned on a joke about the All England club’s “grass”, he did a piece to camera in which he joked that tennis was a “crap version of ping pong” and made some gags about drug dealing. It’s a short video I defy you to get through without hiding your face in mortification.

The other Baron Cohen characters haven’t aged well, either. Does anyone want to see the comedian as Bruno, a straight guy playing a screaming gay that plays on a tonne of homophobic tropes, ostensibly to flush out the bigotry of its targets but which invites the audience to recoil alongside them? Borat was the best of the bunch, somehow managing to retain an endearing core that gave the character more humanity than the others and lacked what feels like the speciousness of Ali G.

Why is he doing this? (One can make a good guess.) Baron Cohen has also directed the movie and surely, nobody wants it. If Ali G had novelty value back in the day, he has long been replaced by characters such as Diana Morgan’s Philomena Cunk, who manage to send up dumb TV culture without humiliating people or trading in caricatures that get a charge off the very thing they purport to be spoofing.

A good end to the week in the form of an outdoor screening at London’s Barbican of the 90s film Beautiful Thing, an adaptation of Jonathan Harvey’s classic coming-of-age play and a movie I must have watched 100 times back in the day. The film, directed by Hettie Macdonald and starring Tameka Empson as Leah and Linda Henry as Sandra, Jamie’s mum, killed me then. This is partly down to the soundtrack from the Mamas and the Papas, and also to all those 90s references – peppermint foot lotion from the Body Shop, anyone? – that feel so far removed they might be signifiers of a lost world in a JG Ballard novel. Of all the film’s lines, it’s strange what sticks and the line I keep thinking of ahead of the screening is: “The whole of bloody Thamesmead can hear you!” More tissues!

Trump’s midterm campaign theme is unrequited love

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 10:00:54 GMT

The president senses a crisis in his cult of personality. He believes the path to victory is through unwavering devotion

Donald Trump has framed his theme for the midterm elections. It has come to him as naturally and inevitably as staring into the mirror, beyond any logic or argument, his definitive answer to no specific issue, providing no understanding of any particular problem, but transcending all of them. His political theme is more primal than programmatic, more instinctive than analytical, a heartfelt expression to protect his greatest romantic attachment, his obsessive fixation, his idealized object: himself.

Trump’s campaign theme is unrequited love. Unlike the pollsters, media consultants and pundits, he alone has grasped the magnitude and the source of the existential crisis threatening his politics. He has identified the problem for the Republicans as the faltering measure of complete devotion to him. His demand has nothing to do with mutual affection. It is a ploy to reassert his slipping control, a manipulative test to prove loyalty to him, or else. There can be no absolute rule without an absolute ruler; no absolute ruler without absolute submission; no absolute submission without the expression of absolute love. His sadness at its fading gives way to anger, paranoia and greater acts of retribution. He equates the fear he instills as a form of love. Trump accepts subservience, from whatever motive, as affection or its closest equivalent. He cares nothing about sincerity, so it’s all in the show. The less love displayed, the more fear required. Yet there is no rebound, but only deeper rejection.

Trump is heading toward the floor for presidential unpopularity – Nixon during Watergate on the eve of his resignation, Truman late in his second term at the depth of the Korean war, and George W Bush at the 2008 financial crash. But Trump’s breakdown differs uniquely from theirs. His decline has come earlier in his term, been more sustained, and his disintegration has not stabilized but is accelerating. He is being crushed by the accumulation of catastrophic events of his own making to which his impulsive response is to double down in each and every area. Stalemated in his reckless Iran war, he has now launched a heedless trade war against Canada that will devastate Republican candidates in the northern tier of states. His latest vanity project is gestural retribution to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America”, a watery ballroom. Admission of error for Trump would be the denial of self-love.

Trump began his campaign on his unrequited love theme on 16 August during a Fox News interview in which he discussed his press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, leaving her job after just having a baby. He had held her up as meeting his highest criterion in remarks last December: “Isn’t she great? Is Karoline great? … She gets up there with that beautiful face and those lips that don’t stop, ba ba ba like a little machine gun.” Now, he tried to make a joke of her departure that expressed resentment at abandonment. “In fact, she likes her children more than she likes Trump. I’m very concerned about that,” he said. Then he repeated his unfunny “joke” at a campaign rally in South Carolina on 21 August: “I just learned she loves the baby more than she loves Donald Trump, and I’m very angry …” Trump’s lame attempt at humor was a rare instance of his truth-telling and self-revelation, a contemporary illustration of Freud’s Jokes and Their Relation to the Unconscious.

Trump was in South Carolina to campaign for his chosen candidate in the Republican primary, Darline Graham, who he had insisted be appointed to the Senate seat of her brother Lindsey Graham after he died on 11 July. Darline Graham confessed to cluelessness when asked in a debate about her position on Taiwan. “National security is not my thing,” she answered. “I’m not … that informed on national security.” But she was fully informed on the necessity of obedience to Trump. “You saved our country, and I want to thank you for that,” she said at the rally. Trump praised his worshipper: “She’s got a good gene pool.” She was born to love him. She stood in stark contrast to the immigrants he had described as “poisoning the blood of our country”.

Then Trump called on the crowd to embrace his new theme. “So what I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot … So just say that I’m on the ballot one more time. You got to say it.” He wishes every candidate to sound like Darline Graham in proclaiming him the national savior. He insists he is beloved, and if those who revere him turn out the Republicans must win. In fact, though he is not on the ballot in the midterm elections, Trump is the central issue. Voters do not have to “pretend, please”.

Trump intuitively comprehends that the midterm elections are about him in a way that makes this midterm unlike any other. In the marrow of his bones, he senses it is a crisis of his cult of personality.

Trump’s Maga was never a new party structure, but constructed on his wreckage of the old Republican party. In its place, every particle of the replacement is connected to the leader to advance his supremacy and self-enrichment. Everything flows upward, all heads tilted, all knees bent. Maga has always been Maga Inc of, by and for one man. The movement is the man.

When charisma fails, the movement implodes. If the leader is not worshipped, his uber-principle – the leader principle – collapses: no fuhrerprinzip, no Führer.

Trump’s plea for their unconditional love – “pretend, please” – defies gravity. He is running against Isaac Newton, and Newton always prevails. Intensity is gauged by “strongly approve” and “strongly disapprove” poll numbers. More than the general statistics of approval or disapproval, these provide insight into the motivation of voters that determine the contour of elections. Trump now stands at 13% “strongly approve” in the most recent Reuters-Ipsos Poll. His “strongly disapprove” rating is at 49%. His total approval is at 33%, while disapproval is at 65%. Those in the “somewhat approve” category include low propensity soft voters especially inclined to skip midterm elections. And this poll was taken before his declaration of trade war against Canada.

All along, the Republicans have been Trump’s indispensable accomplices. Even if they were disposed to object, they could do nothing to draw him back from his “pretend, please” campaign. His anxiety to rescue his invincible image from the reality he’s created makes him more inescapable than ever. Any effort to restrict him will provoke his rage. He will not diminish himself for the sake of the party or even his own future. He plans to spend millions from his Maga Inc political action committee to tell the voters that they have never had it so good – “the greatest economy we’ve ever had, by far”, he says. He has mocked the suggestion that “affordability” might be a problem for many – it’s “a word they”, the media, “devised”, he has said. Trump intends to stage a mini convention in Dallas on 9 September, featuring Donald Trump to “celebrate … our achievements”. Republicans are locked almost uniformly into blind support, with the Maine senator Susan Collins venturing hollow criticism of the Canadian tariffs that makes her seem powerless and infuriates the remaining Maga base. Just as Trump has trapped himself, he has trapped the Republicans. The expenditure of tens of millions to depict his dire consequences as paradise on earth will have the unintended effect of supercharging the already motivated “strongly disapprove” voters and disillusion those who cannot help but be aware of the actual conditions of their own lives.

The sudden surfacing of Natalie Harp as a meme at this particular moment propitiously coincides with the wobbling of Trump’s cult. The 35-year-old is his model of the perfect staffer, perfect companion and perfect American citizen. If unrequited love is the problem, she is the solution. In Trump’s hierarchy of need, his pyramid of status, love and self-actualization, she is at the apex.

Harp is his “binky”, as Maggie Haberman of the New York Times has called her, his comfort blanket, his plush bunny rabbit. The “human printer” who trails after him, pressing the button to churn out an endless stream of adulatory articles, conspiracy theories and “alternative facts”, has become an extension of his nervous system. The former anchor at the fringe far-right One America News Network serves as Trump’s personal anchor. Harp broadcasts around the clock to an audience of one. She is the connector to the neurons of the far right, serving as a conduit to dodgy characters such as Laura Loomer with her lists of national security officials who were supposedly disloyal. Harp is Trump’s neurotransmitter who distributes a steady supply of dopamine and delusion.

Harp’s self-abasing devotion to Trump, expressed in her letters to him, serves as a kind of inadvertent political manifesto for the cult, a template for followers. Harp tellingly muddles a line from Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice – Mr Bennet blessing his strong-willed daughter Elizabeth in her engagement to Darcy – to demean herself and offer subservience to Trump: “To modify a classic, ‘I could not have parted with you, to anyone less worthy’ – And, I will add, it is I who is unworthy.” In another letter, after self-disparaging apologies, Harp writes: “You are all that matters to me. I don’t want to ever let you down. Thank you for being my Guardian and Protector in this Life … With all my Heart.”

As public opinion curdles on Trump, no longer able to “pretend, please”, Harp has not come to the wisdom of Conway Twitty in his 1959 rockabilly hit:

My only prayer will be Someday you’ll care for me But it’s only make believe

Sidney Blumenthal, former senior adviser to President Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton, has published three books of a projected five-volume political life of Abraham Lincoln: A Self-Made Man, Wrestling With His Angel and All the Powers of Earth. He is a Guardian US columnist and co-host of the Court of History podcast

Burnham electrified the Labour party by talking about electoral reform – now he needs to act on it

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 07:00:50 GMT

The prime minister has lifted the spirits of the public and party members, and must use that goodwill to push through change

He bounded into the packed rally, a spring-heeled intruder whose very presence announced a coup at last year’s Labour conference. And so it was. Andy Burnham spoke with ebullient self-confidence, yet without aggression or a barrage of insults. They tried to stop him with a bogus constitutional fix barring him from standing in Gorton and Denton. But those Labour hierarchs lost it without him. His subsequent Makerfield victory proved their mistake and opened the door right into No 10 without dispute.

At that standing-room-only rally on proportional representation he made a pitch-perfect noteless speech of personal passion about the failure of politics to connect, the decline of Westminster, the public’s distrust and the risk of this lost public belief in democracy. His hands were clean, he never benefited from the monster majority that first past the post had delivered so unfairly to Labour MPs: he wasn’t there at the last two elections. He quit out of despair, returning to repair.

Now here we are with an amendment to the representation of the people bill next week that calls for a national commission on the electoral system. A new YouGov poll finds that most Labour MPs support it, by 55% to 29%. Many new MPs sitting on wafer-thin majorities, who don’t know which system helps them personally, are voting purely on principle.

If, as expected, Burnham gives a clear signal that he intends to put electoral reform into the next manifesto to get public consent, if he confirms it needs a national commission ahead of the election, the amendment may be withdrawn with no needless division.

Meanwhile, the Labour conference next month is likely to vote strongly for a motion put up by Labour for a New Democracy, backed by many constituencies, calling for a national commission. In the face of all this groundswell, it would plainly be good for Burnham to get ahead of the mood and own the initiative.

This surge in support for proportional representation has been electrified in the past two years by the rise of Nigel Farage. The threat to democracy became brutally real when his party soared 10 points ahead, though thanks to Burnham he now roughly level pegs with Labour. What was once a constitutional nice-to-have reform, not a priority for Labour people, has become an essential safeguard in the face of real danger to democracy. The prospect of Farage winning a landslide on even less than Labour’s 34% that won 63% of the seats is unconscionable. In May’s council elections, some candidates won seats on little more than 20% of the vote. Imagine the rebellion if Farage became prime minister despite being by far the most disliked political leader. That would feel like the complete breakdown of democracy, where the “losers” would no longer peacefully consent to be ruled by “winners” who had been rejected by about three-quarters of voters.

Burnham’s magnetic performance at that rally set him on the path to leadership in a party now strongly supporting PR, with 66% of members backing it, and similar public approval. Tony Blair knew reform was necessary when he commissioned Roy Jenkins to draw up a system that compromised between absolute proportionality and keeping the constituency link. But he backed off when confronted with the bared teeth of old-time opponents, the unions plus John Prescott and Jack Straw. Keir Starmer plainly supported reform, but then backed off – goodness knows why – as in so many of his self-inflicted errors. It’s Burnham’s time.

More puzzling is Burnham’s retreat on capping party donations. The bill will do away with the worst aspect, banning donations of more than £100,000 from foreign donors. But the unions have balked at having UK donations limited, and with it their sometimes threatening influence. Large political donations are a prime cause of corrosive public cynicism about Westminster politics for sale. Burnham’s authenticity is worth many more votes for Labour than can be bought with political advertising. Think again.

These have been precious days since Burnham walked through that black front door on 20 July, when you meet people everywhere expressing a rare optimism. Often those who are not natural Labour supporters will confess to unaccustomed hope. Burnham has lifted national spirits through small gestures that address people’s feelings of gloom. Keep that flame alight, don’t drop that Ming vase. Perversely that requires not caution, but boldness.

Dear culture-war motorists, look to the future. We’ll all be driving at 20mph soon

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 05:00:48 GMT

There are howls of protest from the right about plans for Birmingham to be a 20mph city. But it will be a good thing, and others will follow

If it can happen in Birmingham, it can happen anywhere. Moves by Birmingham city council to impose a 20mph speed limit on all roads, apart from a few major thoroughfares, marks a turning point in transport policy that could and should attract imitators.

Remember that in the 60s Birmingham was the city that had a racetrack ​style networks of roads at its heart, ​and a tangle of elevated ro​utes and roundabouts that pushed pedestrians underground and ensured no one would be mad enough to try to cycle. Moreover, it was the headquarters of the UK’s car industry, and its roads were designed more as a test track for new models than a way for people to get to the shops. The emphasis on roads above all else was a deliberate strategy by a city that saw its future inextricably bound up with motoring manufacturers.

This ode to the motorcar has gradually been dismantled over the past couple of decades, with the removal of roads turning the city centre into a far more pedestrian-friendly environment. The tram system is being expanded and soon – well actually, not that soon, thanks to endless delays – there will be a new station to accommodate high-speed rail services. Birmingham has been changing, but this latest move will accelerate the process. The imposition of a 20mph zone throughout the city seals the deal. No longer will the needs of cars dominate. Instead, walking, cycling and public transport will be the modes of choice, as car travel becomes slower and more of a hassle.

The opposition, Conservatives and Reform alike, are already on the warpath, emphasising that this is part of a “war on the motorist” – the cliche brought out whenever any politician attempts to redress the balance between speed and livability in the urban environment. Gradually, far too slowly, they are losing the war, even if they occasionally win the battles: in Toronto, the Ontario premier, Doug Ford, is planning to rip out 19km of cycle lanes.

Diehards such as Ford are on the losing side of history. Birmingham’s shift of emphasis in the urban realm is part of a global phenomenon that is manifested in numerous ways: a pedestrianised main street in Vancouver, a congestion charge in New York City, 500km of new cycle paths in Bogotá and so on. Sadiq Khan has got in on the act with the imminent pedestrianisation of Oxford Street (a measure I advocated in a 1998 Evening Standard op-ed).

Wales has led the way with “20’s plenty”, the brilliant campaign founded by Rod King two decades ago that has influenced policymakers across the country. All Welsh local urban roads were restricted to 20mph in September 2023. Though a few busy streets have reverted to 30mph, by and large the concept has been accepted – and research has shown reductions in road deaths and injuries.

In the global race to sustainability and livability, the leader is probably Copenhagen, where ambitions of having a 50% modal share of cycling for commuters may already have been achieved and there are ambitions to go further. Paris, however, is quickly catching up – and demonstrates that change can be rapid once momentum picks up. Since the election of Anne Hidalgo as mayor in 2014, the transformation has been astonishing. It has involved a raft of measures, building on the creation of Paris’s large bike hire scheme in 2007 and the pedestrianisation of the left bank of the Seine in 2013. There has been a comprehensive refocusing of the city’s roads in favour of cyclists and pedestrians, with more than 1,000km of cycle lanes, the removal of thousands of parking spaces, the closure of dozens of school streets and the creation of low-traffic neighbourhoods.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

And here’s the rub: ultimately, the opponents are right. This is an attempt to make life more difficult for motorists, in order to improve the situation for people not travelling in large metal boxes. That does and should involve a raft of measures. Parking spaces need to be removed, access to town centres limited to deliveries, congestion charges imposed. This will give rise to noisy opposition, such as the fanatics in London who broke cameras monitoring compliance with the ultra-low emission zone (Ulez).

We need politicians to explain – and to keep explaining – why the unrestricted use of cars in urban centres is damaging to the local economy as well as to the environment, to people’s health and to the overall feel of a place. It’s no good dodging the fact that the policies that prevailed until the late 1960s, and which still seem to be favoured by backward-looking opponents, were a mistake. Brave politicians need to take on opponents without compromise. Khan did this with the Ulez, standing firm against critics even though some were inside his own party, and the success is for all to see. Not only does research show that children’s lungs are becoming bigger because the air is cleaner, but just go to Parliament Hill in Hampstead Heath and look over London: there is no longer a foul yellow miasma permanently overhanging that famous view.

Khan could push through his Ulez because he has some mayoral powers, though less than those of his counterparts abroad. Hidalgo and her successor, Emmanuel Grégoire, have powers that British mayors can only dream of. However, opportunity is at hand. Andy Burnham’s emphasis on devolution may offer the opportunity for brave new mayors to follow the examples of Paris, Bogotá and Copenhagen – and Birmingham. Twenty is plenty: get used to it.

Christian Wolmar is the presenter of the Calling All Stations podcast and writes a weekly Substack entitled Transport News

What could Meta’s US settlement mean around the world – and what now for other claims against firm?

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 04:00:48 GMT

Other governments could seek similar concessions, while separate legal action is pending in places ranging from Kenya to the Netherlands

In October 2021, Abrham Meareg’s father, a professor of chemistry in Ethiopia’s northern town of Bahir Dar, was shot at close range and died outside his family home. This was in the middle of the country’s civil war.

For weeks, Facebook’s algorithm had actively promoted posts calling for the academic to be murdered, according to Meareg and Foxglove, a nonprofit organisation supporting Meareg’s lawsuit against the company in Kenya. These posts included photos of his father and his home address.

Meareg filed the lawsuit in 2022. He said he repeatedly asked Facebook to remove the posts and the company did nothing. Nearly four years later, the case has still not been heard. Foxglove said Meta, Facebook’s parent company, had “fought tooth and nail to avoid responsibility”.

Meareg said: “It’s a matter of numbers to them, a matter of statistics. It has been proven multiple times that our lives do not matter to them.”

On Wednesday, Meta settled a lawsuit brought by 29 US states who argued it had designed addictive products that hooked young people. The social media company agreed to pay $18bn and to change certain features of its platform in the US. California’s attorney general said it was a victory that would make “a world of difference for children and their families”.

But elsewhere in the world, in jurisdictions as far flung as Amsterdam and Nairobi, other claims have yet to be heard. Far bigger questions about the power of a single US technology company to shape politics and democracy everywhere on Earth are still to be answered.

For the US, the settlement is a victory. A jury has done what the US Congress could not – put controls on a powerful tech company. As a part of the settlement, Meta has said it will set time limits on children’s use of its platforms Facebook and Instagram and block night-time usage.

For Meta, the settlement is also a victory. Its share price rose in the hours after the deal was announced. Its CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, was not forced to testify. The sum it is to pay, while not meaningless, is far less than the states had sought – $200bn – or the amount Meta itself had suggested in a court filing it might have to pay, which was up to $1.4tn.

For the rest of the world, however, the picture is more mixed. The limits Meta will put on its US platform are, in large part, similar to limits the UK and Australia have already achieved through regulation. There are certain concessions Meta has now made that other governments could also demand: for example, while the UK plans to ban under-16s from social media platforms, it may wish to ask Meta to impose a default daily use limit of two hours for under-18s, which is what the company has agreed to in the US.

None of this meaningfully changes the equation for Meareg or what his case represents, which is that a massive US company, unaccountable to voters, unbound by transparency requirements, owns a worldwide digital commons that shapes reality for billions of people.

Whether courts and governments outside the US have the power to confront this fact is a far thornier question.

The central issue of Meareg’s case is Meta’s algorithm. This is the system that decides what content to show users of Facebook and Instagram. It sees you linger over a video about knitting sweaters, for example, and then decides you’ll like one about how to care for your spider plant.

It sees teenage girls watch diet content and shows them anorexia influencers. It sees young men search for bodybuilding content and shows them Andrew Tate. It is alleged to have amplified content that promoted the ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya in Myanmar. It contributed to the election victory of Donald Trump.

Meareg’s lawsuit rests on the claim that this algorithm promoted the posts that called for the death of his father, and that Facebook’s sparse moderation in east Africa did almost nothing to prevent this.

In the early days of the Meta trial in the US, it seemed plausible that states would push the social media firm to finally make some changes to this algorithm. Those changes had the potential to fundamentally alter how the company does business. Meta’s algorithm is intended to keep users scrolling, stuck on the platform, and then it shows them ads.

But that is not what appears to have happened. The terms of the settlement will slightly change what is shown to minors, in that they will not necessarily have personalised feeds. But it is hard to see this concession changing the equation in war zones or creaking democracies.

Arturo Béjar, an ex-Facebook employee and whistleblower, said the limitations were “the equivalent of saying: ‘Well, you can smoke as many cigarettes as you can in two hours a day.’ It doesn’t make the cigarettes any safer.”

It may be up to groups and individuals elsewhere in the world to try to push for these larger changes. It will be an uphill struggle.

Sign up to TechScape

A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives

after newsletter promotion

In Kenya, the high court recently ruled that Meareg’s case against Meta could go ahead, after years of legal manoeuvring from the company to try to prevent it. It could now be heard in the next year.

Rosa Curling, Foxglove’s co-executive director, said: “Meta’s lawyers have spent years trying to prevent this important case being heard, thankfully without success. We hope that the news from the US is a sign that Mark Zuckerberg’s time is finally up.”

In the Netherlands, Repro Uncensored, a nonprofit organisation tracking digital censorship, hailed the US settlement as a “major victory”. Repro Uncensored has an ongoing legal case against Meta in the Netherlands for alleged discrimination against queer accounts, and plans further action in other European countries.

Martha Dimitratou, Repro Uncensored’s executive director, said: “The next stage of accountability must address not only addictive design but algorithms, discriminatory moderation and automated decision-making. These systems shape civic participation and democracy, and the companies controlling them must be held accountable globally.”

The European Commission released a charge sheet against Meta this summer saying the company’s features, including its infinite scroll, contributed to “unhealthy habits and compulsive use”.

That charge sheet is part of an investigation into Meta that the commission launched in 2024. It may lead to Europe pushing for larger changes from Meta, including to its personal algorithm.

It is unclear whether any of these groups or parties can succeed. Meta appears to fear US regulators and courts: after all, it caved after just four days of its US trial. It does not appear to be as intimidated by regulators elsewhere.

Earlier this year it managed to dodge a class-action lawsuit brought by a group of Rohingya refugees over its alleged role in contributing to a genocide in Myanmar. It will have the help of the Trump administration in opposing any EU regulation that could curb its reach in Europe.

Meta declined to respond to questions about either Meareg’s or Repro Uncensored’s cases. In an earlier response to whistleblower allegations that it fuelled violence in Ethiopia and Myanmar, it pushed back forcefully, saying it was “just not true” that the company put profits over safety. Regarding Meareg’s case, it has said it employs staff with local knowledge and expertise to “catch violating content” in Ethiopia.

Meareg said he believed that Meta expected him to give up. “They don’t know how I am determined for justice,” he said. “It is the thing you do for the person you love. If you love someone – and I loved my dad from my heart – then he needs justice. He needs a public apology. There has to be accountability.”

For Trump, the Iran War Is Stuck Between Combat and Genuine Peace

The New York Times August 28, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

news Analysis

The war has deteriorated over the past six months into Mr. Trump’s own version of a “forever war,” with no clear goals and no end in sight.

By Peter Baker

Peter Baker is the chief White House correspondent and has covered five presidents who managed overseas wars.

President Trump the other day posted a heroic image of himself backed by an aircraft carrier, warplanes and American flags. In the lower left corner was former President George W. Bush and a sign, “Mission Not Accomplished 2001-2021.” In the other corner was a sign referencing himself saying “Mission Accomplished 2026.”

Except that it is not. Mr. Trump’s war in Iran, which hit the six-month mark on Friday, is anything but accomplished. Half a year in, the conflict has deteriorated into a quagmire of the president’s own making with no clear goals, no obvious strategy and no end in sight. Mr. Trump, who came to power running against Mr. Bush’s “forever wars,” has staked his presidency on his own version.

For Mr. Trump, it may be the worst of both worlds. He finds himself stuck in a maddening purgatory between full-fledged combat and genuine peace. He is reluctant to resume an all-out bombardment despite his thunderous threats, yet has been unable so far to broker an agreement to end the war on satisfactory terms. He has no victory to take credit for, yet is paying the political price in terms of the toll on the American economy and his party’s chances in the fall elections.

This sort of in-between stasis could in theory extend for a long time, a far cry from the four-to-six-week lightning strike that Mr. Trump predicted when he ordered Operation Epic Fury at the end of February. With no breakthrough in sight, both sides are testing the other’s staying power and Mr. Trump, despite a history of impatience, has made clear that he is “not in a hurry,” as he put it earlier this week.

“There’s not a lot to speak to,” he told reporters on Thursday, disavowing interest in negotiating with Iran at this point. “We don’t want to speak to them; we’re not looking to meet or anything. The strait is open; we’re taking a lot of boats — millions and millions of barrels of oil are coming out of the strait every day.”

In fact, the Strait of Hormuz remains a volatile passage with only a fraction of its prewar shipping traffic, leaving oil markets in flux. While the war killed Iran’s supreme leader, he was replaced by his son and the brutal regime in charge six months ago remains in charge today. Iran’s nuclear program has been damaged but Tehran still refuses to give it up.

“This has been a fiasco,” said Richard N. Haass, who was director of policy planning at the State Department when Mr. Bush invaded Iraq in 2003. “That’s the harsh reality. He can declare ‘mission accomplished.’ He can try to sell the argument as he often tries to, almost to create reality. But it’s going to be a hard, hard sell. There’s nothing to point to that will suggest either that we are better off or that the war was worth it.”

Supporters of the war have counseled forbearance, arguing that Mr. Trump has succeeded in substantially weakening a radical and dangerous Iran with far fewer American casualties than during Mr. Bush’s ground wars in Iraq or Afghanistan. If Mr. Trump sticks with it, they said, he may yet force Iran to back down through military force or economic pressure, making America safer in the long run.

“I know this cuts against the conventional wisdom, but I believe President Trump is winning the confrontation with the regime in Iran,” said Mark Dubowitz, chief executive of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies. “The Islamic Republic has never been weaker in its 47-year history. And it was forced to play its most important card — the Strait of Hormuz — from a position of extraordinary weakness.”

Mr. Dubowitz said that Iran now is left deciding whether to negotiate seriously or spend the next two years under relentless pressure. “We are not at peace, and we aren’t in major combat operations,” he said. “President Trump may instead have found the strategic sweet spot between the two: sustained coercive pressure without either a major war or an unacceptable agreement.”

However it turns out, the war in Iran has become arguably the biggest gamble of Mr. Trump’s presidency, at least in foreign policy, and a case study in how he has approached his second term differently than his first.

While his original four years in power were defined by a more inward-looking America First policy in reaction to Bush interventionism, Mr. Trump returned to the White House last year more willing to wield power overseas and seemingly more intent on reshaping the world to his liking.

His decapitation of Venezuela’s leadership, his threats to take over Greenland, the Panama Canal and Cuba, even his renaming of Lake Ontario as Lake America this week all speak to a legacy-minded president looking to leave his mark beyond U. S. borders. Any hopes that Iran would be a quick and decisive success, however, have long since been dispelled and now the main aim is how to find a way out that can be framed as a victory of some sort.

“It strikes me that Operation Epic Fury is quintessentially Trump,” said Steven A. Cook, a longtime Middle East scholar at the Council on Foreign Relations. “It is no doubt bold, but its orchestrator is mostly careless and unprepared, prosecuting a conflict on the seat of his pants and a lot of bluster.”

Mr. Cook added: “The U. S. could win in the end, but it would only be because it is powerful despite Trump’s mistakes and the Iranians are relatively weak, not because the president pursued an effective strategy.”

Victor Davis Hanson, a senior fellow at Stanford’s Hoover Institution, disagreed, saying that Mr. Trump is pursuing what he called “an anaconda Civil War strategy” that will eventually pay off.

“He’s going to squeeze them as much as he can, and as they start to pop, they will send off missiles or drones from their vestigial fleet, and he’ll hit them hard,” he said in a Daily Signal podcast this week. “And he hopes that will continue, that containment will continue to the midterms.”

Mr. Hanson added that the economic pressure on Iran could ultimately generate popular uprisings or further depress the country’s capacity. “Is that victory? I don’t know,” he said. But he added that it could stop Iran from developing a nuclear weapon at a cost in lives and treasure far below Mr. Bush’s wars. “Take that versus a trillion dollars in Iraq and probably $2 trillion in Afghanistan over 20 years,” he said.

Putting aside dollars and cents, the story of Mr. Trump’s war in its first six months can be told in five numbers: Sixty-three, 12, 1.10, 18 and 759. The first measures public opposition to the war. Just 31 percent support it, while 63 percent are against it, according to the latest Ipsos survey, the kind of figures reminiscent of the darkest days of the Vietnam War.

The second reflects the number of ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz each day, averaging about 12, compared with 130 before the war. The third reflects the average price of gas in the United States, which is about $4.09 a gallon, or $1.10 higher than it was at the start of fighting.

The fourth reflects the 18 American military personnel killed so far in the war. And the fifth is the estimated number of Patriot interceptors left in U. S. arsenal, down from 2,330 to as low as 759 a month ago, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a nonpartisan think tank.

As for the goals that Mr. Trump outlined at the start, most remain unmet. He likes to boast that he has destroyed Iran’s air force and navy, but Tehran remains capable of firing at U. S. bases and allies in the region. The day of liberation he forecast for the Iranian people throwing off their oppressors never arrived. Iran’s ability to support proxy terrorist groups in the region has been diminished but not eliminated. And its nuclear program has been seriously damaged but the regime refuses to abandon it and could reconstitute it, according to analysts.

“President Trump has entangled the United States in a foreign policy failure of historic consequence,” Senator Jack Reed of Rhode Island, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee, said in a statement on Friday. “Six months later, not a single objective has been achieved. Indeed, he has weakened our position in the Middle East and the world significantly.”

Mr. Haass, who was skeptical of Mr. Bush’s plan to invade Iraq while working in his administration and later wrote a book about its failure called “War of Necessity, War of Choice,” said that paradoxically both that conflict and Mr. Trump’s have left Iran stronger.

In the case of Iraq, Iran became a dominant force inside its next-door enemy after Saddam Hussein was toppled, Mr. Haass noted, and now Iran has demonstrated its ability to roil world energy markets by choking off shipping through the strait. “Iran is the strategic beneficiary of both wars,” he said.

Mr. Trump, of course, would dispute that. In fact, he has argued time and again that he has already prevailed against Iran. “We’ve already won,” he declared on March 7, barely a week into the war. “We won everything; we have all the cards,” he said on April 25. “We already won the war,” he said on May 6. “I don’t know if you heard, but we ended the war with Iran today,” he said on June 11.

His “Mission Accomplished” social media post this week was a play off Mr. Bush’s own ill-fated speech in front of a banner with those words aboard the U. S. S. Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier just weeks after the original Iraq invasion in 2003, a pronouncement that later was taken as a metaphor for premature declaration of victory. If Mr. Trump saw the irony in invoking it himself, he did not indicate it, but many others did.

“Trump is clearly wrong to say the U. S. has won,” said Brett H. McGurk, a longtime Middle East adviser for presidents of both parties, including Mr. Bush, Barack Obama, Mr. Trump in his first term and finally Joseph R. Biden Jr. “Few of its stated aims have been met. But Iran has not won either.”

Mr. McGurk, who was a key architect of Mr. Bush’s second-term military surge and strategy shift in Iraq that helped turn the war around, said that experience showed that even a president in his final two years in office can have an impact. And he noted that Mr. Trump seems more committed to seeing the Iran war through than many had presumed.

“Six months is a blip in the Middle East,” Mr. McGurk said. “This war, like many, will not have a clean endpoint. It will merely shift advantage in an ongoing contest. And it’s too early to call where average ultimately settles.”

Peter Baker is the chief White House correspondent for The Times. He is covering his sixth presidency and sometimes writes analytical pieces that place presidents and their administrations in a larger context and historical framework.

How Rising Temperatures Likely Contributed to Nepal’s Deadly Flood

Wired August 26, 2026

Roughly 160 people are dead and hundreds more—including dozens of international tourists—are missing after flash floods hit a region on the mountainous border of Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday. Devastating footage posted to social media shows people fleeing a wall of water that washed away buildings and vehicles.

Initial analysis of satellite imagery and reports from the Nepalese government indicate that the flooding was likely triggered by a landslide caused after a piece of a glacier fell hundreds of feet.

As the region warms, its ice is becoming increasingly unstable, raising the risk of catastrophic flooding.

“The glaciers over there are definitely in retreat,” says Joseph Shea, an associate professor of geography at the University of Northern British Columbia. “There’s a lot of glacier mass up there, but we’re seeing thinning, we’re seeing retreating.”

Since 2000, the world’s glaciers have lost 5 percent of their ice, with much more drastic impacts in certain regions. Nepal’s glaciers lost nearly a quarter of their area between 1970 and 2010. More than 160 smaller glaciers in the country, research has found, have vanished entirely.

A recent study finds that 40 percent of the world’s glacial ice could disappear if the world does not keep warming under 1.5 degrees Celsius.

Before and after imagery shows debris left behind by the floods.

The impacts of warming on glaciers in Nepal can cause cascading effects. Shea points out that retreating glaciers can help trigger landslides as they get smaller and can no longer hold back sediment. As these glaciers retreat, many are leaving large, dammed lakes at higher elevations. “If you have a landslide suddenly into a lake, you get an overtopping of the dam, and then the whole thing can collapse catastrophically,” Shea says. Known as glacial lake outburst floods, two of these events hit Nepal last year, and research shows millions of people are living in harms way around the world.

Wednesday’s disaster was more likely due to a glacial collapse that fell into the valley below. Daniel Shugar, a geologist at the University of Calgary in Canada, told The New York Times that satellite imagery suggested that a 2,000-foot-wide piece of ice may have fallen almost 4,000 feet, “[pulverizing] the ice into water” with the force of its fall. And while Shugar emphasized that it was still too early to make conclusive statements about the cause of the floods, he noted to Reuters that snow that was present on the glacier earlier in the week may have melted due to warm temperatures.

The collapse and debris flow were so large and forceful that they registered as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event, according to the US Geological Survey.

Glaciers elsewhere have broken apart with destructive results. That includes the collapse of a Swiss glacier last year that buried a town, while on a smaller scale, a glacier collapse in Italy in 2022 killed 11 mountaineers. Both were linked with rising temperatures.

There are a lot of factors in a warming world, Shea says, that can play on each other to destabilize glaciers.

“It’s summertime,” he says. “There’s lots of warming, lots of melt happening, lots of water around. There’s also things like alpine permafrost thaws: The ground temperatures warm up, and big blocks and chunks that would have been frozen in place are now suddenly becoming mobile.”
